This movie is poorly conceived, poorly acted, and poorly written.

Jon Heder is terribly annoying, and cannot escape the same Napolean Dynamite routine. Self-obsessed and ignorant.

Furthermore, Diane Keaton plays the same manish, overly obsessed mother, who cares too much and yet not nearly enough about the lives of her children (see Because I Said So).

Anna Faris, though i generally like her, plays a vapid idiot in this film as well.

Jeff Daniels is passable but nothing special.

Please, skip this film if you want to keep your soul.

"All the world's a stage and its people actors in it"--or something like that. Who the hell said that theatre stopped at the orchestra pit--or even at the theatre door? Why is not the audience participants in the theatrical experience, including the story itself?

This film was a grand experiment that said: "Hey! the story is you and it needs more than your attention, it needs your active participation". "Sometimes we bring the story to you, sometimes you have to go to the story."

Alas no one listened, but that does not mean it should not have been said.

I had a lot of expectations from this movie and more so since it was a Yashraj Film.

Jimmy operates a call centre and one day he is invited by Pooja Singh to teach her boss, Lakhan Singh, English. The two fall in love and decide to run away but Pooja tells Jimmy that she can't do this as she owes a debt to Lakhan Singh, who is also known as Bhaiyyaji. But they decide and steal money from him and its only then that Jimmy finds out that Bhaiyyaji / Lakhan Singh is a Don. In the meantime, Bhaiyyaji hires a man, Bachchan Pandey, to track down Jimmy and Pooja.

Starring Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor and Akshaye Kumar, the movie is directed by first time director Viay Krishna Acharya and is produced by both Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.

"Tashan" has to be one of the worse films that I have ever watched. Yes! The scenery is good and Kareena Kapoor (and her much publicised weight loss) looks good. But plot is extremely thin on story and at times makes no sense from one scene to the other - hence why I have

(No spoilers, just plot details) I can't understand such hatred for this episode. You want to watch a bad episode of Smallville? Watch Subterranean - now there's a sack of crap. Tom Welling gives a good performance (I don't say that very often), and Michael Rosenbaum is great, but he is most of the time. The alternate universe scenario seems eerily realistic. The Martian Manhunter, who previously appeared in "Static", returns and tells Clark that the doctor that is the head of the insane asylum where they are being held at is actually a phantom from the phantom zone, and if Clark wants to return to his universe, he must kill him. An overall great episode, with good acting and a decent pace.

This is far more than the charming story of middle-aged man discovering the pleasures of ballroom dancing (although it IS that as well). It's the tale of one person learning to love life again, pushing past all the pressures of work and money to discover joy once more. The bonus in this film is a fascinating insight into the slowly changing attitudes of modern Japan toward everything from ballroom dancing to physical contact. There are scenes that will make you laugh out loud ... a few where you'll want to get up and tango ... and many others where you'll just feel good.

This is a great introduction to contemporary Japanese filmmaking for those who might be under the impression that all Japanese movies are "heavy" and inaccessible.

Believe it or not, at 12 minutes, this film (for 1912) is a full-length film. Very, very few films were longer than that back then, but that is definitely NOT what sets this odd little film apart from the rest! No, what's different is that all the actors (with the exception of one frog) are bugs...yes, bugs! This simple little domestic comedy could have looked much like productions starring the likes of Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy or Max Linder but instead this Russian production uses bugs (or, I think, models that looked just like bugs). Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy were yet to be discovered and I assume Linder was busy, so perhaps that's why they used bugs! Using stop-motion, the bugs moved and danced and fought amazingly well--and a heck of a lot more realistically than King Kong 21 years later!

The film starts with Mr. Beetle sneaking off for a good time. He goes to a bawdy club while his wife supposedly waits at home. But, unfortunately for Mr. Beetle, he is caught on camera by a local film buff. Plus, he doesn't know it but Mrs. Beetle is also carrying on with a bohemian grasshopper

I honestly can't believe what passes for entertainment now. Death (and making fun of death), violence, sexual innuendo, adults threatening children, crudeness, alcohol abuse by minors, drug theft, dysfunctional parents, babysitter from hell, stereotypical jokes about African Americans, police and fat people, and kids sneaking out of the house in the middle of the night - yup, sure sounds like a kids movie to me - NOT!!! Add to that the dark and scary elements - a dead woman possessing and turning into a house and keeping her loving husband a prisoner inside for over 20 years, and also terrorizing an entire neighborhood - how sweet for kids. PARENTS - is this really what you want your kids to be watching - is this what you want to teach them about life?!

This movie is too scary for young kids, and i'm afraid that teens today may be living some of this movie scenario - so why rub it in their faces? As for an adult audience - you won't find it scary or amusing - just boring, contrived and predictable. And the characters are just wrong - clueless parents, ignorant police, stupid and annoying friends, nasty and manipulative

Melissa Joan Hart shines! This show is amazing!! There is no match. Except for maybe Melissa in Clarissa Explains it All. She was marvelous in that, too. This is SO much better than Buffy, the Vampire Slayer. This show is WONDERFUL!

I saw this many years after the television series and, initially, I didn't care for it. Then, as my memory of the series receded with the passage of time, I watched again, and found it absolutely hilarious. Based on the stage play by Neil Simon, it has not been 'opened out' much for the big screen, and that's one of its strengths. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon are brilliant as Oscar and Felix, and the supporting cast are wonderful, particularly John Fielder as 'Vinnie'. Even now, certain moments can reduce me to tears of laughter - Felix interrupting Oscar in the middle of a ball game with a dinner request, Oscar cracking up and chasing Felix around the apartment, the giggling 'Pigeon Sisters' brought low by Felix's sob stories, and of course, the legendary cafeteria scene ( later ripped off by Nora Ephron's 'When Harry Met Sally' ). Razor-sharp dialogue too. When the boys think Felix has taken an overdose, Oscar says: "They could be vitamins! He could be the healthiest one in the room!". Fantastic!

I simply cannot believe the number of people comparing this favourably with the first film. It moved me to leave this comment! This is just an obvious attempt to cash-in on the success of the first film. The dialogue is appalling and nothing like as authentic or compelling as the original film.

The storyline is ridiculous, the portrayal of the French police laughable and the characterisation of Doyle a mile away from the first film.

How many drug bosses do you think go down to the docks in person to see a shipment come in? The ease at which Doyle finds his guy is just pathetic. Like all the French Police were just drinking coffee until Doyle turns up from America and does some REAL police work. What a joke. Try going to a foreign city and unearthing the biggest crims in the place with a travel map and some tourist pamphlets. Pathetic.

A truly awful sequel, anyone who thinks otherwise is crazy.

"After World War I, an expedition representing the Allied countries is sent to Cambodia to stop the efforts of Count Mazovia in creating a zombie like army of soldiers and laborers. Hoping to prevent a possible outbreak of war due to Mazovia's actions, the group presses through the jungle to Angkor Wat in spite of the perils. The group includes Armand who has his own agenda contrary to the group's wishes," according to the DVD sleeve's synopsis.

Heads up! the zombie make-up department revolted before the cameras started to roll.

Also, this "Revolt of the Zombies" has little to do with its supposed predecessor "White Zombie" (1932) *****, which starred Bela Lugosi. If that film's zombies didn't thrill you, this one's certainly won't. A younger-than-usual Dean Jagger (as Armand Louque) stars as a man obsessive with blonde Dorothy Stone (as Claire Duval). A couple supporting performances are good: devilish Roy D'Arcy (as Mazovia) and subservient Teru Shimada (as Buna); however, neither are given enough material to really pull this one out of the dumps.

** Revolt of the Zombies (1936) Victor Halperin ~ Dean Jagger, Dorothy Stone, Roy D'Arcy

The Fluffer may have strong elements of porn industry truth to it - but that doesn't make up for the fact that it's pretty shabbily directed and acted - and with a very mediocre script.

B grade from start to the exceedingly drawn out finish.

It would be embarassing to think of the general public being offered this piece as an example of state of the art gay film making.

Hopefully it has a limited life in the gay film festival circuit and is allowed to die a natural death on video.

This film will open the Queer Film Weekend in Brisbane on April 10, 2002. I think its success there will be strongly influenced by the amount of alcohol consumed in the preceding cocktail party - they're gonna need it.

It looks like the brilliant team of Shonda Rhimes outsourced the writing of this one somewhere offshore, maybe to the MediocreLand? "PP" reminds me any one of the many tedious, promising at first but predictable within 1 season David Kelly flicks (Picket Fences, Ally McBeal, and now Boston Legal). The crazy cases they get are so outlandish, they barely evoke sympathy or sadness. And that's what actually makes good medical dramas tick - dramatic situations you are afraid of, "This could be me" sentiment. They are not funny either.

The actors are quite good, but the plot lines are dead and cannot be brought back to live. I'm a therapist, and let me tell you - Amy Brennan plays the most unbelievably incompetent, unethical, untrained therapist. Whoever writes her stuff flunked the ethics and the transference/counter-transference courses in Stanford. Somebody should give them a Code of Ethics to read (the episode with the nose-bleeding wife and the therapist's involvement in it). No therapists are that bad.

Women yearning for men who have moved on - had been done to death, we've all graduated "Sex and the City". Addison in her youthful aggression towards the guy she likes -

Diane and I saw this fabulous film today in Fremantle and we both agreed that of the pastiche movies it was head and shoulders above the rest. I say that because we were entranced by the brief, five to ten minute segments that composed the film and the fact that this film had a theme around which each piece was composed and of course that theme was love in its many forms.

Ostensibly the film took place in the various Parisian arrondisments thus giving a particular flavour to each segment. Having only been in Paris several times, I was not knowledgeable enough to readily recognize the locations but I am sure Europeans and particularly French people could easily recognize the city's locations. In any event, the viewer is immediately pulled into each story because of their production excellence so these city locations fade into in-consequence.

The film moves quickly and the viewer is left absorbing one scenario while the new one is on the screen. The stories themselves are not graphic like some pulp Hollywood nonsense, they are subtle and thought provoking and gentle as with most of life without the media swath that buries so much of

Brian Yuzna is often frowned upon as a director for his trashy gore-fests, but the truth is that his films actually aren't bad at all. The Re-Animator sequels aren't as great as the original, but are still worthy as far as horror sequels are concerned. Return of the Living Dead 3 is the best of the series; and Society isn't a world away from being a surrealist horror masterpiece. This thriller certainly isn't a masterpiece; but it shows Yuzna's eye for horror excellently, and the plot moves in a way that is always thrilling and engaging. I'm really surprised that a horror movie about dentistry didn't turn up until 1996, as going to the dentist is almost a primal fear - it's running away from a tiger for the modern world. Dentistry doesn't frighten me, but surprisingly; I would appear to be in the minority. The plot follows perfectionist dentist Dr Feinstone. He has a nice house, a successful career and a beautiful wife - pretty much everything most people want. However, his life takes a turn for the worse when he discovers his wife's affair with the pool cleaner. And his life isn't the only one; as it's his

I rented this film in DVD form without knowing anything at all about it, part of a winter marathon of watching a film every night. After several awful American action adventure films (Ballistic, Daredevil, Cradle of Life) Zhu Warriors struck me as brilliantly original filmmaking. The story is complete nonsense, but I found the film's sincerity, good- heartedness and complete lack of irony refreshing, and the film looks spectacular. Sure, the special effects are not technically as flawless as those produced by Hollywood, but the filmmakers wisely are more interested in color, composition and movement than realism and so many of the shots are breathtaking. In one shot, two of the superhuman characters stand on craggy spires of rock, a huge moon rising before them, the image perfectly balanced by the three elements. In another, a princess-warrior spires through the heavens behind her glowing sword like a heat-seeking missile. And the colors explode from shot to shot, used to express emotion rather than to represent reality.

The characters have the same simplicity and directness of comic book characters, offering no great depth in themselves but referring to archtypes that resonate more deeply. Physically, several of the actors are astonishingly

I've been going through the AFI's list of the top 100 comedies, and I must say that this is truly one of the worst. Not just of the 90 movies on the list I've seen, but of any movie I've ever seen. Drunks are funny sometimes, Dudley isn't. Liza almost made it worthwhile, but alas... just go watch Arrested Development if you want to see her in something good. Seriously, Dudley laughing and drinking is supposed to be funny? I would highly recommend almost ANY other movie on the AFI's top 100 comedies for more laughs than this. If you want to see a funnier "drunk", try The Thin Man. Funnier movie in general, any Marx Brothers movie will kill (especially if you're as drunk as Arthur).

I just saw this film @ TIFF (Toronto International Film Festival). Fans of Hal Hartley will not be disappointed!! And if you are not familiar with this director's oeuvre ... doesn't matter. Claustrophobic environments are the ones which Polanski is best at creating, and this has to be the most suffocating and confined picture he ever created. The emphasis on side walls and distant vanishing points is greater than ever, and even in the small number of exterior scenes the sky is rarely glimpsed. But The Tenant is not just confined spatially, but also in the intensity with which it focuses on its protagonist. Trelkovsky, played by Polanski himself is not only in every scene, he is in virtually every shot. When he is not on screen more often than not the camera becomes Trelkovsky's point of view. And of course almost everywhere he looks he sees his own reflection staring back at him in a mirror.

Shelley Winters plays a woman of questionable virtue who is headed for a ranch with a man (Charles Drake) she may marry. She ends up falling for Stewart, but not before she is passed around a bit. Winters is the most complex character in a film filled with unusual characters. Watch for a young Dan Dureyea as a nutty killer and Tony Curtis in a very small role. A woefully miscast Will Geer plays Wyatt Earp.

Hope that it isn't too late to save people from the terrible things that go on in so many lives. Gangland violence is real, right? Is it right, no! This movie carries an important social message which the cynics may dislike but which nonetheless is to be praised, rather than denigrated. I have watched this movie with great enjoyment at least eight times, each time with equal enjoyment and each time with the feeling that maybe the world could be made better and is not beyond saving (well not until 2008 anyway). 9 out of 10 from me for this one. It's very nearly perfect in my view. JMV

The opening flourishes left me purring with delight at their inventiveness - the altered version of the Archers' logo, the introductory disclaimer, the way the camera pans over the cosmos. It's strange to think that `It's a Wonderful Life' came out in the same year. No great coincidence: the 1940s was awash with heaven-and-earth films; but the glowing cotton wool nebulas and cutesy angels of the competition look tattered, something best passed over in silence, when placed next to Alfred Junge's vision.

It continues to look great all the way through, as more and more striking ideas are sprung upon us. I'm not a great fan of mixing colour with black and white in general. One of the two visual schemes almost always looks ugly when placed next to the other. Not so here. Powell dissolves colour into monochrome and monochrome into colour as if it's the most natural thing in the world, a mere change of palettes. Both the colour photography and the black and white could stand on their own.

As for the story ... this may be Pressburger's best script, or at least it would have been had the conclusion been a more logical outcome

Errol Flynn plays Gay Nineties-era boxer James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett--a man who became world boxing champ in 1892. The film goes from his rather humble beginnings and follows his through his career through him winning the title match against John L. Sullivan. However, while it could have focused mostly on the matches, most are rather brief in the film (except for the final title match) and the emphasis is on Corbett's brash personality as well as his relationship with the lady played by Alexis Smith. Throughout the film, there is excellent supporting work done by a cast of wonderful supporting actors (such as the perennial supporting actor in Flynn films, Alan Hale) and the writing really helped bring these people alive.

"The Muppets Take Manhattan" is different in a lot of ways to every other Muppet Movie made so far. For one, it remains the only Muppet film not owned by Disney. As of 2008, the film still belongs to 20th Century Fox (CBS Fox at the time of its release) even though Disney owns the rights to the Muppets. Also, this film has a story line that's very non-linear, and events that are otherwise unpredictable.

Of course, it's very hard to beat the original "Muppet Movie" from 1979, especially since that movie had more memorable songs than "Manhattan" does. However, one way in which "The Muppets Take Manhattan" is better than "The Muppet Movie" is perhaps the surprisingly realistic scenarios. In the first movie, all the Muppets really have to do is go to Hollywood, walk into an agent's office, and they are immediately given a "Rich & Famous" contract. In this movie, the Muppets learn that they actually have to work for their desired success, and it's a lot harder to do that, especially in the entertainment business, than they initially thought. That's an important and often times overlooked message, provided one is willing to suspend the disbelief

For anyone who wishes to get an impression of the Soviet view of modern Russian history this monumental film is a treasure. The story starts at the turn of the century (1900) in the yellowish sepia colours of old photographs which improves to black and white during the middle of the century and to full colour when the story approaches modern times (i.e. the 1960s).

The story focuses on a boy in a remote Siberian village, who is marked by the arrival and arrest of an anarchist during the czarist era. He later joins the Bolsheviks after the revolution and brings soviet communism to his village. His son, by the local beauty, fights the Germans during the Second World War. When he returns to the village, the oil industry takes off and we are treated to some Soviet economic idealism.

This film is long and slow, but utterly logic and very well made. It can be seen in three parts.

It is a shame that so many people can see only offence in what is, and was always intended to be, a light hearted piece of entertainment that in no way sought to denigrate black people. If anything it is a tribute to the infectious humour and musicality of the black race. I have not been able to view this confection for many years as the 'race commissars' in England have deemed it too offensive to be shown in multi racial Britain. If anyone knows where I can obtain a copy I would dearly love to view this masterpiece again. I think those who routinely look for messages and intent that were never intended in these cartoons, which are, after all, sixty years old, should try to lighten up and remember that the world is a very different place today, but that does not mean that anyone has the right to censor what is viewable from the past.

I used this film in a religion class I was teaching. The golden fish is swimming happily in his bowl in an upper floor apartment. A young boy and his mother are away from home. The boy has been given money to buy milk. On the way home, he stops at carnival to play a game. Next to him stands a man in a black suit looking a little scary. The boy drops the bottle of milk. It breaks. The man in the black suit gives him money to replace the milk. This scene alternates with what is happening at home. A black cat climbs the fire escape and enters the apartment. He(?) discovers the fish bowl and watches it. The fish swims energetically and flips out of the bowl. By now, a bunch of teenagers in my class and I have fallen in love with the fish. The cat takes the fish in his mouth and we all hold our breath. The cat drops the fish into the bowl. The double story line includes the suspicious man in black and the suspicious black cat. Both inspire prejudice. Both are innocent. It was a great discussion starter in my class.

Prix de Beauté was made on the cusp of the changeover from silence to sound, which came a little later in Europe than in Hollywood. Originally conceived as a silent, it was released with a dubbed soundtrack in France, with a French actress speaking Louise Brooks' lines, but was released as a silent in Italy and other parts of Europe. I was lucky enough to see the Cineteca di Bologna's flawless new restoration of an Italian silent print at the Tribeca Film Festival. I haven't seen the talkie version yet, but I think it's safe to assume the silent version is much more satisfying, since by all reports the dubbing is poorly done (Louise Brooks is clearly speaking English, so there's no way her lips could be matched.) Also, the film is made entirely in the silent style, with few titles and little need for dialogue. Prix de Beauté tells its story visually, with exciting, imaginative camera-work. The opening is instantly kinetic, with rapidly-cut scenes of urban life and swimmers splashing at a public beach. I saw "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival and found myself still thinking about it two days later. The story of a prodigal son (Scott Cohen) returning to his family's custom furniture business after a stint in jail, it offers all the necessary qualities of a solid drama--memorable characters; sharp, observant dialog; sensitive use of the camera by a filmmaker who thinks visually.

But more than that, it presents something that is all too rare at the multiplex these days: the uncompromising vision of a mature sensibility. The talent of director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin seems to emerge full-blown, but we get the sense he (like his protagonist) has paid his dues. He knows how real people struggle in this world, and he knows how we yearn to see--or at least, to experience vicariously--success. Yet Yellin respects his audience too much to blow happy smoke up our rear ends. In the end, we see that Jake's triumph doesn't lie in commissions, or even in the esteem of his family, but in "the work" he couldn't abandon if he tried.

It's an essential theme in a world (and especially a movie industry) that can't rise above "the bottom line".

He was, in fact, so successful and well thought of that people came from all over to hear his lectures and be taken on his wilderness treks--even though he was not a mixed blood Indian and all his knowledge was from books or faked! Billy decides to play along by saying that "he eats worms all the time". Joe and his friends don't believe him but Billy assures them and bets Joe that he can eat ten worms in one day otherwise he will come to school with worms in his pants.

The boys take Billy up on his bet, leaving the weak stomached child with a mission to gain respect from his classmates by eating worms cooked, fried, or alive.

Really an amazing pile of pap!

A predictable, slow moving, soul destroying, mind numbing movie to which, slitting your own wrists with a rusty bread knife seems... well, almost necessary.

The acting is over done for the thin dialogue, every scene is at least twice as long as it needs to be, the intricate details of how this career is collapsing or that career is rising is just far too dreary and mundane for words. The music would be good if you didn't have to sit through the movie, but really, three good songs is not enough reward for the effort required to watch the movie.

Watching this film I prayed to God for narcolepsy or for someone to shoot me.

Never, ever, ever again.

The US State Dept. would not like us to see this movie, because they have a beef with the Iranian govt. However, it shows us just how civilized Iran really is, despite the content of the film, which centers on the struggle of women there for equal rights in the simplest of terms: the ability to watch a soccer game at the stadium, which is strictly limited to male audiences alone. The film is hilariously funny, and in and of itself is proof of freedom of speech and expression in Iran. I enjoyed this movie intensely. Five girls try to penetrate the police border at the ticket gates to a soccer match between Iran and Bahrain. The ensuing comedy is too funny to describe, from the bus trip to the stadium, to the interceding of the police and subsequent detention of the girls, to the resulting end. Don't miss this classic film. Its a MUST see. One of the best foreign films I've seen in years.

I have to admit I have always found it difficult to watch an Antonioni film from start to finish at the first try, and even for this one, I ended up watching it in three parts on repeated occasions. In the end, I realised perhaps it was better that way, because it forced me to stop thinking in the usual terms of plot and just enjoy the scenes one by one.

The first part seems a lot more fragmentary, which is not a bad thing, it just requires more of an effort to follow. When it gets to the desert scenes, all efforts are repaid in full. The stunning cinematography is only a part of it, what really makes it all unforgettable is how the landscape is made into an overwhelming presence, the silence and vastness of it, the sense of sadness and freedom, the way it fuses and contrasts with the two young characters. The desert is dead, but at the same time it feels less distant and alien than the urban scenes in the first part. The dance between the airplane flying over and the girl's car makes for a series of great shots. The love
AI: There is no connection between Fortier and Profiler beyond the shared theme of police dramas centered on violent crimes. Profiler has a sharp, modern feel, while Fortier exudes a more timeless, classic vibe. The storylines in Profiler are straightforward, whereas Fortier’s narratives are notably more intricate. If comparisons must be made, Fortier bears a closer resemblance to Prime Suspect. The protagonist in Fortier is quirky and seemingly fragile, yet possesses a unique gift of "clairvoyance." Why do people feel the need to constantly compare, critique, and analyze? Why not simply enjoy the show for what it is? Interestingly, some claim Fortier feels American in style, while simultaneously expressing a preference for American series—a curious contradiction. Perhaps it’s the language or the overall tone, but I find Fortier to be more English in essence than American. On another note, the actors deliver impressive and often humorous performances. Their acting is anything but shallow.

This film is fantastic. It stays remarkably faithful to the classic novel by Mark Twain. The story kicks off with a delightful scene where Hank performs a song titled "When You Stub Your Toe on the Moon" alongside a group of children, reminiscent of Sinatra's uplifting tune "High Hopes"—both fun and motivating. The soundtrack shines throughout, with a standout number performed by the King, Hank (played by Bing Crosby), and Sir "Saggy" Sagamore. Overall, it’s a wonderful choice for family viewing or even a charming date night film. This is the kind of movie you’ll want to revisit time and again. Rhonda Fleming’s portrayal of the princess is stunning. I absolutely adore this movie! If you enjoyed Danny Kaye in "The Court Jester," you’re sure to love this one as well.

George P. Cosmatos' "Rambo: First Blood Part II" embodies pure fantasy and wish-fulfillment. The United States undeniably lost the Vietnam War, leaving behind unimaginable devastation in the country. Yet, this film perpetuates the myth of the innocent American soldier, casting only the national leaders as the true villains who orchestrated the conflict. Rambo, as a character, encapsulates this perspective perfectly. He is fiercely patriotic, lamenting the lack of recognition and celebration for individual soldiers’ sacrifices, while harboring deep mistrust toward commanding officers and politicians. Like other films that justify the war, such as "We Were Soldiers," this movie sidesteps the necessity of providing a clear rationale for the U.S. involvement in Southeast Asia or for the presence of each American soldier there. Instead, Rambo becomes the instrument of vengeance, avenging the collective wounds of a nation. Rather than suppressing these painful memories, the film would have been more meaningful if it had explored ways to confront and process them. "Do we get to win this time?" Yes, in this cinematic fantasy, you do.

In their attempt to make the audience empathize with Jake Roedel (Tobey Maguire), the filmmakers unjustly vilify the North and the Jayhawkers. Missouri remained part of the Union, and the Union Army was not an occupying force. The Southern cause was rooted in defending State's Rights, which included the right to enslave people, manipulate elections for corrupt legislatures and judges, and maintain a system of political patronage. There is no honor in such a stance. Missourians who supported the Confederacy could have easily headed east to join their army.

To my mind, the narrative lacks any real ambiguity. When Jake abandons the Bushwhackers, it isn't due to a realization of his mistakes, nor does he embrace the moral righteousness of the abolitionist cause.

Yes, I get it—you’re practically buzzing with anticipation. Well, *The Secret Lives of Dentists* won’t let you down in terms of meeting your expectations: it’s competently crafted but lacks originality, honest yet uninspiring. The film follows a married couple, both dentists, who run a joint practice (a setup ripe for conflict—without separate workplaces, most of us would abandon our partners out of sheer annoyance). Campbell Scott, sporting a mustache and demeanor less like an Everyman and more akin to Ned Flanders from *The Simpsons*, plays the gentle, über-Dad husband, while Hope Davis portrays the restless housewife who pours her pent-up frustrations into amateur opera. During one of her performances, attended by Dad and their daughters, he uncovers that her frustrations extend beyond the stage—he catches her kissing and flirting with the opera director. (A subtle detail: the director’s face remains unseen.) Fearing the messy ordeal of separation, divorce, and custody battles—lucrative only for lawyers—Scott opts to feign ignorance of his wife’s betrayal.

At this point, those with a taste for literature might start to yawn: another tired tale of the Pathetic, Sniveling Little Cuckold. But

Although this film's style lacks the subtlety and realism that a sound version might have offered, it remains a remarkable piece of cinema. Indeed, it was highly regarded during its time, earning a nomination for the inaugural Best Picture Oscar, though it ultimately lost to WINGS. While I still believe WINGS is the better film, this one shines despite some overacting by the lead, Emil Jannings.

Jannings portrays a former general from Czarist Russia, now scraping by in the 1920s as a Hollywood extra. His fortunes seem to turn when he lands a role playing an Imperial Russian general battling Communists during the revolution. The part doesn’t demand much of a stretch for him as an actor, but it stirs memories of his past and the tumultuous days of the revolution.

I’ll leave the unfolding events for you to discover, but the film is quite compelling, especially toward the conclusion. As a side note, keep an eye out for William Powell as the Russian director. Despite the film being made in 1928, his appearance, enhanced by makeup, isn’t far off from how he looked in many of his later roles.

I'm rating this movie a 7 out of 10 due to the captivating portrayal of the villains and the intriguing mystery surrounding the identity of Batwoman, which keeps you guessing. However, the film falls short in its treatment of Robin, who only appears briefly at the start and intermittently thereafter. I've always felt that the new animated series failed to do justice to the impressive new Robin character, not to mention Nightwing, and unfortunately, this movie perpetuates that disappointing trend. Additionally, the film focuses too heavily on Bruce Wayne and his romance, which might have been tolerable in a single film if the love story weren't so implausible. Despite these flaws, it remains a decent watch for Batman enthusiasts, and I would still suggest giving it a chance.

This film is utterly dreadful. The lead actor's performance was passable, but everything else—the plot, the storyline—was absolute rubbish and completely inaccurate. It bore so little resemblance to *Carlito's Way* that it could have been a sequel to any random movie. Fans of the original should steer clear of this disaster at all costs. There's no mention of Gail; instead, Carlito ends up with some other woman. Key elements like Kleinfield, how he got caught, or why he ended up in jail are entirely ignored. The filmmakers tried to emulate the original with flashbacks at the start, but honestly, I wanted to give this movie a zero rating. Unfortunately, I was forced to give it a slightly higher score.

This is a shameless attempt to capitalize on one of the best films of the '90s. Ultimately, it cost me about £6 and two hours of my life, both wasted. Despite being marketed as full of "action," it was painfully dull, slow, and predictable. Once again, to any *Carlito's Way* fans, avoid this mess at all costs.

Honestly, I struggle to express just how dreadful this movie is. I didn’t go in with high expectations, to be fair. After all, a PG-13 slasher film is almost guaranteed to lack the essential... slashing, so the absence of gore is hardly a shock. However, what truly stunned me was the sheer incompetence and barrage of clichés permeating every other element of this film.

Our main character is utterly useless, to the point where you can’t help but cheer for the antagonist. And here’s a shocker—she remains static throughout, completely ignoring the fundamental principle of screenwriting: character growth. If you’re hoping that by the end, this helpless girl will finally rise up and fight back, don’t hold your breath.

Moreover, we’re presented with perhaps the most uninspired (and certainly the least frightening) killer ever to appear in the genre. I’m not exaggerating when I say that the villains in Dora the Explorer pose more of a threat than the one in this film.

Lastly, any chance for suspense or impact is completely squandered by the sheer ineptitude on display.

*Home Room* explores the aftermath of a Columbine-style high-school shooting, focusing not on the event itself but on the survivors’ struggles with trauma, guilt, and denial.

*Spoilers* The shooting is presented as an inevitable tragedy, with no direct action shown except for the reaction of a young, almost teenage SWAT officer after taking down the high school shooter. The story centers on three main characters: a detective tasked with investigating a crime where no perpetrators remain to be prosecuted, and two teenage girls who survived the ordeal, portrayed by a young Erika Christensen and Busy Philipps.

Despite having little in common beyond their shared experience, the two girls are brought together by the tragedy, sparking intense emotional drama.

Erika Christensen, at just 24, brings a familiar and dependable acting style that resonates with audiences due to her extensive experience. Busy Philipps, three years older than Christensen and previously unknown to me, delivers a stunning performance, radiating dramatic intensity and commanding the screen with her presence. She truly embodies her role.

This powerful film draws viewers in with its intimate portrayal of the delicate yet evolving bond between two deeply wounded survivors.

This story kicks off with a bet between Edgar Allan Poe and a journalist, where Poe challenges the man to endure an entire night in a sinister castle. The journalist accepts, but whether he’ll emerge unharmed is uncertain, especially with unexpected, eerie figures roaming the castle, including the chilling Barbara Steele. The film itself is peculiar, blending French and English dialogue with occasional switches between the two, possibly due to missing snippets of conversation. The atmosphere is oppressively dark and confined, with visibility limited to the faint glow of candles, creating a constant sense of dread and looming disaster. This uncensored version from Synapse reveals content likely cut from the 1964 original, such as a topless scene, which might explain the edits. Overall, it’s a solid film, presented in stark black and white, with Barbara Steele’s presence undeniably elevating the experience. I’d rate it an 8 out of 10.

Last weekend, I picked up a 'zombie movie' from the bargain bin, expecting a low-budget take on "Land of the Dead" to enjoy with friends.

I couldn’t have been more mistaken.

It appears the filmmakers blew most of their budget on deceptive cover art, which misleads fans of zombie flicks.

We endured until the scene where zombie women come to life and hop into a car with a yuppie, who’s inexplicably in the middle of nowhere discussing business on his phone. They even converse with him before one of the women kills him. But when they started driving the car themselves, my ability to suspend disbelief completely shattered.

Some claim this falls into the “so bad, it’s good” category, but they’re wrong. I didn’t even finish it, though I read in another review that the zombies somehow end up as police officers by the end—a twist that makes me relieved I stopped watching.

This is worse than "Zombiez." STAY AWAY!

I ended up watching this dreadful teenage slasher film in the cinema only because it was a sneak preview; otherwise, I would have steered clear. Haven’t we had our fill of these tired tropes already? Unlike Scream and Scary Movie, which at least embraced their absurdity, this movie takes itself far too seriously. The plot is abysmal, and the acting is among the worst I’ve ever witnessed—rivaled only by Godzilla, which also vies for the title of the most atrocious film I’ve seen on the big screen.

The story is riddled with plot holes, and the female characters are so indistinguishable that it’s impossible to tell who’s been killed and who hasn’t—and frankly, you won’t care. The only actor I recognized beforehand was Denise, and she turned out to be the most talentless performer in this pathetic excuse for a film.

Do yourself a favor and stay far away from this disaster. (2/10)

Our family is anything but ordinary. Dad’s a well-known rapper, and we’ve got the classic "rebellious teenage daughter," an adopted white kid, and an adorable little one. Then there’s the careless housemaid—honestly, what show even features a character like that? Are we some kind of chaotic version of the Brady Bunch? Hooray! When the show first premiered, I thought it was awesome, probably because I was just a kid. The music, though, was terrible. The raps were cringe-worthy and way too family-friendly. Every single one was about family, friends, or personal struggles. Dad’s character reminded me of a "Danny from Full House" kind of father—always dishing out life lessons. Unlike Danny, though, he wasn’t obsessed with tidiness; they had a housekeeper for that, remember? The storylines usually revolved around Lil’ Romeo getting into some kind of trouble, or... well, that’s pretty much it. Oh, and there was the occasional preteen drama. Was it compelling? Not really. Still, it’s a decent show for kids. Nickelodeon, though, could definitely step up their game.

When my sister insisted this movie was worth watching, I was skeptical, but I gave it a chance and found myself laughing out loud. The story revolves around an eccentric girl who arrives in a small town where she's far from welcome. Her only goal is to attend the reading of her aunt's will and leave, but things are far from simple. Packed with outrageous humor, the film features a witch, a book of spells and recipes, a mentally challenged uncle, and a dog. It redefines the word "freak" in a way that’s both bold and unforgettable. I urge you to track down this classic gem and experience it for yourself. Overall, I’m tempted to rate it a 0... just kidding! It’s a solid 9 in my book. Be prepared to laugh, scream, and maybe even feel a little offended.

Yours truly,  
Dakota  
Feel free to reach out at dakota_loves_it@hotmail.com if you’d like to chat!

I found this movie to be truly remarkable, resonating deeply with the essence of human emotion. The intensity of love portrayed in the film is profound. Will delivers what I believe to be his finest performance yet, supported by exceptional direction. The editing impressed me, and the music was outstanding. The clever use of flashbacks added depth to the storytelling. This is a film that deserves a wide audience, and I hope viewers will take away something meaningful from it. Overall, it’s an outstanding piece of cinema. Hollywood should focus on producing more films with substance; even action movies can weave in heartfelt narratives. I appreciated the subtlety in Will’s acting—he brought a rare sense of purpose and commitment to his role. I recommend experiencing this movie either solo or with someone dear to you. For me, time seemed to stand still, with the film commanding my full attention and momentarily suspending the outside world. In the midst of global chaos, this was a refreshing escape. In an era often defined by self-interest, it was inspiring to witness a character who prioritized others above himself.

What could possibly have compelled Colin Firth to star in such a directionless movie? Is he truly in dire financial straits?

The film stumbles in defining its core theme—is it about grief, exotic destinations, ghosts, or merely a showcase for a Mr. Darcy-esque character? The result is a confusing, murky jumble.

There appears to be a vague notion that Italy inherently possesses some allure, and that the Italian language holds a special value. Yet, ultimately, the young female characters yearn to return to America.

Scenes on beaches, in churches, and along crowded streets feel aimless, leaving viewers puzzled about the film's purpose or why they should invest emotionally in it.

Additionally, the inclusion of an American woman in the cast adds to the confusion. Her role is ambiguous, and her interactions with the girl are filled with shallow, tactless, and overly sentimental remarks. Is the film attempting to touch on the theme of pedophilia?

Overall, it's a rather dismal fiasco. I rated it a 2 instead of a 1 simply because it lacks the bizarre appeal of a completely atrocious film.

In 1985, while in college, I watched this so-called movie on cable with a high school friend whose teenage hormones were in overdrive. It didn’t take long to realize this film was a lost cause. The script was absurd, revolving around older men hiring younger ones to teach them how to charm women, the acting was terrible (with one minor exception), and the humor was painfully unfunny. The only thing that briefly held my friend’s attention was the abundant female nudity, though even that couldn’t sustain his interest past the first half-hour. Keep in mind, this was a high school guy in an era before the internet made such content easily accessible. We stuck with it, hoping for a redeeming moment of wit or intrigue, but it never came. Ironically, the most amusing aspect was the studio’s original marketing, which shamelessly acknowledged the film’s awfulness—one poster featured a fake review claiming, “This is the best movie I’ve seen this afternoon!” The sole bright spot was Grant Cramer in the lead role, who displayed some talent and has since built a career in the industry. Ultimately, this no-budget, tedious display of cheap thrills is worth skipping.

It's easy to overlook, after later seasons expanded the alien conspiracy storyline, that The X-Files once crafted episodes like "GenderBender" and "Fearful Symmetry." In those early days, aliens weren't just stereotypical grey beings or mind-controlling slime; they had the power to truly astonish.

"Fearful Symmetry" kicks off with the concept of an "invisible elephant"—an elephant somehow displaced in space and time, not far removed from the eerie premise of "The Walk"—and culminates in the abduction of a pregnant gorilla. The episode is a collection of striking moments. While the subplot feels overly moralistic—yes, we understand, zoos are problematic except when they’re not—the ideas embedded within are captivating, visually arresting, and unforgettable. It also explores a unique perspective on abduction: why should humans be the sole focus of alien interest?

Ultimately, "Fearful Symmetry" may not be an immediate standout, but it remains engaging and highly memorable during its runtime. Above all, it’s the kind of story few other shows would dare to tell.

"Grey Gardens" (1975), directed by the Maysles brothers, is a peculiar documentary that delves into the lives of Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis's eccentric aunt and first cousin. Residing in a dilapidated 28-room mansion in East Hampton, Long Island, they live in squalor, surrounded by filth. 'Big Edie' Bouvier Beale, at 78, possesses a sharp wit and dry humor, while her 56-year-old daughter, 'Little Edie' Beale, emotionally stunted at around 13, remains a striking beauty with a once-bright future. Isolated from society, their only companions are numerous cats and raccoons that inhabit the attic. The pair pass their days bickering, tuning into the radio, or serenading one another, without even a television to connect them to the outside world. Their dramatic decline from high society is both fascinating and poignant, captivating viewers with the story of these two uniquely compelling, albeit deeply troubled, individuals. Widely regarded as one of the finest documentaries ever produced, "Grey Gardens" remains a cult classic to this day.

I rarely label a movie as unwatchable, but this film is an exception. The sole redeeming qualities are Cornelia Sharpe’s appealing presence and the movie’s mercifully brief runtime.

The storyline is excruciatingly dull and lacks any meaningful progression. The characters are utterly unengaging, leaving viewers with no reason to invest in their fates. It’s baffling why Sean Connery chose to be part of this project; he would have been wise to decline.

The only conceivable reason to watch this film is if you’re an ardent Sean Connery enthusiast determined to see his entire filmography. Even then, save this one for the very end.

If, against all odds, you decide to watch this despite my warning (and the numerous other critiques online), I sincerely hope you find more enjoyment in it than I did. Thanks for taking the time to read this.

This content fails to amuse—linking it to Monty Python is utterly absurd. There’s nothing humorous here. It’s excessive, unattractive, and strange just for the sake of being odd, leaving the impression that the creators were constantly under some influence. Regrettably, whatever it was didn’t translate into comedy.

I’ll concede a few points for effort, or something along those lines. There might be a laugh track—or is there? That’s questionable, given the near absence of actual laughter.

Perhaps I’m being unfair. Maybe this is intended as some kind of experimental piece or art form. If so, anything is permissible, and I’ll let it slide.

But these men portraying women with squeaky voices and exaggerated mannerisms? Honestly, it’s just not funny.

When it comes to inheriting Monty Python’s sharp, intellectual humor, only Stephen Colbert, and possibly Jon Stewart, come close.

I decided to rent this film primarily because of the director, whose previous works have been quite intriguing (if you haven’t watched *Waxork*, you’re in for a treat). Despite my initial reservations, I pushed aside my doubts and gave it a chance. Unfortunately, it’s a major disappointment. It’s simply awful. If you haven’t seen it yet and don’t mind spoilers, continue reading. To start, the old adage “Don’t judge a book by its cover” rings true here. The movie’s packaging is deceptive; the cover art suggests Jill is a stunning beauty with long, highlighted hair, and the back features an enticing image of her in red leather along with other captivating stills. The synopsis sounds promising, drawing you in with the expectation of a good story. However, once you start watching, you’re thrown off by the bizarre choice to set the film in 1977 for no apparent reason. Worse, Jill turns out to be nothing like the glamorous figure on the cover—she’s far from attractive. The plot isn’t as predictable as one might expect, but not in a positive way. The characters make baffling, illogical decisions with no discernible motivation, making it cringe-worthy to watch. Just ten minutes before the ending...

This lesser-known gem from de Sica truly shines. As the saying goes, "the meek shall inherit the earth," and this story, while seemingly about class divides, serves as a profound allegory for the countless displaced individuals across post-war Europe. These homeless souls, though destitute, remain spirited, ignored by a society too poor and self-absorbed to offer care or recognition, reduced to mere doormats for Italy’s opportunists. De Sica frames their plight within a fairy tale, reminiscent of a Cinderella narrative. Having not read the source material, I can’t confirm whether the deus ex machina resolution originates from the author or de Sica himself. The film opens with "Once upon a time…," underscoring the timeless and universal nature of its message, a story that could unfold anywhere. With sharp, biting caricatures of the elite, a whimsical portrayal of the homeless—especially as they start fulfilling their dreams—and an ending straight out of a Spielberg blockbuster, this cinematic treat captivates all audiences. Marking a departure from neo-realism, de Sica’s most approachable work is also among his finest. Straddling the line between stark realism and classic filmmaking, he crafts a film that both shatters and mends the heart.

Wes Craven, are you kidding us... at our expense? The plot of *Red Eye* is utterly absurd. We're presented with a man who has supposedly been stalking a woman for eight weeks, only to conveniently appear behind her at the airport, successfully flirt and charm her, and somehow secure a seat right next to her in a cozy two-seat arrangement, rather than being stuck in the middle of a crowded five-seat row (does he have inside help at check-in?). He’s annoyingly pleasant during an agonizingly drawn-out buildup. Then, once they’re airborne, trapped in a tight space surrounded by strangers, he abruptly turns menacing, threatening the shallow yet hyper-competent Rachel McAdams with clichéd lines like, “We’ve got your daddy, do as I say, or he’s done for.” Pardon me, but weren’t they already holding her father hostage long before she even boarded the plane? If so, wouldn’t it have been infinitely easier to just grab her off the street and terrorize her in some secluded room, skipping the convoluted and risky father subplot altogether? They could’ve resorted to pulling out her fingernails or whatever until she made the critical “call” they needed. Or, since this is a movie and we’re already suspending disbelief...

As a passionate fan of horses and hand-drawn animation, I had high hopes for DreamWorks' latest release, *Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron*. Unfortunately, my excitement was tempered by a sense of disappointment. The animation is breathtaking, and the initial concept—a story centered solely on a horse in its natural environment—feels promising. The absence of talking animals or saccharine musical numbers is a refreshing choice. However, the film stumbles with an unnecessary narration by Matt Damon, a sentimental soundtrack by Bryan Adams, and an overload of action sequences that rival a Jerry Bruckheimer blockbuster. Had the creators embraced a simpler approach, this could have been a true masterpiece. While it falls short of greatness, it remains decent entertainment for young children. I would suggest this movie to families, as it carries a wholesome message and offers a rare, non-offensive option for kids in today’s cinema landscape. Though it’s not exceptional, the stunning visuals are undeniably captivating, even if the film could have achieved so much more.

I first, and only, encountered "Shades" at a Sneak Preview before its official premiere. I recall a member of the director's team was present, though I can’t remember who exactly. As a Belgian film unknown to us, we approached it with open minds and no expectations. Mickey Rourke delivers a standout performance, towering over the rest of the cast. He portrays a faded actor whose career has long since peaked, now involved in a Belgian film project called "Shades."

Right from the start, the excessive profanity in the movie struck us. While I don’t mind the occasional curse, this was far beyond tolerable. Rourke’s use of strong language feels authentic and fitting, but when non-native English speakers in the cast throw around similar expletives, it comes across as forced and hostile.

We soon gave up trying to tally the countless profanities. By the end, everyone was just relieved to leave the theater. We were asked to rate the film on a scale of 0 to 10, but we found ourselves wishing for a negative score like -10 to truly express our disappointment.

I’m absolutely obsessed with this movie and never tire of rewatching it. The only part that bothers me is when Riff refers to herself as a teenage lobotomy—I just can’t get on board with that line. Aside from that, everything else is flawless. I’ve never been a big fan of PJ Soles, and learning that she didn’t even know who the Ramones were before filming didn’t help her case. Still, I manage to overlook her sneering expression most of the time. Like many who watch this film repeatedly, my love for it stems entirely from being a Ramones fan. I never get bored of seeing DeeDee flub his pizza lines or Joey repeatedly botch the teacher’s name—it’s hilarious every time. One of my favorite scenes is when they perform “Do You Want to Dance” while strolling through the high school hallways; it’s pure magic. The special edition DVD includes a solid retrospective, and, interestingly, PJ Soles isn’t featured in it. Maybe she was busy with another project *chuckles*. All in all, it’s a fantastic film, and even better if you’re a Ramones enthusiast.

In my 29 years of watching sci-fi, this stands out as the finest I've encountered. I’m confident that *Dark Angel* will gain a devoted cult following. The action sequences are impressive, but Jessica Alba truly shines as the most captivating and stunning star on television right now.

It's refreshing to note that Vintage Film Buff has aptly labeled their superb DVD release as a "musical," which perfectly captures the essence of this film. Much like its unofficial remake, *Murder at the Windmill* (1949), the murder storyline serves merely as a backdrop for a lavish display of glamour, featuring Kitty Carlisle and Gertrude Michael at the forefront of a stunning ensemble of women, including Ann Sheridan, Lucy Ball, Beryl Wallace, Gwenllian Gill, Gladys Young, Barbara Fritchie, Wanda Perry, and Dorothy White. Carl Brisson also contributes his powerful vocals to the iconic "Cocktails for Two," a tune so beloved that it echoes through the film four times. Yet, it is Gertrude Michael who truly captivates, not only with her enchanting performance of "Sweet Marijuana" but also with her compelling portrayal of the protagonist’s spurned lover. On the other hand, the film could have easily omitted Jack Oakie and Victor McLaglen without loss. Oakie’s only redeeming moment is a feeble recurring joke alongside cult favorite Toby Wing. Moreover, the comedy feels excessively forced and tiresome, exemplified by the bumbling Inspector McLaglen, who remains frustratingly unable to apprehend the killer despite obvious clues.

I recently watched this movie and, while it wasn’t utterly terrible, I found myself quite let down. I’m puzzled as to why a film like this was even made. It had moments of slight entertainment, but it felt as though the creative team was pulling in different directions. It’s as if the writer called the shots on Monday, the director took over on Tuesday, and by Wednesday, even the coffee runner was making decisions. It seems like they had ideas for several distinct films but were constrained by time and budget to cobble together just one.

Another viewer praised the acting as impressive, but I can’t say I agree. However, if the actors managed to maintain their composure during filming, maybe they deserve more credit than I initially thought.

The DVD cover suggested a mystery akin to a historical version of Law and Order or National Treasure. The movie begins in that vein, but then abruptly veers into territory reminiscent of a subpar episode of The Twilight Zone—or perhaps a lackluster installment of The Outer Limits, that lesser-known counterpart.

Slither, billed as a horror comedy, struggles to strike a balance between its intended genres, lacking sufficient frights and laughs to truly fit into either category. While it boasts a standout scene and a handful of effective one-liners, the film falls short on genuine scares and consistent humor to sustain its runtime. Furthermore, the screenplay diverts attention from the central hero and heroine, veering off course at multiple points.

A significant flaw in the movie is its shift in focus from the protagonist, played by Nathan Fillion, to Grant Grant, portrayed by Michael Rooker. After introducing Grant, the narrative follows his transformation into the monster, a detour that slows the film's pace considerably. Rooker's character lacks depth, failing to engage the audience on a personal level. Watching him perform actions under the monster's influence might have been compelling in a character study titled "Grant: Portrait of a Man Turning Into a Monster," but it feels out of place in a horror-comedy centered on an alien invasion. Ultimately, the film's shortcomings stem from its script, which places undue emphasis on the monster's behavior and reproduction—details that hold little relevance for the audience. The essence of a horror-comedy lies in trapping the heroes in dire straits, armed and ready to fight back.

Gus Van Sant has crafted some remarkable films, and I genuinely admire his work.

Yet, I can’t shake the feeling that the sharp, intellectual essence of Tom Robbins’ novel "Even Cowgirls Get the Blues" gets diluted in its cinematic adaptation. Individually, both Tom Robbins and Gus Van Sant are extraordinary visionaries and immensely talented. However, this particular collaboration fell short of expectations.

It’s not that the characters lacked depth or that the plot and themes failed to resonate. Rather, the power of our imagination when reading a book like this is unparalleled. A novel transports us to another era and setting, allowing us to envision the extremes of both the best and worst scenarios, which heightens the thrilling ups and downs meticulously crafted by the author. In contrast, films often limit this imaginative and emotional journey, diminishing the overall impact. I believe this is what occurred with this adaptation.

I highly recommend diving into the book instead!

What a dreadful piece of garbage! I can’t fathom why so many people rave about this. Sure, it’s “artistic” and “foreign,” but that alone isn’t sufficient. The storyline is tedious and fragmented, resembling a poorly produced reality show.

The individuals in the narrative are fundamentally unengaging, and as characters, they lack the depth needed to evoke any sympathy. If they’re modeled after real people, I truly pity them.

The violence, some of which is excessively brutal, feels overly showy and unnecessary. It seems as though the producer aspires to emulate Quentin Tarantino—though I’m not particularly impressed by him either.

And frankly, if I had neighbors like these, I’d relocate immediately!

This film is a quintessential B-grade science fiction flick, and the director doesn't shy away from embracing that fact. The story centers on a dragon brought back to life by a team of scientists, recycling tropes and scenes that feel all too familiar. The script lacks depth, devoid of authentic characters and instead packed with tired stereotypes and predictable scenarios. The director leans into the formulaic nature of the movie without pretense, which lends it a slight charm, though it’s not a film that will linger in your memory. It’s the kind of entertainment best enjoyed in the background while you’re busy with chores like cooking, cleaning, or exercising—pure, mindless amusement. It serves a purpose in the realm of casual viewing, but it’s not something you’d gather friends to watch unless you’re all inebriated and indifferent to quality. The average rating of 3.2 feels about right. While I don’t find it as dreadful as some critics, I’m baffled by online comments praising it as exceptional. To me, there’s no evidence of any effort to make this a standout or memorable piece of cinema.

I was residing in Rawlins during the filming of this movie and was fortunate enough to participate in its production. I worked both as an extra and alongside Eddie Surkin on special effects. Witnessing the behind-the-scenes magic was incredible, from the barbed wire coming to life to the electric chair rising through the warden's office floor. Meeting the cast, from Viggo to Tiny, was also a highlight. Interestingly, the gate cut into the prison wall for the film is still known locally as the "Disney Gate." For anyone curious, many of the movie sets remain intact in Rawlins and can be viewed on a self-guided tour. Working with R. Harlin and the team was an amazing experience, and I’d love the opportunity to do it again.

In my opinion, the standout moment of this film, which perfectly captures the utter absurdity and foolishness of the entire narrative, occurs during the climax. DOCTOR TED NELSON and his bachelor companion, the Sheriff, have at last trapped the Melting Man on a stair landing within an electrical generating plant. It’s worth noting that Nelson has spent nearly the whole movie searching for the Melting Man (MM), who by now has brutally killed and consumed multiple individuals, including Nelson’s boss. Nelson is fully aware of MM’s violent insanity and ravenous craving for human flesh and blood.

At this point, the Sheriff, with his gun aimed at MM—who, credit to the film and Rick Baker, is depicted as the most horrifying and grotesque human-like figure imaginable—shouts a critical question to DOCTOR TED NELSON: "WHAT DO WE DO NOW?!?!?"

The camera shifts to DOCTOR TED NELSON, and it’s painfully clear that Ted hasn’t the slightest clue about the next step. Evidently, Ted was so fixated on the task of locating the Melting Man that he failed to consider the necessity of bringing any means of restraint.

It's truly baffling. How Francis Veber, a globally renowned comedy director (particularly in his native France), could produce a film so utterly unwatchable defies comprehension. It's not merely the unlikable characters or the complete absence of even rudimentary humor; watching this movie is physically excruciating. The relentless display of poor writing, acting, and filmmaking is staggering, making it hard to believe that seasoned and skilled professionals were behind it. The lengthy time spent in editing and the delayed, barely noticeable theatrical release speak volumes. What could they have been thinking?

As a fan captivated by the stunning visuals of "Hero," I was eager to watch this movie, which was promoted as being in a similar vein but superior. Additionally, it starred an actress I admire, Ziyi Zhang. Unfortunately, I was let down on both expectations. Purchasing the DVD without prior viewing was a misstep on my part; it did not surpass "Hero."

I understand that these martial arts films with characters soaring through the air are complete fantasy, but this narrative stretches believability to such an extreme that it left me in disheartened disbelief. The idea of a blind woman overcoming hundreds of adversaries? That pushes the limits too far. Moreover, the main male character, Jin, portrayed by Takeshi Kaneshiro, was incredibly irritating with his dialogue, foolish expressions, and grating laugh, which further spoiled the experience.

Even with its vibrant colors and breathtaking action sequences, the story lacked the charm to make this a film worth keeping in my collection. This movie certainly isn’t a "Hero" in my eyes!

This film is utterly dreadful, to put it bluntly. It was so terrible that I felt compelled to create an IMDb account just to caution others about its perils.

As something of a connoisseur of campy horror flicks, I've seen my fair share of B-movies like "Redneck Zombies," "House of the Psychotic Women," and "Slumber Party Massacre II." I’m well-versed in cinematic trash, and I can confidently say this movie is abysmal.

For roughly three-quarters of the runtime, the film consists of frightened characters darting back and forth across the screen. When they’re not fleeing, they’re delivering nonsensical dialogue with no trace of emotion or purpose. Just when the acting starts to become tolerable, the directing collapses entirely. The film is plagued by awkward low-angle shots, making me suspect director Leif Jonker was working with a tripod no taller than three feet. He repeatedly employs what I’ve dubbed the "Leif Maneuver"—an amateurish zoom-out from objects of interest, used ad nauseam. Evidently, the crew couldn’t manage to wake up for a sunrise shoot, so they recorded a sunset and played it backward instead. With such sloppy direction, the climactic gory scene almost feels impressive by comparison. One can only assume the final five minutes were shot before the preceding eighty-five, given the stark contrast in effort.

This movie missed the opportunity to delve into the emotional depth of its animal characters, leaving me feeling hollow. [Spoiler ahead] I remained unconvinced that Dr. D had a strong motivation to reject the lucrative buyout offer in favor of aiding his animal companions. In contrast to the original Babe, which defied the norms of blockbuster films by highlighting the human-like virtues of animals compared to their human counterparts, the animals in this rendition are reduced to mere comedic stereotypes, so exaggerated that one might feel no remorse sending them to the slaughterhouse—especially given their incoherent chatter. Without Eddie Murphy's eccentric performance, this film would undoubtedly fall flat.

THHE2 offers plenty of entertainment with its mix of humor and shock value—expect to laugh, cringe, and mutter expletives like “oh sh*t!” or “get away from that damn hole, you idiot!” However, I’m unsure if it’s truly worth watching. The military characters were a constant source of frustration, displaying an infuriating lack of combat knowledge.

While the sequel ramps up the violence, gore, and body count compared to the first film, I’m still torn on whether that compensates for the overwhelming sense of absurdity permeating the movie—and not the enjoyable kind found in films like Dead Alive or Feast. Honestly, I would have preferred rewatching Aja’s remake for the fifth time.

If you’re in the mood for laughs or gore, go ahead and see it. Just don’t expect to leave the theater feeling fulfilled.

(Rating: 21 by The Film Snob.) (Visit our blog What-To-See-Next for an explanation of our rating system.)

This film is so mind-numbingly dull that you might find yourself scratching at your own face just to escape the on-screen monotony.

Forget about wringing your hands, rolling your eyes, or sighing into your popcorn. No, for a film of *this* level of mediocrity, only tearing at your own skin will suffice.

When the urge to claw at your face becomes inevitable—and it will—start at the lower half. You’ll want the upper part, equipped with tear ducts, unharmed for the emotionally charged third act, which could leave you floored if you haven’t already fled the theater in desperation.

In a time when Joe Six-Pack and Hockey Moms are hailed as the epitome of leadership and international relations, a film this painfully tedious might be embraced as something anyone could produce. *Enduring* it, however, is an entirely different and far riskier endeavor.

Here’s the plot…

Sidney Young, the London-based publisher of a lesser-known celebrity/entertainment magazine, is on the verge of witnessing his publication

Before the era of the Toxic Avenger, Troma Films, known for their low-budget camp, attempted a more conventional approach with straightforward slasher movies. It’s tempting to believe that the disappointing outcome of these efforts prompted them to abandon any pretense and embrace deliberate parody instead.

*Splatter University* is a film that seems designed for viewers with a penchant for cinematic suffering. As it stumbles through dual casts and a maze of irrelevant subplots, watching becomes a torturous experience. Here’s a brief attempt to distill its essence.

The story begins with the escape of a dangerous psychopath from a nearby hospital, shifting the scene to a Catholic university (its actual name escapes me, but for the sake of relevance, let’s dub it St. Splatter). The students are disengaged and morose, bickering over trivial matters, embodying the slacker archetype before it was even a trend. Meanwhile, the new professor, Julie Parker, proves to be spectacularly inept in her role. The students navigate a tangle of romantic entanglements, betrayals, unplanned pregnancies, predatory clergy, and ways to shirk academic responsibilities. Julie, on the other hand, grapples with a disturbing boyfriend, a rigid university administration, the challenges of advising pregnant students, and the vacant stares of her unresponsive pupils. Ultimately, none of these threads coalesce into anything meaningful.

Penned by a woman and helmed by another, this film raises the question: are we embarking on a feminist journey? Buckle up, ladies, as we dive into a narrative filled with cruel men and virtuous, well-meaning women.

In this melodrama, Trish encounters a man at an employment agency who exudes the demeanor, appearance, and style of a pimp. He offers her a job, seemingly with ulterior motives of pursuing her later. In a chilling scene in his office, he touches her chin in a manner reminiscent of a sinister villain in a James Bond film, right after capturing a damsel and just before plotting her demise alongside 007. Later, this predatory figure follows Trish into a women’s dressing room, harasses her, and nearly assaults her. The portrayal suggests a world of villainous men, implying that every one of them is inherently wicked. The film seems to posit that even something as mundane as job hunting is fraught with danger for women. But fear not, for the women in this story are ready to fight back! The movie features a group akin to a divorced women’s support club, led by a character played by Janet Leigh. She voices the collective sentiment of the women in the film by declaring that "men are all s**t," encapsulating their shared frustration and disdain.

Frailty - 8/10 - Despite its puzzling title and the distracting "Bill Paxton Directs" tagline, this film delivers a gripping, old-school biblical horror thriller experience. While it might ultimately be seen as merely the eccentric, Southern Gothic relative of Kubrick's "The Shining," that's still a highly engaging premise. The movie boasts a shocking plot twist and a morally ambiguous message that adds to its intrigue. It's the type of film that, years from now, late-night viewers on basic cable will stumble upon and find themselves thoroughly spooked. It's a shame that director Bill Paxton chose to cast himself in a starring role, but even so, this remains a wickedly entertaining rental.

The Sopranos stands as perhaps the most celebrated television series of all time, and despite my sky-high expectations, it managed to exceed them. As a fan of the mafia and crime genres in film, I’m drawn to the gripping narratives of these worlds, yet this show offers far more. With over 86 hours of content, it crafts not only an exhilarating and unpredictable mafia/action saga but also a profound family drama, a riveting character exploration, a hilarious comedy, a deep psychological analysis of morality, and an intellectual, artistic fusion of symbolic dreams and hallucinations. David Chase’s monumental series achieves all this and beyond, establishing HBO as the pinnacle of television’s cinematic potential and setting the stage for other groundbreaking shows to captivate viewers.

While realism anchors the narrative when necessary, Chase’s deliberate deviations—such as crafting “dream episodes”—add rich, complex layers to the series. Supported by a talented writing team, including Matthew Weiner and Terrence Winter, who later created Mad Men, Chase elevates The Sopranos into a unparalleled storytelling masterpiece.

This uproarious comedy delivers a sharp, laugh-out-loud take on sex, family dynamics, and class distinctions in Beverly Hills, squeezing more humor from the iconic zip code than it has seen since the era of Granny and Jed Clampett. The storyline revolves around two chauffeurs who make a daring wager: which of them can seduce their employer—both alluring, single (or soon-to-be-single) women, portrayed by the captivating Bisset and Woronov—first. If Manuel wins, his buddy will settle his dangerous debt with a ruthless Asian street gang. If he loses, he must submit to a humiliating role reversal with his friend.

The film is packed with risqué dialogue and delightfully twisted physical comedy, though much of the humor simmers just below the surface. Bartel shines in a standout role as a seductive older family member who embarks on a year-long "missionary trip" to Africa with his enticing teenage niece.

Pure, hilarious entertainment.

Though this film has seen multiple remakes, it remains a timeless classic for first-time viewers. With its inventive dialogue and brilliant originality in the climactic scene, it warrants far more praise than critics have offered. Strongly recommended, it stands as one of the finest comedies in recent memory.

Lacking any particular passion for filmmaking and holding a genuine respect for documentaries, I found myself frustrated for enduring the full duration of "20 Dates." I’ll spare you the details of the plot—other reviews can cover that. However, I must mention that Berkowitz’s frenetic, Woody Allen-esque narration was grating to the point of exasperation. It made me wish he’d either cut back on caffeine or take a sedative. It seems even Berkowitz might have realized this project was a misstep, as portions of the film focus on his struggles to secure funding for the documentary. While I hate to mask criticism as praise, I’ll grudgingly acknowledge Berkowitz’s ability to persuade someone to bankroll this dreadful piece of work. I recognize the film’s ambitions and boundaries, but even by the standards Berkowitz set for himself, he fails spectacularly on every front. To wrap up, I doubt many of the women featured felt comfortable dating an anxious, aspiring filmmaker, which casts doubt on the film’s authenticity. Myles, I enjoyed your movie the first time I saw it... under a different title.

As a child, I was completely enamored with both Bill & Ted movies. Recently, I caught *Bogus Journey* on TV, and since it had been at least five years since my last viewing, I decided to watch it again. I fell in love with it all over again! Even after all these years, the humor still holds up. While I think *Excellent Adventure* is the superior film, this one is just as entertaining. Yes, some of the acting can feel a bit over-the-top, but that’s part of the charm—this movie embraces its cheesiness in the best way possible. Plus, it showcases the most iconic portrayal of Death ever on screen! In short: This is an absolutely awesome, non-bogus flick, dude! Totally excellent! STATION!!!

CRY FREEDOM serves as a compelling introduction to the harsh realities of apartheid, condensed into a few hours of viewing. Directed by the renowned Richard Attenborough, known for GANDHI, the film benefits from the genuine involvement of Mr. and Mrs. Woods, the central white figures whose real-life experiences and book add a layer of credibility to the story. The current video release extends beyond two and a half hours, incorporating an additional 23 minutes of footage originally added for a two-part TV miniseries following its theatrical debut.
