While this extended duration amplifies certain shortcomings—such as inconsistent character development and broad stereotyping—it also highlights a potential strength: the focus on the white characters’ journey. When viewed as a political and historical educational tool rather than solely for its artistic value, CRY FREEDOM addresses a narrative all too familiar to black Africans, though it may resonate more powerfully with younger audiences through this visual medium. Ultimately, the film and the book target a white audience, aiming to provoke reflection and awareness.

This film mirrors reality in the sense that very little occurs over its roughly two-hour duration, with no clear direction or storyline apparent, largely due to a cast that often remains unseen because of the so-called "experimental" lighting noted by numerous critics.

It's utterly tedious. It's unsurprising that Altman directs this, given his inconsistent track record (while "Gosford Park" was a hit, can we forget "Pret A Porter," "Kansas City," or "Dr. T and the Women"? Dreadful). Yet, considering the source material is a John Grisham story and the talented cast, barely visible through the dimness as you struggle to stay awake, this film emerges as a remarkable example of cinematic failure. And no, it doesn't even achieve the status of "so bad it's good."

It's simply awful.

I have watched "Miracles Still Happen" at least four times, and I never grow weary of this incredible film. From the opening scene, it captivates the viewer’s attention. As the story unfolds and the plane crashes, the tension escalates, drawing us into the harrowing journey of a young girl struggling to survive alone and terrified in the Amazon after being the sole survivor of the disaster. The added heartbreak of losing her mother in the crash intensifies the drama, as we witness the immense challenges she faces during her ten days in the wilderness. The reality that this event actually occurred feels almost unimaginable, and the idea that anyone could endure such an ordeal is beyond comprehension, especially as we see the threats of wild animals, snakes, and other reptiles, alongside the vast forests, diverse wildlife, and swarms of insects. As the film continues, we are shown the numerous dangers this girl must confront while following a river, clinging to the hope that it will guide her to safety. She recalls her father’s advice that a stream will always flow into a river, and then into an even larger one, eventually leading to civilization.

I'm uncertain about its global availability, but if anyone involved in selecting content for videotapes and distribution to video clubs is reading this, I urge you to acquire it! To be absolutely clear: PLEASE GET THIS MOVIE INTO VIDEO STORES!

It’s impossible to describe—you simply have to watch it!

About a year ago, I caught a news segment on TV about a zombie movie being shot in my area. Since that moment, I’ve closely followed the progress of the film, titled 'Fido,' from its completion to its debut at various festivals. Two weeks ago, 'Fido' premiered at my local theater. Just yesterday, I came across a newspaper article reporting that, while 'Fido' struggles to draw crowds in its limited release elsewhere, it’s a hit at our local venue. Surprisingly, at The Paramount Theater, it’s outperforming all other films, including '300.' This local enthusiasm is likely due to residents eager to see their city on the big screen or to catch a glimpse of themselves as zombies. For any locals who haven’t yet watched 'Fido' but are thinking about it, you’ll recognize plenty of familiar sights—from the school and city park to the forbidden zone. These scenes showcase the Okanagan Valley’s stunning beauty, an unexpected highlight in a zombie flick! Beyond the scenery, 'Fido' stands out as a genuinely good film. Despite a few shortcomings, it surpasses most of the other 20 movies currently showing locally.

I watched this during a test screening and, frankly, I'm at a loss for words. What on earth did I just witness? This movie stumbles through its runtime with the grace of Mickey Mouse attempting to recite lines from "Scarface." It's not just confusing; it’s utterly nonsensical, and even if you try to switch off your brain, the absurdity is so overwhelming that it fails to elicit even a chuckle.

The storyline centers on crocodile hunter Steve Irwin endeavoring to "rescue" a crocodile that unwittingly holds a CIA probe. When the CIA tracks down Irwin to recover their device, he misidentifies them as poachers and resolves to thwart their plans.

That’s the extent of the narrative depth here. The remainder is filled with exaggerated parodies of Australian stereotypes—think endless "Didja see dat?" and "Crikey!"—paired with awkwardly staged action scenes. In one particularly surreal moment, Irwin leaps onto a speeding RV and engages in a knife fight with a CIA operative on its roof. Yes, you read that correctly: Steve Irwin, in a knife duel atop a moving vehicle. Let that image be your benchmark for the sheer awfulness of this film.

I believe this celebrity skit show is quite impressive. Greg Kinnear's stint as host was particularly enjoyable. While Hal Sparks did a decent job, I often find myself wishing Greg Kinnear had stayed on. It feels like no one commits to a TV show for its full duration these days. Nevertheless, I appreciated the different hosts and cast members parodying celebrities, which I found hilariously entertaining. I must admit, I do miss this show. In closing, I strongly recommend it to all dedicated sketch comedy enthusiasts—you’re sure to love it.

My enduring admiration for Italian actress Lucianna Paluzzi, whose role in 1965's "Thunderball" ignited my adolescent fascination, has guided me to some rather unique cinematic discoveries. A prime example is the 1959 British gem "Carlton-Browne of the F.O.," where Lucianna appears in one of her early roles as a princess. Though her part is not the focal point, the film serves as a brilliant stage for the comedic prowess of Terry-Thomas and Peter Sellers, both of whom were gaining prominence at the time. This charming and often hilarious movie introduces us to Gaillardia, a Madeira-esque island nation that was once a British colony until 1916, after which it faded into obscurity. Forty-three years later, the island captures global attention and becomes a hub of international intrigue when rich cobalt deposits are unearthed. Her Majesty dispatches the inept Carlton-Browne from the Foreign Office to oversee the situation. Terry-Thomas delivers a delightfully understated performance in the titular role, matched by Sellers as the Prime Minister Amphibulos of the small nation. (Notably, this was Sellers' second film of 1959 involving a small country outsmarting the world, the first being "The Mouse That Roared.") Ian Bannen nearly overshadows them both with his charismatic portrayal of Gaillardia's debonair king.

**Highlights:** This indie horror flick offers some truly inventive and chilling effects that are sure to unnerve even the most hardened genre enthusiasts. It steers clear of overused jump-scare tactics like sudden soundtrack jolts, opting for more subtle shocks. Even if you think you’ve seen it all, this movie has a few surprises up its sleeve that will leave you stunned.

**Areas for Improvement:** The acting occasionally falls flat, lacking the depth needed to fully convince the audience. Certain scenes have a “shot-on-video” aesthetic that, while mostly effective in creating the intended mood, can feel amateurish. The cinematography overuses close-ups on trivial actions, which detracts from the storytelling. While the effects are unsettling, they are sometimes overdone, diminishing their impact. Additionally, the ending feels hurried, skimming over potentially powerful moments, and leaves viewers to piece together key details not out of intentional mystery, but due to apparent oversight by the filmmakers.

Overall, this is a solid indie horror film that rises well above the genre’s typical offerings. It’s definitely worth a watch for fans looking for something fresh.

Bloodsuckers holds the promise of being a somewhat acceptable film, with its intriguing premise of military personnel hunting and fighting vampires in outer space, tapping into the more playful, campy side of the genre. The notion of a universe populated by diverse vampire species, each with unique traits—many still unknown to the characters—adds an interesting twist. However, the concept of most galactic life beyond Earth being vampiric raises questions about logistics, given the traditional nature of vampires. If nearly everyone is a vampire, it’s unclear who they are supposed to feed on, a detail the filmmakers seem to gloss over. Ultimately, the movie feels like a budget-conscious blend of Firefly/Serenity, classic vampire tales, and a hint of Aliens.

The action sequences are fairly standard and unoriginal, heavily reminiscent of Serenity, but they are competently handled and include enough gore to satisfy vampire movie fans, with some humorously exaggerated blood gushing. The film also delves into character dynamics, though much of this feels dull, stemming from conflicts among characters who often come across as petulant and immature.

I've fallen asleep during movies in the past, but never has a single film managed to do so twice, requiring me to watch it over three separate sessions to finally get through it. The dialogue was abysmal, with women delivering lines awkwardly and men portrayed as mere stereotypes. Additionally, two characters meant to be Japanese appeared Chinese, bore Chinese names, and spoke with distinct Chinese accents. I’m still puzzled by the unnecessary sexual entanglement among the Emmenthal men. With a calculation of 10 minus 8.5, I’m left with a difficult decision: should I rate this movie a one or a two?

It is clearly against the law. Pedophiles exploit content like this. How was this movie even allowed to be produced? This film can be described in a single word: disturbing. What drives individuals to create and view such films? While watching, I couldn’t believe they would depict a child, perhaps only 12 years old, in an intimate scene with an adult woman. Apologies if this ruins the plot for anyone, but I wish I hadn’t seen it myself. Where has the moral judgment of these filmmakers gone? Could it be that the creators themselves have predatory inclinations? Our society is rife with sexual predators targeting children, and yet filmmakers produce content that seems to encourage such behavior. I also noticed a comment asking if there’s a version showing nudity. This involves a child, and someone is making such a request? What is wrong with this scenario?

I'm an avid follower of the comic book series, yet this film was a massive disappointment. I was hoping for a vibe reminiscent of Heavy Metal 2000—deliberately paced, with campy dialogue and plenty of gore—but this movie was far worse than I could have ever anticipated.

While the storyline mirrors the comic fairly closely, that's where the similarities end. The characters lack the vibrant energy and charisma that captivated me in the original series. The film adapts only a fragment of the comic, choosing a particularly dull and sluggish segment over the more engaging later sections. It fixates on trivial moments rather than the compelling overarching narrative of the source material.

Had the right team been behind this project, it could have been extraordinary. Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case, resulting in another forgettable film that few will watch and even fewer will cherish. My copy is destined to gather dust for years before I eventually discard it.

If you're a fan of gangster films, this should be at the top of your must-watch list—either buy it or rent it without hesitation. Al Pacino delivers an exceptional performance, and the story is nothing short of iconic. A perfect 10/10! It's baffling that this movie isn't included in the TOP 250 list.

Although the 3-D animation, the standout feature of the film, was executed impressively, nearly every other aspect failed to deliver. It seemed as if the creators assumed that the 3-D effects would compensate for a lackluster plot and shallow character development. The fact that this is a children's movie offers no justification for such shortcomings. Audiences are just as captivated by deeply developed characters (like Shrek or Nemo's father) as they are by stunning 3-D visuals. Among the main characters, only the two-dimensional Scooter showed any notable trait, sporadically driving the storyline with his insatiable appetite for everything around him.

The real disappointment, however, comes at the film's conclusion with Buzz Aldrin's cameo. After enduring an hour and a half of a stiff, cartoonish depiction of this historical figure, Aldrin himself appears only to dampen the mood. He labels the film's protagonists as "contaminants" and declares the depicted scenario to be entirely implausible.

Seriously? Why not just shatter the children's illusions about the Easter Bunny and Santa Claus while you're at it?

Ariauna Albright is a talented actress, and her decision to star in this poorly written debacle is baffling. What had the potential to be an engaging film ends up as a tedious bore. Ariauna's standout quality is her ability to deliver a compelling performance while exuding undeniable allure, in stark contrast to her co-star Lilith Stabs, whose striking appearance is overshadowed by a clear lack of acting skill—suggesting her training funds might have been spent on spa treatments or beauty salons instead. This production desperately needed some provocative elements and, with a creative scriptwriter, could have seamlessly incorporated them into the storyline. Despite the limitations, Ariauna makes the best of the situation and manages to somewhat preserve her reputation. The Tempe company should take note that casting two attractive women in revealing fetish cop uniforms naturally raises expectations for corresponding content and playful themes. That's all that needs to be said.

It's peculiar to watch a movie where certain scenes fall flat, especially when measured against the legacy of its predecessors, while others in a secondary storyline or subplot resonate with unexpected power and depth. Sudden Impact is a prime example of this contrast, with Clint Eastwood taking on the roles of star, producer, and director. He demonstrates both his finest moments and his weaker ones as he navigates a crime/mystery/detective narrative within the iconic Dirty Harry series. The famous 'make my day' line emerges here, but unlike the playful yet cool 'do I feel lucky' monologue from the first film—which hardened into something fierce by the end—in this installment, the tone feels reversed. As expected, Eastwood's character once again clashes with the department, stubbornly fighting crime on his own terms. This is evident in scenes like a diner robbery (a possible influence on Pulp Fiction?) and a high-speed chase involving a bus full of senior citizens. When he's ordered to 'take a vacation,' it's the furthest thing from his mind. The main plot, however, lacks conviction beyond the predictable storyline and dialogue, which only heightens the viewer's frustration. Yet, before long, his journey intertwines with a compelling subplot that Eastwood...

THE SUNSHINE BOYS is a delightful 1975 film adaptation of Neil Simon's play, centered on a retired vaudeville duo portrayed by Walter Matthau and George Burns. Having parted ways on bitter terms, the two are now faced with an opportunity to reunite for a television special. The catch? They still despise each other and have no interest in working together again. Richard Benjamin plays Matthau’s nephew, a theatrical agent tasked with the daunting challenge of orchestrating this reunion. This heartwarming and funny comedy serves as a touching tribute to the bygone era of vaudeville, succeeding largely due to one of Neil Simon’s finest scripts and the exceptional performances by Matthau, Burns, and Benjamin. Burns earned the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his role, but Matthau truly steals the show with his impeccably comedic portrayal of Willy Clark. Though nominated for Best Actor, Matthau was overshadowed by Nicholson’s performance in ONE FLEW OVER THE CUCKOO’S NEST; in a different year, his work here would have been a strong contender for the award. Matthau dominates the screen with a performance that is perfectly timed and utterly authentic, without a single misstep. The audition scene, in particular, showcases his brilliance.

This review focuses on The Wizard, distinct from The Wiz or Mr. Wizard. The Wizard is a film from the late 1980s that centers on a quiet boy with an extraordinary knack for video games, showcased as he walks through the entire opening sequence. For clarity, The Wiz is an unneeded remake of The Wizard of Oz, and Mr. Wizard is the character known for quirky experiments like connecting 100 straws for a child to sip tang through.

With those distinctions made, I must emphasize there’s little justification for watching this movie. It essentially functions as a 100-minute advertisement for Nintendo, spotlighting products like the Power Glove, The Legend of Zelda, and Super Mario Brothers 3. I use the term "functions" very loosely, as the script appears to have been hastily thrown together over a weekend by individuals unfamiliar with Nintendo games. Furthermore, the direction lacks any discernible style, perhaps even less than what my grandmother might muster. Had the writer and director taken the time to play these games themselves, they might have recognized the mediocrity of their project and opted instead for a practical career path, like learning to install car audio systems.

This is arguably one of the dullest slashers ever made—if it can even be classified as one. I wouldn’t bother watching this, even if it veered into adult film territory, which it strongly resembles. Enduring a poorly acted story about a small group of middle-aged individuals wandering through the woods is utterly tedious. These types of films are typically geared toward teenagers, so it’s unclear who the target audience was for this snooze-inducing disaster. The only redeeming aspect of this movie is its cover art, which is the sole reason I decided to track it down as part of the Suspense Classics 50 Movie Pack. However, after viewing the other films in this collection, it’s evident this one couldn’t fit anywhere else. If you’re craving a solid woods-based slasher, I suggest checking out Just Before Dawn or The Final Terror instead.

I found Cinderella 2 and Jungle Book 2 deeply underwhelming, but this sequel might be even more disappointing. To begin with, the animation was subpar, resembling a low-quality Saturday morning cartoon, and at times, it was even worse. While I appreciated a few characters like Thunderbolt and Patch, others, such as Cruella, fell flat. Cruella, who was a captivating villain in the original, lost her edge in this follow-up; her dialogue was unremarkable, and her animation was frankly unappealing. Her artist sidekick, Lars, felt like a complete caricature, and Roger’s sudden abandonment of smoking seemed implausible. On a positive note, the voice acting was generally strong, particularly Barry Bostwick’s performance as Thunderbolt, though Jodi Benson’s accent was a major misstep for me. There were a handful of decent moments, but the plot felt overly drawn out and reminiscent of a stretched-out TV episode. Ultimately, this sequel is a significant letdown compared to one of the most iconic Disney films of the 1960s, alongside Jungle Book. Regrettably, I can only rate this a 3/10; it simply didn’t resonate with me.

To me, this story begins with amusing jokes about Frank's fantasies while he’s navigating a staircase or sitting through business meetings. However, after watching the movie for an hour, the same fantasies and humorous scenarios are repeated endlessly. It becomes too predictable, resembling a TV show where you can step away and return without missing anything significant.

While I appreciate Felix Herngren’s portrayal of Frank, that alone isn’t sufficient. Even as a comedy, the film needs more variety and a meaningful message for its audience.

"Ruby in Paradise" is a captivating coming-of-age tale that follows Ruby Lee Gissing, a young woman breaking free from her oppressive background to discover her true self. Ashley Judd delivers a masterful performance as the titular character in what might be her debut film role, one that she can take immense pride in. However, the story steers clear of the clichéd pursuit of fame, avoiding any resemblance to becoming the next iconic figure like Madonna—be it the biblical mother or the provocative pop star.

Instead, the film focuses on the importance of trusting one’s instincts and engaging in self-reflection to evolve into one’s ideal adult identity. A word of caution: this is not an action-packed flick. It features occasional voice-over narration by Judd as Ruby journals her thoughts—a detail that might deter some male viewers. Yet, I urge patience with this exquisite film, which reveals that true contentment can be found in the simplest of acts, like carrying water or chopping wood.

Todd Field, known for his role as Nick Nightingale in "Eyes Wide Shut," also directs, writes, and co-stars as Ruby’s dignified love interest. His character plays a crucial role in helping her reshape the notions of relationships ingrained from her childhood.

However, even his presence isn’t the ultimate solution for Ruby Lee. The film avoids imposing an external savior, emphasizing that her journey and growth are her own.

This film marks at least the third iteration of the same story, so a feeling of familiarity while viewing it shouldn’t come as a shock. The creators have merely shifted the setting and altered the storytelling approach, yet these changes lack depth or impact. Unfortunately, the movie doesn’t improve upon its source material, largely due to an inherently flawed plot that consistently fails to deliver. Much like the earlier versions, the acting remains unremarkable.

While the plot does offer a surprising twist at the conclusion for first-time viewers, this ending feels disconnected from the rest of the narrative. If the film had concluded ten minutes sooner, it could have been far more effective and rewarding, leaving a stronger impression. However, I must reveal a spoiler: the story ultimately suggests that crime pays, as the perpetrator escapes justice. This is a message I find deeply unsatisfactory in any film.

Fortunately, the film avoids excessive, meaningless violence and unnecessary filler. However, it lacks depth in thought and a coherent narrative flow. While the story showed promise, it seems the director lost focus on the central theme. The plot feels fragmented, veering off into odd, unresolved directions. Additionally, the portrayal of a golf country club environment feels inauthentic, with several depictions bordering on the ridiculous. Overall, the film fails to captivate.

Seriously, I'm not joking. That's exactly what's written on the video case.

Plot summary in brief: A beautiful woman simply stands there smiling, and inexplicably, this causes men to turn on each other with deadly intent.

"Find Ariel... Where's Ariel... Can't find Ariel..." Come on, she's literally right behind you, fool...

It appears that everything worth saying about this awful little Space Opera has already been covered.

A group of cheesy actors, mostly portraying convicts, enters the scene after the initial cast is swiftly eliminated. Then, they too meet the same fate. Every plot twist is telegraphed a full fifteen minutes ahead. It’s as if the actors drew straws to determine who gets the most screen time and a fatter paycheck. The alien virus/hologram/VR witch/glitch appears utterly powerless and contributes nothing. Why doesn’t she just remain in the computer instead of performing her "teleporting vampire" act? (Honestly, it would’ve been more captivating if she were an actual vampire, or did anything beyond merely standing and staring at people—which is her only activity. Somehow, this alone drives all the men to slaughter each other. Figure that one out...)

In truth, this hardly qualifies as a space movie.

"Strange Case," while not John Cleese's most triumphant television endeavor, carries the raw energy of a first draft thrust into production without the benefit of polishing edits. The series sprinkles in a mix of absurd and occasionally sharp ideas, yet the narrative fails to coalesce into a compelling whole.

Arthur Lowe, however, shines as Dr. Watson, bringing humor and charm—bionic enhancements included. "Good Lord."

I absolutely adored the first *Scary Movie*. As a devoted fan of parody, which I consider the pinnacle of humor, I believe it’s often seen as the sharpest type of comedy. The Wayans brothers nailed this in the original, though they seemed to lose their touch in the sequel. I view the Wayans family as comedic masterminds, but even the best can falter at times.

The sequel starts with potential. The parody of *The Exorcist* had me hooked, particularly the “come on out, ma” bit—classic Wayans brilliance. However, beyond that, I only found myself laughing on two other occasions: 1) the scene where Tori Spelling’s character is wooed by a ghost at night, only to turn overly attached and bring up marriage, while he protests, “It was just a booty call!” That got a chuckle out of me. 2) The *Save the Last Dance* spoof, where Cindy accidentally pummels a girl while showing off her dance moves. Even these brief moments of humor pale in comparison to the uncontrollable laughter induced by the original *Scary Movie*.

The remainder of the film is a disappointment, littered with crude, lowbrow gags. Many of the subtle jokes from the first film are lost here, replaced by cheap attempts at shock value.

I can’t understand why some of you aren’t impressed by the thrilling car action scenes and Jessica Simpson’s stunning presence in this movie. Clearly, it’s not meant to be a cinematic masterpiece, and that’s perfectly fine. It’s entertaining and humorous, capturing the same vibe as the original show, even though I wasn’t a fan back in the day and only recently watched an episode. The theater seats were practically vibrating with excitement, and the car sequences kept me engaged without dragging on, unlike some overly long scenes in *2 Fast 2 Furious*. Jessica Simpson is undeniably attractive, and I only wish she’d been featured more in the action. Overall, I had an absolute blast watching this film, and I’m eager to see it again soon and add the DVD to my collection. My advice? Just enjoy it for the fun ride it is.

This film was an absolute disaster, deserving a capital "C" for crap. The opening scene hinted at potential, but that hope was quickly shattered as the direction of the plot became painfully clear.

As for Morty, the eerie wooden statue from the original movie, he’s reduced to a laughable caricature in this version. It’s painfully obvious he’s just a man in a tacky plastic costume. (And honestly, who finds "Morty" even remotely terrifying? It’s as menacing as "Jimmy" or "Fred" in the horror genre. Why not just call the statue Henry-freakin'-Kissinger? “Flee, it’s Dr. Kissinger!” That would be about as frightening as "Morty.")

Then there’s a scene where the so-called "hero" attacks his father’s tombstone with—what, a sledgehammer, you might think? A two-by-four, perhaps? No, he furiously whacks it with a twig—a pathetic little twig. Even more absurd, after the characters leave, the tombstone inexplicably starts to bleed. Ridiculous!

Lastly, there’s a Native American character living with the protagonist’s grandparents who seems to have no purpose other than tending to Morty. He spreads eerie tales about the statue, issues warnings to skeptics, and even repairs Morty’s arm when it gets damaged.

Brokedown Palace follows the journey of two close friends, Alice and Darlene, who embark on an impromptu adventure to Thailand, only to find themselves imprisoned when drugs are discovered planted in their luggage. This premise held the promise of a profound and emotional narrative akin to "Return to Paradise," yet the film opts to emphasize the dynamics of the girls' friendship rather than the gravity of their predicament.

Claire Danes and Kate Beckinsale deliver compelling performances, with the heart of the film lying in the complex interactions between their characters—marked by suspicion, envy, and the constant probing of their bond, culminating in profound sacrifices for the sake of friendship. The movie largely sidesteps deeper political commentary and the brutal realities of prison life, which are somewhat downplayed, choosing instead to highlight these personal themes.

However, the film is not without its flaws, including noticeable plot inconsistencies and elements that strain credulity. The true dread and despair of the protagonists' circumstances are not as deeply felt as they could be. Additionally, the world beyond the prison walls remains underdeveloped, exemplified by Bill Pullman's portrayal of a seemingly dubious character.

I’m genuinely shocked that the talented Alan Ball is associated with this disappointing project. After watching the first two episodes, I can confidently say this series won’t be on my must-watch list. It’s plagued by numerous flaws that undermine its potential.

The casting choices leave much to be desired. Anna Paquin, portraying the protagonist Sookie, delivers a surprisingly weak performance. I recall her being far more compelling in previous roles, so perhaps the script is to blame. Additionally, her appearance doesn’t captivate; at times, she looks rather unappealing. The actor playing Bill fares slightly better, largely because his character is meant to be stiff and distant. The supporting cast struggles as well, burdened by stereotypical roles and challenging accents. Tara, for instance, is painful to watch, with Rutina Wesley’s attempt at the accent being excruciating—like fingernails on a chalkboard. Nearly as grating is Nelsan Ellis, whose dialogue is often hard to decipher. Both his character and...

I adore this film, with its stellar cast including Jouvet, Arletty, Blier, and the masterful direction of Carné. While much has been discussed about the movie, there’s a particular aspect I’d like to highlight: none of the footage features the actual Hôtel du Nord, which I believe still stands (or does it? I’ve heard rumors of its potential demolition...). Instead, the entire scene was meticulously recreated on a set, primarily because halting traffic on the St Martin canal for weeks was simply not feasible.

'Presque rien' captures the tender story of two young boys discovering love during a seaside summer. I’ll refrain from detailing the plot, as its allure lies beyond the narrative (though rest assured, it’s both captivating and unique). What truly elevates this film is its cinematography. The visual artistry of 'Presque rien' is breathtaking, earning the highest praise and leaving viewers enchanted by its sheer beauty.

The storyline unfolds in a non-linear, somewhat intricate manner. It defies straightforward chronology and leaves some questions unanswered, yet this complexity only adds to the film’s intrigue. I wholeheartedly recommend 'Presque rien' to those who value the artistic essence of cinema; they will undoubtedly find it a rewarding experience.

French director Claire Denis has earned her place among the world's most distinctive and accomplished filmmakers with works like *Chocolat* and *Beau Travail*, and her 2004 film *The Intruder (L’Intrus)* further enriches her remarkable body of work. This cinematic poem evokes a profound sense of lingering loneliness and loss, offering a window into the mind of a man grappling with physical and mental decline as he journeys across the globe in search of redemption and peace—elusive goals that remain just out of reach. Inspired loosely by Jean-Luc Nancy’s memoir of a heart transplant, *The Intruder* is a film of such intense opacity that even multiple viewings leave it challenging to articulate in anything beyond subjective, impressionistic language.

Louis Trebor (Michel Subor), a man in his seventies, faces a likely fatal heart condition. Much like the professor in Ingmar Bergman’s *Wild Strawberries*, he seeks to reconcile with the regrets of his past while time still remains. Despite his evident physical toughness and considerable wealth, he appears emotionally exhausted, his face marked by a look of quiet surrender. Though we are shown only fleeting glimpses of his inner world,

I've seen this film twice already, and I intend to watch it once more. It immerses you in the director's perspective, exploring both his romantic entanglements and the political climate in Israel. Additionally, it brings tears to my eyes as it evokes memories of a beautiful era, contrasted with the tragic murder depicted in the story. It’s truly a must-see.

This isn’t your conventional vampire tale, far removed from the works of Bram Stoker or Anne Rice. Instead, it presents a genuinely unique vampyre narrative. These vampyres are genetic mutants, unaffected by sunlight, and embody pure malevolence.

The movie isn’t without flaws. Many of the actors are evidently novices, though the two leads portraying Van Helsing and Rally, the vampyre woman, deliver commendable performances. The film is extremely violent, which might unsettle some viewers. Additionally, it is packed with complex scientific details that could be difficult to grasp, potentially leading to disinterest. Despite these issues, I was captivated by the ingenious plot and the standout performances. With a larger budget and wider distribution, this film’s potential for success could be limitless.

At first glance, one might assume this is a biography of Claude Monet, but instead, it’s a tightly woven narrative centered on the complex dynamics among three teenage girls on a French synchronized swimming team. The story excludes parental figures or teachers, omits any mention of school, and relegates boys to a single minor character, the attractive yet perpetually baffled Francois, who drifts in and out of the plot.

Pauline Aquart, the youngest of the trio, dreams of earning a spot on the team she idolizes. Her appearance is unconventional—still navigating the awkwardness of adolescence with long, gangly limbs, oversized feet, and a flat posterior. Her protruding jaw and full, pursed lips give her an unusual look, though over time, her unique features become oddly captivating, even striking from certain perspectives.

Adele Haenel, by contrast, is older and more physically mature. She exudes allure in her swimsuit, strutting confidently, playfully taunting boys, and tossing her long blonde hair. Yet, there’s an enigmatic quality to her—her true nature remains elusive. Is she as she appears, or is there more beneath the surface? I couldn’t quite pin it down. The French penchant for contradictions over clarity might explain why Francois always seems to be hovering, intrigued yet perplexed.

Those who criticize this film might be harboring resentment from past romantic disappointments. This movie is a gem for anyone who can appreciate the timeless charm of songs like Johnny Mathis's classics, Bobby Darin's "Beyond the Sea," or Stan Getz's "The Girl From Ipanema," among others.

I gauge a film's worth by how often I feel compelled to rewatch it before feeling fully content. "Chances Are" drew me back multiple times, and each viewing was a delight.

Additionally, I pay attention to the chemistry between the actors, and in this case, I found their collaboration to be seamless and engaging.

Open your heart and allow the comedic enchantment of this movie to sweep you away.

- Alan

It's evident that the production budget for this movie was minimal, perhaps as low as $5. Watching it feels like a complete waste of time. There’s nothing even slightly redeeming about this film. I’m not sure why I continued to watch it myself. The lead actress isn’t appealing, and the acting is downright terrible. You’d be better off doing literally anything else, like watching TV or playing subpar video games. I feel cheated out of my time. This is the first movie review I’ve ever written, which might be obvious, but I felt compelled to warn others who might check IMDb for opinions before deciding to watch. There’s no action, no attractive characters, no discernible budget, and the acting is atrocious. The movie screams low quality, and to top it all off, the entire film takes place in a single room.

It's challenging to pigeonhole this film—maybe it's best described as an avant-garde spy thriller. *Mother Night* is an exceptional novel by Kurt Vonnegut, and arguably one of his most adaptable works for the big screen. The movie stays remarkably true to the source material. Opting for an "indie" production style likely proved more successful than if a major Hollywood studio had bankrolled it. In today’s climate, it’s doubtful that a cerebral book like *Mother Night* would even get a nod from the major Hollywood powerhouses. Typically, that would be a shame, but not here. *Mother Night* boasts sharp direction and a strong ensemble. Nick Nolte, who seems to land increasingly compelling roles with age, retains that relatable "everyman" quality, enabling him to embody a diverse array of characters. Sheryl Lee, as always, is captivating and delivers a stellar performance. I’ve long felt she deserved more recognition from the entertainment world. Starting her career playing a deceased character with minimal screen time in *Twin Peaks*—even if the show became something of a cult hit—was hardly the ideal launchpad. Regardless, this film is thoroughly engaging, and you don’t need to have read the book to appreciate it.

Upon reviewing the extensive feedback on this movie, it becomes evident that science fiction audiences are divided into two distinct groups. The first group consists of highly educated, well-read, and discerning individuals. They are deeply familiar with the genre's history and understand the remarkable potential it holds when crafted by a talented writer. For many years, science fiction was relegated to the fringes of literature, often dismissed by critics as mere tales of ray guns and aliens, suitable only for young teens. However, today's knowledgeable fans are acutely aware of this past and revere the great authors—Asimov, Heinlein, Bradbury, and Ellison—who elevated the genre from obscurity. Through their work, these pioneers produced thought-provoking, intelligent narratives that pushed boundaries and redefined what it means to be human. These informed fans approach Hollywood's offerings with a critical mindset, not out of mere cynicism, but with a discerning perspective shaped by Hollywood's often underwhelming track record. For them, the story reigns supreme; they are unimpressed by superficial elements like dazzling CGI or relentless action sequences. When the content lacks substance, they see through the facade.

This film was incredibly thought-provoking. I've watched it multiple times, initially at the age of four, when it left a lasting impression, and again at twelve. The core message the director imparts is a call to awareness, urging us to include God in our daily lives and to avoid the error of disregarding or disrespecting Him.

A remarkable film for both skeptics and the faithful!

A film devoid of moral grounding. A drifter accepts a mobster's offer to commit murder for cash, only to be betrayed by them. As the story unfolds, he develops a romantic connection with the widow of his victim, moving in with her while she remains unaware of his dark secret. Tragedy strikes when he "accidentally" kills her upon her discovery of the truth. In a style reminiscent of WALKING TALL, he then seeks vengeance against the mobsters who deceived him. The core issue lies in the drifter's initial decision to accept the hit job, which strips him of any redeemable qualities, sympathy, or heroic traits. This leaves the audience unable to find any moral anchor in the narrative or to invest emotionally in such a character. Meanwhile, the widow, portrayed compellingly by the captivating Kari Wuhrer—known as the sheriff in EIGHT LEGGED FREAKS—runs a shelter for the homeless, yet diminishes her own likability by quickly becoming intimate with the drifter, despite her vulnerable state following her husband’s death. Furthermore, her reaction upon learning his true identity—locking him inside her home—stretches believability, as if every house is equipped with such inescapable security.

Two decades ago, young Michael Hawthorne, then only five years old, witnessed a horrific tragedy: his father brutally murdered his mother with an axe on a desolate road before taking his own life. In the present, Michael (Gordon Currie) gathers his girlfriend Peg (Stacy Grant) and close friends—Chris (Myc Agnew), Jennifer (Emmanuelle Vaugier), Lisa Ann (Kelly Benson), Ned (Brendon Beiser), Mitch Maldive (Phillip Rhys), and Trish (Rachel Hayward)—to celebrate Halloween at his grandparents' farm in the countryside. He instructs everyone to dress in costumes symbolizing their deepest fears. Alongside his Native American friend Crow (Byron Chief Moon), they plan to conduct an ancient ritual using a carved wooden figure named Morty (Jon Fedele), intended to banish their fears permanently. Michael's own terror is rooted in the dread of turning into a serial killer like his father. However, the ritual spirals out of control when Morty transforms into a manifestation of Michael's father, unleashing a deadly rampage on his friends.

"The Fear: Resurrection" emerges as a lackluster and aimless slasher film that squanders the intriguing premise of confronting and eradicating personal fears. The screenplay is marred by clichés and lacks coherence. Performances range from over-the-top, as seen with Betsy Palmer, to notably underwhelming.

There have been dark times in my life, moments of confusion and deep sadness. Watching *Rancid Aluminium* ranks among them.

The red flags were glaring. No premiere—apparently even the cast avoided it—and a complete absence of reviews in any publication. The sole reason I endured the movie was the faint hope of catching up on sleep.

The film made no sense whatsoever. The narration was absurd. At one point, I found myself cheering when the protagonist seemed to have been shot, only to sink into deeper disappointment when it turned out he was unharmed. I genuinely wish those responsible for this cinematic disaster face severe repercussions.

There were a few redeeming elements, mostly unintentional comedy. One particularly bizarre scene had the main character inexplicably engaging in a private act in a bathroom stall while instructing the occupant next door to cover their ears.

Words fail to capture the frustration I feel, so I’ll end with this:

*Rancid Aluminium*: a film solely for masochists, idlers, and those regressive enough to willingly subject themselves to such torment.

Roughly five years ago, I watched a film that continues to linger in my mind with an unsettling presence. Despite being forewarned about its notorious reputation, I chose to ignore the warnings, holding myself solely accountable for the experience. As a fan of Sandler, I was skeptical that any of his works could truly be as dreadful as critics claimed, dismissing the backlash as mere prejudice against him. How mistaken I was.

This so-called comedy fails to deliver even a fleeting moment of humor across its entirety. Achieving a complete absence of laughter in a 90-minute film is, in a twisted way, remarkable. One might expect at least an accidental snippet of amusement, yet this movie offers nothing but disappointment. It doesn't even reach the level of "so bad it's good"; it simply wallows in awfulness. There's no humor to be found in its failures—only a sense of despair. You keep waiting for a joke, a quip, anything to elicit even a slight smile, but such relief never arrives.

Consider the horror movie *The Ring*, where viewing a cursed tape means death within seven days. If this film were that tape, viewers wouldn’t last the week—they’d likely end their torment immediately, overwhelmed by the sheer agony of enduring it.

Many war movies produced in the US during World War II were entertaining but lacked realism, as their primary purpose was to serve as propaganda to boost morale on the home front. I'm not criticizing these films, as many remain enjoyable to watch. Yet, their frequent departure from reality often prevents them from achieving true greatness. A prime example is the John Garfield movie *Air Force*, where a single B-17 seems to nearly decimate half of the Japanese air force. In contrast, *Pride Of The Marines* stands out as a refreshing exception, earning praise for its relatively accurate depiction of a true story. Initially, I doubted the film’s authenticity because the events seemed far too extraordinary to be real. However, after further research, I discovered that it closely mirrors the astonishing true account of two men whose remarkable actions earned them the Medal of Honor. This is a rare instance where reality appears more unbelievable than fiction!

I came across this film after delving into the book that served as its inspiration. While it isn’t a precise biographical account, it is "loosely based" on real events. Nevertheless, I found it to be a gripping and unsettling delve into the themes of evil and insanity, with Michel Serrault delivering a truly haunting performance as Dr. Petiot.

The movie is filled with striking visuals; the image of Petiot gliding through the night like a vampire, his black cloak billowing behind him, feels almost legendary. There are also distinct expressionistic elements—Petiot’s distorted silhouette ascending the stairs from the cellar, where the dismembered remains of his victims await incineration, evokes chilling scenes reminiscent of 'Nosferatu.'

However, the film’s most captivating aspect for me was its sound design. The soundtrack brims with foreboding tones, beginning with the sinister music of the opening credits paired with eerie, wordless cries. Petiot resides and operates his medical practice in a bustling complex of small shops, where the constant sound of knives being sharpened lingers in the background, alongside a peddler playing haunting melodies on a saw. Animal sounds add to the unease—the concierge keeps a goat, unseen cats wail in the distance—and as the film progresses, these elements intensify the atmosphere.

This movie lacks any artistic merit to warrant an award, and frankly, it doesn’t even deserve an audience. Ironically, it’s been nominated for cinematography, yet the camera work is, at best, disorienting. With every frame, it feels as though the view is being unnecessarily cropped, preventing you from seeing the complete picture. The storyline is abysmal. To be candid, I couldn’t endure watching the entire film. The most cringe-worthy moment was witnessing soldiers reveling in their barracks, with one being pressured to drink alcohol. Scenes like these, among others, strongly echoed the style of Steven Seagal.

Heed my warning and avoid this dreadful film at all costs.

Creating a film like this demands a profound lack of understanding of Nietzsche’s philosophy, personality, psychoanalytic methods, and the history of Vienna. Choose a renowned genius whose works you’ve never studied, portray him as unhinged, surround him with eccentric doctors attempting to treat him, throw in a few moderately attractive women, cast an actor with an outrageously large mustache to play him, ensure every character speaks with an exaggerated accent, depict absurd dream sequences, introduce another unrelated but famous figure (like Freud), sprinkle in a handful of terms from the genius’s writings, go overboard with every element—especially the music—and there you have it. To the audience: steer clear.

As the nephew of the director, it took me years to obtain a copy of this film, and I can attest that it truly ranks among the worst movies ever made. I even checked with my uncle, who no longer possesses a copy himself. I’m excited to surprise him with one.

At present, the film holds an average rating of 1.9/10. From what I’ve gathered, this score would likely place it in the mid-30s of IMDb’s "bottom 100," but with only 206 votes, it hasn’t yet earned a spot on the list.

It’s unfortunate that the film doesn’t even receive the dubious honor of being recognized in the bottom 100.

On a lighter note, I’m planning to gift copies of the movie to family members this holiday season. Could this be the best—or worst—gift ever?

Initially, I hesitated to join the masses in watching "Lost," but a chance viewing of an early Season 1 episode—the one featuring the polar bear—completely captivated me. The show, not the bear, has held my rapt attention ever since. So please indulge me as I attempt to express my enthusiastic, somewhat disjointed admiration for it.

"Lost" starts with a straightforward concept: a passenger plane crashes on a deserted island. Yet, it transforms this premise into something remarkable by delving deeply into each character’s psyche—exploring their motivations, identities, and pasts. It quickly becomes apparent that the island isn’t just a backdrop; it’s a pivotal link in their lives, whether they are escaping their pasts (like Sawyer and Kate) or seeking spiritual connection (like Locke and Claire). Moreover, "Lost" intricately examines the island itself, unveiling the enigmatic and terrifying secrets it holds, all of which appear to be mysteriously interconnected.

Though television actors often lack the reputation for nuanced or exceptional performances, the majority of the "Lost" cast truly shines in their roles, bringing a surprising depth and authenticity to their characters.

I watched this movie late on a Saturday night, stretching into Sunday morning, with my brother while we were having a few drinks. It’s hands-down one of the most hilariously terrible films I’ve ever seen, perfect for tearing apart. The so-called 'luxury' ocean liner is blatantly a 'roll on, roll off' ferry, decked out with cast iron everything. The doors, slapped with cheap adhesive stickers labeled 'staff,' are reused in different contexts throughout the movie, making the lack of continuity glaringly obvious. It’s so bad, it’s almost impressive—you can’t help but notice the plot holes as they practically slap you in the face.

In the climax, the main character jumps off a lifeboat with the ferry visible in the distance. The scene cuts to his son and new girlfriend (who, by the way, is the ship’s PR director, a kung-fu expert, and a former cop fired for doing things her own way—yes, really) speeding away from an explosion on the ferry. Then, out of nowhere, the dad is suddenly there, hugging them. How did he get there? No explanation—it’s pure magic, and honestly, who cares? This film has zero redeeming qualities. The casino onboard is laughably tiny, the size of a large bedroom with just one table. And when the characters are chased by the villains, there’s conveniently only one place to hide—you can probably guess where.

A string of murders plagues a small town in the Texas desert, leaving residents questioning who could be behind the killings. While the film offers minor twists of mystery and touches on racial tensions—an element that feels somewhat out of place—its primary appeal lies with slasher enthusiasts. Fans of the genre will likely enjoy the familiar staples of graphic violence and nudity that define such movies.

Dana Kimmell, known for her role in FRIDAY THE 13TH PART 3, plays a spoiled, amateur sleuth teenager at the center of the story.

*1/2 out of ****

MPAA: Rated R for graphic violence and gore, nudity, and some language.

While this movie carries an R rating, I suspect it will only appeal to teenagers. The reason being, it lacks a coherent plot, any meaningful character growth, and genuinely humorous moments.

The film’s primary draw is its abundance of nudity, featuring numerous scenes with scantily clad or completely naked women, who are, admittedly, quite attractive.

I’m puzzled as to why this film bears the American Pie name, as it fails to effectively blend elements of an erotic film with comedy, falling short in both genres.

I’d recommend watching this movie solely if you’re interested in seeing nudity but are hesitant to rent or purchase an explicitly erotic film.

I rated it 1/10 for the couple of times I managed to smile during the film, and an additional 2/10 for the attractive women featured.

Once again, a cult emerges with its questionable teachings. This isn't a plot twist, as the true revelation unfolds when you investigate the group behind this tedious, pseudo-scientific infomercial—Ramtha's School of Enlightenment.

Whenever a religion or philosophy resorts to hiding behind a veil of deception reminiscent of the Wizard of Oz, I choose to disengage. I’m grateful to Ramtha that I watched a borrowed copy of this film on a so-called "friend's" suggestion. Spending any valuable time or money on this mind-numbing New Age propaganda would have been a travesty. I can only wish that those who "truly believe they can walk on water" would follow that belief to its "logical" end—either walk, sink, or stay silent. As a film, it barely earns a "1" for entertainment, largely due to crafting the most insufferable character in cinematic history (the photographer's roommate—unbearable!). If you're compelled to watch this, make sure to borrow it from one of the indoctrinated individuals who suggested it.

This early Adam Sandler movie echoes his personal journey as a comedian in 1989. The character's persistent recognition of his own untapped comedic brilliance and frustration with his material feels more like Sandler’s own sentiments than scripted dialogue. Compared to his later blockbuster hits like Big Daddy or the quirky Billy Madison, this film falls short. At the time of its release, Sandler had yet to master a consistent, successful, and humorous style of self-expression, mirroring the struggles of his on-screen persona. Most of the film’s humor stems from Sandler’s soliloquies, often centered on his overlooked talent and self-deprecation over his appearance and romantic failures. Additionally, the movie is difficult to endure as it lacks the polish of a serious production. Sandler frequently breaks the fourth wall, addressing the audience directly with comments on the film’s meager budget and dubious content. Ultimately, the film is cringe-worthy and uncomfortable to sit through. After watching, I was eager to erase it from memory, worried that its discovery by a wider audience might tarnish Sandler’s reputation. I recommend skipping this one.

Individuals who can endure this film and still consider it a commendable piece of cinema clearly lack an appreciation for quality filmmaking. Watching this movie felt like an affront; the direction and cinematography were reminiscent of a high school project. Even The Blair Witch Project, a film I deeply dislike, boasted superior cinematography. The storyline held the promise of becoming a gripping and compelling narrative, yet it disappointingly fizzled out within the first ten minutes and failed to recover. Some have suggested the movie explores a child’s imagination, which is a valid concept, but the execution of the script was sorely lacking in creativity and depth. Take, for instance, the scene with the Indian in the store. Did the child glance at a small idol and conjure up an entire tale of an Indian spirit named Wendigo? The child mentions this to the store employee, who nonchalantly responds that she is the only one working there, hinting at a potential ghostly encounter. However, the moment passes uneventfully as she haggles over the idol’s price, and the child's vision of the mysterious figure is simply brushed aside.

To everyone who believes 1. This was a dull broadcast and 2. Halle Berry and Denzel Washington didn’t earn their Oscars,

Please, keep quiet! This was among the finest Academy Awards shows for several reasons. First, it marked a historic moment with a Black actress winning the Best Actress Oscar. For years, many of our Black sisters have been overlooked by the Academy. Honestly, I had stopped tuning into the Oscars due to the glaring lack of diversity among both winners and nominees. It often felt like just a group of white individuals congratulating each other. The Academy had numerous opportunities to honor outstanding Black actresses like Alfre Woodard, Whoopi Goldberg, Diana Ross, and Mary Jean Baptiste, yet they consistently failed to do so.

Second, Halle Berry absolutely deserved her Oscar—there was no contest. The Academy was long overdue to recognize her, given how many deserving actresses have been ignored by a predominantly white voting body. Yes, Nicole Kidman gave a lovely performance in *Moulin Rouge!*, but it was high time Black talent was acknowledged at these awards. As for Denzel Washington, the Academy owed him a great debt after previous oversights.

If you were captivated by *Deep Cover*, you're likely to enjoy this movie too. Many of the poetic passages Laurence Fishburne delivers in *Deep Cover* originate from the eloquent script of *Once In the Life*, a film adapted from a play he authored. If you're as enamored with Fishburne as I am, you'll be thrilled by this film, which showcases him in all his intense, fully realized glory. Naturally, as a gangster film, it includes elements of violence and drug use, but the script shines with beauty, and the story is deeply moving, even veering into romantic drama territory.

This is an INCREDIBLE film—dark, thrilling, seductive, and full of suspense. If you've ever slipped out at night or spent time in a secret hideout, you'll feel the weight of the claustrophobic sets, which symbolically reflect the characters' entrapment in their circumstances. Packed with subtle foreshadowing and intricate relationships, the film is masterfully crafted, with every emotion echoed in the set design and cinematography. OUTSTANDING WORK!

May 1938. Hitler visits Italy, setting the stage for a historic encounter with Mussolini. Amidst a backdrop of emotions, tensions, and the search for self-affirmation, a deserted town becomes the meeting point of two contrasting worlds: a lonely housewife and a journalist. For the housewife, Antonietta, this encounter offers a fleeting refuge from her sorrowful existence, a brief respite for a classic victim of circumstance. This is a tale of solitude and silence, exploring the hidden corners of life and the raw, combative nature of longing.

At the heart of the story is a poignant gesture—a book given on a spring afternoon, symbolizing a profound connection. The film unfolds as a poem, masterfully capturing the nuances of shared loneliness. It is a quiet plea for an indescribable bond with reality and the inner self. Images of Il Duce loom large, while Antonietta’s awkwardness, Gabriele’s patient yet fragile demeanor, and the director’s skillful touch imbue the script with elegance. Two exceptional actors elevate this work to sublimity, offering a delicate foretaste of life’s hypocrisies and the harshness of arbitrary judgments, while illuminating the essence of existence and the ugliness of tyranny.

Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni deliver performances of breathtaking intelligence, cementing their mastery. This film stands as a clear masterpiece.

Despite the numerous negative reviews, I nearly skipped this film, but I'm glad I didn't. To my surprise, it turned out to be a reasonably entertaining horror flick. While the acting was generally subpar, Alice Krige's performance stood out as exceptional. Additionally, some of the dialogue, like the line "Just consider yourself lunch," added a humorous touch.

Overall, this Stephen King adaptation is better than average - I'd rate it a 7/10.

Somewhere out there, a definitive list of the worst gay films ever produced must exist. These are the movies with interminably long camera shots of actors gazing thoughtfully into the void, or scenes that linger far too long on irrelevant details, like cats slurping spaghetti. This particular nauseating film tells the tale of two boys who live, love, swim, and find themselves trapped in grottos. One boy has a melancholic mother, while the other has no mother at all. They talk, walk, swim, make love, get drunk, and eventually part ways. One ends up in the hospital for eight days, only to be released later. The movie is riddled with fast-forward and rewind sequences, alongside extended, brooding shots of a character staring into space or simply sitting idle. It feels like a pretentious filmmaking trick, or perhaps the film is so devoid of substance that these prolonged, empty scenes are necessary to pad the runtime. Without them, relying solely on plot or story, the movie would barely last 14 minutes. To be clear, this is about the 30th gay film I've...

If Akira Kurosawa erred in the creation of Dodes'ka-den, it was in collaborating with the "four knights"—a group comprising Kobayashi, Ichikawa, and Kinoshita. Their aim was to launch their partnership with a major commercial success, but Kurosawa, often seen as the leader of the pack, instead crafted an abstract, deeply human art film. Set in a ravaged slum, the movie portrays characters grappling with profound tragedies. Had Kurosawa chosen a more independent path or partnered with a different studio, the outcome might have been different. However, this decision, compounded by other financial and creative struggles, contributed to his 1971 suicide attempt. Nevertheless, as an artist, Kurosawa remained true to his reputation in dramas, showcasing the resilience of the human spirit against all odds. The unconventional setting of the film should not be overlooked, yet it is hardly a flaw on Kurosawa’s part.

The content of Dodes'ka-den captivates, though not in the typical style associated with the director, primarily because it prioritizes character over plot. There are elements that

As a dedicated Pokémon enthusiast, I thoroughly enjoyed this film. It introduces new legendary Pokémon, as is customary with each installment, and deepens the connections between characters. However, I doubt that those unfamiliar with Pokémon, including most adults, will find it appealing. Some dialogue felt cliché, which is somewhat inevitable during the English dubbing process. The animation was stunning overall, though a few scenes fell short in quality. While the villain came across as somewhat cheesy, I appreciate how the franchise consistently varies its antagonists, ensuring they aren’t all the same. To those who didn’t enjoy it, I respect differing opinions, but I’m confident that Pokémon fans will adore this movie.

What unfolds when a coalition of derogatory stereotypes, including Mexican immigrants, Middle Eastern individuals, and atheistic Eastern European communists, amasses their forces along the southern border? Gary Busey, naturally, takes them on with gusto. A prime example of the absurd cultural narratives from the Reagan era, *Bulletproof* squanders a talented supporting cast, including notable performances by L.Q. Jones and Thalmus Rasulala.

This is the quintessential Lars von Trier film, my top pick, surpassing both "Breaking the Waves" and the more recent "Dancer in the Dark." I’m captivated by the stunning visuals and the uniquely creative framing. The performances are exceptional, making this an absolute must-watch.

I believe the criticism labeling the show as cheesy is somewhat overblown. When someone sits down to watch a TV series, what are they seeking? Primarily, it’s enjoyment, unless they are a critic or someone dissecting the narrative. For the majority, however, watching TV is about unwinding and having a good time. FULL HOUSE serves as the perfect escape after a taxing day at work or school. It brings laughter and offers more than just comedy.

Admittedly, the Tanner family represents an idealized, almost unrealistically perfect household. If such a family existed in reality, they would undoubtedly be a benchmark for others to emulate. Yet, as a fictional depiction on television, there’s no harm in showcasing such an ideal. The show’s long run is a testament to its popularity and the enjoyment it provided to viewers, regardless of any subsequent critiques.

Additionally, FULL HOUSE appeals to viewers of all ages, not only entertaining them but also imparting valuable lessons, no matter how simple they might seem.

After being compelled by my children to view this film at least ten times during each of the past two Christmas seasons, I believe I’m well-equipped to critique this adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ timeless story. Frankly, it falls short. To begin with, living up to the brilliance of Chuck Jones’ animated TV special is a tall order for any production, yet this version feels overly forceful and unnecessarily drawn out, resulting in a dull experience. I’ll admit there are a few clever jokes, but on the whole, the movie seems like a blatant attempt to capitalize on the holiday spirit while ironically criticizing the commercialization of Christmas. Jim Carrey’s performance is characteristically exaggerated, which clashes starkly with the essence of the Grinch. Unlike Boris Karloff’s portrayal of a subtly menacing, cunning character, Carrey’s approach lacks depth and deliberation, marking just one of many missteps. Additionally, the talents of actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Christine Baranski are squandered in this production. Universal, what were you thinking? While I recognize that Anthony Hopkins, much like his compatriot Michael Caine, often accepts a wide range of roles, this particular project should have been declined.

This film, the most expensive Canadian production ever filmed in British Columbia, is also arguably the worst, never even making it to release. Directed by a British filmmaker rather than a Canadian, the movie glaringly reflects this outsider perspective. It portrays Canadians as over-sexed, drug-addicted fools, completely lacking the essence of Canadian identity—ironic, given that public funding supports such projects for cultural representation. Predictably, the British character is depicted as the only sane one, while the rest are reduced to tired sitcom clichés—think "Norm!!" from Cheers. The cinematography swings wildly between picturesque postcard shots and dim, shadowy indoor scenes. The actors appear visibly restless, leaving one to wonder if they’re as disengaged as the audience or if this is the director’s misguided vision of artistry. Skip this disaster and instead explore the works of Bruce McDonald, a genuine Canadian talent with fresh, cinematic stories to tell. You won’t feel the urge to leave his films just ten minutes in.

This movie ranks among the most disappointing I've ever watched. I attended its premiere at SXSW and left utterly underwhelmed. The director's limited knowledge of John Lennon was evident, a fact they even admitted during the event. Intended as a drama, the film instead provoked unintended laughter from the audience due to its overwhelming cheesiness—a clear indicator of its failure. The only redeeming elements were the performances of Dominic Monaghan and Jason Leonard as Livien's roommates and bandmates, who brought humor to an otherwise overly serious film. The frequent, awkward insertion of Beatles lyrics felt ridiculous. On a positive note, the soundtrack stood out as the highlight of the movie. Unless you're an ardent fan of Dominic Monaghan, I’d recommend skipping this one.

"Fear of a Black Hat" is an exceptionally well-made film. I found myself laughing nearly non-stop from beginning to end. If you have the opportunity, I strongly suggest watching this movie. Without a doubt, it’s the most hilarious film I’ve ever had the joy of seeing. Get ready and go watch it!

Why should you dive into the captivating nature documentary "Earth"? I could go on endlessly about its brilliance, but I’ll keep this concise while standing firm on why it’s an absolute must-watch. The film takes you on a breathtaking journey along the migration routes of three animal families: a polar bear mother with her cubs, accompanied by a gripping subplot of the father bear braving a solitary hunt for food; a whale mother and her calf embarking on an epic migration in search of prey; and an elephant mother guiding her young (though not so small, given they’re elephants) across the African landscape. Directors Alastair Fothergill and Mark Linfield have done an extraordinary job, not only showcasing these three compelling animal families but also highlighting the survival skills of numerous other species with stunning visuals. The cinematography team—Richard Brooks Burton, Mike Holding, Adam Ravetch, and Andrew Shillabeer—demonstrates exceptional talent, capturing awe-inspiring natural landscapes and instinctive animal behaviors, with slow-motion predator-prey sequences that are nothing short of mesmerizing.

The central romance of the film, which serves as its primary focus, is engaging and well-executed. Yet, the backdrop to this love story feels overly poetic, visually exaggerated, and detached from reality. More concerning is the main character’s psychology, which comes across as strange and baffling, much like the film’s confusing conclusion. If the movie piques your curiosity, go ahead and watch it, but keep your expectations in check.

I'm not shocked that even cowgirls get the blues, judging by this film. I had higher hopes for Uma Thurman, which is the only reason I endured this disappointing ordeal. It's a terrible movie, with the soundtrack being its sole saving grace. It's unfortunate that we can't rate films a 0 out of 10 in these reviews, as this one truly merits such a score.

This film, running at 2 hours and 20 minutes, manages to encapsulate much of the renowned Pearl Buck novel, covering extensive narrative territory.

While it occasionally veers into melodramatic territory, it also features striking visual sequences, culminating in a breathtaking locust invasion at the climax. Given that this movie dates back about 70 years, the special effects team delivered an impressive feat.

Paul Muni and Luise Rainer, both celebrated award-winning actors of their era, deliver compelling performances. However, the authenticity is undermined as Caucasian actors portray all the Asian characters, with some, like Walter Connolly, appearing unconvincing. A remake featuring an all-Asian cast would enhance the film's realism and credibility, not merely for political correctness, but to better reflect the story's cultural context.

Thomas Clay has been associating with the wrong crowd. That’s the problem with today’s youth—they lack respect.

Honestly, this film is one to steer clear of at all costs. The action throughout most of the movie drags, feeling heavy and uninspired, meandering toward a drug-fueled conclusion as if, much like its director, it has no better direction to take. We meet the protagonist, a quintessential outsider, struggling to find his place both at school and at home, grappling with the typical awkwardness of adolescence. Robert eventually falls in with a rough group, begins skipping school, and experiments with drugs, soon spiraling into becoming a violent predator.

At its core, the film reveals Clay’s complete inability to grasp the connection between violent imagery and real-world violence. Clay appears to believe that a generation of deranged young people is corrupted by war footage on television, yet he has created a film featuring an utterly repugnant scene of SIMULATED violence. Does he truly not see the irony?

If Clay is unfamiliar with platforms like YouTube, he might be dangerously naive, oblivious to how the shocking climax of his film could be misused or misinterpreted.

Emily Watson's portrayal of Natalia is hands down the most endearing and romantic protagonist I’ve ever witnessed on screen. She reigns supreme as the heart of this film, unquestionable in her dominance. Or perhaps, has she been transformed into a kingly figure? The intricate, almost brutal interplay of chess matches and the families’ relentless battles for dominance, power, and triumph is nothing short of breathtaking. Much like the chess grandmasters depicted, the director skillfully juggles multiple mental games with the audience simultaneously, each thread weaving into either dominant or subtle patterns. The era, costumes, and visuals of early 20th-century Italy’s lake district are captured with breathtaking splendor. Every inch of the frame is utilized with purpose.

Countless brilliant moments fill the film, too many to list. I strongly suggest allocating time to view this masterpiece twice, perhaps with a week in between, as it’s impossible to fully absorb the poetic depth of its 64-square, yet multi-layered structure in a single sitting.

I haven’t read Nabokov’s novel, but to draw a parallel, what I’ve experienced evokes memories of another romantically victorious film that blends poetry and play—Barry Levinson’s *The Natural*. It boldly discarded the bleak conclusion of Bernard Malamud’s fatalistic novel, opting instead for a vision of romantic impressionism.

This so-called movie is utterly devoid of substance! It seems Rachel Griffiths was desperate for a paycheck. The production clearly operated on a shoestring budget, as the lighting was practically nonexistent. I swear, if I ever cross paths with Pete Postle-whatever-his-name-is, I might just lose all hope. I’d love to know if this film even had 1) a storyline or 2) a script. My greatest regret is squandering my time on this absolute garbage.

Is it fair to call this movie "All shock, no plot"? So many potential storylines in this film were left untouched. The history of the room is barely mentioned beyond the deaths associated with it. *Why* is the room evil? What caused it to become that way? Why does it operate on an "hour" countdown? Additionally, there are several intriguing hints that go nowhere. For instance, we *see* a camera in the air vent, as mentioned by the character, but when he climbs into the vent, the camera mysteriously disappears.

What about the fact that all the ghosts appear "digital," and objects "wink out" with a static noise before hitting the ground? When you piece these clues together, room 1408 starts to resemble a high-tech haunted attraction. Yet, there’s no further exploration or explanation of this idea.

And let’s not forget the inconsistencies with electronics in room 1408. Supposedly, electronics don’t function there—except for the TV, which works perfectly. The cell phone has no signal, but somehow the wireless internet operates without a hitch. How many contradictions can one film stack up? Regrettably, this movie is just a series of cheap shocks. It’s all recycled tropes: reflections in mirrors, things lurking just out of view, shifting paintings, bleeding walls, and the tired "Was it all a dream? No, it wasn’t" twist. If the room is meant to be the centerpiece, it fails to deliver anything fresh or meaningful.

My girlfriend and I stumbled upon this movie while flipping through channels. We were both anticipating a heartwarming, family-friendly Christmas film, but we ended up deeply disappointed.

The actor portraying the soldier displays a complete lack of emotion. His expression remains unchanged whether he's cutting down Christmas trees, witnessing the girl he loves being kissed by her boyfriend, or experiencing a joyful surprise from her. His performance is dreadful, and all we could do was laugh at how absurd it was.

Then there's the stereotypical cute blonde girl, whose talents seem limited to counting dots and betraying her boyfriend. What a gem! Her life’s ambition appears to be living with her parents and counting even more dots.

Essentially, the plot revolves around an emotionless man who falls for a girl whose main skills are dot-counting and infidelity. The story is utterly predictable and a complete waste of time. You gain nothing from watching it, except perhaps a few awkward chuckles due to its sheer corniness.

I did find it amusing when her dad mentions that he only eats french fries and not...

I might be among the few who truly appreciated this film. I watched *Up the Academy* when it was first released, and I concur with the previous comment that it was ahead of its time. The humor is classic *MAD* magazine style, and I’m puzzled as to why *MAD* didn’t fully embrace this project. Additionally, it was one of the rare films from the early '80s to feature an incredible soundtrack, showcasing emerging punk and new wave bands from L.A. I still own the soundtrack and play it regularly even now. Honestly, there are far worse movies out there. I don’t find *Porky’s* as amusing as *Up the Academy*, which delivers solid laughs with jokes often centered on stereotypes or sexual escapades. Let’s be clear, no one expected this to be *The Maltese Falcon*.

While I'm not an obsessive John Cleese fan, I did find "Fawlty Towers" utterly brilliant and count myself among his admirers. So, when I stumbled upon this gem, languishing on a shelf at my local Blockbuster, I couldn’t resist giving it a chance. What I discovered was a delightful surprise, easily one of the funniest 50-minute viewing experiences I've ever had. The script embodies classic English "goon show" humor, reminiscent of something you'd hear on a "Firesign Theater" record if it were just an audio sketch. Yet, the flawless execution and impeccable timing transform "Strange Case" into a mesmerizing performance, capable of turning anyone into a lifelong devotee of British comedy.

The British have a unique talent for blending broad, satirical parodies with subtle, well-observed character quirks and precise timing, and the creators of this piece utilize both masterfully. Cleese's take on "Holmes" seems to draw inspiration from the bumbling charm of Arkin’s and Sellers’ "Inspector Clouseau," but his exceptional flair for physical comedy ensures he stands out on his own merit. The real standout, however, is Arthur Lowe as "Watson." Lowe portrays him as a friendly yet hopelessly obtuse fool with such brilliant timing and delivery that he steals the show, becoming the highlight of this comedic masterpiece.

Do you recall the early days of Pay Per View? I certainly do, and I can almost still remember the phone number you had to dial to rent a movie on your TV. As kids, we were always tempted to rent something like Playboy, but that meant actually speaking to someone at PPV to request it. When you finally mustered the courage to make the call, you’d end up watching hours of disappointing soft-core content with terrible angles. I mention this because this movie was also on PPV back then, and I can vividly recall nearly every scene from its trailer. In recent years, I’ve been on a mission to collect all the amazing films I watched as a child, and this one is on that list. It’s the kind of movie that’s hard to turn off once it starts. Featuring an all-star cast, it follows a group attempting the perfect bank heist, only for everything to go hilariously wrong.
