There are many great spoof bank caper films out there, and this one definitely belongs in that group. With a perfect blend of action and humor, it’s highly entertaining. Give it a watch if you’re up for it!

Honestly, producing this type of film does little to benefit the Australian film industry, as it lacks any meaningful values. Perhaps it might appeal to a niche audience with time to spare, but that's about it. Australian filmmakers should aim to showcase our country's incredible talent on a global stage, and this film simply doesn’t serve that purpose. Frankly, it comes across as cheap and tasteless.

To begin with, I never thought of myself as someone who disliked Uwe Boll, mainly because I don’t recall ever watching any of his films. However, after enduring the abysmal film titled "Seed"—named after the serial killer central to the story—I’m on the verge of joining the critics. This movie is utterly incoherent; the plot is laughable, and despite Boll’s obvious attempt to garner attention through shock value, 90% of the film is simply tedious. Here’s a breakdown of the film:

1. The film starts with a hooded killer watching disturbing real-life footage of animals being tortured at pelt farms on television. It opens with a flimsy justification of “commenting on humanity” and even provides a PETA address. Given that the movie carries no meaningful message and stands as a deplorable example of torture porn-exploitation, it gives viewers an immediate reason to despise it from the outset.

2. There’s a scene involving death by electrocution, accompanied by on-screen text that blatantly foreshadows later events, ensuring that even the least attentive viewer can follow along.

3. Police officers are shown watching videos depicting the horrific starvation of animals, babies, and women, further adding to the film’s grim and pointless tone.

John Carpenter's *Halloween* is, without question, a horror masterpiece. It recounts the chilling tale of Michael Myers, an escaped mental patient who returns to his hometown on Halloween night to terrorize and murder a group of babysitters.

This film, the original and undeniably the finest in the *Halloween* series, showcases Carpenter's remarkable restraint. He paces the story deliberately, allowing tension to build while crafting relatable, likable characters—a rarity in the horror genre.

Even more striking is the absence of blood and gore, yet it stands as the most terrifying entry in the franchise to this day. Imagine that!

*Halloween* also introduced Jamie Lee Curtis to the silver screen and served as a career-defining moment for the late, great Donald Pleasence. A genuine classic.

While viewing this film on video last night, I experienced recurring chills that convinced me of its lasting impact. I suspect I will return to this movie repeatedly in the years ahead.

It possesses every enduring trait one could desire in a narrative or cinematic work. Although certain cultural references remain unfamiliar to me as a Western audience member, at its heart, this story resonates universally.

Disavowed by director Richard C. Sarafian, this cinematic catastrophe first fouled up theaters in Japan before limping to the U.S., where it bypassed theaters entirely and landed straight on video. It vanished into obscurity until the Turner networks, desperate for content to fill the dead hours between 3am and 6am, dredged this relic from the depths of their archives as an alternative to infomercials. The pseudonym "Smithee" is typically slapped on a film when studio meddling mutilates it beyond recognition, prompting the director to detach their name from the wreckage. However, Sarafian can’t entirely pin the blame on the studio for this fiasco. The cast, seemingly fresh from a crash course in "Overacting 101," hams up every cringe-worthy line with gusto. The storyline is a tangled mess, the special effects are lackluster at best, and the moments that aren’t unintentionally hilarious are simply tedious. One can only assume the original script or source material held some promise—how else could talents like Palance, Matheson, Boyle, or Heston have been lured into this disaster? Yet, somewhere between script and screen, everything went disastrously awry. In short: Steer clear. It’s not even terrible enough to qualify as a so-bad-it’s-good guilty pleasure.

In the traditional framework of the four humors, which extends beyond mere comedy or entertainment, Altman's "H.E.A.L.T.H." brilliantly addresses each humor with humor and charm. Lauren Bacall embodies Phlegm through her character Esther Brill, a cautious and defensive woman obsessed with maintaining the illusion of youth and beauty, often at the expense of her own health. Paul Dooley portrays the Choleric Dr. Gil Gainey, floundering like a fish out of water—or perhaps a seal—energetically flopping about and rallying the masses with his eccentric, water-centric fervor. Glenda Jackson's Isabella Garnell captures Melancholy, reminiscent of Shakespeare’s brooding, self-righteous Hamlet, complete with introspective soliloquies. Henry Gibson’s Bilious Bobby Hammer adds to the mix with his mantra, "The breast that feeds the baby rules the world." Amidst this array of exaggerated personalities are Harry Wolff and Gloria Burbank, played by James Garner and Carol Burnett, who stand as relatively grounded figures, navigating the chaos of extreme humors gathered at H.E.A.L.T.H.—an organization akin to a global trade entity, ironically focused on anything but actual health.

I was in France around March 5th, and I’ve always loved attending film festivals. I had heard of the Cinémas d'Amérique Latine de Toulouse but had never been before. This time, I made the decision to go and ended up watching *Cero y van 4*.

The film left me in awe. Though it didn’t resonate with me as deeply as it might have with Mexican audiences—likely due to the French subtitles—it was still profoundly impactful.

*Cero y van 4* is a biting satire on urban violence, focusing on kidnapping and street crime in Mexico. It paints a raw, unfiltered picture of the city, a sprawling metropolis. I found parallels with *Secuestro Express*, another satire on kidnapping featuring a remarkable performance by Mia Maestro. While *Secuestro Express* adopts a more serious tone, both films seem to share a thematic connection—perhaps a shared exploration of redemption and the question of how much is too much. Similarly, *Man on Fire*, with its intense and powerful depiction, offers a stark, non-satirical look into Mexico’s streets. It also reminds me of *The Brave One*, a film that delivers a visceral punch to the gut. Like *The Usual Suspects*, *Cero y van 4* is filled with unexpected plot twists and turns, keeping you on edge throughout.

Is this the most misogynistic film ever made? By 1968, shouldn’t Hollywood have progressed past casting white actors in brownface to portray Native Americans? My favorite moments, if you can call them that, are when the women giggle and blush while being dragged off by bikers for gang rape—apparently, rape is entertaining! Who would have thought? Then there’s the shameless imitation of "The Hustler," with the overweight boss character scheming to ruin the Native Americans while playing pool with the lead rebel. Add to that the atrocious acting, the painfully obvious music cues that practically dictate what to feel, and the complete absence of any actual Native American representation in the cast. Who are we even supposed to cheer for? It’s no surprise that Quentin Tarantino is a fan of this film. Despite his movies often showcasing strong female characters, I’ve come across at least one account claiming he’s a misogynist in real life. Why did I even watch this, you wonder? Let’s not get into it.

SPOILERS

Jean-Paul Sartre once said, "Hell is other people," and in "The Odd Couple," Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau bring this sentiment to life with striking precision. Playing Felix Ungar and Oscar Madison, respectively, Lemmon and Matthau portray two close friends who decide to share a home. As their differences start to grate on each other, the comedy unfolds at a rapid pace, culminating in Felix’s departure, which leaves Oscar transformed into a tidier version of himself.

Jack Lemmon delivers a stellar performance as Ungar, the neurotic, cleanliness-obsessed divorcee navigating single life. In sharp contrast, Walter Matthau shines as Madison, the messy sports writer whose main concern is playing poker to cover child support payments.

The brilliance of Lemmon and Matthau in their roles owes much to Neil Simon’s masterful script, as well as their seamless chemistry as a duo. Despite their contrasting lifestyles, both characters share common ground in their strained relationships with ex-wives and children. These two legendary, late actors forge a partnership that feels utterly unique and nearly impossible to replicate, leaving audiences clamoring for more.

To start with, there’s no hint of flirtation in this movie, whether with Anthony or any other character. These individuals don’t engage in playful banter—they simply act on their desires. The initial challenge for viewers is enduring over 15 minutes of graphic violence and sexual deviance. This might be tolerable—I’m as drawn to dark themes as the average critic—but without a meaningful context, it becomes off-putting. Once you push through the brutality and chaos, the story introduces Donna, and the film shifts into an entirely different genre, though not necessarily an improvement: it becomes a road movie devoid of emotional depth. There are feeble stabs at humor through cameos, which are over-the-top in both writing and performance by personalities like Judy Tenuta and Mink Stole, alongside a few prostitutes and drag queens. They all merit stronger material. The cinematography is deliberately disorienting, so if you’re prone to motion sickness—or any kind of discomfort—this film is best avoided. Honestly, it’s unclear who the target audience for this movie might be, aside from perhaps gay and bisexual S&M enthusiasts who enjoy poorly written, poorly filmed independent projects centered on their own subculture.

What a disappointing decline for Sean Ellis.

You invite a group of friends over, buzzing with excitement for Sean Ellis's latest project. You have a rough sense of the storyline, carefully avoiding spoilers to preserve the thrill, and your expectations are sky-high.

It's late at night, the ideal setting for a film like this.

Fifteen minutes in, you reassure yourself that the pace will surely pick up. By the 25-minute mark, you're contemplating whether to call it a night and revisit the movie when you're better poised to catch the subtle nuances you anticipated but haven't seen. Past the half-hour point, you notice that half of your enthusiastic crowd has dozed off, and you decide to end the session.

A few days later, having run out of other content to watch, you give it another shot, this time in broad daylight, hoping your energy will keep you engaged. Ten minutes in, you're skipping through excruciatingly slow and unnecessary transitions and visuals. With any other film, you'd have abandoned it by now, but the lingering charm of *Cashback* and its reputation compels you to persist. Yet, even that legacy can only sustain your patience for so long.

This might be among the most disappointing films I've ever watched. Despite what critics might claim, I found it to be terrible. I believe the issue lies with Kundera's novel. It's not that it can't be adapted to film; rather, like the vast majority of his writing, it feels pretentious and overly protracted. Kundera appears to be infatuated with his own ideas, his characters often seem self-obsessed, and his works frequently come across as misogynistic. I've read several of his pieces, including his Socialist Realist poetry—which was particularly dreadful—and I still can't grasp why there's so much acclaim surrounding him. The traits in his novels, such as the self-absorption, are frustrating to read, and in the film adaptation, all the aspects of Kundera's style that I dislike were even more pronounced. Perhaps I overlooked something, but I doubt it. As an aside, I'm astonished that this film is part of the Criterion Collection. I can't see how it could be considered that significant.

Reunion shows come in various forms. One type features veteran actors dusting off long-forgotten roles to reprise characters they haven’t portrayed in two or three decades. The outcomes of these revivals are often uneven. For instance, 'Return to Mayberry' managed to be decent despite some absurd moments, while 'Return to Green Acres' was dreadful (Eddie Albert’s harsh critique of the script, which I won’t quote, matched the film’s poor quality). 'Rescue from Gilligan's Island' addressed a missing piece in the castaways’ tale, though the show itself was overly comical, even by the standards of the original series. Generally, these reunion specials suffer from subpar scripts, often laced with a self-aware humor that proves deadly in comedy—characters should never seem aware of their own jokes. Additionally, new characters are often shoehorned in, clashing with the established ensemble. Overall, these revival attempts tend to disappoint.

Another type of reunion show involves the cast setting aside their former roles to gather and share memories, interweaving anecdotes with clips from the original series. Then there are films inspired by these shows, which seldom succeed, as well as movies that delve into the backstory of the series, such as those based on 'The Brady Bunch.'

I rated Timecop a perfect 10, but this movie gets a mere 1 from me.

The storyline is incredibly dull and barely connects to the original Timecop. Many elements from the first film were discarded and replaced with nonsensical new content. The plot is set in 2060 (if my memory serves me right), yet inexplicably, time travel has become more perilous.

The action sequences are largely disappointing. Only the opening scene stands out as impressive, but overall, there are very few action moments, and those that exist are frustratingly brief.

At one point, the protagonist jumps through time multiple times in just a few minutes—actually, I think it was just twice.

In summary, don’t bother with this film; it’s simply not worth your time.

This film feels like one we’re supposed to admire, but I couldn’t connect with it. It strives excessively to appear 'artistic,' prioritizing style over substance. While individual scenes are visually stunning and enjoyable in isolation, stringing them together transforms the experience into a tedious chore. I rented it based on the enthusiastic reviews on the box and my love for Shakespeare, but I ended up deeply disappointed. Ultimately, I found it somewhat pretentious and, at moments, dull.

Following the traumatic assault on Harry Reems' young girlfriend by Zebbedy Colt, known as The Night-Walker, Reems falls into a state of despair and seeks solace in the company of lesbians. Colt, characterized by his cane and magician-like attire, continues his spree of violence against women. Determined to stop him, Reems sets out to hunt Colt down and put an end to his crimes. Although filmed on celluloid and possessing a slight edge of nastiness, the movie resembles a typical 1970s adult film and suffers from poor execution. The depiction of rape and abuse is unexpectedly tame, and the attempt to emulate "Death Wish" comes off as absurd. R. Bolla, known from "Cannibal Holocaust," appears as a police officer. Colt, typically known for exaggerated performances, has moments of intensity in a few scenes, but overall, he remains too restrained for my taste. This gritty film had the potential to be far more daring.

Ugh! My brain is throbbing! And no wonder, after slogging through this grueling cinematic ordeal. I have no idea how I resisted the urge to fast-forward through the entire thing.

Perhaps it's just me. Maybe I'm missing the film's supposed premise... or failing to grasp its so-called mystical vibe. Honestly, though, I found the movie about as mystical as a quick stop at McDonald's.

Moreover, the characters were utterly terrible, with more depth to be found in a Tom & Jerry episode. Argh! Why do I subject myself to such rubbish? Why do I even bother with this nonsense? It's enough to make someone flee to a monastery or enlist in the Foreign Legion! ARGH! This film is absolutely atrocious in nearly every way. Other than that, it's not half bad.

This film is truly exceptional, and I’ve found myself rewatching it with delight on multiple occasions. Michael Caine delivers a stellar performance, as always. Though he’s often critiqued for accepting roles in films of varying quality, his portrayal of Sidney is undeniably impressive. The screenplay is outstanding from the very beginning. It’s surprising to see Ira Levin, known for penning chilling tales like *The Boys from Brazil* and *Rosemary’s Baby*, craft something so sharp and witty. With a cast featuring talents like Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan Cannon, and Henry Jones, and under the direction of Sidney Lumet, it’s hard to imagine this movie being anything less than remarkable.

I hesitate to say more, as revealing any details about the plot would be a disservice. Simply watch it and let yourself be captivated.

Oh my goodness! It's rare for a "horror" movie to leave me so uninterested or to elicit as many laughs as this one did. It kicks off with an engaging premise and a lively beginning, but quickly devolves into little more than a typical slasher film, sprinkled with some supernatural and sexual diversions. The typically outstanding Alice Krige is unfortunately underutilized here, and the plot twists are simply absurd. Skip this unless you're truly out of options. Rating: 3/10.

I caught this film during a Monstervision marathon on TNT, hosted by Joe Bob Briggs. Even his commentary couldn’t salvage the experience. The sole reason I endured to the end was my role as a video production teacher—I needed to ensure my students would never produce anything this dreadful. It took every ounce of willpower to sit through it. Imagine the discomfort of witnessing your great-grandmother awkwardly flirting with a teenage boy—that’s the level of cringe this movie delivers.

If you were to douse the film reel in paint thinner and watch it dissolve, it’d still be more captivating. I’m not exaggerating.

If you ever spot this movie in the bargain bin at S-Mart, retreat as if you’ve stumbled upon a venomous snake.

Typically, I steer clear of Farrelly brothers’ films. I don’t think I’ve ever sat through one. Nor do I remember watching a Jimmy Fallon movie—well, except for *Taxi*, but I’ve atoned for that lapse in judgment and been absolved. However, this movie featured Drew Barrymore, and I find her utterly charming. There’s something about her that keeps me smiling throughout every scene she’s in. She has this captivating quality that draws me in. I even endured an Adam Sandler movie just to watch her in *50 First Dates*. How pathetic is that? This wasn’t meant to be the ultimate baseball film, and it isn’t. Instead, it’s a heartfelt love story about a forlorn soul clinging to the one constant in his life until he discovers something—or someone—worth sacrificing it for. The ending was predictable, but the journey to get there was filled with moments that made it all worthwhile.

I’m somewhat ashamed to admit that I only recently watched this film, 13 years after it first premiered. The narrative resonates deeply with any father or brother, portraying one sibling as somewhat untamed and the other as the quintessential responsible older child. While Craig Sheffer’s portrayal of the eldest brother feels a tad too reserved, Brad Pitt delivers a remarkable performance, and Tom Skerritt is impeccably suited to the role of the father. The fishing sequences, captured in the stunning landscapes of Montana, are visually captivating—I never realized fly fishing could be so mesmerizing. The film stays true to the original book, with just a few alterations to better fit the cinematic format. In contrast to many book-to-film adaptations, this one holds its own. It’s an ideal choice for anyone seeking a serene evening with a poignant and emotionally engaging story.

This Cheech & Chong movie boasts the funniest jokes among their entire catalog. It was my first introduction to their comedic duo, and I found it thoroughly entertaining. My dad, an incredible role model, was the one who suggested I watch it, and surprisingly, my grandma purchased it for me, fully aware of its content. I’m truly blessed with such a unique family. Overall, this film is quite enjoyable and a fantastic choice for renting when you’re in the mood for a classic comedy. However, I should note that it’s not hysterically funny; it has its humorous peaks but doesn’t reach the level of hilarity found in There’s Something About Mary. Give it a watch regardless—I’m confident you’ll get a few laughs, unless you’re staunchly opposed to drug-related humor.

This film was an utter waste of my time, and the director should feel ashamed for producing such a disgrace. I will never understand why individuals feel compelled to create such meaningless movies. The ending, where she died, was so poorly executed that it made me laugh out of sheer disbelief. I had to switch channels multiple times during the film because the acting was so cringe-worthy that I felt embarrassed just watching it. I sincerely hope the actor who portrayed Heath never finds another role. Furthermore, I hope the director is barred from ever making another movie and is forced to return the money paid for this dreadful production. {0.2 out of 10}

This film fails to engage, with fleeting glimpses of nudity thrown in as a feeble attempt to maintain the audience's attention, though they ultimately fall flat.

The standout element of the movie is Lena Olin, who delivers a captivating performance in her role. In contrast, Day-Lewis struggles, mumbling through much of his dialogue.

Kaufman appears to lack a clear vision for directing this piece. The jarring shifts between domestic and marital tensions and political turmoil feel mismatched and poorly executed. Characters’ perspectives shift inexplicably, leaving the narrative fragmented and disjointed.

I approached "Still Crazy" without much expectation, assuming it would be just another rock'n'roll movie, likely appealing to baby boomers with a dose of nostalgia. While it does offer that to some extent, the film surpasses those initial assumptions. Directed by Brian Gibson, who previously crafted a biopic on Tina Turner, the movie reflects his adept style. It feels poignant that this was his final work.

The ensemble cast is impeccably selected. Bill Nighy delivers a flawless performance as the band's lead singer, while Bruce Robinson, now a director but once an actor, portrays the band's faded guitarist with remarkable skill, especially considering he hasn’t been on screen since the late 1970s. If you're in search of a film that’s both heartwarming and humorous, complete with fantastic music, this is it.

Rating: 7.4 out of 10

For my 8th birthday, I received the book version of *Kazaam*, and while people often claim that books outshine their movie adaptations, this was an exception where they were mistaken. At least the movie ends quickly.

The acting in the film is dreadful, which I anticipated from a production starring Shaq as a magical, rapping genie who emerges from an outdated ghetto blaster—perhaps there was a valid reason for his imprisonment. The child actor portraying Max is insufferable and lacks any talent. His character, constantly whining, is bullied by local kids, and honestly, I can’t fault them; Max comes across as an annoying brat.

The storyline is utterly ridiculous and painfully clichéd. It revolves around a boy whose father is perpetually absent due to work, until he discovers a new companion who transforms his life and ultimately facilitates a reunion with his dad.

Even at the tender age of 8, I found this concept absurd. It’s astonishing that anyone involved in this film managed to sustain a career afterward, as it’s a complete embarrassment and should never have been produced. I could go on at length about the movie’s flaws, but

What a dreadful movie! It’s astonishing that it was even considered for a Golden Globe; it must have been competing with some truly terrible films. The story of the first renowned female Renaissance painter has been completely distorted, rendered unrecognizable. My issue isn’t with the creative liberties taken—had the narrative been compelling, I’d have no objections. However, the plot is utterly perplexing. By all accounts, the artist’s real life would have made a much more captivating film, so why opt for this incredibly dull screenplay? Perhaps the true story lacked the sensationalism of nudity that seems to be a prerequisite. The film is abruptly concluded with a rushed summary of the artist’s life—if only the same conciseness had been applied throughout, we could have spared ourselves a tedious two hours.

Indeed, this film is essentially a carbon copy of the original, yet they couldn’t even manage to align the timeline of events properly. Whether this was a deliberate choice stemming from laziness or sheer indifference is unclear, but regardless, this production is an absolute disaster. It hardly qualifies as a movie. I encountered this travesty as a supposed second feature on the disc with the original *The Boogeyman*. I felt like my brain might implode, and I strongly advise you to steer clear if you’re unfortunate enough to cross paths with it. It ought to carry a warning label, something like: "Caution—exposure may significantly lower your IQ." For me, there’s no question; this debacle earns a solid 0/10.

In my opinion, this movie is rather peculiar, packed with plenty of humor. I wouldn't classify it as particularly frightening, but rather entertaining, especially if you're a fan of horror films. The Scarecrow reminded me somewhat of "Children of the Corn," though it's not quite the same. When comparing the two, this one is definitely more enjoyable to watch. =)

Alright, alright, don't get upset. I was just joking.

"Bustin' Out" is honestly a more fitting and accurate title anyway.

Racism and crime dramas receive a sharp satirical treatment from our X-rated animator buddy, Ralph. And he delivers one of his finer works here.

On the crime side, it portrays a harsh reality: they build their empire, protect it fiercely, but boredom and tougher competitors often lead to their downfall (or close to it). Watch it yourself to see how it all unfolds.

Racist? I'm not so sure. With Scatman (RIP) and the love walrus (also RIP) as central black characters providing the main perspective, it felt more like a critique of racism to me. The fact that Richard Pryor approved of it speaks volumes too. Plus, seeing a young (pre-"Miami Vice") Phil Mike Thomas was a pleasant surprise.

It's an animated "Blaxploitation" film, and that's a positive in this case. It's executed skillfully and with impact. Some scenes, like the lynching, might make viewers uncomfortable, but sadly, they’re rooted in reality.

Still, Ralph really should have reconsidered that title.

I finally managed to watch "Starlight" on TV last night, and I'm at a loss for words—simply, wow! It's tough to decide where to start critiquing—the laughably cheesy special effects (don’t miss the laser beams blasting from Willie's eyes!), the dreadful acting, the painfully slow dialogue, the jarring incorporation of stock footage, or the pervasive sense of self-important pretension that permeates the whole show. This is genuinely a unique spectacle, and we should probably be grateful it stands alone. I propose Jonathon Kay as the rightful successor to Ed Wood!

I disregarded the reviews and decided to watch it for myself. Unfortunately, the critics were spot on. Given the film's budget, it was a complete waste of money.

Thankfully, I watched *Kill Bill* afterward, which was a much better experience.

If you’re looking for a truly terrifying movie, *Crossroads* might be the one!

In conclusion, I’d rather watch *Girl in Gold Boots* than this rubbish.

I wholeheartedly concur with jamrom4. This film is, without a doubt, the worst I’ve ever endured. It was absolutely dreadful. Despite being cautioned against watching it, I foolishly disregarded the advice. Just ten minutes into this torturous ordeal, I lost all hope for any redeeming qualities, yet I forced myself to sit through to the end, purely as a test of endurance. Regrettably, I now wish I hadn’t. It was revolting, utterly devoid of substance, and the ending felt sanctimonious. No film this abysmal deserves to exist. I strongly urge everyone to avoid the horrors of *Fatty Drives the Bus*. If only I had taken the same advice. Please, spare yourself from this cinematic disaster. I suspect those who gave it high ratings are connected to its production and, frankly, their judgment is questionable at best.

This is, without a doubt, my all-time favorite movie. I've seen it at least ten times, and each viewing leaves me in tears. My family pleads with me to avoid watching it, worried about my inevitable emotional breakdown. What I adore just as much as the film itself is that it’s a true story, penned by Antwone himself. The acting is exceptional, with every actor perfectly cast in their role. Denzel Washington, one of my favorite actors, delivers his best performance yet in this film. 

I once cared for a little boy who, like Antwone, was born in jail. He was the sweetest child I’d ever met. Thankfully, after a nearly two-year battle, he was adopted by a loving family. I watched this movie during that uncertain time in his life, and I’m overjoyed to know he’s now safe and cherished. I’m equally thrilled that Antwone found his family and happiness. 

I’m eager to learn more about Antwone’s life since reuniting with his family. I simply can’t praise this movie enough!

I've never really admired Farrah Fawcett—until now. Her performance in this film was nothing short of remarkable. The emotional toll of repeatedly filming such intense scenes is unimaginable. This movie was incredibly difficult to watch, with its deeply disturbing subject matter leaving you feeling powerless as you witness a woman enduring endless abuse. However, the tension seemed to dissipate when her friends came back to the house, and I found the ending to be quite unconvincing. The director's focus on height in his framing and frequent use of mirror reflections was notable, but I think he should have prioritized maintaining the pacing in the latter half of the film. While I’m sure this story would be incredibly impactful as a stage play, as a movie, despite its strengths, it ultimately didn’t quite hit the mark for me.

Avoid wasting your time and money on renting this dreadful film! I’m baffled as to how it even got produced. (I’m not sure why a minimum of 10 lines is required... I’ve already encapsulated the essence of this terrible movie, but anyway...) The performances were atrocious, as if the cast desperately needed acting classes. The storyline was flimsy, and the conclusion was utterly disappointing. The cinematography was perhaps the only aspect that wasn’t a complete failure, and the sound design was passably minimalistic. On a positive note, if a film like this can be made and even turn a profit, there’s hope for aspiring screenwriters with genuine, creative concepts. So, take encouragement from this! The same applies to actors—if this cast got paid for their work, there’s definitely a chance for you to succeed as well!

**POTENTIAL SPOILERS:**

This film was a disappointing experience. It treads familiar territory as a Catholic, superstitious suspense thriller, recycling themes seen in countless prior movies.

It features the archetypal doubting priest, the tension between sexuality and priesthood, the intersection of politics and religion, church hypocrisy, conspiracies within the church, and the emergence of a sinister new era. The narrative is further muddled by overdone battles of dark magic between good and evil.

The plot is weak and uninspired, hinging on two main ideas: Absolution, often referred to as the Sacrament of Anointing the Sick, which are the final rites a person can seek to purify their sins on the verge of death; and Excommunication, the act of severing someone from the Church. An excommunicated individual is barred from receiving Absolution. This is where the concept of the Sin Eater comes into play, though I'll refrain from further details. Combine this with the clichéd elements mentioned earlier, and you get "The Order."

I found the sex scene involving the priest, intercut with imagery of the Virgin Mary, to be particularly offensive to Catholic sensibilities. The film concludes with Heath Ledger delivering a line (paraphrased) like, "I am the one who redeems and condemns sins, I exist without love, and so on," followed by a shot of him walking into the darkness.

HAH! So this is the film the "Next Action Stars" were involved in. I’m relieved I didn’t take part or win...

Isn’t it amusing how you can judge a movie within the first 10 seconds? Seriously, just take a look at those opening titles! I caught part of this so-called "teleplay" (since it was made for TV) one evening during my military service. My fellow viewers were a typical mix of regular guys who occasionally tune into shows like Las Vegas purely for the eye candy. Expectations weren’t exactly sky-high—after all, the most popular movie among us was The Girl Next Door, and not for its stellar screenplay, if you catch my drift. Yet, this film’s complete lack of originality, poor acting, terrible script, and absence of anything remotely redeeming made it effortless for us to switch over to Las Vegas (or maybe it was CSI? I can’t recall) without a single objection from the group. And trust me, that’s saying something! For the love of all that’s good, don’t buy this movie! If it’s airing on TV, just keep flipping channels.

I'm concerned that you'll notice a significant number of people rating this movie a perfect 10 are deeply religious, particularly Christian. I am not part of that group. If you're in search of a film with a strong Christian message, this might be a good choice. However, if you're after a quality film for a general audience, I suggest looking elsewhere.

The characters in this movie irritated me with their unreasonable actions. The central idea seems to be that teaching morality without acknowledging Jesus as its foundation is misguided. There's a particular scene where the protagonist instructs a young boy that stealing is wrong, then attributes this moral principle to Jesus. I found this troubling: are we really to think that the concept of "do not steal" originated with Jesus? Does this imply he authored the Ten Commandments? Was stealing considered acceptable prior to that? I rented this film from Netflix and, in hindsight, should have paid closer attention to the reviews which hinted at its thematic content. Lesson learned.

This film is not only a delightful source of entertainment, boasting stellar comedic performances, but it also offers intriguing political insights. Filmed during the twilight of the Soviet Union, it thoroughly satirizes the Soviet mindset. Set in the nascent days of the Soviet era, the narrative challenges the logic underpinning the revolution from both cultural and practical perspectives. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, the stringent controls of Soviet society had begun to loosen, yet the underlying ideology and mindset persisted, ripe for critical examination. Fortunately, this profound philosophical critique is delivered within a humorous and engaging framework!

I absolutely adored this movie! As a devoted Tom Hanks enthusiast, I’m consistently amazed by his versatile performances. He shines in intense, dramatic roles like *Cast Away*, *The Green Mile*, *Saving Private Ryan*, *Forrest Gump*, *Apollo 13*, and *Philadelphia*. Equally, he brings laughter in comedic gems such as *A League of Their Own*, *Turner and Hooch*, *Catch Me If You Can*, *The Ladykillers*, *Big*, and, of course, *Toy Story*. However, Hanks isn’t the sole standout in this film. Tyler Hoechlin, a rising talent with immense potential in Hollywood, plays Hanks’ son and delivers an outstanding performance. He’s definitely an actor to keep an eye on; I’m confident he’ll achieve remarkable success in his career. Paul Newman, as always, captivates with his brilliance on screen—a true icon. We must also acknowledge the supporting cast who, though in smaller roles, contribute significantly to the film’s success. The stunning and exceptionally talented Jennifer Jason Leigh, whose unforgettable performances in *Bastard Out of Carolina* and *Single White Female* remain etched in my memory, graces the screen as Hanks’ wife, bringing elegance and depth to her role.

The movie is pure entertainment, especially for those of us who were young and ardent fans of "The Ramones" during the era it was released. I've revisited this film countless times, both solo and with friends, and it never fails to feel fresh and hilarious. While it may seem a bit earnest to say, the idea of idolizing a particular band is evergreen, as is the universal high school experience of being bored by the monotony of certain classes.

Moreover, the film is packed with memorable lines and scenes. It pokes fun at the notion that our "permanent record" from high school will haunt us forever (I can confirm, having been out of high school for quite a while now, that it doesn’t). There’s the iconic "static" exchange ("I'm getting some static"..."Not as much as you're going to get," as Principal Togar looms closer), the hilariously frail school board member flanked by nurses, the Nazi-like Hall Monitor's unsettling fondness for "body searches," Principal Togar’s dramatic declaration of "the final solution" while torching Ramones records (a nod to the pre-CD era), and, of course, Joey Ramone’s classic observation, "Things sure have changed since we got kicked out of high school," followed by Togar’s pointed question.

I thoroughly enjoyed this show; it seems we only received the first—and apparently only—series here in the UK on Channel 4. The characterization was spot-on, reminiscent of The Simpsons, as it captured the diverse personalities of a small-town community with precision.

The absence of a laughter track was a refreshing choice. At the time, I hadn’t seen this approach in an American TV comedy, aside from The Larry Sanders Show, and it worked brilliantly here. It amplified the impression that these eccentric cops were genuinely quirky, not just playing up for an audience.

Overall, this offbeat gem hit all the right notes for me. I can’t help but wonder if it failed to resonate with some viewers due to poor timing or exposure. Had it aired at a more suitable hour in the UK, I believe it could have become a cult classic.

To wrap up, I’ll pose my usual question: Does anyone know where I can find this series to rewatch it? Any suggestions?

It might be surprising to learn that this film was condemned as immoral by more religious leaders than any other movie before the strict Hayes Code was enforced. Indeed, clergy warned their congregations that watching this film constituted a grave sin.

I’m not fabricating this. Their objections were based on several points, outlined below:

Firstly, Jane’s evident enjoyment of intimacy is highlighted. In one scene, she and Tarzan are seen waking up in their treetop home. Jane stretches languidly and, with a playful glance, teases, "Tarzan, you've been a bad boy!" This implies not just intimacy, but a playful, perhaps unconventional kind. Later, under the Hayes Code, portraying characters—particularly women—as taking pleasure in such activities was frowned upon.

Secondly, Jane’s preference for Tarzan, a candid yet cunning and resourceful wild man, over Holt, a conventional and civilized nine-to-five gentleman, was controversial. Initially, Holt impresses her with a beautiful dress from London, causing her to hesitate in her loyalties. Her doubt deepens when Holt attempts to kill Tarzan, and both believe him to be dead. However, upon discovering Tarzan is alive, the allure of civilized life dissipates for Jane. And why wouldn’t it? Tarzan’s allure is undeniable.

In 1959, THE BRAIN THAT WOULDN'T DIE was deemed so offensive that it required multiple edits and a three-year delay before its release in 1962. Now, it's hard to fathom how anyone could have taken the film seriously even back then; it's not only sensational and crude but also absurdly over-the-top in a brazen, almost comical manner.

The plot revolves around a doctor obsessed with limb transplantation. When his girlfriend dies in a car accident, he frantically transports her severed head to his hidden laboratory. Using little more than telephone wires, a few clamps, and what appears to be a shallow baking tray, he miraculously revives her head. However, gratitude is the last thing on her mind. She’s furious, especially upon learning that the doctor intends to graft her head onto a new body.

As it turns out, the doctor is quite particular about this new body—he’s looking for one that’s “built for speed.” He prowls city streets eyeing unsuspecting women, frequents strip clubs, attends bodybuilding competitions, and seeks out pin-up models in his relentless quest.

That enchanting juncture in life, poised between the pure simplicity of childhood and the tumultuous storm of adulthood, is the essence of this film.

At the outset of the movie, Danni, portrayed brilliantly by Reese Witherspoon, finds herself at this pivotal crossroads. She is enamored with Elvis, endlessly playing his songs and daydreaming about romance. Her sister Maureen, soon to leave for college, effortlessly attracts attention from boys, exudes beauty, and appears to have everything under control—though she secretly struggles. Maureen dates a local underachiever whose father also pursues her, all while longing for a worthy suitor to sweep her off her feet. Like many adolescents, Danni yearns to be someone else, believing her own identity falls short. She idolizes Maureen, blind to her own unique beauty.

The intrusion of adulthood into Danni's world begins with her first encounter with Court Foster. Having recently lost his father, Court has relocated with his mother and two younger brothers to work on their family’s old farm.

Emma remains my favorite Jane Austen novel, largely due to the endearing nature of its protagonist. Despite her imperfections, Emma's good intentions shine through, allowing readers to both forgive and adore her. Her relationship with Mr. Knightley is a delightful blend of warmth, familiarity, respect, and playfulness, sparking that delightful, heartwarming romantic thrill. Mr. Knightley epitomizes the ideal man, while Emma represents a near-perfect embodiment of an independent, intelligent, and confident woman for her era. At just 21, she still has room to grow and overcome her shortcomings. Who wouldn't aspire to be Emma? Who wouldn't relish a gentle rebuke from Mr. Knightley? 

However, this particular adaptation of Emma falls short of capturing the qualities I cherish in the character. I found it so disappointing that I couldn’t even finish watching it. The portrayal lacks the warmth and generosity that make Emma so lovable in the novel—her patience and affection toward her father, and her close bond with Mrs. Weston, which highlights her selflessness in prioritizing her friend’s happiness over her own by encouraging Miss Taylor’s marriage. Additionally, Mr. Woodhouse in this version comes across as strangely eccentric rather than charmingly peculiar.

I made a genuine effort to enjoy this show, going as far as purchasing the pilot film on both VHS and later DVD. Despite my attempts, I couldn’t connect with the story, largely due to the two main characters, David (Bruce Willis) and Maddie (Cybill Shepherd), who seemed overly self-absorbed. I will acknowledge that the show featured some sharp dialogue, which was undoubtedly a significant factor in its success, and I did find much of that writing impressive.

In essence, the series echoed the classic screwball comedies of the 1930s and 1940s, full of male-female banter. There’s plenty of arguing, accusations, and shouting, which seems to appeal to many viewers. However, I personally dislike that kind of constant conflict, so I never became a fan of *Moonlighting*.

The only standout for me was Allyce Beasley as the endearing but underutilized aide, Agnes. It’s a shame she didn’t get more screen time. While Shepherd was visually appealing, and I’m sure many would say the same about Willis, the relentless bickering between the leads ultimately drove me away.

This movie has haunted me ever since I first watched it.

My mother saw it on television back in 1992. I recall being jolted awake in the middle of the night by her tearful outbursts as my father guided her up the stairs.

She kept muttering something like, "Don't let her take me," or words to that effect. Curious about what had distressed her so much, I asked, and she revealed she had been watching *The Woman in Black*.

Naturally, I felt compelled to see it for myself, and despite being only eleven, she allowed me to watch it. It terrified me beyond words. Since then, no other horror movie has managed to affect me the same way!

This production feels more like an expensive children's TV show than a proper film. From what I can discern, the antagonist appears to be a massive horde of chocolate-coated espresso beans, a notion seemingly confirmed by the subtitles naming it 'Insomnia.' Initially, when it's stated that a civilization was destroyed by insomnia, I got excited thinking, "Wow, a nihilistic martial arts movie!" But unfortunately, that wasn't the case. However, one might label it experimental cinema, especially with a scene where the villain is choked by an elderly man's lengthy, white eyebrows. Whether the subtitles are enabled or not, Zu Warriors remains equally nonsensical—a troubling indicator. As for the special effects, they strike me as rudimentary, landing somewhere between the stop-motion of Ray Harryhausen and the low-budget flair of Xena: Warrior Princess.

I've long admired Woody Allen and will continue to appreciate much of his earlier work, but even the most devoted fan can't overlook the tedious, pointless, and pretentious nature of this film, compounded by its dreadful acting. It feels like an empty exercise in self-indulgence, built on shaky and inconsistent foundations. The decision to mold Will Ferrell into a contrived "Woody Allen doppelgänger"—mimicking Allen's mannerisms and dialogue as if Allen himself were playing the role thirty years younger—was a catastrophic misstep, resulting in an absurd and laughable performance. As for the dialogue, what was meant to be profound philosophical musings devolves into an unintentional parody of intellectual thought, oblivious to its own comedic irony. It's truly disappointing.

This underappreciated film is a relaxed and easygoing entry in the giallo genre. It deviates from some of the typical tropes, embracing a more fluid style. The story follows a woman desperate to find her missing lover, a psychiatrist who has inexplicably disappeared. Her investigation brings her to a villa inhabited by a quirky cast of characters, and, in classic giallo fashion, murder lurks just around the corner.

The ensemble cast is impressive. Notable performers include Aldofo Celi (Thunderball), Alida Valli (Suspiria), Horst Frank (Cat o' Nine Tails), and a young Sybil Danning, who would later become an '80s scream queen. Rosemary Dexter, though lesser-known, delivers a strong performance as the film’s lead.

A standout element of Eye in the Labyrinth is its unconventional music. Unlike most gialli, it features a jazz-rock fusion soundtrack composed by Roberto Nicolosi, reminiscent of Miles Davis’ work on In A Silent Way. This exceptional score sets a unique tone for the film, enhancing its leisurely vibe and perfectly complementing the sunlit, coastal landscapes that dominate the visuals.

An actor's debut film is typically one you can skip—it's frequently that initial project where the inexperience of everyone involved is glaringly obvious, and this movie is a prime example.

Even by 1982 standards, this film is so terrible that it becomes unintentionally hilarious. Shot entirely in the Chicago area on a clearly limited budget, the performances by the entire cast are rigid, lifeless, and exaggerated, resembling a mix of a high school production and subpar community theater. Background traffic noise often overwhelms the dialogue, which is itself cringe-worthy, overly explicit, and feels forced rather than natural. The scenes are awkward and disjointed, and despite the story spanning several years, neither the children nor the adults show any signs of aging.

I believe a Christian film can appeal to a broad, secular audience, but too often, the filmmakers become so preoccupied with 'The Message' or, in this case, their personal connection to the story that they neglect essential elements of good filmmaking.

The Unborn is a commendable low-budget horror film that taps into the anxieties surrounding pregnancy. Brooke Adams delivers a consistently strong performance, alongside b-movie veteran James Karen, though the rest of the cast falls into the typical b-movie mediocrity. Surprisingly, the soundtrack by Gary Numan stands out as a highlight. Henry Dominic’s screenplay shows a surprising depth for this genre, despite a subtle undercurrent of misogyny. Rodman Fender’s direction is passable at best, with a few gratuitous jump scares that feel unnecessary. If you admire Brooke Adams—whose film career deserves far more recognition—this movie is worth watching for her reliably excellent performance.

The BFG, a beloved classic by Roald Dahl, fails to capture its enchanting essence in this animated adaptation. While the storyline closely follows Dahl’s original tale, absolving John Hambley’s script of any major fault, the film falls flat due to its uninspired animation, sluggish pacing, and underwhelming voice performances. One would anticipate a lively, colorful, and joyful cinematic experience, but instead, the movie is a dreary ordeal that quickly becomes tiresome to watch. For children unfamiliar with the story, the book should be their first encounter with this tale; the film risks turning them away from a true children’s masterpiece.

Sophie, a young orphan voiced by Amanda Root, resides in a harsh orphanage run by the unkind Mrs. Clonkers. Late one night, while gazing out the window, Sophie catches sight of a towering figure stealthily moving through the village. Noticing it has been spotted, the figure extends a giant hand through the window, plucks Sophie from her bed, tucks her into a vast pocket, and vanishes into the darkness. Soon, Sophie learns she has been taken by a giant from a mysterious realm.

What a travesty...

You forgot to brush your teeth, and somehow that trivial oversight becomes the premise for a drags-on-forever 30-minute episode. Picture this: a couple of kids causing a ruckus, followed by the inevitable dad stepping in to deliver a stern lecture because, well, that’s his role.

Of course, Uncle Joey can’t resist chiming in with his bizarre sound effects and goofy expressions. Then there’s Uncle Jesse, strolling in with his signature black leather jacket and jeans, striking a pose for a few minutes while everyone reminisces about how Mom would have handled things if she were still here.

It’s all a series of quirky, pointless escapades, spun into an unnecessarily drawn-out narrative with no real substance.

Full House doesn’t just bore you to the brink of tears—it practically fast-forwards your aging process by a factor of twenty.

This film ranks among the most iconic representations of French sexual liberation in the 1970s, featuring Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere in sharply sardonic roles. It also belongs to the wave of dark psychological dramas from the 1970s and 1980s, alongside works like *Serie Noire*, *Buffet Froid*, and *Beau Pere*, all directed by Bertrand Blier.

On a separate note, I’d like to address a prior comment about the movie: the English translated title significantly deviates from the original French. While it’s accurate that the main characters are metaphorically “going places,” the French title could be directly translated as “the waltz dancers,” a subtle reference to the motion of the testicles.

Mesmerizing to behold, but what would be your initial reaction upon discovering Atlantis yourself? Dive in and explore! This was a unique chance to transport audiences to an extraordinary realm. Regrettably, Disney fell back on its predictable, formulaic storytelling.

This movie is simultaneously the worst and the best I’ve ever watched. Sci-Fi original films are expected to be terrible, and that’s exactly what makes them so entertaining! The line, “I like my dinosaur meat well done!” might just be the greatest quote of all time. The plot feels like it was conjured up in a haze of a pot-fueled daydream. I can picture it: the writers stumbling out of a long night of getting high and battling it out on Dance Dance Revolution, only to cobble together this wild concept—space marines landing on an alien planet crawling with dinosaurs and dotted with medieval houses, all to safeguard a science team researching the bizarre world. Absolute genius! It ticks every box on the Sci-Fi original movie checklist: guns, dinosaurs, medieval vibes, space travel, and, of course, atrocious acting.

So, definitely give this movie a watch, but don’t bother buying it.

The characters are utterly unappealing, with the protagonist embodying the most grating traits of Woody Allen, Paul Provensa, and Paul Reiser combined. The forced and predictable scenes, such as the painfully obvious setup of the kid on rollerblades inevitably knocking someone over, were simply nauseating in their awfulness.

The film was understated yet remarkably touching. It portrayed the often harsh reality of gender segregation in society with a subtle finesse. There was a sharp, bittersweet humor woven into the narrative. The use of non-professional actors lent the movie a raw, authentic feel, enhancing its realism. Additionally, the film carried a documentary-like quality. Among the most compelling moments were the scenes where the girls, forbidden from watching the game, listened intently to a soldier—who was meant to supervise them—narrating the match with fervor. For Iranians, the familiar scenes of jubilant cheering and street dancing after a victory evoke a deep sense of national pride. Even for those unfamiliar with Iranian culture, the universal appeal of these moments is undeniable!

As the traditions of Christmas have transformed over time, whether focused on religious or secular aspects, it remains a season when people are expected to treat each other with greater kindness. However, this sentiment seems to have eluded Ebenezer Scrooge, a merchant and moneylender in 19th century London.

Scrooge's nephew remarks that his uncle completely disregards Christmas, dismissing it as mere humbug. The compassion that once resided in Scrooge has long since vanished, leaving him as cold and unyielding as his 20th century parallel, Mr. Potter of Bedford Falls, New York.

Yet, in Charles Dickens' narrative, it is never too late for redemption. A solitary ghost and three spirits visit Scrooge, guiding him toward a profound transformation.

A Christmas Carol stands as a perennial holiday classic, often overshadowing its role as a poignant social critique of 19th century Britain, much like Oliver Twist. The characters depicted in this story belong to the middle and lower classes. The Cratchit family, though slightly better off than the street dwellers in Oliver Twist, must still fight to maintain their modest status.

This film is a masterpiece of design, utterly flawless in every aspect. The set, lighting, sound, and plot are all crafted with perfection. The script serves as an enticing invitation to a sophisticated game, centered around a deceptively straightforward mission.

Paxton delivers a stellar performance, showcasing impeccable mannerisms and vocal nuances without a single misstep. Every frame is carefully constructed, and as the movie progresses beyond its first hour, unexpected twists emerge in rapid succession. While it may not claim the title of the year's best film, it is undoubtedly a brilliantly polished gem, crafted for those with a taste for complexity.

As a child, my babysitter was an avid fan of Scooby Doo, so I ended up watching numerous older episodes. Personally, I’m not a fan of the franchise, which makes it puzzling why I even had the TV on when this new show premiered. To my surprise, I actually enjoyed it. For me, Shaggy and Scooby have always been the only captivating characters—*bracing for backlash from other character enthusiasts*—so I appreciate that this version centers solely on them. However, this focus might not sit well with fans of the classic series. I’m impressed by the voice acting, particularly Dr. Phinius Phibes, whose performance I admired even before learning it was Jeff Bennett. Additionally, Jim Meskimen’s portrayal of Robi feels vibrant, as if he’s truly relishing his role. I also find the techies amusing, with their slightly quirky, perhaps autistic-like traits, and their eagerness to engage in role-playing games similar to Dungeons and Dragons or reenact scenes reminiscent of Star Wars (though not explicitly named as such in the show).

"The Crush" offers a fairly enjoyable romantic comedy experience for its initial two-thirds, aiming to emulate a British version of "Sex and the City" with its focus on 40-something friends navigating love. 

I was particularly amused by the reversal of the typical trope with the young, attractive male lead, though his character lacks depth (and, frankly, we see little of his physical appeal, despite Kenny Doughty’s evident charm deserving more screen time). 

The film places significant emphasis on the age disparity in a younger man/older woman relationship, far more than was highlighted in either adaptation of "Sabrina" (both of which I dislike) or in real-life pairings like Douglas and Zeta-Jones or Dion and her Svengali-like partner.

Andie MacDowell, playing an expatriate, is surrounded by familiar faces from British drama and comedy, including the sharp-witted Anna Chancellor, whose presence adds a delightful edge.

However, the plot takes abrupt, contrived turns toward the conclusion, feeling like forced resolutions. It wasn’t until the credits rolled that a deeper issue dawned on me. Much like "Sex and the City," the writer and director—here, debutant John McKay—is male, and it seems he may have intended to craft a story about three gay men, possibly exploring their journey of coming out.

I first encountered this film on MST3K, and while the humor had me in stitches, I don’t believe the movie itself was terrible. Admittedly, it was somewhat difficult to follow and clearly made on a shoestring budget. However, it boasted a plot reminiscent of Hitchcock, and I can sincerely say that I found the non-MST3K version quite engaging. This film is practically begging for a Hollywood reboot.

Redline is a cheap imitation of Fast & Furious, lacking any of the charm or redeeming features that might salvage it. It doesn’t require a complex narrative filled with unexpected twists, but it desperately needs SOME substance! This film is akin to a adult movie, with a flimsy storyline and dialogue squeezed into a mere 60 seconds at the start and finish. Yet, it’s even worse here, as it fails to deliver any value for your money. The film is excruciatingly dull, featuring implausible race sequences and a tragic misuse of stunning, expensive cars that almost seem tainted by their association with this disaster. Yes, the lead actress is attractive, but who is so desperate for on-screen eye candy to endure this? It feels as though the director randomly pulled dialogue and plot fragments from a hat, consulting a magic 8-ball for every scene change. No serious racing enthusiast or anyone with even a basic understanding of the sport could watch these race scenes and find any enjoyment.

Kirstie Alley appears slightly trimmer in this film, though the difference is minimal. She stars alongside a man resembling MacGyver, complete with bleached blond hair. The movie's central idea revolves around an older woman—shockingly labeled as 50!—who struggles to get her screenplay produced due to ageism. To circumvent this, she enlists her younger nephew to pretend he’s the writer. The concept isn’t fresh, and the execution falls flat with poor acting, absurd dialogue, and a far-fetched plot. A secondary storyline involving a writer harboring a crush or admiration for Alley’s character feels inexplicable and unnecessary. The actor playing Kirstie’s brother delivers such a stiff and ill-suited performance that their shared scenes are painful to endure. In short, there’s little to praise about this film. Steer clear.

This might just be the absolute worst film I’ve ever watched. Once again, I fell into the trap of purchasing a movie based on an intriguing synopsis on the back and an appealing front cover. After this disappointing experience, along with another film, "Malevolence," which I’ve also reviewed, I’ve definitely learned my lesson. I’m a fan of horror movies set in remote locations like woods, deserts, or farms. This film claims to be set in the Texas woods, but it looks more like it was shot in someone’s backyard. The production quality is arguably the poorest I’ve encountered. The acting was utterly dreadful, and the storyline bore no resemblance to the description on the cover. I even attempted to sell it to F.Y.E. and a local store that purchases used DVDs, but neither would accept it—that’s how abysmal this sorry excuse for a movie is. I’ve seen my share of terrible films (like "Troll 2"), but this one truly stands out as the worst. I didn’t think anything could surpass "Troll 2" in awfulness, but I was sorely mistaken. Do not purchase this movie unless it’s given to you for free, and even then, think twice.

This visually refined and clever game unfolds as 'a story within a story.' The central character, scriptwriter Bart Klever, is locked in a relentless battle with his latest script—which also happens to be the screenplay of the film we are viewing. Within the movie, Bart is depicted as a scriptwriter crafting the very script that defines his struggle, making his creative conflict a core theme of the narrative. The setting, primarily the apartment where Bart works and looks after his young daughter, becomes a character in itself. This intimate space provides a rich playground for illusions created through manipulations of space, light, color, and the presence of a pair of cats. The seemingly straightforward world of the room grows increasingly complex due to the fluctuating dimensions of the script, which is shaped by the filmmaker's interventions and displayed on a computer monitor, acting as a contrasting element to the ever-shifting surroundings. The continually changing perspectives deepen the mystery, prompting questions like: What constitutes 'truth' versus 'illusion'? Which of the worlds we observe holds prominence over the others? Is there any fixed point of reference within this narrative landscape?

This film, with its tacky appearance and lack of charm, failed to captivate even the children in the audience, save for a single, somewhat funny bathroom gag. Christopher Lloyd, clearly beyond his best days, comes across as weary and unengaging in this part, not aided by the pitiful attempts at humor from the writers. Elizabeth Hurley's performance in what was meant to be a comedic role is painfully unpolished. Jeff Daniels and Darryl Hannah manage to escape embarrassment. Ultimately, there seems to be no justification for producing this movie, particularly when inevitable comparisons arise with Robin Williams's frequently masterful spontaneity in Mork & Mindy.

This film falls short in every way compared to its predecessor: it lacks energy, flair, and actors willing to embrace over-the-top performances. Even the script feels subpar. I was left puzzled by several plot points. If Farrah isn’t truly committed to a career, why does she have a manager—and why is he investing his time in her? If Kate and Barney are supposed to be serious “artists,” why would they join something as gimmicky as The Mother of All Jiggle Shows (reminiscent of the "Brady Bunch" movie where Robert Reed dreams of Shakespeare but ends up on a kitschy set)? They weren’t household names, but they weren’t struggling unknowns either. While the film gets some historical details right (like the poster release predating Farrah’s show), it fabricates events like Silverman dismissing pitches for "Funniest Home Videos" and "American Idol," and Spelling promising his daughter Tori a future show of her own—none of which happened.

What troubled me most was the misrepresentation of Spelling’s role. He’s portrayed as the show-runner and creator, which is far from the truth. The depiction of how he supposedly “conceives” the idea for CA is downright absurd.

Moreover, how could Spelling and Goldberg enforce Farrah’s oral contract while the others had formal agreements? And why didn’t Farrah or Bernstein speak up about this discrepancy?

In fact, this 1999 film boasts impressive production quality. The cast is both visually appealing and moderately skilled. Thankfully, it avoids the cliché of countless goons firing endlessly without ever landing a shot, and there are no over-the-top car chases or crashes that senselessly destroy expensive, stunning vehicles.

The interior sets appear convincingly contemporary from an architectural standpoint, and the technology seems up to par. However, there’s a notable exception in the high-tech computer room, which looks like it’s stocked with relics from a 1950s electronics lab. Additionally, the makeup on the corpses had me chuckling—it’s not traditional pancake makeup but rather something resembling dried pancake batter smeared on their skin. This is presumably meant to suggest calcification of the bodies, though the film leaves the explanation of how a virus could cause such a transformation as a puzzle for the audience to solve.

And speaking of the virus, I wish I could say this isn’t the most absurd premise I’ve encountered in a sci-fi horror film, but that would be dishonest. A computer virus that spreads through television or computer screens and somehow morphs into a deadly biological agent? Honestly, it’s a stretch too far. Warp drives, in comparison, seem almost plausible.

This film is exceptional for three primary reasons. Visually, it’s a feast for the eyes with its stunning aesthetics. I was captivated by the vibrant color palette that runs through the entire movie, complemented by remarkable costumes and breathtaking sets. The cinematography, which appears high-end (though it likely wasn’t), enhances the overall visual impact. Additionally, I’m a sucker for narratives about outsiders and misfits uniting to form a family. While such stories can sometimes feel clichéd, this one avoids those pitfalls. The ensemble cast brilliantly brings to life characters who are deeply flawed yet incredibly endearing. Alan Larkin stands out as particularly impressive (his presence, along with the van and the road movie vibe, reminded me of last year’s favorite, *Little Miss Sunshine*). I was also introduced to Fabrizio Bentivoglio, a fascinating actor, though I found Til Schweiger’s performance occasionally grating. The opening scene, along with the moments where their tricks go hilariously wrong, brought plenty of laughs. The film masterfully balances humor and heartfelt emotion throughout. I was especially fond of the ending. Above all, the central magician theme ties it together beautifully—a skilled magician directs the audience’s gaze to craft an illusion, and this movie does exactly that.

The title alone speaks volumes. I watched this movie with my father when it was released, and as a Korean War veteran, he held immense respect for the man portrayed. However, a major drawback of the film is its narrow focus on just a brief segment of his life. The full scope of his story could have been transformed into an extraordinary biographical epic, though the production costs for such a project would be staggering to consider.

Some reviews criticize the man’s flaws, which feels like taking cheap shots. The film’s central theme, "Duty, Honor, Country," isn’t just empty rhetoric from a decorated officer; it represents a profound testament to one man’s unwavering commitment to his nation.

Ironically, Gregory Peck, known for his liberal views, seemed to deeply understand the essence of the man. He delivers a compelling performance, skillfully balancing the portrayal of a fearless general with the compassionate, human side of the figure.

This clever film explores romance across different eras, following Keaton as he searches for his beloved in the Stone Age, ancient Rome, and the modern 1920s. In each timeline, Keaton plays his iconic timid character, competing against Wallace Beery for the affection of his lady love. Among the three settings, the Roman segment stands out as my favorite, despite its admittedly cheesy elements. I was particularly entertained by the lion—clearly a man in a costume—and the bizarre snow-covered chariot race. Above all, Keaton’s incredible acrobatics stole the show. While each era offers its own delightful, old-fashioned charm, this film may not be his finest work, but it remains a remarkable and entertaining piece. Definitely worth a watch!

When I first got involved with this movie, I anticipated that it would be widely mocked. To my surprise, it garnered appreciation from viewers over the age of 7. Personally, I found some enjoyment in it, but mainly because my 10-year-old sister and I spent the entire time poking fun at it.

I apologize, Jordan, but I found the acting to be subpar. A film is often doomed when the lead actor struggles to deliver a convincing performance. Additionally, the script and plot offered little to salvage the overall experience. The character Pamela, in particular, struck me as incredibly weak and almost pitiful.

Despite these criticisms, I did appreciate the performances of a few actors, including the talented Spencer, Hollywood, and Ronnie. Unfortunately, their efforts weren’t enough to save the film.

There are two aspects of this movie that continue to baffle me:

1.) The idea that Spencer’s character would fall for her. Frankly, it felt off-putting. Although I researched and found that in real life, he is only about four years older than her, the age gap in "Go Figure" appeared much more significant. While Jordan is undoubtedly attractive, her portrayal in the film made the pairing seem implausible.

I might be giving this movie more praise than it warrants, perhaps because it’s Halloween, and I’m fresh from a visit to "Knott's Scary Farm," feeling in the mood for an over-the-top, cheesy Halloween flick.

Plus, it only set me back a single dollar.

Normally, I’d fast-forward through a film like this to reach the highlights, but for some reason, I held back this time, though I’m not entirely sure why. Right from the opening scenes, it was clear this wasn’t a "serious" film, not even qualifying as a B-movie. It falls more into the realm of DeCoteau’s so-called "horror" flicks like "The Brotherhood," shot on film-look video with a budget that seems barely more than pocket change (I kept half-expecting one of his stereotypical buff college guys to stumble into frame, awkwardly adjusting his underwear). The production lacks cutaway shots (likely due to the cost of multiple camera setups) and features flat lighting, yet... it’s difficult to describe. There’s something oddly captivating about seeing a director with virtually no budget manage to create a somewhat passable film. The mere fact that he pulls off a half-decent job is impressive in itself. This movie isn’t without its strengths— the acting is passable, the cinematography is decent (though overly bright for a horror vibe), and there are

Sidney Franklin's "The Good Earth" has earned its place as a classic due to its enduring narrative and exceptional performances, particularly by Luise Rainer, who received an Oscar for her role as O-Lan. Rainer's portrayal is so transformative that she becomes almost unrecognizable. With minimal dialogue in a lengthy film, she conveys profound emotion through her facial expressions and physicality, embodying a Chinese character so convincingly that those unfamiliar with her work might believe she is of that heritage.

The film's relevance persists as it delves into a rags-to-riches tale and the universal themes intertwined with such a journey. After enduring years of hardship and scarcity, Lung and O-Lan attain wealth, only to discover that material gain brings an empty existence. It is not until they reconnect with the land, battling a dramatic locust invasion—rendered with still-impressive and visually striking special effects—that they rediscover true contentment. This familiar storyline, presented through the distinctive lens of a Chinese family’s experience, especially groundbreaking for 1937, cements the film’s classic status. Ultimately, it powerfully underscores that wealth holds little value without the bonds of friends and family.

All the criticism labeling this as a bad movie is absurd. In fact, I consider it the finest film I've ever watched. The storyline is outstanding, and the performances by the actors are among the best I've seen. I wouldn't dream of criticizing any of them. This movie stands as the greatest, and it will remain so in my eyes.

Busy Phillips delivered an outstanding performance, excelling in both comedy and drama. While Erika Christensen was solid, Busy undeniably dominated the screen. Her work here is a refreshing highlight following her role in The Smokers, a film that fell short of expectations. If Busy doesn’t earn a nomination for this movie, it would be a travesty. Skip Mona Lisa Smile and watch Home Room instead.

I have a strong dislike for Hollywood, yet my passion for cinema compels me to sit through subpar films in theaters. I had high hopes for *Vanilla Sky*, wishing it would either stay true to the original *Open Your Eyes* or carve out its own unique path. Unfortunately, it attempted to do both and failed miserably.

The film started off promisingly. I’m a big fan of Radiohead and wished there had been more of their music. However, by the end, we’re subjected to *Good Vibrations* by The Beach Boys—an jarring shift from great to terrible. There were a couple of decent tracks in the club scenes and perhaps a few others, but why did they have to blast *Good Vibrations* during the climax? It was more irritating than confusing or even intentional. Worst of all, it had no relevance to the plot. If you’re going to include songs, at least give them some thematic weight. Something like Radiohead’s *Kid A* would have been far more fitting. Oh well.

The director did manage to create a standout club scene, which was impressive. Beyond that, though, the movie felt like a pretentious mess, as if it assumed audiences would automatically grasp its meaning. Those who could appreciate its depth likely prefer subtitled films, while the rest are left baffled.

Upon the United States' entry into World War I, the government compelled Hollywood to produce propaganda films. Among these, THE LITTLE American stands out, largely due to the presence of Mary Pickford.

Pickford portrays a young woman caught in a romantic dilemma between two suitors: Jack Holt, who is German, and Raymond Hatton, who is French. The escalating war interrupts her choice as both men join the military.

Tragedy strikes when the ship carrying Pickford is sunk by the Germans, reminiscent of the Lusitania disaster, due to its cargo of munitions. In a powerful moment, Pickford, standing on a lifeboat, confronts the German commander with fervent accusations. Her journey takes a dramatic turn when she encounters Holt and Hatton again while held captive at a château.

Director Cecil B. DeMille crafts a memorable scene as Pickford and Holt traverse a devastated village. They come upon a church reduced to a single standing wall, against which a large crucifix is mounted. In a striking visual, the wall falls away, yet the figure of Jesus remains, eerily floating in the air—a surreal highlight in a film that otherwise adheres to a direct and unadorned narrative style.

Pickford, as always, captivates with her performance.

Last night, I watched "I, Robot" on DVD and this morning, curiosity led me to peruse the reviews. It appears that the movie has sharply divided opinions among IMDb's critical audience, sparking not just debate but also a fair share of derogatory exchanges.

I'm somewhat taken aback by this division, as the film doesn't strike me as exceptional or even particularly good, nor does it sink to the depths of awful or truly bad. Instead, what "I, Robot" truly embodies is a sense of disappointment. It's disheartening to see how eagerly American moviegoers consume and praise trite, clichéd remakes as if they were groundbreaking masterpieces. The film screams "recycled" from every angle—be it the storyline, which clumsily blends Asimov’s themes with contemporary high-octane action, or Will Smith’s portrayal of a quick-witted, indomitable cynic, or even the special effects that seem lifted straight from "The Matrix" and other sources.

Sadly, "I, Robot" might just be the quintessential action flick for the current demographic: a shallow narrative, banally clever dialogue, and an overload of adrenaline-pumping sequences. Smith delivers a lackluster performance, reinforcing the notion that Hollywood's ongoing quest to mold him into a black Bruce Willis continues to fall flat. The plot is riddled with inconsistencies and gaps of varying significance, though I doubt many will pause to ponder them.

In Bridgeport, Richard Fenton (Johnathon Schaech), a disturbed high school teacher, becomes dangerously fixated on his teenage student, Donna Keppel (Brittany Snow). Donna is forced to watch as he brutally murders her family in a twisted attempt to keep her close, but he is ultimately captured and sentenced to life in prison. Three years on, Donna, still grappling with trauma, is undergoing therapy and reliant on medication. On the night of her prom, she attends a celebration at the Pacific Grad Hotel with her boyfriend Bobby (Scott Porter) and two other couples. Unbeknownst to them, Richard has escaped from prison and is now hiding on the same floor of the hotel, relentlessly pursuing Donna while slashing through her friends and hotel staff who stand in his way.

The slasher film "Prom Night" is a forgettable amalgamation of tired tropes, displaying a complete absence of originality. The plot is superficial and absurd, compounded by Johnathon Schaech's unconvincing portrayal of a deranged killer.
