The screenplay is so predictable that viewers can easily guess the unfolding events of each subsequent scene. My rating is a three.

Title (Brazil): "A Morte Convida Para Dançar" ("The Death Invites to Dance")

This film is arguably one of the most disappointing I've encountered in some time.

Is Heath Ledger considered a heartthrob? I found his appearance rather unappealing. Had I been aware that he and Naomi Watts are a couple in real life, I might have been less baffled during the interminably long two hours, trying to understand her attraction to him.

Orlando Bloom as a heartthrob? With his unkempt beard and perpetually startled expression, I struggle to see the appeal.

Rachel Griffiths delivered her typically stellar performance, but Geoffrey Rush seemed eager to leave the set at the earliest opportunity.

Am I expected to sympathize with bank robbers and killers? This movie pales in comparison to Butch Cassidy, which genuinely entertained. Instead, this was predictable, full of clichés, and utterly dull. We remained in our seats, hoping for improvement, but it never came.

The final 10-15 minutes were inadvertently comical. Heath and his crew are barricaded in a frontier hotel, with women and children suffering due to their actions, which is hardly amusing. However, the sight of them emerging from the hotel in armor was unintentionally funny, as it reminded us of the Black Knight.

I found it difficult to connect with this film on any level—intellectually, emotionally, or aesthetically. The dialogue felt heavy and failed to draw me in. I struggled to form any attachment to the characters, leaving me indifferent to their stories, and I’m at a loss to highlight many positive aspects of the experience.

I’ve come across opinions suggesting that a deeper understanding of obscure Catholic theology is necessary to fully grasp the film’s meaning. As an atheist, I acknowledge that I may lack familiarity with the intricacies of Catholicism. However, I’ve watched numerous films exploring religious themes that have resonated with me due to their universal relevance to the human experience, without requiring specialized knowledge or specific beliefs.

"The Bourne Ultimatum" kicks off in the midst of a breathless chase, erupting into a heart-racing thriller as Jason Bourne (Matt Damon, in top form) hunts for the architects of the CIA black-ops program that molded him into a lethal assassin, all in a desperate bid to uncover his true identity. David Strathairn brings a chilling intensity as the shadowy figure pulling the strings, joining the familiar ensemble of Joan Allen (outstanding) and Julia Stiles (barely noticeable).

As with the second film in the trilogy, I found myself wishing that Paul Greengrass would steady his jittery handheld camera during the brief moments of calm. Yet, this frenetic style brilliantly captures the tense, suffocating atmosphere of close-quarters combat and proves just as effective in the predominantly foot-based chases across rooftops, punctuated by the occasional massive vehicular collision. A key charm of the Bourne saga lies in its relentless globe-trotting and the almost fantastical manipulation of technology and communication, which appear to defy the boundaries of physics and modern capabilities. The Bourne universe thrives in a gritty, hyper-realistic realm laced with tech-driven wizardry, where coincidences stretch believability as characters inexplicably converge at just the right moment.

This animated film, though peculiar at times, offers a surprising depth and emotional resonance compared to many other cartoon movies. It centers on a young girl at a camp, struggling with low self-esteem and lacking friends, save for a brother and sister duo who share her misery. Her despair reaches a breaking point, leading her to make a desperate pact with a devilish demon. Despite its dark turn, the story feels strikingly real. At her lowest, the girl recognizes her mistake, experiences genuine remorse, and undergoes a transformation. In doing so, she teaches the sinister, mystical creature the human capacity for love. The sibling twins also grow, finding their own sense of self-worth by aiding small bear characters. While certain aspects of the movie may seem odd, it delivers a powerful, positive message for children and remains an enjoyable watch. The music, composed by Stephen Bishop (known for *Tootsie* songs), further elevates the film’s charm.

This film is perfect for unwinding with a glass of wine, a cozy fire, and your feet propped up. It’s easy to follow, requiring little mental effort, making it an ideal choice after a tiring day. Don’t expect realism—if you’re looking for something profound, this isn’t it—but it’s incredibly humorous. The idea of a businessman willingly living in a slum for a time, and even growing to like it, is absurdly amusing. I highly recommend giving it a watch.

Undoubtedly, Ealing comedies are exceptional, yet this particular film shines as one of the finest in my opinion.

The core idea of the movie revolves around a tiny section of Pimlico in London being revealed as part of Burgundy rather than the UK. The story unfolds as we witness the residents' struggle to protect a treasure unearthed after a bomb detonation, while fending off black market traders who quickly exploit the absence of UK law and rationing in this unique territory. Tensions rise when the government seals the border, turning the residents into captives on their own street, prompting a fierce resistance against the establishment.

Forced to ration water and food in their quest for justice, the residents find themselves in a worse state than before the ordeal began, which introduces the film's moral lesson. Their spirits plummet as they lose all their food supplies, leading them to consider surrender. However, in a heartwarming turn, the entire city of London rallies to their aid, sending an abundance of food that reignites their resolve to fight on.

This film strikes the perfect chord from start to finish, with outstanding performances by the cast.

I recall being five years old when my parents mistook it for a typical animated film, only to be shocked when the scenes turned provocative and violent. I must admit, this movie has the potential to offend just about everyone with its indiscriminate satire, yet it’s undeniably hilarious and surprisingly profound. I highly recommend it to fans of cult classics. Additionally, check out *Fritz the Cat* and *The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat*. If I’m not mistaken, these were also directed by Ralph Bakshi. They follow a cat navigating tough times with family, life on the streets, and various jobs. When I was old enough, I rented all of these films. Due to its controversial title at the time, *Coonskin* was alternatively released as *Street Fighter*. Ralph Bakshi also directed *Cool World*, featuring a young Brad Pitt. Another animated film, *Heavy Traffic*, explores the gritty street life of a young man.

Drones, tribal drumming, grating synthesizer sounds, and children’s voices fill the soundtrack. This is "world music" at its most condescending. The film feels like a poorly made travelogue, utterly failing to engage. Its fatal flaw lies in the disjointed sequences—jumping from India to Egypt, South America to Africa, and beyond, with no transitions or visual logic to explain the abrupt shifts across continents. There's no deeper message conveyed through the imagery, just clips of people from developing nations, often carrying "baskets on their heads," as another critic noted, trudging along as if this mundane act holds profound significance. If the filmmakers aimed to create a music video showcasing the Third World, they could have simply traveled a few hundred miles south from where the strongest scenes of *Koya* were filmed and shot in Mexico. That would have been a far more fitting backdrop for a theme like "life in transformation."

Instead, they opted for a chaotic global tour, pieced together with overprocessed, tedious slow-motion shots that numb the mind. The sole redeeming quality of this film is that it isn’t quite as unbearable as *Naqoyqatsi*.

Allow me to begin by saying that I generally appreciate Renny Harlin's directorial approach, and the cinematographer deserves praise for certain captivating shots. While I thoroughly enjoyed Harlin's works like "Elm Street 4" and "Die Hard 2," there’s a crucial element absent from this film. That element, unfortunately, is a decent script. While dialogue in such films often falls short, this movie sets a new benchmark for inanity. The lines are so poorly written that I’d rather not recall a single one. Moreover, the delivery of these lines is lamentable, more fitting for a low-budget adult film than an action-adventure flick. It seems as though Harlin believed that dragging out the dialogue could somehow salvage the script. Regrettably, that assumption was incorrect.

What’s truly disappointing is the waste of talented actors in ill-suited roles with abysmal dialogue. I’ve never been particularly fond of Stallone, but when he outshines Lithgow, Turner, and especially Rooker—the weakest of the lot—something is clearly amiss. Lithgow delivered an unforgettable villain in "Ricochet," yet here, his performance fails to impress.

Lessons from "The List":

Even with a competent cinematographer, a talented actress, and Malcolm McDowell, this film still falls flat.

Don't expect a refund from Blockbuster.

Despite his reservations about the script, Malcolm McDowell gives his all.

Chuck Carrington is in dire need of acting lessons.

Invest in a skilled screenwriter.

It feels like a personal punishment, perhaps even from Jesus, to have spent $5.50 on this film.

When crafting a movie, an ending seems optional. Just leave the story vague, unresolved, and dull enough to lull the audience to sleep before the credits roll. Brilliant.

Apparently, any ordinary landlord can reverse death with a simple cross drawn on a window. Better start networking.

Your maid might just have the power to sing you back from the dead.

Chuck Carrington really needs to work on his acting skills.

Bringing this movie home will earn you nothing but scorn and ridicule from your roommate.

Sorry, but apologies won't cut it.

There's a certain charm to the cheesy horror films of the '70s that you can't help but adore. Unlike the predictable slasher movies of today, these K-tel gems manage to evoke genuine fear without leaning on overused tropes.

This particular B movie delves into the chaotic production of another B movie, with disastrous consequences. Faith Domergue, known from *This Island Earth*, plays a washed-up B movie starlet who is cast in a film about a string of gruesome murders that haunted a family’s home. Her boyfriend, who also directs the film and bears a striking resemblance to a gruff Gordon Jump, is racing against time to shoot on location. Meanwhile, the Ken doll-like co-star stumbles upon a book of Tibetan chants, which they decide to incorporate into the script for added "authenticity"—a decision they soon regret.

John Carradine, far removed from his days of searching for the elusive 17th gland in *The Unearthly*, now plays the humble caretaker of the estate. He goes about his routine tasks, though he frequently clashes with the irritable director.

The tension escalates gradually: a dead cat appears, John Carradine is seen near a grave, and the horror crescendos with a staggering seven murders—at least the body count lives up to its promise. It's a pity, though, that the ghoul in the story didn’t quite grasp the bigger picture.

Could anyone identify the specific model of pickup truck John T drove? It appears to be a mid to late 1970s Ford. This film holds a special place in my heart, and it’s also my wife’s favorite. It was the first significant movie we watched together after getting married. I’m particularly interested in the pickup because it resembles the first truck I ever drove, and I recently acquired a similar one. My goal is to restore my truck to match the one featured in the movie. Additionally, the soundtrack was fantastic, and the acting was impressive. Does anyone know the current whereabouts or background of the actress who played John’s aunt? I’m also curious if John had a stunt double for the tower scene where he nearly fell. Lastly, what year was the Mustang that Debra W drove in the show? It seemed to be a 1960s model. Thanks!

This Three Stooges film ranks equally with my other favorite, "Disorder in the Court." It's a hilarious riot that any fan of the Stooges will thoroughly enjoy.

In this movie, the Stooges are working as janitors at a recording studio when they overhear the talented Christine McIntyre perform a stunning rendition of "Voices of Spring." Christine is on the verge of signing a record deal, but she's hesitant to reveal her career aspirations to her father and demonstrate her true singing talent. After she and the others leave the studio, the Stooges decide to have some fun by playing her record and dressing Curly up as Christine. A key figure in the music industry, who could launch Christine's career, mistakes Curly for the real Christine and invites him to perform at her party. However, a disgruntled man at the event, whose solo performance is ruined by the Stooges in front of everyone, vows to seek revenge.

This is an exceptional Stooges film that should not be overlooked!

10/10

The College Girl Murders is a whirlwind of intrigue and suspense. A deranged scientist invents a nearly undetectable toxic gas, but before he can profit from his deadly creation, a mysterious hooded monk wielding a whip ends his life. The terror escalates when a college girl is murdered in a church by the same gas, prompting Scotland Yard to step in. As the murders persist, the question looms: who can apprehend this elusive killer who moves freely through the college undetected?

**What Works:**

- **The Killer's Persona.** There's an undeniable allure to a murderer cloaked in a striking red outfit reminiscent of the KKK, complete with matching red gloves. The white whip he brandishes cuts a stark contrast against the vibrant red robe, making for a visually arresting image. While the notion of a killer in such a conspicuous, fiery red, pointed hood prowling a girls' school stretches believability, the costume ranks among the most menacing I've encountered.

- **Swinging 60s Soundtrack.** The title track of The College Girl Murders is a standout, with its cool, jazzy 1960s vibe that I found irresistible. I’m eager to uncover more about this captivating piece of music.

- **Quirky Elements.** Beyond the killer's distinctive appearance, the film is peppered with odd and eccentric details that add to its unique charm.

I was deeply impressed by the film's central theme of identifying "intruders"—the Others within the fragile Self—on multiple levels, predominantly subconscious but occasionally more symbolic. These intruders permeate the entire movie: they appear at the Swiss-French border where the protagonist lives in isolation, in his persistent daydreams and nightmares, and within his deteriorating body following a heart transplant. In the latter half of the film, the protagonist himself becomes an intruder, returning to an ancient French colony in an attempt to seek redemption for past sins.

The overarching mood of the film is more bitter than tragic, steeped in regret and guilt, with a prevailing sense of failure. It paints a stark portrait of old age—seemingly independent on the surface, yet profoundly empty and lonely within. The director crafts the visuals to evoke fleeting feelings of anxiety and longing rather than to convey overt messages. Some of these images are captivating and, despite the somber tone, not without humor, resembling an absurd theater that only a sleepwalker could conjure.

(MAJOR SPOILERS) Having previously watched Takashi Miike's unsettling and violent film 'Audition,' which delved into Japanese notions of femininity, I approached 'Visitor Q'—likely shorthand for 'Visitor Question'—with curiosity. In this movie, Miike explores the dynamics of a dysfunctional family in a profoundly disturbing and grotesque manner. His surreal take on family life attempts to echo David Lynch’s disorienting and innovative style but falls short in terms of finesse and captivation. From the outset, viewers are thrust into a series of bizarre situations, starting with a scene where the father (Kenichi Endo, delivering a commendable performance) engages in a paid sexual encounter with his estranged daughter (Fujiko). Later, upon returning home, the father is struck on the head with a large rock by a mysterious figure known as "the visitor" (Kazushi Watanabe). Inexplicably, they both end up at the family’s residence. The mother (Shungiku Uchida) suffers abuse from her son (Jun Muto), who in turn is victimized by his schoolmates. The visitor, upon entering the household, imposes himself ominously into the family structure. Over time, with the visitor’s influence, the family starts to mend their fractured bonds through shocking means, including acts of lactation, violence, and murder.

I am continually struck with both awe and revulsion by the atrocities committed throughout history under the guise of religion, and the actions of the Catholic Church in Twentieth Century Ireland stand out as particularly egregious, especially when one considers that the lessons of history and the enlightenment of modern times should have served as a moderating influence.

*A Love Divided* recounts the true story of a family torn apart by senseless bigotry and prejudice, all justified by a baseless Church doctrine. The film opens with a glimpse into the idyllic life of a small Irish village, where Sheila and Sean Cloney enjoy a contented marriage and are raising two young children. Despite Sean being Catholic and Sheila Protestant, she willingly agrees to their children being brought up in the Catholic faith. Initially, there is no hint of discord between the Catholic and Protestant communities in the village. However, this harmony is soon destroyed when Sheila voices her wish for their older child to attend the Protestant school. The local priest deems this choice a "sin" and intervenes, quickly turning Sheila’s husband and the entire Catholic community against her.

This film serves as a classic case of seasoned directors of music videos and commercials venturing into their first feature-length project. Visually, the film excels with stunning imagery, impeccable camera work, sophisticated lighting, impressive CGI, and top-notch sound design, all contributing to a sleek, high-budget aesthetic. The actors also display promising talent, though even their strongest performances cannot salvage a weak storyline.

In this instance, the issue isn't just a poor plot—it's the near absence of one altogether.

Roughly half of the dialogue is reduced to repetitive exclamations like "What the hell was that?", "What was that?", and "What the hell was that?" Unfortunately, neither the characters nor the audience receive even a sliver of clarification. Much of the remaining dialogue feels so disjointed that it seems as though there was no script to begin with, leaving the actors to improvise without a clear understanding of the story.

The standout performance by Skye Bennet, portraying an autistic girl, likely shines because her role spares her from the cringe-worthy lines burdened upon the other actors.

Are you a fan of unraveling mysteries and intricate storytelling? If so, this film is tailor-made for you. Directed by Francis Leclerc, the son of the iconic French Canadian singer Félix Leclerc, this movie is a brilliant and ingenious piece of cinema. Leclerc’s signature flashy cinematography and sharp editing are on full display, complemented by an outstanding performance from Roy Dupuis, who delivers a captivating portrayal in the lead role.

The story centers on Alexandre Tourneur, a veterinarian in his 40s, who awakens from a coma after someone mysteriously unplugs his life support. As Tourneur grapples with fragmented memories, he tries to uncover who struck him while he was tending to an injured deer on the roadside. Amidst his struggle, he exhibits strange behavior, as if something—or someone—has taken control of him.

While not outright eerie, the film brims with suspense and mystery, delivered through exceptional acting. The ambiguous ending invites multiple interpretations—personally, I suspect the accident was caused by the Indigenous character—but it remains open to speculation.

I highly recommend this film and rate it an impressive 9.5/10.

This film shines like a small beacon of light amidst a gloomy season, championing the simple virtue of genuine kindness. Morgan Freeman embodies a character reminiscent of himself—a seasoned actor nearing 70. He visits a modest, somewhat dingy grocery store to study for a potential role as a store manager. Before long, he wins over the staff and shoppers, particularly a charming yet irritable young woman (Paz Vega) who manages the "10 items or less" checkout line.

"10 Items or Less" doesn't aim to deliver profound messages, nor does it claim to. It traces the burgeoning friendship between Freeman and Vega, with the older man providing guidance while she, in return, offers him a ride home after the movie company's assistant fails to show up and Freeman realizes he's forgotten his own phone number, leaving him unable to seek assistance. On a dreary Sunday afternoon in New York City, feeling a touch of melancholy, this movie lifted my spirits and banished my blues.

Ladies and Gentlemen, do not be misled by the label of "A Stanley Kubrick" film. This movie is profoundly disappointing, despite being lauded as one of the most terrifying horror films in history. True horror should instill a deep, lingering fear that haunts viewers in the dead of night. However, *The Shining* utterly fails to deliver genuine frights, presenting instead a clumsy and ineffective attempt at creating spine-chilling terror. It's clear that efforts far removed from realism rarely succeed. The only redeeming qualities of the film are the breathtaking views of the snowy valley and the striking appearance of the hotel where much of the action unfolds. As for the performances, Jack Nicholson seems utterly lost and lethargic, unsure of his role throughout. Little can be said about the bald, supporting actor, who spends most of his screen time fussing over a young child actor. While the harsh weather conditions during filming might be a temptation to blame for the film's shortcomings, they are no excuse for the tragedy that this movie represents. Sadly, with Kubrick no longer with us, there is no chance for revisions or redemption.

I’m astonished that this film was released as late as 1984. The acting is downright comical, and the storyline is among the most absurd I’ve ever encountered. Why would anyone choose an overweight Texas sheriff like Joe Don Baker to escort an Italian, whom he illegally detained in Mexico, all the way to Italy? Additionally, the movie’s title is utterly uninformative, offering no hint of the plot and serving as one of the most uninspired names for an aspiring action or cop flick I can imagine.

I’m thankful I watched this through the lens of MST3K, with Mike and the bots providing a comedic buffer. Their commentary includes jabs at the female lead’s likeness to Elaine from Seinfeld with lines like, “None of them are spongeworthy,” and relentless quips about Baker’s size. While this film might not be worse than "Mitchell," Baker’s notoriety certainly sets the tone. Right at the start, when his name appears on screen, Tom quips, “I wish I was illiterate so I wouldn’t have to read that.”

The film boasts a compellingly crafted story within its genre, encapsulating all the classic elements of a Columbo narrative. It showcases Lieutenant Columbo's unique method of engaging with his suspect, the gradual unraveling of the mystery, the presence of Columbo’s beloved dog, and the captivating cat-and-mouse dynamic, which is especially well-executed here. Additionally, the movie is peppered with refreshing humor, primarily centered around Columbo himself. Remarkably, the script shines even though the concept of Columbo pursuing a detective/murder mystery novelist isn’t entirely new, having been explored in previous Columbo films.

Under the adept direction of James Frawley, who went on to helm five more Columbo movies during the 1970s and 1980s, the film is imbued with a distinct style and features several standout, memorable scenes.

Though it ranks among the slower-paced Columbo films, it doesn't overstay its welcome with an excessive runtime. While this leisurely pacing can sometimes hinder a Columbo story, it works effectively here, likely due in no small part to the strong performances by the cast.

As with many Columbo films, the cast often includes either a prominent, well-known star or a veteran actor from the golden age of cinema.

I must confess that Al Pacino is something of a guilty pleasure for me. He was a remarkable actor until his performance in *Scent of a Woman*, where he seemed to irreversibly overindulge in his own persona. I had hoped that *City Hall*, a film I knew little about from my childhood, would turn out to be a hidden treasure—an underappreciated, forward-thinking, and captivating political thriller set in an urban landscape. Sadly, it falls short of that mark.

*City Hall* overwhelms its narrative with an excess of characters, names, and "authentic" citywide issues, creating the illusion of a sprawling, intricate plot. For a time, it seems as though the revelations will be earth-shattering once the truth unfolds. In reality, however, the numerous subplots and tangents lead to rather predictable and clichéd urban storytelling tropes like Corruption of Power, Duplicitous Politicians, and Mafia connections to law enforcement. On paper, this setup could generate gripping suspense, with the constant threat that no character is safe and anything might happen. Yet, once again, the film fails to deliver on this potential.

Regrettably, the events that unfold are entirely foreseeable, leaving us with a series of "confession" monologues. These are presumably intended to coalesce into a contemporary fable, offering a lesson on the moral ambiguity inherent in the "real world" of politics.

Let's start with the iconic theme song performed by Christopher Cross, titled "If You Get Caught Between the Moon and New York City." Even after all these years, this song remains a timeless classic, never losing its charm. It beautifully captures the essence of New York City. Moving on to the film, the talented Dudley Moore CBE takes on the role of a spoiled, drunken millionaire engaged to Jill Eikenberry’s character. Jill would later gain fame on *LA Law*. Moore’s character is attended by his exceptional British butler, portrayed by Sir John Gielgud OM, who earned an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his remarkable performance. In the story, Arthur falls for Liza Minnelli’s character, whose acting is flawless in this role, rivaling her Oscar-winning performance in *Cabaret*. Though Liza doesn’t sing in this film, she shines as a diner waitress. I also adore Geraldine Fitzgerald as the Bach family matriarch, who controls the family fortune. Her performance is outstanding, and she deserved a nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the Academy Awards. Barney Martin, widely recognized as Jerry’s dad on *Seinfeld*, plays Liza’s father and delivers a fantastic performance as well. Overall, the movie is brilliantly written, superbly acted, and masterfully executed.

Robert Duvall delivers an utterly disappointing performance in this film, mimicking William Buckley’s tone throughout with distracting consistency. His over-the-top, melodramatic style strips away any potential for genuine dramatic engagement. Whether this was intentional scene-stealing or simply a misstep, it remains the sole memorable aspect of an otherwise forgettable movie. This film ought to be used in amateur acting classes as a cautionary tale of what to avoid. Fortunately, Duvall later moved on to more significant roles and abandoned the forced cultured accent. While he excels as a character actor, that seems to be the extent of his range. In stark contrast, Klaus shines with a subtle and remarkable performance that truly stands out.

This captivating film chronicles the life of Grey Owl, a man living in 1930s Canada, and ranks alongside emotionally powerful movies like 'Rudy' and 'Awakenings'. The story begins in the later years of Grey Owl's life, guiding viewers through his most challenging yet impactful times.

The narrative centers on a Canadian Indigenous trapper who becomes an advocate for the endangered beaver, over-hunted to the brink of extinction. He also forewarns of diminishing natural landscapes and the excessive exploitation of the planet's resources—a radical idea for the 1930s, yet astonishingly well-accepted. His influence grows, transforming him into a prominent speaker with an eager audience.

Pierce Brosnan's casting might raise eyebrows, but it is far from a misstep. Skeptics should watch the film to appreciate his compelling portrayal. Alongside him, Annie Galipeau delivers a strong performance, her chemistry with Brosnan feeling genuine and unforced, a stark contrast to the contrived pairings in recent Bond movies.

I highly recommend this film to anyone who enjoys compelling drama, stunning landscapes, or stories tied to environmental advocacy. It's also suitable for family viewing, though children under 10 may struggle to follow the plot, depending on their maturity level.

I can’t recall who suggested this film, but they claimed it was among their favorites. It’s undoubtedly an odd one, akin to staring at a car wreck on the highway.

As the saying goes, truth is stranger than fiction, and the reality depicted here is truly remarkable. I’m puzzled by the idea of a fictionalized version of this documentary being released this year. How could it possibly surpass the original? The story follows Jackie Kennedy’s aunt and cousin, who withdraw from New York’s elite society to seclude themselves in the Hamptons. Over time, they become hermits, epitomizing the stereotype of “crazy cat ladies.” They might have remained out of sight if the city hadn’t threatened to condemn their property due to its squalor, prompting a rescue by Jackie herself. This documentary, filmed after the intervention, constantly leaves you wondering, “How much worse was it before?” It offers a glimpse into the underbelly of high society, and it’s absolutely riveting.

I was eagerly anticipating the release of this film during its production, but it ended up being a massive disappointment. It strayed far from the enchanting, whimsical essence of Dr. Seuss, instead coming across as crude and distasteful. I doubt Dr. Seuss himself would have given his blessing to this adaptation. In contrast, *How the Grinch Stole Christmas* was far superior, with subtle adult humor that thankfully went over my children’s heads. However, *The Cat in the Hat* was blatantly vulgar, and my kids picked up on much more than I would have preferred. Having grown up with Dr. Seuss’s stories, it was disheartening to see this beloved classic butchered on the big screen. I’m curious to see how they handle *Horton Hears a Who*. I sincerely hope it honors Dr. Seuss’s legacy in a way this one failed to do.

Unbelievable! This movie is an affront to anyone's intelligence. Seriously, who believes three kids could defeat 30 to 40 ninjas? And don't get me started on the mindless humor sprinkled throughout. This film is absolutely terrible. It’s a warning sign, only useful as a way to waste time or for accidental chuckles.

According to the DVD sleeve's synopsis, a theater troupe is gripped by fear as a mysterious murderer dubbed 'The Fiend' begins targeting them. Two reporters, accompanied by their bumbling photographer, dive into the story of 'The Fiend,' only to discover they too are in the killer's sights. Just when it seems the trio has unraveled the mystery, a surprising twist leaves the true identity of the murderer in question.

Bringing a Hollywood twist to "The Hunchback of Notre Dame," producer Sam Katzman’s "A Face in the Fog" benefits from the absence of studio sets, lending an intriguing authenticity, particularly in scenes featuring 1930s traffic toward the film’s conclusion. However, the direction leaves room for improvement, with the camera angle during the fight scene proving less than ideal. The production budget seems minimal, yet the cast, comprised of actors transitioning from silent films to talkies, delivers amiable performances under the given constraints.

**** A Face in the Fog (2/1/36) Robert F. Hill ~ Lloyd Hughes, June Collyer, Al St. John

"... for Paris is a moveable feast." — Ernest Hemingway

Countless brilliant minds have captured the essence of Paris through art, literature, music, poetry, poignant quotes, and of course, cinema. The renowned filmmaker Max Ophüls once described Paris with vivid imagery:

"It presented the glistening, rain-slicked boulevards under the glow of street lamps, morning breakfasts in Montmartre with cognac warming your glass, alongside coffee and barely warm brioche, and the nightlife of gigolos and prostitutes. Everyone in the world claims two homelands: their own and Paris."

Paris is synonymous with love and romance, a theme beautifully explored in "Paris, Je T'Aime," subtitled "Petite Romances." This anthology of short films, crafted by 18 diverse directors from across the globe, offers glimpses into the City of Light's 20 arrondissements. Each story introduces us to Parisians of varied ages, genders, ethnicities, and backgrounds, all navigating the multifaceted nature of love. In some of these "petite romances," we witness serendipitous meetings between strangers that spark immediate attraction, intimacy, and the potential for deeper connections—such as the encounter between Podalydès and Florence Muller on a Montmartre street in the opening segment.

I've been eager to watch this movie for ages, as James Merendino is a fantastic director. SLC Punk ranks among my top films, and initially, I found the first ten minutes of this movie to be a promising sequel. However, it soon started to lose momentum. The acting and direction were impressive, and overall, the film had a smooth flow, with the exception of the script. At certain points, the only thing holding my interest was the presence of Claire Forlani, whom I consider the most beautiful woman in the world. While the movie was decent, I had hoped for something more exceptional.

P.S. Keep an eye out for excellent cameo appearances by Chi McBride and Chris McDonald.

Without a doubt, this is the funniest movie I have ever watched. From the opening scene where four troublemakers are dispatched by their fathers to Wienberg Military Academy, the film establishes a comedic tone that persists throughout this zany adventure, never relenting for a moment.

Describing this movie is a challenge; the humor is so perfectly executed and ingeniously crafted that at first glance, it might seem like just another silly 80s teen comedy centered on lust. However, it is far beyond that! Born from the creative minds at MAD Magazine, *Up the Academy* delivers a unique formula and style that remains unmatched by any of Hollywood's so-called "funniest" releases in recent years. The film is packed with such juvenile, slapstick content that you might think the script was penned by a pair of 14-year-olds. If you enjoy embracing your "immature" side, this movie is a must-see. A true classic. *****

I must confess that my sole motivation for purchasing this movie was my admiration for Gackt and my utter devotion to Hyde. I anticipated a visually appealing film with plenty of eye candy for female viewers, paired with a somewhat clichéd plot. The synopsis, after all, seemed quite far-fetched. However, having just finished watching it, I am compelled to proclaim its brilliance to the world! Both Hyde and Gackt delivered profoundly moving performances, leaving my eyes still burning from tears that streamed through the latter half of the film. The story draws you in completely, making you deeply empathize with the characters by the end. The theme of vampirism, which I adore but can easily overpower or derail a narrative, is woven into the plot with such subtlety that it feels exotic yet seamless within the context, rather than a forced or extraneous element. Initially, I rated it a 9 out of 10, but upon reflection, I struggled to justify withholding that final point.

This film is simply outstanding. If you get the opportunity to watch it, don’t hesitate—rush to see it. Although it bears little resemblance to the 1932 original, Al Pacino delivers a remarkable performance as Tony Montana, truly embodying the character.

Pacino possesses a unique talent for delivering lines in a way that makes everything sound extraordinary. If you enjoyed the sharp dialogue and profanity in *Pulp Fiction* (assuming you’ve seen it), then *Scarface* is a must-watch for another perspective on how an actor can master such language. (It’s quite impressive.)

Despite the movie’s intense action and rapid pacing through time, which doesn’t always maintain a realistic timeline, it remains easy to follow. However, you need to stay alert to catch every detail. Personally, I’ve found that watching this film makes three hours fly by effortlessly—it’s truly that captivating.

This is one of those rare films that is so brilliantly acted and directed that you completely lose yourself in it, forgetting it was even made in a different era.

I discovered Act-I purely by chance over ten years ago, and the content wasn’t even what the tape’s cover label indicated. It left me astounded, overwhelmed, and in awe. Over time, I forgot about it, but nearly a decade later, it resurfaced in my thoughts. I tracked down both acts and found them even more impressive than my initial experience.

My only critique is that the Tank Police constantly emphasize their war on crime, justifying the use of tanks and heavy weaponry. Yet, they seem to struggle with criminals in a way that’s either not depicted or exaggerated. Most of the time, they appear rather lax. If their claim of being in a state of war is mere propaganda, that angle hasn’t been clearly portrayed.

I doubt the original Japanese version could match the quality of the Americanized adaptation. As for the storyline, some explanations seem to have been muddled in translation, though this flaw can be overlooked.

Chris Rock headlines this updated take on Warren Beatty's *Heaven Can Wait*, which was itself a reimagining of the 1941 film *Here Comes Mr. Jordan*. This comedic tale follows a man who dies prematurely, before achieving his lifelong aspirations, and embarks on a journey in a new, temporary body. While Beatty's character was a backup quarterback for the Los Angeles Rams, Rock's modern twist transforms the protagonist into a struggling, untalented standup comedian.

It's a riot to watch the razor-witted Rock portray a terrible comic, akin to witnessing Tom Hanks flub his way through a role as a dreadful actor. Lance Barton, Rock's character, dreams of performing at the iconic Apollo Theater on a professional night. Yet, each time he tests his material, the crowd jeers him offstage with gusto, earning him the unfortunate moniker "Booie." His jokes fall flat, and his delivery is cringe-worthy—Lance embodies everything Chris Rock is not in real life.

Beyond the stage, Lance works as a bike messenger, pedaling through city streets en route to yet another doomed performance when—BAM!—a truck collides with him. Perhaps his departure from his body was just a fraction too soon.

I received the first Bill and Ted movie as a Christmas gift, and when I spotted the sequel in a store, I couldn’t resist buying it. I found this one to be just as humorous as the original, though the storyline was significantly stranger. The concept of their personalized versions of hell was amusing, and I loved how they had to challenge Death himself. What made it even funnier was that they outsmarted him in silly games like Clue. My only critique would be the inclusion of Station and Death in the band; aside from that, I thought it was fantastic.

Whoever created this film must have been pulling a massive prank.

To begin with, the idea that this movie was produced in 1993 is utterly implausible. The clothing styles and soundtrack scream 1980s. My theory is that this film languished in obscurity for years before some eccentric distributor dusted it off and unleashed it upon an incredulous audience.

There is a storyline—sort of. A peculiar loner encounters a bearded stranger who claims that by meditating and singing his favorite tune, the loner can transform into anyone he desires. I must note here that the loner’s cherished song is none other than "London Bridge Is Falling Down." Why this particular song? Simply because he’s portrayed as utterly clueless. Barely a minute into the movie, and the level of absurdity has already hit a staggering peak. And believe it or not, it spirals even further into nonsense.

The loner, aptly dubbed the nostril picker, earns his nickname through two distinct scenes of nose-picking. That explains the title. He then opts to morph into a girl to get closer to his target.

A captivating film by Powell and Pressburger, whose body of work I’m now eager to delve into further. The story explores the blurred lines between perception and reality, highlighting the challenge of distinguishing one from the other. Stunningly filmed and performed, though David Niven appears older than the 27 years his character claims to be. It was a delight to spot a youthful Richard Attenborough. This movie provoked thought both during the viewing and long after it ended.

If you're interested in grasping the fundamentals of quantum mechanics, invest your $9 in a secondhand textbook rather than this film. I’m somewhat concerned that the money I paid might be funding Kool-Aid shipments to Guyana.

I doubt the directors successfully conveyed any clear message, though it seems they attempted to touch on multiple ideas: 1) Science can account for all our actions, suggesting our lives are predetermined; 2) Science falls short in explaining everything we do, implying we possess free will; 3) Science is, like, totally awesome, dude; 4) We are divine; 5) Reality exists solely in our perception; 6) Sarah Norman is a challenging character to portray; and 7) here, place this small paper tab on your tongue and prepare for some mind-blowing visuals.

This film is the epitome of what I dread most in cinema. It is both arrogant and reckless, offering a portrayal of the Colombian conflict that is so stereotypical and simplistic that it feels like a slap in the face to every Colombian. The acting is atrocious across the board—from Grisales, whose nude scene is downright embarrassing, to Bejarano, to Fanny Mickey, who seems like a character straight out of a Tim Burton horror, to Díaz, who struggles valiantly to breathe life into a role so flat, clichéd, and poorly scripted that all he has to work with is a mustache. Then there’s the gratuitous ending, a gore-filled mess so over-the-top and cheap it would make even Ed Wood wince. The movie fails on every level: cinematography, art direction, costumes, makeup, editing, and above all, directing. Jorge Alí Triana has never been a strong filmmaker, but even his earlier works had a shred of dignity—this one has none. I can’t find a single positive thing to say about this wasteful disaster, other than my hope that Colombian filmmakers take this malicious flop as a lesson in honesty, integrity, and responsibility.

I must begin by sharing how I discovered this film. It was during a harsh winter in Alaska, around 1990. A friend from Australia was staying with me and my girlfriend in our cramped, tiny apartment. Alaskan winters are notoriously brutal, driving most people indoors to pass the time with heavy drinking and watching whatever flickers across the TV screen. I stumbled upon this movie outside a thrift store, half-buried in a snowbank, and instantly recognized it as a hidden gem. It might just be the greatest bad movie ever made. Over the next two weeks, we watched it repeatedly while drinking like there was no tomorrow. We became so obsessed that we’d even flip the TV sideways or upside down for a fresh perspective. It’s an absolute treasure. The laughter is relentless, and the memories are unforgettable. If you ever spot this movie for rent at a video store, don’t hesitate—grab it. You won’t be disappointed!

I initially assumed *The Sentinel* would be an average film, but I was pleasantly surprised when I watched it. While it’s not a cinematic masterpiece, it’s highly entertaining, with well-executed action sequences. The movie evokes the style of TV series like *24* or *Alias*, and it also brings to mind Wolfgang Petersen’s thriller *In the Line of Fire*. If you’re expecting a groundbreaking or iconic thriller, you might be let down. However, if you approach it with modest expectations, you’re likely to enjoy *The Sentinel*.

Rating: 7

You're looking for the film "THE Gamers" by Dead Gentlemen Productions, but this isn't it. This movie lacks humor and is simply a waste of time.

Many of the positive reviews appear to be penned by thinly veiled fake accounts. It seems the creators are trying to fabricate interest in their work.

This film fails as a mockumentary. Drawing parallels to "Spinal Tap" or Christopher Guest's works feels like an affront.

The film's tone is so harsh that it's hard to believe anyone acquainted with the subject would find it amusing. Self-deprecation is valuable, but if you're the target of such mockery, you'd need to loathe yourself to appreciate this.

The movie isn't provocative due to bold satire of controversial issues; rather, it's offensive in its relentless, pitiful mediocrity.

This film ranks among my all-time favorites. The dialogue is sharp, brimming with clever puns, the cast delivers outstanding performances, and the storyline is remarkably unique.

Experience it for yourself and see why I rave about it.

THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS boasts a constellation of talent that could light up a new galaxy, yet the end result remains highly questionable. The film’s intentions and messages are undeniably admirable, and most would likely nod in agreement with its core values (Liberal Democracy is virtuous, violent fascist regimes are vile; open-mindedness is commendable, racism is deplorable). Regrettably, these themes are hammered into us with the finesse of a sledgehammer, lacking any trace of nuance.

In the end, we’re left watching a clash between utterly flawless, noble heroes and despicable villains who possess no redeeming traits whatsoever. The tension feels as contrived and predictable as a poorly staged professional wrestling bout.

Jeremy Irons portrays the patriarch, a character rife with contradictions. Meryl Streep plays his clairvoyant wife, while Glenn Close takes on the role of her sister-in-law. When the camera lingers on these central figures, the film gains momentum and becomes genuinely engaging. However, THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS stumbles by juggling far too many subplots. Characters flit in and out of the narrative like targets in a carnival shooting gallery, leaving us with little chance to connect with or care about them. The inevitable outcome is a sense of ennui.

Under the direction and screenplay of Bille August, adapted from Isabel Allende’s work, the film struggles to maintain focus amidst its sprawling ambitions.

This episode marks the first regularly filmed installment of the Columbo series, though it was broadcast as the second, following Steven Spielberg's "Columbo: Murder by the Book." Remarkably, it also stands out as one of the finest in the series!

Bernard L. Kowalski proves himself to be an exceptionally creative director with this film. It's no surprise that he was later invited to helm three additional Columbo movies. The film features inventive and striking shot sequences, crafted with evident style, passion, and meticulous attention to detail. Every frame is purposeful, elevating this movie above the typical made-for-TV fare and making it one of the best-directed entries in the Columbo catalog.

This particular Columbo episode is notably unique for several reasons. The murder itself is almost accidental, a spontaneous act rather than a premeditated crime. As a result, the killer has no opportunity to orchestrate the 'perfect murder' beforehand and must scramble to cover their tracks and dispose of the body after the fact. Furthermore, the portrayal of the killer deviates from the norm; rather than being depicted solely as the perpetrator, he is also presented as a figure who assists in unexpected ways.

Sandra Bernhard is a true original, undeniably one of the most hilarious women alive. She kicked off her career as a stand-up comedian in the 1970s, but her major breakthrough arrived in 1983 with a standout role alongside Jerry Lewis and Robert De Niro in Martin Scorsese's underappreciated gem, *The King of Comedy*. Despite this, her film career didn’t fully soar. She starred in a few quirky yet captivating movies like *Dallas Doll* (1994) and *Dinner Rush* (2000), but her most remarkable work came from the roles she crafted for herself.

*Without You I’m Nothing* stands out as her finest achievement. Adapted from her wildly successful off-Broadway show, it catapulted her to stardom and even made her Madonna’s close friend for roughly four years. Across ten impeccably choreographed and staged sequences, Sandra transforms from Nina Simone to Diana Ross, shares stories of her childhood, Andy Warhol, and San Francisco, and delivers renditions of songs popularized by Burt Bacharach, Prince, and Sylvester. Under the direction of John Boskovich, Sandra delivers a 90-minute powerhouse performance that’s both alluring and hilariously distinctive. For any Bernhard enthusiast, this film is unmissable—a celebration of her (uniquely) striking beauty and her extraordinarily unconventional talent.

I snagged this for just 50 cents at the flea market and was thrilled at first.

For about 15 minutes, I was captivated, but then it became monotonous and boring.

It’s cool to see Mick and the crew in their heyday, though I wish the dialogue wasn’t so heavily overdubbed—I wanted to hear their actual words and music.

The skits feel outdated politically, overly simplistic, and naive, like a poorly scripted Monty Python on a bad trip. I found myself more interested in the late '60s England scenery than the absurd skits themselves.

This film serves as a stark reminder that times change, and what once mattered can quickly seem trivial. The song is great, but this DVD has overplayed it to the point of exhaustion.

I've recently acquired the restored edition of a film I fondly recall from my childhood, and it has provided an intriguing afternoon of entertainment. In its complete form, Bedknobs makes much more sense, with the reinstated deleted scenes—particularly those featuring McDowall—seamlessly connecting the storyline. However, the remastering of these scenes is somewhat unsettling. It appears the original soundtrack for this footage was either lost or damaged, prompting someone at Disney to overdub the scenes with new dialogue. This might have worked well, but many of the original cast members were unavailable to reprise their roles (for various reasons), resulting in a somewhat sloppy execution. The lip-synching is noticeably off in places, and David Tomlinson’s voice is replaced by an actor who sounds nothing like him—there’s even a faint German accent, I believe. On a positive note, it’s delightful to hear the full versions of the songs (though 'Step in the Right Direction' is still missing), and the film’s magical moments continue to captivate. I dare anyone not to chuckle when young Paul looks at Angela Lansbury with such innocence and coos.

I’m clearly not the intended audience for this movie. As a man approaching 50, I’ve only recently ventured into the realm of independent cinema, quite by chance. It began late one night when I came across a film called *Clerks* on TV. Two things immediately stood out: 1) its technical roughness and 2) its exceptional writing. My curiosity piqued when I read an interview with this film's director in the local paper, mentioning *Clerks* as an influence. When he cited *The Station Agent*—a movie I’d watched on DVD just a week earlier—as his primary inspiration, I knew I had to see his work. The result echoed *Clerks* in some ways, though the two films differ vastly in content. Both are marred by technical flaws but are redeemed by outstanding writing. While *Clerks* portrays a day in the life of a man with little to show for himself, hesitant to confront deep personal questions, *Less Like Me* centers on a man who appears to keep himself perpetually occupied,

I approached this film with the understanding that it was a drama centered on a man with a supernatural ability, ostracized and turned into a monster by society. Needless to say, my expectations were completely upended, but in the most delightful way. My friend and I found the movie to be deeply romantic—undoubtedly aided by the charming male lead—and it offered a well-rounded mix of plot progression, action, and even humor. A particular moment of comedy, where the characters don’t learn each other’s names until the third act, had the entire theater in stitches. In summary, it wasn’t what I anticipated, but it turned out to be a wonderful surprise. I’m definitely planning to purchase this film on DVD when it’s released.

For years, this much-anticipated television reunion of two iconic sitcom characters was reportedly sidelined, only to launch with a disappointing start and spiral further downward. Mary Richards, played by Mary Tyler Moore, and her longtime friend Rhoda Morgenstern, portrayed by Valerie Harper, reunite in New York after years of estrangement to share updates on their lives. What could have been a fresh and exciting premise falls flat, as, regrettably, neither character has experienced anything noteworthy in the time apart—nothing compelling enough to justify a film. Instead, the script resorts to tired, overused plot devices, mostly centered on the challenges faced by older women in the workplace, while entirely lacking the unique charm and wit that made the original series a success. The supporting cast fails to leave an impression, the humor is absent, and the once-sparkling chemistry between Moore and Harper has vanished. Rumor has it that Moore delayed this project for years, holding out for the “perfect script” before agreeing to participate. If this script was deemed “perfect,” one can only imagine the quality of those she rejected. The downfall of this reunion isn’t due to the characters’ age, as the passage of time is inevitable.

In my opinion, this might just be the most hilarious film I've ever watched. Robert Harling's screenplay is almost flawless—take a peek at the "quotes" section, or better yet, rent the DVD to experience the impeccable delivery that truly brings the dialogue to life.

Sally Field delivers a wildly comedic and exaggerated performance unlike anything she's done before, while Kevin Kline is effortlessly funny. Robert Downey, Jr. shines with his usual brilliance, and even in a brief role, Kathy Najimy is uproarious as the overwhelmed costumer. I’ve never been a big fan of Elisabeth Shue, but she excels here as the lone grounded character amidst a cast of over-the-top personalities on the set of "The Sun Also Sets." That shaking you sense might be Hemingway turning in his grave—or perhaps he’s laughing uncontrollably.

Five stars. Hilarious through and through.

Monty Berman and Dennis Spooner, after their work on 'The Baron,' created this fantasy series featuring three superhuman spies, a concept that predated 'The Six Million Dollar Man.' As a child, I was captivated by it, and I still find pleasure in revisiting the show. The on-screen dynamic between Stuart Damon as Craig Stirling and William Gaunt as Richard Barrett was undeniable, while Alexandra Bastedo brought a sultry charm to her role as Sharron Macready with her signature pout. Anthony Nicholls delivered a memorably gruff performance as Tremayne. The standout episodes were penned by Tony Williamson, Terry Nation, and Brian Clemens, with Spooner’s own 'The Interrogation' holding its own against 'The Prisoner.' I’m disappointed that a second series was never made; the premise had immense untapped potential. Could there have been a romantic rivalry between Craig and Richard for Sharron? What if Tremayne had discovered the Champions’ extraordinary abilities? Were there hidden powers beyond those revealed? Sadly, these questions remain unanswered.

This movie presents an unconventional romance narrative. While it might not be particularly remarkable, Nicole Kidman single-handedly elevates the film, overshadowing a mostly forgettable supporting cast. However, Ben Chaplin delivers a commendable performance, and the depiction of Hertfordshire life, with scenes of St Albans and Hemel Hempstead town centers, authentically captures the region's spirit. Initially resembling a typical episode of the well-known British series "Heartbeat," the story quickly evolves into a intense gangster escape thriller. Despite its modest scope, nothing particularly striking occurs, making it a reasonably enjoyable option for weekend viewing. It's worth a watch, especially for those in their thirties feeling isolated like the protagonist, John, as they might relate to his experiences.

It seems inevitable that everyone gets a shot at redemption eventually. In "The Best of Times," Jack Dundee (Robin Williams), a humiliated resident of Taft, is determined to seize his. Known for his wild radio antics in "Good Morning, Vietnam," Williams now trades the microphone for a football, aiming to recreate a pivotal high school game that lost his team a coveted championship. However, convincing his former teammate Reno Hightower (Kurt Russell) to join this nostalgic rematch proves to be a challenge.

Admittedly, this film isn't the pinnacle of either actor's career. Nevertheless, Williams and Russell form a surprisingly effective comedic duo. Plus, some of the character names alone are bound to tickle your funny bone. It's definitely worth a watch.

Steer clear of this film under any circumstances. It is, unquestionably, the most dreadful movie I have ever watched. While many films possess at least a single redeeming quality, this one offers absolutely nothing. Utterly abysmal!

In a summer filled with disappointing films like *Snakes on a Plane* and *The Da Vinci Code*, making a strong critique feels daring. Yet, I stand firm in my opinion. *Superman Returns*, much like *King Kong* from six months prior, is excessively long, self-indulgent, and overloaded with CGI to an overwhelming degree. Honestly, this overreliance on digital effects is becoming unbearable.

Richard Donner, in his two Superman films, embraced a "keep it real" philosophy, and I believe his approach to special and optical effects remains the most effective. In contrast, Bryan Singer inundates us with so much CGI that it pulls you out of the narrative, constantly reminding you that you're watching a would-be blockbuster. This film seems to believe that the only way to captivate an audience is by throwing $250 million—an utterly reckless sum—at flashy visual effects that fail to deliver on their promise. We've already seen all that CGI can offer; there's no fresh territory here. The result is a lack of genuine atmosphere or emotional engagement. When a movie is 95% composed of such superficial elements, the conclusion is clear.

I've come across numerous reviews from enthusiastic critics claiming the film possesses "soul" or...

I was just thirteen when I first encountered this series, and now, more than three decades later, I’m revisiting it on DVD. The imagery from the opening credits has stayed with me all these years, profoundly shaping my perspective on the world and its diverse inhabitants. My parents, who were still with me at the time, watched the series alongside me, and our post-episode discussions became cherished memories. This experience ignited a passion for history in me, which ultimately led to achieving top scores in my school’s public exams.

Sir Laurence Olivier’s voice and narration are eternal and flawless. I believe those who lived through the era would recognize this as their definitive account of World War II history. I can’t fathom ever tiring of watching it. Perhaps a comparable series on the Cold War could be considered, though finding someone to match Sir Laurence’s gravitas seems nearly impossible.

Don’t hesitate—purchase it!

Mario Lewis from the Competitive Enterprise Institute has authored a comprehensive 120-page rebuttal to this deceptive film, which might as well be called A CONVENIENT LIE. His detailed critique, titled "A SKEPTIC'S GUIDE TO AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH," is available at www.cei.org. For a more concise version, a 10-page summary can be accessed at www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf. After reviewing these thorough analyses, you'll see that the so-called "global warming" crisis is as unfounded and overhyped as the Y2K panic of 1999, which Al Gore also supported, alongside the scientifically dubious film THE DAY AFTER TOMORROW, based on a book by Whitley Strieber, who claims to have been abducted by UFOs. Much like James "The Amazing" Randi debunks psychics, Philip Klass dismantles UFO claims, and Gerald Posner refutes JFK conspiracy theories, Mario Lewis effectively dismantles Al Gore's film and the broader "global warming" narrative.

Scott Henderson (Alan Curtis) is wrongfully charged with the murder of his cheating wife. On the fateful night of her death, he was in the company of an enigmatic woman who kept her identity a secret. When accused, the police retrace his steps with her, but witnesses recall seeing him alone. Condemned to death, Henderson’s devoted secretary (Ella Raines) takes it upon herself to uncover the real killer, driven by her love for him.

Produced as a low-budget B movie by Universal, the film features a cast of character actors alongside a fading star, Franchot Tone. Despite its modest funding and lesser-known ensemble, this picture emerges as one of the standout film noirs of the 1940s. Under the skilled direction of Curt Siodmak and adapted from a compelling novel by William Irish (a pseudonym for Cornell Woolrich), the movie boasts a sharp script and striking visuals. Its pacing is brisk, and the cinematography is captivating. A particularly memorable scene is the charged jam session featuring Raines and Elisha Cook Jr., which crackles with raw sexual tension—remarkable that it passed the censors unscathed.

While nearly flawless, the film is not without its shortcomings. Tone's performance is notably weak, detracting from the overall impact.

Anyone who praised this film with glowing reviews clearly needs to broaden their cinematic horizons.

The story follows a down-on-his-luck character who obsessively films his dysfunctional family. The film is overrun with foolish characters and even features distasteful moments like "teabagging," which pretty much encapsulates the entire experience.

Save yourself the trouble. You might be tempted to watch until the end, hoping for some redemption or improvement, but trust me—it never gets better.

I was incredibly eager to watch this movie, hoping that Australia had finally produced a stellar film. Unfortunately, my expectations were shattered.

This film is arguably the most dismal attempt at a slasher flick I've ever encountered. I pity Molly Ringwald for traveling all the way to Australia just to star in such a dreadful production.

The performances were abysmal, particularly the Australian actor attempting an American accent, which was painfully unconvincing. The storyline itself was equally disappointing.

Initially, I scoffed at the film's title, finding it as clichéd as the mock movie "Stab" from Scream 2. Nevertheless, I was prepared to overlook this if the movie proved worthwhile.

WARNING!!! MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD!!!

The most egregious flaw of the film was its conclusion. I anticipated a shocking reveal about the killer's identity, but the twist—that the killer wasn't even human—transformed a potentially grounded slasher into a terrible horror flick.

I advise against watching this movie; it's likely to leave you utterly disappointed!

Among the three remakes of this storyline, I enjoy each one and own all three on VHS, plus a DVD copy of this particular version. The scripts vary just enough to keep each film entertaining and worth rewatching. Has any other movie been remade three times with such impressive all-star casts in every iteration? While the lead actors in this version are outstanding, the supporting cast shines as well. I'm especially fond of William Tracy's performance as Pepi; he’s such a captivating presence that I’ve sought out other films he’s in, though many are unfortunately unavailable. Echoing other reviews, I highly recommend purchasing this one.

If this movie was indeed backed by a $20 million budget, I’m utterly baffled as to where the funds were allocated. The CGI effects are so poorly executed that a monkey could have produced something more impressive. I will concede, however, that the machines and Martians might have looked striking in a retro video game on the original PlayStation 1 or mid-90s PC titles, had one been developed. The burning question remains: where did the money disappear to? For the same budget, Pendragon Films could have crafted a remarkable film using classic models and computer-controlled cameras in the style of George Lucas from 1975-83, paired with actors who at least appear invested in their roles (or in this case, seem to care about the disaster they’re part of). This might just be the most abysmal film ever created! I’d sooner endure a 24-hour marathon of *Ishtar* than subject myself to this travesty again. I loathed every second of it! Let me clarify: this IS the WORST film ever made. Unlike other notoriously bad movies such as *Plan 9*, *Killer Tomatoes*, or *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*, which are so terrible they earn a peculiar kind of affection, this film offers no such redemption.

Rated NR (equivalent to R for pervasive strong language and crude sexual humor). Quebec Rating: 16+ (should be 13+). Canadian Home Video Rating: 18A

Eddie Murphy's *Delirious* marks his debut stand-up comedy performance, released in 1983. During that era, Murphy was gaining fame through roles in films like *48 Hrs.* and *Trading Places*, as well as his appearances on *Saturday Night Live*. He produced two stand-up comedy specials, *Delirious* and *Raw*. While I personally found *Raw* funnier due to its subject matter, *Delirious* is equally hilarious, featuring Murphy's nostalgic reflections on childhood and his comedic takes on celebrities like Mr. T and Michael Jackson. Any stand-up comedy enthusiast should definitely watch Eddie Murphy's *Delirious*.

I settled in to watch a documentary on Puerto Rico, but instead, it focused on Nuyoricans. When I visit Puerto Rico, I often miss the reality of the 50% living in poverty. The struggling individuals I do notice are typically recent arrivals from Haiti, the Dominican Republic, or Cuba. I believe there’s no such thing as Spanglish; you either speak Spanish or you don’t, and from what I’ve gathered, you don’t. Pedro Albizu Campos doesn’t hold the same significance for me as Martin Luther King Jr. does. While MLK was undeniably a great man, Campos is revered only by the 1% who advocate for independence. To the majority, he’s viewed as extreme, akin to someone like Osama Bin Laden. I find Puerto Ricans pushing for independence to be misguided. For those dreaming of an independent Puerto Rico, just look at the state of Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, and much of South and Central America, as well as Mexico. Their independence has hardly been a success story. Ultimately, this documentary wasn’t truly about Puerto Rico; it centered on the struggles of Nuyoricans.

To the individual who felt there wasn’t enough focus on African influences in the program, the documentary was intended to cover Puerto Rico, not Africa. I’m sure Denzel Washington will produce something on that topic soon.

I’m fascinated by early color films—turns out, the 1940s wardrobe wasn’t just shades of gray!  

Margaret Rutherford steals the show in this film. Her “quirky” outfits are surprisingly appealing, and she boasts a striking hourglass figure. However, I think she was given too much freedom with her performance. Likely having honed this character through numerous roles, it seems no one advised her to cut back on the over-the-top antics with the adage, “If it gets a laugh, ditch it.” She overdoes the zany behavior when her character is meant to be unexpectedly grounded. The humor in Madame Arcati lies in the subversion of the typical medium stereotype—ethereal women draped in flowing fabrics. Instead, Arcati comes across as a retired headmistress with a no-nonsense attitude (“Let’s give it our all!”). Yet, the contrast between her practical demeanor and her outlandish beliefs isn’t fully explored.  

And just because nearly all the actors are English (except for Cummings), it doesn’t mean Americans need to lean on tired clichés like “Brit,” “stiff,” “lip,” and “upper.” Enough already! The three main characters are far from reserved—they frequently lose their cool and toss around suggestive quips (“Did he make love to you?” “Yes, but very discreetly—he was in the cavalry!”).

A remarkable series and an underappreciated gem, The League of Gentlemen stands as one of the finest modern comedies of our era.

With its dark, eccentric humor that eclipses the predictable, repetitive style of its lesser-known yet more widely recognized successor, Little Britain, The League of Gentlemen was a truly unique presence during a somewhat stagnant period in British comedy.

Before its debut, there had never been anything quite like The League of Gentlemen. At first glance, it appears to be a straightforward sketch show, but it quickly reveals itself as a vibrant, eerie, and uproariously funny world teeming with unforgettable comedic characters. What truly distinguishes it from its competitors is its storytelling method. Instead of recycling indistinguishable sketches, the show follows individual characters or groups through their distinct arcs and narratives. Each encounter with them feels fresh, consistently delivering unexpected twists.

Over the course of three series and a Christmas special, the fictional town of Royston Vasey becomes a bizarre yet hilarious landscape filled with a captivating cast of grotesque characters.

As other critics have pointed out, the movie loses its momentum in the final half-hour. Prior to that, it struggles with a predictable plot and a remarkably shallow performance by Kate Capshaw, who seems utterly disconnected from her role and drags down every scene she appears in. Connery and Fishburne deliver solid performances, but the majority of the scenes feel contrived for dramatic impact rather than authenticity, casting a pervasive sense of artificiality over the film. The ending, meanwhile, is outright strange. It’s evident that the filmmakers, aware of the disjointed mess they had created, tried to salvage it with an excessively loud and "dramatic" soundtrack. Every minor jolt is punctuated by an overblown orchestral swell, which eventually becomes comical. If you're looking for a prime example of a disastrously bad major film, this is worth a watch; otherwise, it's best to pass.

Ettore Scola stands out as a significant figure among Italian filmmakers. One summer evening, my parents and I sat down to watch "C'eravamo tanto amati." While we enjoyed it, our appreciation didn't match the deep affection we felt for "A Special Day." I feel Scola is often underappreciated, perhaps due to the lackluster reception of his more recent works. Last night, my mother and I settled on our couch to revisit this cinematic gem. The screenplay, direction, cinematography, music, and production design were all restrained yet precise, but what truly captivated me was the dynamic between Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni. Both deliver exceptional performances as Antonietta, a housewife trapped in a marriage with a fervent Fascist and mother to six children, whose husband desires another child to win a prize for large families, and Gabriele, an outspoken Anti-Fascist. Their shared day, set against the backdrop of Hitler's 1938 visit to Mussolini in Rome, is nothing short of extraordinary. I’ll refrain from revealing more about the storyline—seek out this film for yourself!

"It evokes the initial rush of pleasure mingled with guilt, the impulsive thrill of youthful allure mixed with apprehension, a crescendo of conflicting emotions," remarked a film enthusiast after watching LOVE AT THE TOP, the often misunderstood title for Michel Deville's sophisticated film LE MOUTON ENRAGE.

In contrast, Vincent Canby of the New York Times, commenting shortly after the 1974 debut, noted: "LOVE AT THE TOP, which premiered yesterday at the 68th Street Playhouse, is a 1973 French comedy that vaguely echoes various nineteen-fifties British comedies centered on the relentless ascent of ambitious, cynical young men both driven by and consumed by their desires." He highlighted a key distinction, however, pointing out that LOVE AT THE TOP does not engage with the British class structure. (January 27, 1975)

While individual critiques have varied, the passage of time has offered its own verdict. More than three decades later, it’s clear that films like LE MOUTON ENRAGE are rare—where decadence seems almost naive, relationships brim with youthful zeal, and emotions are portrayed with striking manipulation.

For admirers of Romy Schneider, it goes without saying that this movie

This rather uninspiring made-for-TV movie premiered on the TBS cable network. The plot follows Antonio and Janine as they pursue a deadly computer virus, and that’s essentially the entire story. Trivia enthusiasts might find it interesting that the film debuted on the same weekend as the real-life 'Melissa' virus, which also emerged in email inboxes worldwide.

Certain movies are so dreadful that they somehow become enjoyable, but this one doesn’t even come close to that category. Supposedly based on a true story, this film strays as far from reality as Pinocchio’s dream of becoming a real boy. The acting is atrocious, the direction lacks any finesse, and the pacing is absurdly rushed. It feels as though the director was in a hurry to wrap up and head home.

Melissa Joan Hart has never impressed me as a skilled actress, though it’s worth noting that her projects often seem constrained by small budgets. In this film, as in many of her others, she undermines her role by overacting and delivering her lines at a frenzied pace, as if rapid speech could heighten the drama. Instead, she constantly reminds the audience of the camera and crew before her, failing to draw viewers into her character. Her performance ultimately drags down the entire movie, stripping away any remaining chance it had to redeem itself.

Perhaps the only redeeming moment is the conclusion when her character faces consequences, but even that fails to deliver any real satisfaction.

This film is utterly dreadful, a textbook case of cinematic failure that fails to captivate even the most forgiving B-movie enthusiasts. I strongly advise against squandering your valuable time on this abysmal piece of work. The acting is atrocious, the direction is abysmal, the script is beyond terrible, and there’s a complete absence of any understanding of what constitutes entertainment. I picked up the DVD for just $3, and I’m tempted to pay someone to take it off my hands. Destroying it wouldn’t even begin to erase the torment this movie inflicted on me. As a fan of B-movies—think killer toys or bizarre lagoon creatures—I can say with certainty that this doesn’t come close to their quirky charm. It’s not even the kind of bad that’s amusing; it’s simply pitiful.

I stumbled upon this film on video around 1990, completely unaware of what I was about to watch. Many horror enthusiasts might have overlooked it, mistaking it for a standard prison drama, and even those who gave it a chance were often disappointed, expecting something different. These factors likely contribute to its low ratings, but I urge genre fans to disregard the scores and give it a try.

The movie excels in every aspect, boasting a compelling script, chilling atmosphere, stellar performances, and a hauntingly authentic prison setting.

A true hidden gem, this film remains in my video collection to this day. Don’t miss out—give it a watch.

52-Pick Up deserves far more recognition than it has received. The film operates on multiple levels, boasting a complex yet coherent plot. The cast delivers some of their most compelling performances, with Ann-Margret, Roy Scheider, and John Glover ideally suited to their roles, bringing profound depth to their characters. Vanity also stands out, displaying surprising talent that could have launched a significant acting career, while Kelly Preston’s portrayal leaves a lasting, unsettling impact. This movie is a must-watch for fans of action paired with a raw, intricate narrative.

Initially, I was uncertain whether I was viewing a documentary, a piece of propaganda, or a dramatic narrative. Considering the era of its creation, it likely blended elements of all three.

While the storyline was fairly predictable, there was a lingering anticipation of captivating scenes as the film progressed. The depiction of training routines and equipment struck me as quite authentic.

The film truly resonated with me towards its conclusion. The scenes portrayed a sense of realism, rare in my experience, allowing me to immerse myself in the action and empathize with the young soldiers’ thoughts. This was juxtaposed with the typical challenges of depicting convincing Japanese soldiers during a period when casting actual Japanese actors was presumably difficult.

This movie serves as a valuable reflection of the American psyche in 1943, amid the conflict with Japan. Additionally, it includes a subtle critique of Japan, referencing past American assistance to the nation.

I typically avoid harshly criticizing films, preferring to highlight the positives over the negatives. However, in this instance, there are scarcely any redeeming qualities to mention. Frankly, if a film is going to be this poorly executed, one wonders why it was made at all. A significant portion of the movie is consumed by prolonged close-ups of Anne’s face as she breathes heavily, accompanied by violin music in the background. The remainder is marred by stiff and unconvincing performances. Rupert Penry-Jones delivers a completely emotionless portrayal, while Jennifer Higham, as Anne’s younger sister, adopts jarringly modern mannerisms.
