Anne herself is depicted as timid and self-effacing, which is acceptable initially, but her character shows no growth throughout the film, leaving viewers puzzled as to why Captain Wentworth would fall for her. Additionally, the production fails to capture the essence of its historical setting, with numerous glaring errors that cannot be ignored—such as characters running out of a concert, kissing publicly in the street, and dashing through town without proper attire like hats (a scene that feels entirely unnecessary, especially when contrasted with one of the most romantic moments in the original book). In conclusion, this film is a profound disappointment and a terrible adaptation.

Pacino delivers a flawless performance in the speech beside the deceased child’s coffin, outshining even Shakespeare’s Mark Antony with his powerful rendition.

Should the praise for the exceptional dialogue go to Paul Schrader or Ken Lipper? The lines are profound, insightful, and a true delight for anyone who appreciates films with strong scripts. The storyline unfolds impressively, maintaining its strength all the way to the concluding voice-over.

Beyond this, the film offers little else to discuss; even John Cusack has portrayed more compelling characters in other works. Notably, the movie is heavily male-centric, with the female characters serving merely as background figures.

Rated 7 for kids and 6 for those who insist they're grown-ups, this semi-sequel to The Lion King shifts the spotlight to fan-favorite sidekicks Timon and Pumba. It reimagines the original tale from their unique perspective, delving into the backstory of their friendship. True to Disney tradition, lesser sequels often emerge alongside TV spin-offs that highlight minor characters from their blockbuster films. While skepticism about such projects is understandable, young viewers and devoted fans are unlikely to mind. Packed with humor, songs, and captivating moments, this film stands out as one of the rare sequels that exceeds average expectations. Its success hinges on the endearing appeal of the beloved protagonists, a brisk narrative pace, clever nods to the original movie, and a sprinkle of witty gags for adult audiences. Though the animation retains its high quality, it’s slightly less vibrant than the first film, aligning with a laid-back storyline that embodies the "Hakuna Matata" spirit.

In the movie, Timon and Pumba settle in to rewatch the events of the original film, often pausing to poke fun at various scenes as if they’re part of the audience. The story also explores Timon’s struggles as an almost-outcast, revealing his feelings of isolation.

This summer has been packed with blockbuster releases and film comebacks, along with the inevitable disappointments of some of those revivals, making it challenging to find a movie I could simply relax and enjoy.

If you’re not inclined to read further (no spoilers ahead), here’s the gist: This film is more mature than *Ella Enchanted*, featuring some potentially disturbing violence, frequent death, and a few scenes with mild gore, making it unsuitable for young kids. However, it avoids being overly cheesy or pushing beyond its scope. Imagine a slightly more serious and magical version of *The Princess Bride*, and you’ll get the idea.

---

I’m not the most frequent moviegoer—perhaps once or twice a month if I’m feeling motivated. As a dedicated Sci-Fi/Fantasy enthusiast, I quickly grow weary of recycled, predictable plots and films that prioritize spectacle over substance. This movie, however, stands out as a rare gem.

By August, I was so disillusioned by the unmet expectations of major releases that I nearly skipped watching *Bourne*.

Michael Stearns portrays Mike, a deeply frustrated man with a peculiar moral stance on sexuality. He has no qualms about leering at nude dancers, yet he becomes unhinged when women engage in sexual acts with men. In his view, a woman loses her "innocence" and "beauty" the moment she becomes intimate. Driven by this belief, Mike roams the Hollywood Hills, spying on couples from afar and ultimately killing the men with a high-powered rifle equipped with a scope.

The film seems to exist primarily to revel in repetitive sexual content, with the plot feeling like a mere afterthought. This focus is likely to appeal to many heterosexual male viewers, as the movie offers numerous extended scenes of nudity—featuring attractive women—and explicit sex, delivering a heavy dose of titillation. However, the voyeuristic lens through which much of this is viewed, often literally through Mike’s rifle scope, heightens the unsettling nature of the film. His prolonged observation of couples before taking lethal action emphasizes a disturbing obsession with watching. This eerie tone is further amplified by a soundtrack that, while somewhat atmospheric, often feels overly intrusive.

In essence, this movie lacks a coherent plot, dragging on for 80 minutes with unhinged characters who are either drinking or delivering terrible jokes. The soundtrack is dreadful, the humor falls flat, and the female characters are portrayed as either promiscuous fools or awkward nerds. It feels as though the script was penned by a 14-year-old boy obsessed with the idea that drinking is impressive, women exist solely for male pleasure, and anyone who disagrees is a nerd. Furthermore, this film has little connection to the original American Pie series, aside from a few familiar names and a minor role for Mr. Levenstein. The only redeeming aspect is the attractive cast of women. I advise against watching this film and caution viewers not to be misled by its 5.4 rating, as it is clearly inflated and deserves no more than a 2.

Trailers for this film might highlight moments of violence or unconventional sexuality, but these are merely fleeting snippets, chosen to draw in viewers. They do, however, reflect the core theme of the movie:

It portrays individuals who, battered by constant degradation in their jobs and personal lives, wield whatever power they possess elsewhere to cruelly dominate others. At the bottom of this oppressive hierarchy, women often bear the brunt of the suffering.

A film as raw and unflinching as *Hundstage* is difficult to watch, yet living through such harrowing realities is far more grueling.

Technically, the movie echoes the style of *Short Cuts*, composed of documentary-like vignettes that showcase ordinary people—neighbors, perhaps—presented in their unvarnished truth. There’s no gloss, no glamour, and most unsettling of all, no trace of hope. The documentary approach intensifies the discomfort, forcing you to confront the reality that such individuals exist in large numbers, hidden beneath society’s polished facade. Somewhere, the porn industry thrives; somewhere, domestic violence goes unreported; somewhere, dreams are shattered. I’ve certainly known people like these.

If you’re looking for a film that strips away illusion and lays bare the harshness of life...

Bogmeister and others have hit the mark on this one. "Shore Leave" represents *Star Trek: The Original Series* (TOS) taking its initial stab at lighter sci-fi, a style they would later master with the iconic "The Trouble with Tribbles." This episode offers a much-needed break for both the Enterprise crew and the show's audience, stepping away from the high-stakes, universe-altering conflicts seen in episodes like "The Corbomite Maneuver."

Seeking a spot for some downtime, the Enterprise stumbles upon a seemingly perfect M-Class planet. An away team is dispatched to investigate, but soon, bizarre events unfold—some appearing dangerous at first glance. What follows is a chaotic tapestry of human emotions, woven through a strange mix of fantastical mystery (McCoy seems to step through the looking glass), psychological tension (Kirk is relentlessly pursued by a tormentor from his past), and romantic comedy (no further elaboration needed).

TOS stands out as the least serialized entry in the *Star Trek* franchise, making it easy to overlook how many first-season episodes leaned into intense, potentially disastrous drama. Unlike the writers of later series, the TOS team wasn’t shy about boldly venturing into uncharted territory for television at the time.

Is it possible that HeidiJean actually watched this film? Calling it a great Christmas movie is a stretch—far from it. The movie is tedious, uninspired, and utterly devoid of creativity or emotion. As I endured it, I couldn’t help but question who decided Carly Pope was suitable for the lead role. She displays no discernible personality and delivers a thoroughly unimpressive performance. Baransky, as always, shines and offers the sole flicker of interest in this otherwise dreary production. It’s likely her participation was the only reason this project got the go-ahead. Perhaps my expectations are too high for a Lifetime movie aired just 15 days before Christmas, but I couldn’t help thinking that with a different director and a recast lead actress who could at least evoke some empathy, this might have been a charming little film.

The movie opens with a voice-over that explicitly informs the audience about the setting and introduces the characters. Right from this point, my appreciation for the film began to wane. Given the vast array of creative tools at a filmmaker’s disposal, resorting to a voice-over to explain the context feels like a simplistic and uninspired choice. In my view, such narration undermines the essence of cinematic storytelling.

I find it particularly frustrating when a voice-over dictates the location, the time period, and, worst of all, the inner emotions and thoughts of the characters. A skilled director should employ visual storytelling to convey these elements, allowing the audience to connect with the characters’ experiences through imagery and action rather than overt narration.

Despite this off-putting introduction, the film soon unfolds into a compelling narrative that sustains interest for a considerable duration. It portrays the dynamics of a middle-class family, capturing the individual lives of its members with remarkable authenticity. The director demonstrates a keen ability to reflect real-life scenarios. For instance, a scene depicting a father making private phone calls from the bathroom might initially seem peculiar, but it mirrors the odd, relatable quirks of everyday life.

I never imagined a movie could be this terrible. The title seemed so full of potential, yet with a cast of 20, you'd expect at least one to deliver a decent performance. My wife couldn't endure it, walking away and heading to bed just 20 minutes in. She made the right choice.

The film is a fully realized piece that captivates from start to finish, weaving together childhood flashbacks and the peculiarities of a strange father with chilling tales of serial murder. The storyline alone is inherently compelling, offering a rich canvas for director Bill Paxton, who masterfully exploits its potential with remarkable depth.

From the opening scene to the final frame, the movie maintains a gripping sense of anticipation about the unfolding events and the direction of the narrative. The creativity infused in the storytelling is exceptional, marking this film as a meticulously crafted work. It stands out as a rare treasure, devoid of any dull moments, with the action transitioning smoothly, briskly, and cohesively between scenes.

Moreover, the film powerfully illustrates the extremes to which individuals may go, committing heinous acts against loved ones and perpetrating evil under the guise of divine will, particularly when gripped by delusion, as depicted in this haunting story.

I get the humor in the show, but it’s simply not funny. The entire series is dreadful. I comprehend it fully, which only makes it worse. The only standout character in the show’s history was the hobo from a single episode, but even revisiting that episode alongside others confirms how awful the series is. It’s not amusing in the slightest—not even close. I’m tired of hearing, “Only intelligent people understand it,” because if these so-called smart individuals are so brilliant, why do they prejudge others without knowing them, claiming they lack the intellect to grasp the show? It’s akin to asserting the sky is red without ever glancing outside. Ultimately, this is hands-down the worst show I’ve ever watched. The jokes are abysmal; yes, I understand them, but they’re still terrible. The controversies surrounding the show are uninspired, and the humor—revolving around fart jokes and bodily fluids—is juvenile and poorly executed with subpar acting. I can’t fathom what these “smart” viewers see in it, but making assumptions about others without any knowledge of who we are is far from an intelligent observation.

Among the numerous modern variations of the sitcom, the classic approach with a live audience and indoor setting remains the most effective. "That '70s Show" serves as a prime example. When the series first aired, actors like Kurtwood Smith and Debra Jo Rupp were relatively unknown, as were the young talents Topher Grace and Ashton Kutcher, who both delivered remarkable performances. (Sadly, both are departing the show this year to explore other ventures.) I wish Topher would reconsider, as the series initially revolved around his character, Eric, and his tight-knit group of friends. Meanwhile, Ashton has become akin to the John Travolta of our era—recall Travolta’s romance with Diana Hyland from "Eight Is Enough," much like Ashton’s relationship with Demi Moore. The relatively unknown cast was a strength, as a high-profile celebrity can often overshadow the story. I miss Mo Gaffney’s portrayal of Don’s girlfriend, Joanne, and Lisa Robin Kelly as the original Laurie—her replacement simply couldn’t measure up, which is a shame. I appreciated Tommy Chong’s role as the endearing, albeit burned-out, father figure to Steven Hyde. Additionally, it was a delight to see Tanya Roberts in a role beyond "Charlie’s Angels."

I would rate it a 2 out of 10.

I found myself deeply disappointed with this production. The storyline lacked depth, with events feeling rushed and superficial, which obscured the intended moral message. While Brenda Song delivered a commendable performance, Shin Koyamada struggled to embody his character convincingly. I understood the inclusion of western influences in the narrative, but felt there was a missed opportunity to incorporate more authentic Chinese elements. For instance, the villain’s design was more reminiscent of a robot than a figure rooted in Chinese culture. Most frustrating, however, were the inaccurate and distorted facts woven into the plot.

Some might argue that as a children’s show, it doesn’t require such rigorous standards. Yet, other Disney productions like Mulan have demonstrated superior storytelling and cultural representation.

Ultimately, I believe Disney should invest more in research and thoughtful planning for their projects. A compelling show cannot rely solely on a sequence of martial arts sequences to carry it.

Anyone dismissing this film as dull is simply a narrow-minded individual better suited to watching fast-paced car chases or lighthearted romantic comedies. This movie is captivating, with not a single tedious moment. The reason lies in its core: it’s built on sharp, intelligent conversations among genuine characters facing a critical situation, showcasing their struggle to overcome it. Let me emphasize—intelligent dialogue! This is a signature of nearly every Rohmer film, and it’s precisely why some viewers turn away. They crave constant action. That’s their choice—let them indulge in action flicks forever, while those of us with refined taste and discernment will keep seeking out gems like this.

Rohmer often faces criticism for being overly "talkative." Yes, he is, but I see that as praise rather than a flaw. Shakespeare, too, was verbose. Is there a play more laden with dialogue than "Hamlet"? When a piece of art explores themes of ideas and value conflicts, it naturally demands discussion of those concepts, and that’s the essence of this film. It delves into tensions like aristocracy and noble lineage versus equality, and the profound test of loyalty to lifelong friends when that bond is pushed to its limits.

Without intending to dampen anyone's spirits, Brad Sykes is behind at least two of the most uninspired and predictable films I've encountered, this being one of them alongside Camp Blood.

The performances are abysmal, the film quality is poor, and every aspect of this movie practically begs the question, "Couldn't you do better on your own?" Perhaps this serves as an invitation for us all to flood YouTube with our own subpar zombie content.

I picked this up for just £1, but keep in mind that 71 minutes of your life is priceless. It's wise to steer clear of this disaster, even if it's dirt cheap.

You've likely heard the advice to live each moment as if it were your last. Regardless of whether that’s true today, I urge you not to squander a single second on this film! Nichole Hiltz offers a few pleasant glimpses of eye candy (though, unfortunately, it remains under wraps), while David DeLuise demonstrates why he’s better suited for small-screen roles or dog food ads. With a superficial, implausible storyline and cringe-worthy dialogue, there is absolutely no "Art" to be found in "Art of Revenge."

I attended an exclusive early screening of this film today. To be honest, I’m not particularly fond of Dane Cook or Steve Carell, so I went in with no real expectations. Surprisingly, I found myself enjoying it quite a lot.

*Dan in Real Life* follows the journey of a widower with three daughters who joins his extended family for a weekend getaway. At a local bookstore, he encounters the woman of his dreams, only to discover she is dating his brother.

The film is crafted with care—the soundtrack, cinematography, and performances, particularly Steve Carell’s, are all impressive. However, I felt the movie fell short in terms of character development, especially with Dane Cook’s role. The dynamic between Dane and Steve’s characters lacks depth, and exploring their relationship further could have better illuminated Dan’s internal struggle over falling for his brother’s girlfriend. Despite this, *Dan in Real Life* remains a heartfelt and well-made film, offering a refreshing change from the flood of horror and action releases this year.

One redeeming aspect of this movie is Lola Glaudini's captivating presence, particularly her striking physical appeal. Regrettably, the film misses the mark by not showcasing more of her allure, which might have salvaged some entertainment value from this chaotic production. Another actress briefly appears topless, but she pales in comparison to Glaudini. Additionally, Armand Assante's aging appearance is notably distracting; he looks considerably worn out. "Consequence" falls into the typical B-movie category, showing glimmers of potential in its storyline but failing miserably in execution. The cinematography is downright unattractive, and the direction lacks any spark, resulting in a dull thriller plagued by predictable twists and faded stars. While Glaudini shines as a seductive femme fatale in a provocative, low-budget manner, even her performance can't rescue "Consequence" from being utterly forgettable and disappointing, lacking even the charm of campy trash.

I came across a comment by Chris_m_grant from the United States.

He stated: "A fantastic documentary from 1924. This early 20th-century depiction of the geography of present-day Iraq was impactful."

I want to express my gratitude to Chris and to everyone who has shown interest in the Bakhtiari Nomads of Iran, the Zagros Mountains, and the stunning landscapes featured in the film *Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life*. The traditions portrayed in the movie have persisted for centuries and will continue to endure as long as life itself. I hail from this very region of Iran and am proud to be a Bakhtiari.

Chris, I apologize for any inconvenience, but I must clarify that the Bakhtiari region of Zardkuh is located in Iran, not Iraq as mentioned in your comment. Iran and Iraq are two separate and distinct nations. Confusing an Iranian for an Iraqi is somewhat akin to mistaking an American for a Mexican. Thank you,

Ziba

Could someone please advise Shaquille O'Neal to focus on his basketball talents instead? This movie failed to entertain even on a basic, mindless level. In it, Shaq portrays a genie residing in a boom box—an unoriginal twist on the classic genie-in-a-lamp concept. His role is to assist a young boy, played by the equally irritating Francis Capra. The storyline is as weak as that of *Waterworld*, the acting is dreadful, and I suspect anyone who enjoys this film would hesitate to admit it publicly.

May and her husband travel to see their children and grandchildren, but the reunion feels strained. There’s an unexpected distance between the grandchildren and their parents, a lack of the familial warmth one would anticipate. After dinner, May’s husband complains of feeling unwell, sharply attributes it to his daughter’s cooking, and grumbles about wanting to return home. Tragically, he passes away that night.

Now a widow, May finds herself adrift. Her marriage may not have been filled with passion or excitement, but it gave her a sense of purpose. She had someone who relied on her, and though her own desires remained unfulfilled for years, her days had structure and meaning.

Overwhelmed by depression and a lack of drive, May moves in with her daughter, Paula. Soon after, Paula confronts her mother, unleashing years of pent-up frustration. She accuses May of never truly being there for her, of failing to provide the nurturing she craved. May appears taken aback and vulnerable, yet she lacks the energy or will to mend the rift. Her response, “I’m your mother and I love you,” feels hollow—an empty declaration that fails to bridge the emotional gap between them.

I never quite warmed to the original "Cube" film. Despite its intriguing concept, the grating performances and unlikable characters prevented me from fully enjoying it. Consequently, I felt no urge to watch its sequel. However, when I learned a third movie was in the works, one that would serve as a prequel to the first, my curiosity was piqued. I hoped it might address the shortcomings of the original and deliver a more compelling ensemble. Unfortunately, I was mistaken.

"Cube Zero" begins promisingly by introducing two characters tasked with monitoring and managing the endless labyrinth of deadly traps that torment the Cube's occupants. The filmmakers effectively create an air of mystery through the depiction of the men’s mundane routines, raising questions about why individuals are sent to the Cube and the true identity of those orchestrating the sinister operation. These mysteries are left for the audience to ponder. Though the acting is somewhat underwhelming, the first half of the film progresses at a decent pace.

As the narrative unfolds, one of the two "watchers" starts to

I missed the opening of this movie, which could explain my strong dislike for it. However, having studied the decline of the Roman Republic extensively, I’m well-versed in the historical context. Ironically, this familiarity might also contribute to my negative opinion of the film.

The movie is riddled with historical errors, far outnumbering the extras on screen. It’s so blatantly inaccurate that it seems the filmmakers didn’t even try for authenticity, which might be excusable if that was their intent. Curiously, though, they occasionally make a significant effort to be historically precise, which only adds to the confusion. For instance, they mention Antonius’ marriage to Octavia, only to dismiss it a couple of scenes later. If it’s irrelevant to the storyline and Octavia never appears, why include it at all? Similarly, they inconsistently refer to Antonius as both Marcus Antonius, his true name, and the peculiar anglicized version, Mark Antony, within different scenes.

Even setting aside the historical inaccuracies, the film could have still been enjoyable if not for the leading actress. She lacks any semblance of poise, portraying her character as overly emotional, theatrical, and utterly devoid of self-control.

Hey there, I'm Paul Raddick, also known as Panic Attack from WTAF, Channel 29 in Philadelphia. Allow me to dive into a truly dreadful movie that somehow kickstarted Adam Sandler's career before fading into digital obscurity.

"Going Overboard" follows Sandler as an aspiring comedian who lands a gig on a cruise ship, only to spectacularly flop—or so I believed. Along the way, Sandler crosses paths with women who are fans of "History of the World Part 1" and "Rebound." These women are supposedly engaged, but in a shocking twist, they meet a grisly fate at the hands of Sawtooth, the most ruthless cannibal ever known. While Sandler struggled in "Going Overboard," he later found success in films like "Big Daddy," "Billy Madison," and Jen Leone's top pick, "50 First Dates." Man, Drew Barrymore was absolutely stunning. "Spanglish" sizzles with appeal, but "Going Overboard"? It’s a complete disaster! That’s all for now.

This movie immerses you in the extraordinary journey of a single family, allowing you to experience every moment of their epic struggle. With stunning performances and breathtaking cinematography, it feels achingly authentic. The final line, imbued with poignant hope, lingers as one of the most unforgettable in recent recollection.

I strongly advise against watching this movie. It’s simply awful and a complete waste of time. I found no redeeming qualities in it. The film is poorly made, with a weak plot and subpar acting. I’d rather endure anything than sit through this movie again.

This film has always been my ultimate favorite from childhood. The special effects, groundbreaking for their time, earned well-deserved awards. The dialogue remains etched in my memory, as vivid as if I’d heard it just yesterday. It’s a classic, enduring adventure that never grows old. The score, composed by the legendary Miklos Rosza, cinema’s greatest, adds to its magic. Sabu shines as the Thief, while Conrad Veidt masterfully portrays the sinister villain. I keep a copy close by, ready for my next nostalgic journey. Hold on—Rex Ingram is itching to escape his genie bottle!

**ELVIRA, MISTRESS OF THE DARK (1988)**

**Directed by:** James Signorelli

**Starring:** Cassandra Peterson, W. Morgan Sheppard, Daniel Greene, and Edie McClurg

**Plot:** Elvira (Cassandra Peterson) abandons her television gig and travels to the conservative town of Fallwell, Massachusetts, to claim an inheritance from her late aunt, dreaming of funding a grand Vegas show. However, her dreams are dashed when she inherits only a eerie mansion, a poodle, and a mysterious cookbook with magical powers. While stranded in Fallwell, Elvira schemes to earn cash, energizes the local teens, flirts with a charming hunk (Daniel Greene), dodges accusations of witchcraft that could lead to her being burned at the stake, and protects the cookbook from her sinister uncle (W. Morgan Sheppard), who aims to use its dark magic to unleash chaos on the world.

**My Thoughts:** I'm a huge fan of both Cassandra Peterson and her iconic character, Elvira. Peterson is a talented, stunning, and witty individual, and as Elvira, she adds a delightful mix of macabre humor and endearing naivety to her persona, not to mention her striking physical presence. This film showcases her unique appeal brilliantly.

The 'fish out of water' theme is a highlight of the movie. Seeing Elvira, draped in her signature low-cut black gown, navigate the uptight environment of Fallwell is endlessly entertaining.

This sequel to Joe Dante's 1981 classic, "The Howling," is a disappointing mess with an unattractive visual style, a weak script, and clumsy pacing. Despite "The Howling" being among the rare elite of exceptional werewolf films, it has unfortunately spawned a series of dreadful and unbearable follow-ups, including this one. As a small solace, "Stirba" is a sequel in name alone, bearing no ties to the characters or storyline of Dante’s original work. The narrative centers on a vicious cult of predominantly female Transylvanian werewolves led by the character Stirba. Portrayed by Sybil Danning, Stirba morphs from a shapely elderly woman into a stunning blonde bombshell (with a striking figure) in an instant, turning furry when overcome by sexual desire. Her nemesis, Stefan Crosscoe, an occult investigator played by a visibly weary Christopher Lee, journeys to Stirba’s realm alongside an American couple mourning the loss of a friend to the werewolf cult. If your sole interest lies in graphic violence and unnecessary nudity, this film might appeal to you. It revels in gory detail with every minor death, even showcasing exploding eyeballs and the gruesome demise of a dwarf who is impaled.

Assessing this film, or any similar production from the early sound era, using standard film critique terminology proves challenging. There is a palpable sense of urgency as numerous silent era stars tentatively explore sound, gripped by the fear of obsolescence—a fate that indeed befell some. Rin-Tin-Tin, on the other hand, appears entirely at ease. Amidst a medley of disconnected scenes, certain performances inevitably shine, with John Barrymore's soliloquy from Richard II standing out as a highlight worthy of preservation. Generally, those with prior stage experience display a noticeable assurance. Overall, the film offers reasonable entertainment and is essential viewing for "film buffs" with a keen interest in the transition from silent to sound cinema.

I had planned to watch this movie in the theater, but it was completely sold out. Instead, I ended up watching *Solaris*, which turned out to be the most disappointing film of 2002.

Victor Rosa (John Leguizamo), a hardened and savvy 'street pharmacist,' is shaken after witnessing a child being shot. This incident prompts him to abandon his old ways and invest all his money with Jack (Peter Sarsgaard). Initially, things appear to be on track, but the situation takes a turn when Jack disappears with Victor's girlfriend, Trish (Denise Richards). This plot point occurs late in the film, and had it not been spoiled in the trailer, it could have been a compelling surprise. Unfortunately, it was revealed, stripping away any suspense.

Ultimately, this movie lacks any engaging elements; the trailer gives away every significant detail. If you've seen even a single preview, you've essentially seen the entire film, so you might as well just piece together the rest in your mind. Visit the website, watch the trailer, and save yourself the $3.99. There are no unexpected turns or surprises throughout the movie, except perhaps for the shockingly poor quality of the soundtrack.

I can only hope that the person responsible for composing the soundtrack was

"The Cobweb" serves as a prime example of films that boast impressive, occasionally remarkable performances and standout moments, yet are ultimately undermined by a convoluted storyline and a lack of engaging content for viewers. The film features Richard Widmark as a doctor at a psychiatric facility, whose personal life spirals into chaos amid family issues and an absurd, overblown conflict that feels trivial at best.

The storyline is utterly implausible. The central issue revolves around choosing new drapes for the library windows of the institution. An elderly woman insists on using her own drapes, while many patients wish to create their own designs. This bizarre and unintentionally comical dispute escalates to a dramatic extent, endangering lives and tearing families apart. It resembles a petty squabble one might expect among very young children rather than adults.

The plot's logic is so questionable that it begs the question of whether only someone detached from reality could find it believable. To be clear, the acting is not the issue. The ensemble supporting Widmark includes other talented performers.

There was a genie, portrayed by Shaq,  
Named Kazaam, and man, he was lack.  
His rhymes were lame, his lines a mess,  
A kid whining over his dad, no less.  
Terrible acting, casting a flop,  
Special effects that make you wanna stop.  
What’s next? This film’s a wreck,  
Probably didn’t earn a twenty-buck check.  
He’s stuck in a boombox, not a lamp,  
Hurts to watch, worse than a cramp,  
Like a soggy food stamp, it’s just damp.  

You get the gist—a rhyming genie with no skill,  
In a awful flick with effects that kill.  
Plus, the plot’s a confusing, tangled hell,  
I won’t drag on, no need to dwell.  
It fits the “so bad, it’s funny” vibe,  
Watch it once with friends, share a jibe.  
But don’t expect brilliance, not even a spark,  
It’s just a laugh in the cinematic dark.

The story of *The Dentist* unfolds on the morning of Dr. Alan Feinstone (Corbin Bernsen) and his wife Brooke's (Linda Hoffman) wedding anniversary. At first glance, the Feinstones appear to lead an idyllic life in their stunning Los Angeles home, with Alan enjoying a thriving career laden with responsibility. However, beneath this polished facade, turmoil brews. Alan uncovers Brooke's infidelity with Matt (Michael Stadvec), their swimming pool cleaner. His humiliation deepens when he learns that Matt is also involved with Paula Roberts (Lise Simms), a neighbor. To compound his woes, the IRS is hounding him over a substantial debt.

Alan's sanity begins to unravel as he becomes obsessed with the notion that everything around him is decayed and corrupt, mirroring the state of his patients' teeth, and he feels compelled to rectify it. That very morning at his dental practice, he starts unleashing his pent-up rage and frustration on his patients. He first harms a young boy, Jody (Brian McLaughlin), then, in a delusional state, mistakes a patient, April Reign (Christa Sauls), for his wife and sexually assaults her. He also intentionally subjects another patient to a needless and excruciating procedure. Alan's descent into madness continues as he...

From the moment I first watched *How The Grinch Stole Christmas*, it captured my heart and claimed the spot as my favorite film. Even after watching it eight times, its magic remains as powerful as it was during that initial viewing.

Screenwriters Jeffery Price and Peter S. Seaman, known for their work on *Who Framed Roger Rabbit*, brilliantly adapt The Grinch's tale for the big screen. Under Ron Howard's skillful direction, the story bursts to life, and Jim Carrey’s vibrant portrayal of The Grinch truly steals the spotlight.

Some critics argue that the film strays from the essence and values of the original story. Having read the source material, I respectfully disagree. The movie conveys the same core message about the true meaning of Christmas as the original. In fact, it deepens the emotional resonance by exploring the personal backstory of The Grinch, revealing the reasons behind his transformation.

*MILD SPOILERS* (These likely won’t spoil the experience, but if you’re someone who prefers to go into a story completely blind and haven’t seen the movie yet, tread carefully.)

I want to commend the series for its remarkable effort. The storyline, while needing some refinement, was quite impressive, particularly in Season 1. However, Season 2 veered into more of a spectacle, losing the original charm that defined Dark Angel. The narrative in Season 1 was more captivating, balancing a lighter glimpse into life at Jam Pony with a gripping, serious plot involving Manticore's pursuit of the X-series. I was eagerly anticipating new seasons, and I still am. I hope the team at FOX and the Dark Angel production crew recognize that many fans are still waiting for the show's return. Even two years after its cancellation, Dark Angel has the potential to make a significant impact if handled with care. I believe a visionary like James Cameron should take on this challenge.

Collusion Course is a disappointing film that surpasses the cliché of the "evil white male corporate capitalist" trope often seen in weekly movies. Watching it is more unpleasant than enduring a toothache. Jay Leno, who can indeed act and showcased his talent in the underappreciated film The Silverbears with a performance suited to his role, is wasted here. In this dreadful movie, Leno's portrayal of a sanctimonious buffoon somehow manages to be less irritating than Morita's character, who comes across as a sanctimonious fool.

A chemist invents a revolutionary fabric that resists dirt and wear, posing a significant threat to multiple industries in this charming Ealing Studios comedy. Guinness delivers a stellar performance as the gentle yet determined chemist. Greenwood, with her captivating voice, portrays the romantic lead, while Parker plays her frazzled father. Thesiger brings humor to his role as a titan of the textile world. Beyond its entertaining narrative, the movie poses thought-provoking questions about science, economics, and politics. Under Mackendrick’s skillful direction—later known for "The Ladykillers" and the brilliant "Sweet Smell of Success" in the 1950s—the film shines.

How far can someone fall in an attempt to relive past triumphs? ST:HF is eager to demonstrate.

If you're accustomed to the elements that defined a great Star Trek series, steer clear of this one.

The writing is disjointed, the actors' performances lack depth, and above all, the design choices are utterly abysmal.

If you admire strong, capable captains, you won’t find them here. If you value the resolute spirit of the Federation, prepare to be disappointed. Starfleet is ridiculed, with ensigns sporting SPIKES in their hair as if it’s a fashion statement.

Meanwhile, a seemingly unhinged captain stumbles through the scenes, and within the first two minutes of the opening credits, Ensign Spikey is already scheming a romantic encounter with an engineer. The quality only deteriorates from there. Even the uniforms are a mess—ill-fitting, with some too tight, others too loose, collars plunging to inappropriate depths, and a chaotic mix of TNG Seasons One and Two outfits alongside Season Three and DS9 designs. The discipline and tradition that marked the original series are completely absent in this production, right down to the smallest details. The only redeeming feature might be the graphics, which show slight improvement with each season. Or perhaps even that’s too generous a claim.

Should Todd Sheets openly confess that this film was crafted as a satire of the zombie genre, I would revise my rating to an eight. Picture a film where each scene, dialogue, and subtle acting choice is deliberately satirical. I could likely scribble nonsense on a page, rearrange the mess, and still produce a superior script. Two specific scenes stand out when recalling this movie. SPOILER ALERT! The first involves Mike's dad and another father calmly strolling—I emphasize, strolling—down a narrow staircase swarming with zombies. Despite brushing against the thrashing undead on this cramped stairwell, they remain unscathed. Upon reaching the bottom, the ex-marine turns, quips, "God, you're a horny bastard," and fires at just one zombie. The second scene occurs in a military complex where a girl stabs a zombie with a machete and instantly finds herself encircled. The camera circles her for about forty seconds as zombies stand mere inches away. Then, almost nonchalantly, she darts through the horde to rejoin the other humans. SPOILER ALERT OVER! These moments are undeniably noteworthy.

At New York University in Manhattan, Robert Wuhl is instructing a group of film students. He delves into historical misconceptions and forgotten truths, making the content incredibly engaging. I find myself wanting more of this captivating series. Wuhl effectively uses examples and interactive "show and tell" methods to illustrate his lessons. For instance, he revealed that Paul Revere wasn’t the actual rider during the famous Midnight Ride; Henry Wadsworth Longfellow chose Revere’s name for its rhythmic appeal in his poem.

I’ve been a fan of Robert Wuhl for years, following his career from stand-up comedy to his role in HBO’s "Arli$$." While he excels as an actor and comedian, his talent as a teacher truly stands out. I strongly encourage you to watch an episode of this show—it’s an enriching experience that’s definitely worth your time.

A lackluster movie.

The narrative introduces Chrissy, the protagonist, as a 'young' and somewhat morose individual who aimlessly drifts through life, contributing little to the plot's progression. It was unsurprising, then, that the focus eventually shifted to her family members. It's a shame, as Chrissy initially appeared to be a potentially intriguing character.

The storyline was unsurprising and often felt overly structured. This raises the question: when will filmmakers like the Campions, Jacksons, and Tamahoris create innovative, visually captivating stories that inspire rather than merely entertain for a couple of hours?

From a technical standpoint, the cinematography was poorly executed.

A mysterious entity is targeting victims, leaving puncture wounds on their jugulars and draining them of blood until they perish. Police detective Karl Brettschneider (Melvyn Douglas, in one of his final roles in B-movie horror before moving on to more prestigious projects) is baffled by the identity—or nature—of the perpetrator behind these gruesome crimes. As hysteria grips the village, Karl turns to the brilliant Dr. Otto von Niemann (Lionel Atwill, delivering another compelling performance as a mad scientist) for insight into the cause of these innocent deaths. Meanwhile, Karl grows increasingly concerned for the safety of his beloved Ruth (the captivating Fay Wray, in her third collaboration with Atwill following *Doctor X* and *The Mystery of the Wax Museum*), who serves as Niemann’s assistant.

Dwight Frye dominates the screen as a deranged village idiot with an obsession for bats and an unsettling presence that makes him an easy suspect amid the town’s escalating paranoia. Maude Eburne brings humor to the film as a gullible and overly impressionable patient of von Niemann’s, convinced she suffers from every ailment she reads about in books near the laboratory. Her susceptibility to suggestion often leads von Niemann to indulge her endless, imaginary maladies with a mix of amusement and patience.

I haven’t watched the first film, and if it’s anything like this one, I have no strong urge to do so.

I just watched it a few hours ago, and I’m already struggling to recall any details.

From what I can piece together, the main storyline revolves around a group of incredibly irritating characters staying at a house with a creepy old woman reminiscent of Friday the 13th, all while being hunted by a man who might as well be a plank of wood.

Some characters meet their demise, the movie concludes, and now I’m considering legal action against the person who sold me this film, seeking compensation for the wasted hours of my life.

I’d pay someone £1 to take this movie off my hands... oh wait, I already passed it on to a so-called “friend.”

...and even so, they could easily skip watching it. Frankly, this so-called film holds genuine appeal solely for enthusiasts of bondage. Fans of Bettie Page will gain no new insights—absolutely none—and won't even find comfort in familiar, beloved, or nostalgic elements.

Forget the dreadful screenplay, the stiff acting that falls below even community theater standards, the complete lack of directorial vision, the poor lighting, or the overall shoddy production quality. This is "Hey, kids, let’s make a movie!" filmmaking at its most abysmal. One might grudgingly acknowledge that at least they figured out how to operate the camera. But sadly, none of these flaws are the core reason this project is so fundamentally *flawed*.

The real issue lies in the casting of the actress portraying Bettie Page. This somewhat fuller-figured woman, whose only similarity to the Queen of Curves is her dark hair and iconic bangs, brings nothing to the role beyond a readiness to be tied up and gagged. While this may have benefited her film career before and after this deplorable piece, it does nothing to redeem the abysmal portrayal.

I recently rented this movie and initially assumed it would be a typical story of a girl trying to make a statement. However, I was pleasantly surprised to find that Diane’s decision to join boxing was driven by her own passion. I thoroughly enjoyed the film and would rate it an 8/10—that’s how much I liked it. Additionally, any movie featuring Michelle Rodriguez is bound to be good, even if she’s only appeared in six films.

This issue exemplifies a growing trend in films where background noise and soundtracks overpower the dialogue. What logic is there in such a choice? This problem isn’t unique to this movie; it seems pervasive across most modern films. For two years, I suspected my TV might be faulty, but even after upgrading to a new one, the issue persists. Background sounds, which could be happening blocks away from the characters, still drown out their conversations.

In this particular film, the problem was even more pronounced because, in the English version at least, the female lead constantly mumbles. I found myself wishing Jean Reno’s character would ask her to speak clearly or remove whatever seemed to obstruct her speech. If you’re watching on DVD and have even a basic grasp of French, I suggest opting for the French version with subtitles for a better experience.

I rate this film a 4, largely due to Jean Reno’s impressive performance in *Leon*. Many praise the film’s scenery, but watching it on a TV, and having lived in the Rockies for several years, it didn’t particularly impress me.

The movie begins at a leisurely pace, introducing Wallace Napalm, a photo-service drop-off station attendant. His wife is confined to their home, bound by an ankle bracelet due to an arson conviction. Wallace, a dedicated member of the local volunteer fire department, approaches firefighting with utmost seriousness.

As the audience observes Wallace's mundane routine, a sudden twist emerges with the arrival of a traveling carnival in town. Among its performers is Wilder Napalm, Wallace’s brother and a clown with a unique ability.

Both brothers share an extraordinary secret: they are pyrokineticists, or "pyrotics," individuals who can ignite fires using only their minds. While Wallace conceals his powers, Wilder openly showcases his to those around him.

Spoiler: Their conflicting attitudes stem from a tragic childhood event in which they unintentionally caused a vagrant's death. Wallace restrains his abilities, whereas Wilder dreams of revealing his talents on national television.

Adding to the tension, Wilder harbors feelings for Wallace’s wife, a woman both brothers once courted. Her presence becomes a source of conflict, ultimately sparking a literal fiery confrontation between the siblings.

The film offers entertainment, though it is not without its flaws.

Allow me to clarify that I’m not from the South, though I am American. Country music isn’t my favorite, but I can tolerate it. You won’t catch me in a cowboy hat, though I do wear hats occasionally. I don’t live in a trailer, but I do enjoy tuna salad and own my own home. Why mention these details? They’re relevant if you’re among those who claim only “country” folks can appreciate this movie. This film, rooted in the classic “they loved and lost” theme, is directed by James Bridges as a quintessential American love story, raw and authentic. In a time dominated by Jerry Springer-style sensationalism and oversharing, this movie feels more genuine than ever.

Bud, a young man coming of age, sets out to build his own life with the support of his aunt and uncle, relocating to the big city with them. Seeking an escape affordable to a blue-collar worker, Bud is drawn into the local honky-tonk scene. There, he meets Sissy, a woman from a similar background, and their intense romance unfolds with a rollercoaster of emotional highs and lows.

Satan's Little Helper stands out as one of the more impressive B Horror films I've encountered, particularly due to its storyline. By "impressive," I refer to the originality of the plot, which offers a fresh take in a genre often riddled with clichés. However, the movie also raises several perplexing questions that linger in your mind as you watch.

I first stumbled upon this film while browsing the Horror section at HMV. Fed up with the overhyped, so-called "terrifying" Hollywood blockbusters, I was on the hunt for something unique. The cover art of Satan's Little Helper instantly grabbed my attention with its eerie allure. Despite knowing it was a direct-to-DVD release, I decided to give it a shot—after all, having endured "Boogey Man" the previous night, I figured it couldn’t be any worse. After viewing, I felt moderately pleased. The plot truly captivated me, especially the unsettling premise of the killer befriending a young boy under the guise of friendship, only to carry out his murderous intentions. In a twisted, disturbing manner, the killer even seemed to believe that he and the boy could form a sinister partnership.

Branagh stands out as one of the rare individuals who grasps the distinction between cinema and theater. His adaptation of Hamlet is arguably the most loyal representation of Shakespeare on screen, while still delivering a vibrant and dynamic experience, akin to an action thriller. The haunting encounter between Hamlet and his father’s ghost is a moment that lingers long after the film ends.

Xizao is a unique gem of a film—unassuming and straightforward, yet profoundly rich in emotion and delight. Its narrative is uncomplicated, and the conflict between tradition and modernity is skillfully woven into the opening scenes. This central theme forms the heart of the film, but its impact would have been lost without the brilliance of its characters and the actors who bring them to life.

Master Liu, the elderly patriarch, embodies a bygone era of China before its rapid modernization. He operates a bathhouse in a quaint, old neighborhood, and every scene within its walls evokes a pang of envy in us, the stressed and discontented. Even the most jaded cynics would struggle to find fault with this enchanting setting.

Equally compelling is Master Liu’s mentally challenged son, Er Ming, whose dynamic with his modern-minded brother adds depth to the story. The interactions among these three characters, along with the eclectic visitors to the bathhouse, are portrayed with remarkable nuance and sincerity. Certain moments carry such intense emotion that they surpass the emotional depth found in most cinema.

Due to its subtle critique of the regime, the film faced censorship and was given disproportionately limited exposure. Whether this was coincidental or deliberate remains uncertain, but the impact of such suppression is undeniable.

This is arguably the worst movie I've ever watched, yet, to be fair, it’s oddly entertaining and quite amusing. It’s clear the filmmakers weren’t aiming for a polished Hollywood blockbuster. Instead, it’s a ridiculous story about a serial killer who gets drenched in toxic waste, triggering a bizarre transformation during a harsh winter. He morphs into a murderous snowman, a concept absurd enough to elicit laughter on its own. The film is utterly nonsensical, but its humor shines through, especially in the over-the-top killing scenes. I wouldn’t recommend purchasing it (I made that mistake after being drawn in by the cover), but if you stumble upon it on TV one night and are in the mood for some silly fun, give it a watch.

Haha! That's quite the opener. I initially believed this movie was unique, only to find out it’s essentially a copy of the 1976 remake of KING KONG. I didn’t watch KING KONG until I was 15, but I caught this flick at the age of 9. The groovy disco soundtrack is incredibly catchy and will linger in your mind, as will the theme song performed by the Yetians. The creature effects are, frankly, the worst I’ve ever seen, yet this movie holds a special place as a cult classic among B-movies. Some unforgettable lines include: "Take a tranquilizer and go to bed," and "Put the Yeti in your tank and you have Yeti power." I still recall watching this on MOVIE MACABRE, hosted by the iconic Elvira. There's a standout scene that flips the KING KONG narrative—instead of climbing up a building with the girl, the creature climbs down and catches her as she falls! That same year, another KING KONG knockoff, MIGHTY PEKING MAN (1977), emerged from Hong Kong. The film is packed with traveling matte shots and mechanized body parts. It’s a guaranteed laugh riot, and as I mentioned, it’s just another in a long line of quirky imitators.

I must emphasize how disappointing it is that the typical viewer often fails to value creativity. The distinctiveness of this show lies in its surreal, dreamlike world. There's no need to question why Ned possesses the power to resurrect the dead, or why this revival lasts merely a minute. Where has the enchanting magic of childhood stories disappeared to, reminiscent of tales like *A Wrinkle in Time*?

I find this series refreshingly innovative because it stands in stark contrast to the flood of overly explicit TV programs that leave nothing to the imagination or sense of awe.

Incorporating a touch of escapism into the viewing experience is a delightful addition.

The surreal atmosphere is what captivates me most about the show. With its 1950s-inspired aesthetic, the pure and unique characters, and the settings and landscapes that defy strict realism, it creates a mesmerizing escape.

Unlike other shows that dwell on the grim aspects of death, this series cleverly conceals its darker themes. While other programs may entertain, they pale in comparison to this one. It has reinvigorated television with a renewed sense of curiosity, creativity, and wonder.

*Pushing Daisies* has swiftly climbed to the pinnacle of my favorites.

I first watched this movie as a 12-year-old and was captivated, though looking back, my young age likely clouded my judgment. Having recently revisited it, I found myself wishing I could reclaim the time spent. Frankly, the film is quite disappointing. Despite my appreciation for actors like Lee Majors, Chris Makepeace—who shines in better films like *My Bodyguard* (1980) or the comedic *Meatballs* alongside Bill Murray—and Burgess Meredith, this particular role did little to enhance their careers.

The story follows Lee Majors’ character, Franklyn Hart, a former race car driver determined to drive his stored race car cross-country to California. However, there’s a significant hurdle: the government has banned all private transportation. While the premise had potential, its execution fell flat, resulting in a deeply underwhelming film.

This film serves as a prime example of how even the most hilarious jokes can fall flat. I had high hopes after watching the incredibly funny trailer, but the movie itself didn’t come close to meeting those expectations.

Strangely, the humor in the film isn’t the issue. The parodies of the smoking ban and references like "Jo Bole..." are genuinely amusing. However, I’m at a loss for who to hold responsible for the movie’s failure.

The likely culprits could be: 1) The actors and actresses, who lack the comedic flair needed to pull it off; 2) The director, who may have mishandled the project; or 3) The person responsible for casting the actors or choosing the director. If you’re absolutely desperate for entertainment—and I mean truly desperate—then consider watching this film. Otherwise, just track down the ads and teasers; they’re far funnier than the actual movie and will have you laughing out loud.

P.S. The only redeeming elements of this film are Mahesh Manjrekar and the humorous Chappu Bhai.

An utterly disagreeable movie. Although Rick Baker's special effects are striking (albeit unsettling), the film lacks any other redeeming qualities. Much like numerous films from the 1970s, it leaves you with a lingering sense of discomfort, as though you need an extended shower to wash away the grime. The characters are consistently unlikeable, and the storyline is incoherent.

***SPOILERS*** In "Omen IV," the malevolent legacy of the late AntiChrist Damien Thorn resurfaces in a chilling new form. This time, the terror manifests as a girl named Delia York, portrayed by Asia Vieira. Delia is adopted by a seemingly worthy couple, Karen and Gene York, played by Fay Grant and Michael Woods, through St. Francis Orphanage, run by the Catholic Church.

From the outset, Delia unleashes her sinister nature, making her presence felt by violently scratching her mother during a house party. Her dark powers soon become evident when she narrowly escapes death by a runaway truck, only to be saved by a mysterious "Devil Dog" named Ryder. At school, Delia deals with a local bully by humiliating him in front of his peers, causing him to wet himself. When the bully’s father threatens the Yorks with a lawsuit, Delia orchestrates a horrific, self-induced traffic accident that results in his decapitation. A clear warning: cross Delia at your own peril.

Meanwhile, Delia’s father, Gene, rises to prominence in the community, or so he believes, securing a congressional seat as an advocate for clean air and environmental conservation, unaware of the dark forces potentially propelling his success.

This story lacked a single fresh concept. Its themes were borrowed from multiple works, including *The Ninth Gate*, *In the Mouth of Madness* (another of Carpenter’s films), and *The Ring*. It even replicated the iconic glowing circle from *The Ring*, shamelessly using it as the film’s title. The soundtrack, composed by Cody Carpenter, was essentially a rip-off of *Suspiria*. I hope no one tries to defend this by tossing around the term “homage.” Yes, I noticed the theater showing Argento’s *Deep Red*, but calling this an homage is a weak excuse. This was the lowest of the low. Simply piling on gore and “shocking” visuals doesn’t create a quality horror film. Carpenter once understood that. He should either retire quietly or find a way to revisit his past genius.

I had the privilege of viewing this film at the Sundance Film Festival, and I was utterly captivated by its profound impact. The movie delves into the psychological toll on our courageous soldiers who enlist with the noble intention of defending and serving our nation with honor, expecting support from our government in return. It meticulously explores the mental transformation that occurs during boot camp, where soldiers are molded into "killers for their country," thrust into combat, and later grapple with the aftermath upon returning home. The film also sheds light on the deep impact that taking a life has on the human mind. Unlike other works, it honors the soldiers without any criticism directed at them, instead pointing a critical lens at a system unprepared to meet the comprehensive physical and psychological needs of returning veterans.

This film is intense, touching, deeply emotional, and intellectually stimulating. It serves as a rallying cry to truly support our troops beyond merely displaying stickers or attending parades—by genuinely listening to their stories and advocating for significant improvements in how their health and well-being are addressed.

Director Vincenzo Natali brought a distinctive flair to this film, employing creative camera angles and impactful close-ups. It was a pleasant surprise to witness Jeremy Northam and Lucy Liu taking on lead roles, showcasing their versatility as actors. Moreover, the movie featured one of the most inventive "escape" sequences seen in recent cinema. The combined talents of the director and cast culminated in a compelling thriller.

While the film's plot was intricate, the narrative unfolded with clarity, peeling back the layers of corporate avarice and deceit.

In his iconic 1949 novel "1984," George Orwell envisioned a future dominated by a totalitarian State that suppressed freedom and controlled thoughts. Intriguingly, this captivating futuristic film presented a different oppressor—not the State, but the corporate realm, which subjugated and devalued the human workforce.

I strongly believe that every horror and cult movie enthusiast should watch this film. I did, and I was thoroughly impressed!

It's truly remarkable—a deeply atmospheric, unsettling, and terrifying experience. What's even more astonishing is how they managed to create such a masterpiece on an incredibly low (practically nonexistent) budget.

Here's a brief synopsis from the film's website: "One morning, an old man ventures into the woods to find his missing cat. Instead, he stumbles upon an orphaned child and a murder without a body..."

Unfortunately, there's no trailer available on IMDb, but I’ve included a link to the movie’s official site, where you can watch a chilling trailer. I highly recommend checking it out.

www.softfordigging.com

Initially, I didn’t mind the Geico commercials; I even found them somewhat witty and entertaining the first 50 or so times I watched them. However, I must ask, is this truly the best concept they could devise? This show is terrible! It’s dull and reminiscent of an episode of "The Office," just with characters dressed as cavemen. (I know many will disagree with me, but "The Office" simply isn’t my cup of tea.) I understand the stereotypes: the downtrodden guy trying to stay out of trouble, burdened by a terrible boss who despises him; the self-proclaimed intellectual who’s barely competent; and the clueless one desperate for acceptance. But honestly, who cares? I’ve encountered these types in real life and found them just as irritating as I do on screen. Why would I spend another 1/336th of my week watching more of these clichéd characters? If, after reflection, you still consider this entertainment, you might want to check with your parents to see if you were dropped on your head as a child.

I immediately realized that this film strayed significantly from Dodie Smith’s original novel. Nevertheless, I found it charming that Pongo and Perdita’s son now had his own litter of puppies. Among them, the most adorable was undoubtedly little Snowball, who remained completely spotless until the film’s conclusion.

Truthfully, I was unsure how to react when Cruella de Vil appeared to undergo a complete change of heart. I had often pondered the idea of her becoming amicable, but her swift reversion to her true, sinister self—declaring herself Cruella once again—left me genuinely concerned for Chloe’s Dalmatians.

Surprisingly, the scene where the puppies watched *Lady and the Tramp* while Chloe and Kevin enjoyed their dinner exceeded my expectations. I was also quite taken with the parrot who mimicked a dog, and I found it remarkable how many tricks the dogs had mastered for the movie.

Naturally, I was relieved that the Dalmatians were rescued in the end, though I couldn’t help but wonder what would happen next to

Before I dive into my thoughts, I must say that this movie is severely underrated.

Sharon Stone delivers a captivating performance as Catherine Tramell, and Morrissey shines as Dr. Glass, an analyst tasked with evaluating her following the death of a sports star. Dr. Glass finds himself entangled in a seductive game orchestrated by Tramell, who skillfully manipulates his mind.

The acting is generally strong, with the exception of Thewlis.

Stone truly excels in this role, embodying a slick, mischievous, and seductive character who appears just as youthful as she did in the original film. Her performance is impressive, reminiscent of her work in *Casino*. Morrissey also stands out, bringing a necessary vulnerability to his character. On the other hand, Thewlis falls flat. His over-the-top portrayal undermines his role, and he ultimately disappoints.

Overall, while this movie doesn’t quite match the impact of the first, Stone is a delight to watch. Just try to overlook Thewlis.

To begin with, it seems the well-known actors were in dire need of a paycheck. The surgical scenes were utterly ridiculous, and surely the cast must realize that anyone with even a basic understanding of medicine would find them completely preposterous. Anesthesiologists don’t just wander out during a heart transplant, nor do such critical procedures take place in a cramped, ill-equipped room lacking essential tools, heart-lung machines, or proper sterilization practices. It’s simply laughable. The absurd surgery sequences made it impossible to focus on the plot—no blood, no supporting staff, and then the heroic doctor swooping in to take charge. This movie isn’t meant for anyone who thinks critically. Additionally, the budget must have been incredibly tight. While the street scenes were passable, one has to wonder who served as the technical advisor. It feels as though the film was directed by someone utterly clueless. Save your money—wait for it to hit DVD, and even then, don’t bother renting it.

Halloween tells the tale of a misunderstood young boy whose inner turmoil leads him to commit a horrific act—murdering his older sister in the film's opening scene. This chilling act marks only the beginning of Michael Myers' dark journey.

Donald Pleasance portrays the doctor who has spent years analyzing Myers. He senses a unique and sinister evil within him, an unstoppable force that refuses to be confined.

Following his escape from a mental institution, Myers sets out to find his younger sister. Killing her might bring an end to the torment of this troubled soul, yet he struggles to complete his mission as others stand in his path. Undeterred, he eliminates these obstacles while relentlessly pursuing the one girl he seeks.

While countless horror films feature teenagers falling victim to masked or grotesque killers, Halloween is often credited as a pioneer of the genre. When we think of iconic horror, names like Freddy Krueger or Jason Voorhees chasing vulnerable victims often come to mind. However, it was Halloween that arguably laid the foundation for these terror-filled tropes.

For those enchanted by the stage musical A CHORUS LINE, the film adaptation proves to be a disappointing replacement. It not only omits several songs but introduces unwarranted plot complications, reimagined dance routines, and frankly, Richard Attenborough lacks the finesse to capture dancers on film effectively.

Onstage, A CHORUS LINE was the embodiment of Michael Bennett's vision. His concept, choreography, direction, and ultimately his gift to Broadway and global audiences, it delivered two hours of raw, unflinching realism that forged a deep connection with the struggles of its “boys” and “girls.” In stark contrast, the film falls short in conveying emotion and substance; the performers appear as though they are merely trying out for A CHORUS LINE rather than living the intense reality of an audition. Every action and line feels overly calculated and deliberate. Michael Douglas, portraying Zach, exhibits such restraint that it's hard to accept him as the notoriously harsh choreographer. Even his outbursts lack authenticity, with every movement, emphasized word, and subtle expression seeming meticulously staged. Additionally, regarding the decision against his dancing: Kevin Kline tried out for the role of Zach on Broadway and impressed Michael Bennett with his performance, but his inability to dance led to him not securing the part.

I ended up with this movie, though not by choice. A few days ago, sheer boredom led me to its intriguing box. I slid it into my ancient VCR and endured the next hour and a half lamenting, "Why, God, why?" The storyline wasn't terrible; as a gamer, I found some elements relatable. If you're a fan of overly nerdy, cheesy romantic moments, this might be your kind of film. Picture lines like, "I've always seen myself as a Vulcan, you know, like Dr. Spock... incapable of love." Honestly, there’s little to praise about this movie—it’s genuinely dreadful. Yet, if you’re in the mood for a spectacularly bad film, this is your pick! The behind-the-scenes story, however, is far more captivating ;)

If I had to describe this movie in a single word, it would be:

LAME

I was completely captivated by this silent action drama. Kurt Russell, and only Kurt Russell, could have delivered such a remarkable performance. Trained from childhood to know nothing beyond war and combat, Todd (Kurt Russell) is abandoned on a distant planet after being replaced by genetically engineered soldiers.

The scene is perfectly set, giving rise to yet another iconic figure in action cinema—SOLDIER. Unlike Rambo, Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Mel Gibson, or Jason Statham, Kurt Russell fully embodies this role, making it uniquely his own with originality, boldness, and a deeply human touch. I regret that no sequels were ever produced.

10/10

-LD

I didn't have high expectations when I watched this film, especially since it came in a bundle of five movies, all of which were disappointing in their own unique ways, and cost less than five pounds. My skepticism was confirmed; they were all awful. This particular movie has a handful of interesting moments—though calling them "interesting" is generous. The occasional camcorder perspective is a nice touch, and the drummer fits the stereotype of being incredibly irritating, but that's about all there is to say. The main issue is that it's excruciatingly dull. What I can only guess was meant to build suspense turns into long stretches of absolutely nothing happening, and when something does occur, it's painfully unexciting. I kept my thumb hovering over the fast-forward button for most of the film but decided to give it a fair chance. Also, I couldn't help but wonder if the lead singer of the band is really as stunning as the characters repeatedly claim. Personally, I thought he resembled a meerkat. I haven’t even touched on the killer, and I won’t bother—it’s simply not worth the effort to explain.

I watched this film solely because of Al Adamson, a director notorious for being one of the worst in cinematic history, ranking alongside the likes of Ed Wood, Jr. and Ray Dennis Steckler in the hall of terrible filmmaking. However, I found myself somewhat let down. While the movie was undeniably poor, it didn’t reach the spectacularly awful depths of Adamson’s earlier, more campy disasters. As a result, it wasn’t as entertaining as I had hoped for fans of bad cinema.

I approached this film with caution due to its suggestive title, "Naughty Stewardesses," which hinted at pornography—a genre I wouldn’t typically review on IMDb. At times, especially in the first ten minutes, it did seem to lean in that direction. Yet, it was evident that the script had been heavily altered during production. For much of the runtime, there’s little to no provocative content, and towards the end, a sudden, violent plot twist emerges out of nowhere, completely devoid of any allure. The outcome is a bewildering mess.

Regrettably, none of the film’s numerous elements are even remotely redeeming. For instance, as an attempt at adult entertainment, it reveals surprisingly little, and it’s baffling why they would include a 71-year-old character in such a context.

This independent film stands out as one of the finest I’ve ever witnessed at the Tall Grass Film Festival. I was thoroughly impressed by numerous aspects of the production. Beyond the film itself, meeting the cast and crew was an incredible experience; their talent and warmth were truly remarkable. Avi delivered a standout performance, and Ricky Ullman, transitioning from Disney's lighthearted teen comedies to a mature, complex role, showcased astonishing versatility and skill.

The talent on display was exceptional, and the cinematography was equally impressive. If you're looking to explore independent cinema, this film is an absolute must-see. I believe Mr. Gruver would have been immensely proud to feature such a remarkable submission in his festival. His parents were so captivated by the movie that, after it won the Audience Favorite award, they watched it again. This film masterfully blends dark humor, sadness, and deep emotion, resulting in a truly fabulous piece of cinema. I’m genuinely captivated by this work and can’t help but feel an overwhelming enthusiasm for it.

This movie is a delight for both adults and children, offering entertainment on multiple levels. It includes everything from thrilling car chases and slapstick humor like pies in the face to clever, subtle jokes tailored for grown-ups.

Glenn Close delivers a masterful performance as the wickedly charming Cruella De Vil, who insists on being called "Ella." After spending three years at Dr. Pavlov's Behaviour Modification Clinic, she emerges seemingly cured of her obsession with fur, including the puppy-skin coats she once coveted. She even locks away all her fur garments in the dungeon of her extravagant castle.

However, a true 'Dalmatian' story wouldn't be complete without Cruella's deceit and plotting. It's inevitable that something will unravel her reformed behavior. This time, her sinister plan requires just one more puppy, bringing the tally to 102 Dalmatians.

Ioan Gruffudd shines as the likable hero who manages the 'Second Chance' dog shelter. Despite his roles in 'Titanic' as Fifth Officer Lowe and in the recent TV adaptation of 'Great Expectations' as Pip, I didn't recognize him—perhaps because I missed 'Great Expectations' and his part in 'Titanic' was minor.

Gerard Depardieu

In an era where Hollywood profits from depicting our flaws, hopelessness, crime, addiction, and conflict, this film emerges as a powerful reminder of the "Indomitable Spirit." If you're feeling defeated, this movie will liberate your thoughts and lift your spirits. We’re all aware of life’s challenges, and sometimes we need a nudge to remember that perseverance and bravery can carry us forward. This film inspired me in that way, and I hope it does the same for you.

I still possess those scratchy, late-night, no-cable, low-quality VHS recordings of this show from ages ago, complete with the old late-night commercials. I used to stay awake until the oddest hours just to catch it on TV and hit the record button.

The series wasn’t truly centered on Freddy Krueger—only the initial episodes featured him in a role beyond that of a Rod Serling-like host. Rather, each episode presented a unique nightmare, delving into classic horror motifs like traumatic childhoods, dating, cannibalism, money, death, and, repeatedly, dating.

From the episode where a teenage boy mistakenly pledges eternal love to the wrong girl and finds himself physically fused to her for a horrifying moment, to another where a young flight attendant goes home with a mysterious man only to discover his cabin houses a trophy room of other flight attendants, and one dimly recalled episode likening blind dates to hockey—with all the injuries and penalties that implies—dating emerged as the most terrifying theme of the series.

In one memorable episode, Jeffrey Combs (known from Re-Animator, among others) portrayed an ambitious pizza vendor with a...

A wildly romantic comedy brimming with seamlessly blended subplots and performances that deliver razor-sharp comedic timing, "Moonstruck" is a captivating spectacle. When Cher's timid fiancé enlists her aid to reconcile with his brooding, estranged younger brother, the ensuing chaos is beyond anyone's wildest imagination. With operatic symbolism, Catholic confessions, love bites, and drifting snow, the film is both timeless and effortlessly charming. It takes roughly 15 minutes for the movie to find its footing—early scenes, like the grandfather with his dogs at the cemetery, feel somewhat uneven, and a subsequent moment with Cosmo and an old man at the gate comes across as cryptic. Yet, the intricate tapestry of the story is woven with finesse, and the film's unsteady tone and eccentric charm prove utterly contagious. ***1/2 out of ****

John Boorman's "Deliverance" follows four suburban men from Atlanta as they embark on a canoe trip down the turbulent Cahulawassee River, a wild waterway soon to be erased by a dam project and the subsequent flooding of its untouched terrain.

The group embodies a range of personalities: a rugged, uninsured outdoorsman who thrives on risk (Burt Reynolds); a dedicated family man with a talent for the guitar (Ronny Cox); a heavyset, single insurance salesman (Ned Beatty); and a reserved, contemplative married man with a young son, often seen enjoying his pipe (Jon Voight).

Their journey quickly turns into a harrowing ordeal as they confront the brutal forces of nature. The film also serves as a profound exploration of morality, illustrating how civilized individuals can succumb to the savage rules of the wild.

Masterfully filmed, this intense adult adventure delivers truly captivating moments that keep viewers on edge.

I’d like to clarify the earlier comment. The plot involving a criminal whose image is stolen by a band is from CB4, not Fear of a Black Hat. It’s easy to mix them up since the two movies share similarities, but Fear of a Black Hat is, in my opinion, the far better film.

How can anyone take her gritty, high-octane bounty hunter tale seriously with *that* accent? It’s simply laughable. Beyond that, the director’s visual approach feels dizzying and overly contrived, the storyline is a superficial, tiresome, and muddled rehash of a gangster flick, and the performances fail to convince. The movie incessantly introduces new characters right up to the end and unfolds through disjointed, out-of-order flashbacks, seemingly designed to keep viewers perpetually disoriented. Worse, it presents events that *aren’t even real*, only to later clarify, “that didn’t happen, this did”—take the (supposed) killing of the (fabricated) ‘first ladies’ as an example. What, then, was the purpose of showing us the initial, incorrect version of events?

Appalling casting decisions, a tangled and chaotic narrative, and a directorial style that leaves you with a migraine. 1/5.

I first watched this movie half a lifetime ago on a black-and-white TV in a tiny Samoan village, and I found it absolutely hilarious back then. Watching it again after all these years, though, I no longer find it laugh-out-loud funny. In fact, I don’t find much of anything hilarious anymore. Still, this remains a clever and breezy comedy that keeps a steady pace without any missteps, and I truly enjoyed revisiting it.

Set in 1945, the story follows Fred MacMurray as a 4F, desperate to join the armed forces despite being deemed unfit. While managing a scrapyard, he rubs a lamp and summons a genie who offers to grant him a few wishes. (A familiar trope, sure, but while the setup is just decent, the ensuing fantasies are quite engaging.) MacMurray wishes to serve in the army, and with a puff of magic, he’s suddenly marching alongside Washington’s troops. He finds himself in a cozy, welcoming USO, where June Haver and Joan Leslie appear in elaborate lace outfits—or something of the sort—and striking lavender wigs.
