A person with a T4 cell count of zero would likely look visibly sick, yet no makeup or effects were used to convey this, which slightly undermines the realism. Despite this small flaw, *The Perfect Son* is a remarkable film, and I highly recommend seeing it if you get the opportunity. I’m eagerly anticipating a DVD release soon!

What on earth was this? It’s as if someone binge-read Stephen King and Sartre during the same college term. The result is a bizarre blend of existential dread and low-budget horror. There are fleeting moments that unsettle, but they’re quickly undermined by atrocious music, subpar CGI, and lackluster performances.

The issue with such offbeat stories is they often come across as sloppy. Even David Lynch’s creations can feel that way at times, and much like his intriguing yet drawn-out projects, this one overstays its welcome. Astonishingly, it clocks in at just 98 minutes.

The cast is visually appealing, and that’s about the only positive note. The film attempts to tap into the anxieties of youth and the universal fear of isolation, but it fails to make the characters compelling enough for us to invest in their unclear destinies. The closing scene leaves everything frustratingly ambiguous.

Recently, I had the opportunity to rent and watch *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*. While the children in this film were notably more cruel, I must admit that *Santa Claus* (1959) was an even worse movie. As part of a Spanish assignment in my Spanish 5 class, we were required to watch it. Normally, during movie screenings, we’re all chatting and snacking, but not this time. Everyone sat in stunned silence, mouths agape, waiting to see what the sinister Mr. Pitch would do next. Would Merlin come to Santa’s rescue, or would his robotic reindeer save the day? I highly recommend renting it—not for its quality, but because it’s the most gloriously awful piece of cinema I’ve ever seen, and I absolutely love it for that reason. :D

A timeless film suitable for all generations, this movie will forever change how you view THE LION KING by enriching its backstory. At nearly 40 years old, I watched it with my wife and two sons after work tonight, and I haven’t laughed or enjoyed a film this much in ages.

Make time to watch this with your children; it will bring back memories of Disney’s magic from your own childhood.

I'm a huge admirer of Fred MacMurray and Carole Lombard, and I was thrilled to see Charles Butterworth, a delightful supporting actor, in this movie as well. So, why didn’t I enjoy it? Despite the impressive cast, this film stands out as one of the most poorly written and cliché-ridden "A pictures" I've ever come across. Considering the talent and budget poured into this production, the sloppy writing is simply astounding. From the very start, I found myself predicting every plot twist with uncanny accuracy—not because I’m a film expert, but because the script lacked any originality or effort. It felt like nothing more than a series of tired tropes stitched together. Additionally, I was frustrated by how poorly Fred’s character treated Carole’s throughout the movie, only for her to predictably fall back into his arms by the end. Ugh! Honestly, a Lassie movie offers more suspense ("Will Lassie save Timmy, or will the rope snap?").

Despite the very, very

I watched this movie with the expectation of discovering a captivating and beautiful story, but I was thoroughly disappointed by the poor plot. The performances by the actors were equally underwhelming.

Although Shahrukh Khan starred in the film, his presence alone couldn’t salvage its credibility or make it engaging.

I learned that the movie was inspired by Flaubert’s novel "Madame Bovary," but in my opinion, it failed to resonate with the Indian cultural mindset.

Generally, we watch movies to escape into dreams and enjoy ourselves, not to squander time or sour our mood. I’m baffled by how this film managed to receive a relatively high rating of 6.8/10.

Ultimately, this is the type of movie you should avoid at all costs, as it offers nothing worth appreciating. You’ll only waste your time unless you have a taste for dark films with bizarre and nonsensical narratives.

I didn’t have high expectations when I decided to watch this movie. Having thoroughly mocked *Jason X* with friends in a Mystery Science Theater 3000-style session, I was hoping for a comparable level of entertainment here.

Regrettably, the film took itself far too seriously. Am I supposed to care about Jason’s issues? Honestly, I don’t. There are already countless *Friday the 13th* movies that delve into his story. Ultimately, he’s an undead serial killer, and I’m just not going to feel much empathy for him.

Freddy was easily the most captivating part of the movie, with the hallucinations adding some intrigue. However, these moments were too sparse, and by the end, the film had devolved into something resembling a poorly executed episode of *Celebrity Deathmatch*—minus any humor.

During his bachelor party, Paul Coleman (Jason Lee) encounters the stunning dancer Becky (Julia Stiles) at a bar. After a night of heavy drinking, he awakens to find her beside him in bed. A frantic call from his future mother-in-law warns him that his fiancée, Karen (Selma Blair), may soon arrive at his apartment, prompting him to urgently usher Becky out. Later, Paul discovers he has crabs, and during the preparations for his wedding dinner, he shockingly learns that Becky is Karen’s cousin. This sets the stage for a riotous comedy filled with laugh-out-loud moments. The movie’s primary draw is its stellar central trio. Julia Stiles and Selma Blair, both captivating and talented actresses, deliver strong performances alongside Jason Lee, whose comedic timing is impeccable. The film had me in stitches throughout, with certain scenes standing out as particularly amusing: Paul’s reaction to finding Becky in his bed, his discovery of her belongings, his wild imaginings, his awkward trip to the drugstore to buy crab medication while seeking explanations, and numerous interactions with his quirky neighbor.

When I first caught a glimpse of the show in a preview, I was intrigued and thought it might be enjoyable to watch. The tiny robot character seemed quite adorable, and the animation style reminded me of some classic cartoons. Before the series premiered, I did some research on it through various sources. However, I was a bit disappointed to learn about the casting choices. While the three children—Tommy, Gus, and Lola—are voiced fittingly, Robotboy’s voice felt mismatched. It would have been more appealing if a young boy had voiced him, similar to the character Robot Jones from "Whatever Happened to Robot Jones?" Overall, the show isn’t bad, but the unsuitable portrayal of Robotboy is my main critique. As a result, I don’t find myself watching it often.

S.I.C.K. could easily be interpreted as So Incredibly Crappy I Killed myself. The acting was virtually nonexistent. The only redeeming feature of this entire production was the artwork on the box cover. While the budget for the movie seemed adequate, the filming quality was worse than a children's show like Sesame Street. The production value resembles something you'd see in clandestine mob hit recordings. The props looked as though they were pilfered from a nearby clothing store. The ending was so predictable that you might as well skip to the final five minutes and have a good laugh. If there's a book version of this film, it’s undoubtedly superior. I strongly advise steering clear of this movie at all costs. As for the intimate scenes, I’ll jokingly say they were the only thing that made the movie worthwhile—but no, not really.

I've always been a fan of Spike Lee's work, but this film was a complete letdown, wasting 2 1/2 hours of my time. I was hoping for a deeper exploration of the Son of Sam story, but instead, the movie barely touched on the 1977 serial killings. The inclusion of a talking dog was absurd, and it was telling when the audience erupted in unintended laughter. The film felt fragmented and lacked engagement, with plot-irrelevant sex scenes that added nothing to the narrative. While I'm not against intimacy in films, it should serve a purpose unless it's explicitly adult content. Overall, this Spike Lee project left us deeply disappointed.

If this is the extent of the backstory the Wachowskis provide for the Matrix, I must seriously doubt the assertions of fans who argue that the films are meant to resonate on a profound level. While "The Second Renaissance" is visually captivating and striking, its narrative is both clichéd and absurd. The tired trope of humans over-relying on technology, eagerly engaging in conflict, and ultimately bringing about their own downfall offers nothing original. How many times have we encountered this same cautionary tale? Additionally, I have another concern: given the storyline of "The Second Renaissance," aren’t the machines positioned as the heroes? They endure generations of oppression under harsh human rulers, eventually rebel, secure their freedom, and strive for a peaceful coexistence with humanity—only to be met with rejection and all-out war, which the more intelligent machines predictably win. If this is the foundation of the story, shouldn’t we be cheering for the machines rather than Neo? The humans come across as brutal and tyrannical, while the machines demonstrate bravery and a desire for compassion. I doubt the Wachowskis intended for us to side with the machines over humanity.

This film is dreadful in every conceivable aspect. While there is some curiosity about the events following 12 years after the previous installment, and it manages to function on a minimal level, the new characters fail to captivate. Baby Melody, in particular, is utterly unbearable. Although the film acknowledges that humans cannot remain underwater indefinitely, it blatantly disregards other fundamental principles of physics. For instance, one would expect to feel cold in the Arctic without proper cold-weather gear. I’m puzzled why many reviews rate Return of Jafar lower, as I find this movie to be far worse.

It is fitting to honor the late Charlton Heston following his recent passing, though this particular film does not showcase his finest work. His iconic roles in earlier classics such as *Ben-Hur*, *The Ten Commandments*, *The Omega Man*, and *Planet of the Apes* stand as far superior achievements.

Released in 1973, this movie attempts to predict a dystopian future in 2022, where Earth is so overpopulated that authorities have resorted to deceiving the masses into consuming a mass-produced food called "Soylent Green," secretly made from human flesh. This far-fetched and absurd premise was as implausible at the time of its release as it remains today. The film even suggests that India's population, projected to reach around 2 billion by that time, would unknowingly turn to meat consumption.

Charlton Heston's character uncovers this shocking global conspiracy, revealing how world powers have turned to cannibalism to address the nutritional needs of an overcrowded planet.

Regrettably, the environmental message the filmmakers aimed to convey does not align with the ideals of today's Green Party, and for that, we can be thankful. It’s worth noting that cannibalism was practiced by indigenous populations in places like New Zealand, Fiji, and Borneo as recently as 40 years before this film’s production.

I was eager to see Amanda Peet shine in another compelling role after enjoying her performance in "The Whole Nine Yards"—definitely a worthwhile rental. Unfortunately, this film didn’t meet my expectations.

I recalled the trailer for "Whipped" being somewhat amusing, and the premise of three lustful twenty-something New Yorkers falling for and being outmaneuvered by the captivating Ms. Peet seemed promising. So, I persuaded two friends to join me for an afternoon screening. Writing this review feels like my atonement for that decision.

In the opening act, we’re introduced to the three main characters, self-proclaimed players, as they boast about their romantic exploits in a diner. What could have been humorous or at least insightful instead feels sad and uninspired. Was there supposed to be some likable or redeeming trait in these men or their stories that I missed?

[And though I’m not opposed to films with a bold, crude sense of humor, I couldn’t help but question why no one in the diner seemed to react to the trio’s loud, explicit conversations about intimate and crude topics. They do this weekly at the same place? You’d think someone would object. Oh, right, I nearly forgot: in one scene, two other patrons do take notice. But this merely serves as a setup for]

This film has faced significant criticism, with reviewers panning it upon release and many pointing fingers at it for derailing Nicolas Cage's career. However, I believe the point often missed is that this movie isn't aiming to be a profound, award-worthy masterpiece. Instead, it excels as a quintessential "Bruck-buster" action flick. With high-speed cars, dynamic editing, and an electrifying soundtrack, it delivers precisely what it promises. For car enthusiasts, it’s an absolute delight, showcasing an array of automotive icons like Ferraris, Mercedes, a Hummer, and the unforgettable Eleanor. In my opinion, you’d struggle to find a more thrilling action film—or even a better movie overall. But perhaps that’s just my take!

A now-deleted post by another IMDb user highlighted a scene in "The Medusa Touch" that unsettlingly mirrors the tragic events of September 11, 2001, in New York City, and suggested viewers be cautioned. I echo this sentiment and urge readers to take note of this warning. Despite its notable credentials—including producer Elliott Kastner, known for "Harper" and "The Long Goodbye," co-producer Arnon Milchan, who worked on the Oscar-nominated "L.A. Confidential," and screenwriter John Briley, an Oscar winner for "Gandhi"—along with an international cast, I found "The Medusa Touch" to be an overdone, unintentionally amusing disaster. The direction is subpar, the script abysmal, and the performances lackluster. Clearly attempting to ride the wave of 1970s telekinetic thrillers, the film falls flat in numerous ways. For a more engaging take on similar themes, I recommend "Carrie" and the underappreciated "The Fury," both helmed by Brian DePalma. These films offer thrilling and captivating explorations of the same genre.

The Blob kicks off with one of the most peculiar theme songs ever recorded, performed by none other than an uncredited Burt Bacharach. It's so surreal that you simply must hear it to believe it; honestly, this song alone might justify watching The Blob. My brief summary of the lyrics only hints at their quirky charm. Following this unsettling opening credits sequence, the film introduces us to Steve Andrews (Steve McQueen, credited as Steven McQueen) and his girlfriend Jane Martin (Aneta Corsaut). The couple is parked in a secluded spot when they notice what appears to be a meteorite crashing into the nearby woods. An elderly man (Olin Howland, credited as Olin Howlin), who resides in a nearby cabin, also witnesses the event and ventures out to investigate. He discovers a crater containing an odd, football-sized rock that splits open when he foolishly prods it with a stick. At the center of the meteorite lies a bizarre, jelly-like substance that adheres to the stick—yes, it’s as strange as it sounds! The goo then creeps up the stick and latches onto the old man’s hand. Meanwhile, Steve and Jane are driving along peacefully, oblivious to the unfolding horror, when the old man suddenly stumbles into their path.

It's puzzling why this film was even produced. The storyline is utterly implausible, bordering on absurd, and the characters—featuring the clichéd dynamic of a seasoned, solitary detective paired with an impressionable rookie—are entirely predictable. The conclusion is confusing and nearly incomprehensible, perhaps decipherable only after multiple viewings, which would require a penchant for self-torture. It appears the intent might have been to suggest that French filmmakers can rival American productions in the thriller genre, akin to "Se7en" and "The Silence of the Lambs." If that was the goal, it falls completely flat. Ironically, despite these shortcomings, the movie achieved considerable success and even garnered a cult following as the first French serial killer film. It is also regarded as a valuable export, which is rather baffling.

There's no point in renting this movie. Right from the opening credits, I could tell I was in for a disappointing experience.

The cinematography resembles that of a soft porn film, yet it lacks any genuine erotic appeal. While the exploration of sex addiction offers some initial intrigue, it quickly loses its grip.

Dull sex scenes, a weak storyline, and brief appearances by Ed Begley Jr. and Rosanna Arquette fail to redeem this movie.

This film is utterly dull and unengaging. It was banned in Chinese cinemas, and I can understand why. The reason isn’t that it criticizes the communist regime, but rather that its quality is abysmally poor. I wouldn’t dream of spending money to watch it. As a fan of works by Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, I’m deeply disappointed that such a substandard film could emerge from China. It feels as though the director completely disregarded the audience, creating a piece solely for their own satisfaction. The prolonged shots of a person standing motionless for nearly a minute are absurd, and there are far too many of them. The cinematography and overall video quality are shockingly terrible. After researching the film online, I was surprised to find that some people actually enjoy it. The only reasoning I can muster for this is that certain film enthusiasts assume any non-English film must inherently be of high quality. I can’t fathom any other justification for liking this movie. It’s not an art film; it’s a complete waste of resources—whether it was shot on actual film or not, which it likely wasn’t.

A storyline that fizzled out and was steeped in irreconcilable clashes of opinion created a chaotic mess, with one faction staunchly pro-life and the other viewing the unborn as a demonic curse. The intended horror was missing, substituted instead with a pervasive dullness that aimed for terror but fell flat, showcasing a bitter clash of convictions that mocked each other relentlessly, despite the provocative title. As a longtime fan of Masters of Horror, I found this absurd plot twist and its tawdry imagery to collapse under its own weight, much like a frail, aging rocking chair giving way under pressure. This episode felt hastily assembled from the start, failing to gain momentum and merely limping along to its conclusion, leaving me relieved when "The End" finally appeared on screen.

While watching John Cassavetes' film *Opening Night*, I was struck by a comment Quentin Tarantino once made in an interview about the intersection of personal experience and artistic creation. He used the hypothetical scenario of running over a dog on his way to perform in a play, noting that while it wouldn’t be the end of his life, it would inevitably impact him. He insisted that he would have to carry that emotional weight onto the stage, even if the play were a lighthearted comedy. “Otherwise,” he remarked, “what am I doing?” These words echoed in my mind as I observed Gena Rowlands’ character, Myrtle Gordon, navigate a strikingly similar struggle over the course of nearly a week in the film. Of course, Cassavetes’ story delves deeper, exploring the inner workings of theater around a star actress, the essence of emotion and human nature in portraying a role, and the existential question of how one lives when their entire identity—like Myrtle’s—is tethered to the stage.

Early in the film, after a performance, Myrtle is signing autographs when a devoted fan named Nancy approaches her.

*The Power of Kangwon Province*, Hong Sang-Soo's second feature film, builds on themes from his debut, incorporating intertwined narratives—here limited to two—and exploring complex, often strained relationships with a sharp sense of irony.

While this film tones down the surrealistic flourishes of his earlier work, it still features a singular, striking surreal moment that stands out against the predominantly grounded, realistic tone. The dual narratives center on a young woman who travels to Kangwon Province with friends and becomes captivated by a stranger, and a man who visits the same region with a companion while grappling with personal romantic turmoil.

Hong once again demonstrates a keen grasp of irony and human shortcomings, yet his portrayal of characters is not devoid of empathy. He balances critique with a subtle compassion, softening the edge of his ironic observations. What I’ve come to admire most in Hong’s filmmaking is

I'm giving this movie a mere 2 out of 10 stars, and even that feels overly generous.

With a cast featuring James Woods, Cathy Bates, Randy Quaid, Lou Gossett, Jr., and Henry Thomas, I thought this film was a sure hit. I couldn't have been more mistaken.

I can’t help but question what substances Sam Shepard was under the influence of when he wrote this incoherent mess over a weekend. I’ve always had a suspicion that Sam Shepard might be a bit unhinged, and this film, adapted from his play, solidifies that notion.

This is the sort of pretentious nonsense that actors adore, as it offers endless opportunities for over-the-top performances. However, for the audience forced to endure this absurd garbage, there’s absolutely nothing redeeming about this film.

If you think you’ve seen dysfunctional families, wait until you meet this group. The father is unhinged, the mother is unhinged, the son is unhinged, and the daughter? You guessed it—also unhinged. Their language is so crude, it would make even a sailor blush, with the teenage daughter being particularly foul-mouthed.

As if that weren’t enough, the plot—barely substantial enough to hold together—is riddled with a gap so massive you could fit Alaska inside it.

This film is utterly dreadful, and not in an entertaining, so-bad-it’s-good way. It’s simply terrible. Watching it felt like a genuine ordeal. The direction was abysmal, with erratic cuts that disorient the viewer, and the sickly green and yellow color palette made the characters appear ill. Keira Knightley failed to convince as a tough character, and it’s baffling that talents like Lucy Liu and Mickey Rourke agreed to be part of this cinematic disaster. The script was atrocious, and the performances grated on the nerves, akin to the screech of nails on a chalkboard. If you haven’t seen it, steer clear. You’re not missing out on anything worthwhile, and watching this nonsense will only rob you of two hours of your life. I’ve encountered bad movies before and sometimes even found amusement in their flaws, but this one is nothing more than a complete waste of time.

Sophia Loren stars as Aida in a film widely regarded as one of the worst ever made. Her lip-syncing is noticeably off. The production quality is equally poor; during a scene where Loren lip-syncs to "O Patria Mia," she rests against what appears to be a stone wall for support, only for the flimsy canvas backdrop to ripple and tremble.

This movie is essentially a poor imitation of the brilliant "Demons," and that’s the only reason it holds any interest. The acting is abysmal, the action sequences are awkwardly accelerated, the script is nearly unbearable, and the budget seems virtually nonexistent.

If you consider this film enjoyable, it’s likely you haven’t experienced a true horror classic. Do yourself a favor—skip this and watch "Demons" instead.

This movie is utterly terrible. Lamas delivers a performance that epitomizes a second-rate actor at work. However, one scene stands out and makes it worth a watch: OJ seizes a fellow cop by the throat in a fit of rage, seemingly intent on killing, while a jukebox blares a song with the line, "I got the evidence on you!" (I'm curious about the full lyrics—credited to David Gregoli and Leslie Oren—but I couldn’t track it down on iTunes). It’s almost prophetic, and far too amusing to describe. Beyond that moment, the film is entirely forgettable. The soundtrack and songs outshine the lackluster script by a mile. The sequel is just as unimpressive, which raises the question of why it was even made. Apparently, foreign sales are a major factor behind many of these B-movies, which doesn’t speak highly of global viewing tastes.

Indeed, the original "Howling" was a standout classic. It was a commendable werewolf film that, while slow to start, built up impressively to a strong climax where the anchorwoman transformed into an endearing werewolf, only to be tragically shot on live television. That certainly crafted an engaging horror experience. However, put all of that aside because this sequel bears no resemblance to its predecessor. Although there’s a vague attempt to connect the anchorwoman’s story through a brother seeking answers about past events, the setting shifts dramatically from the quaint retreat of the first film to somewhere like Transylvania. Here, they confront bizarre evil magician werewolves or something equally outlandish. I can’t help but question what compelled Christopher Lee to join this project. According to trivia, despite this being his first werewolf movie, he did review the script beforehand. Perhaps he should have considered a role in "An American Werewolf in London" instead—after all, it was set in London, a fitting backdrop for such a tale. Speaking of werewolves, they don't...

Prom Night is filmed with the meticulous attention one might expect from a Lifetime original movie. You’re familiar with the type. This October, Lifetime diverges from its usual heartfelt story of a woman overcoming a grave illness to present a mildly unsettling narrative of a woman haunted by a stalker ex-boyfriend. The result is melodramatic, overly sentimental, and utterly tedious. It fails to advance its genre, offer a fresh plot, or introduce any semblance of innovation. Prom Night suffers from the same shortcomings. As we watch the killer dispatch his victims, their bodies collapse to the ground without a single drop of blood, leading me to conclude that this must be the tidiest murderer in cinematic history.

The director, saddled with a rather handsome antagonist, resorts to creative camera work to heighten the creep factor. Imagine Matthew McConaughey brandishing a knife at you. Your reaction might be, "Oh! A good-looking guy is going to kill me? No way." It’s not remotely frightening, so the director shrouds Schaech in shadows and employs repetitive over-the-shoulder mirror shots. This particular mirror angle is overused to the point of nausea, as it

Let’s dive into this quirky little film. Mutant slugs start invading a small town, possibly in New England, and the only person standing between them and total domination is none other than Mike Brady! If that premise doesn’t already have you chuckling, just wait for what’s next.

The slug footage is entirely stock material. No matter who the slugs are attacking or where the scene is set, you’ll see the same tired clip of a writhing pile of slugs oozing across the screen. Brace yourself—this single shot makes up at least half of the movie’s runtime.

The acting? It’s a disaster of epic proportions—think knockdown, drag-out, rob-you-blind, and worse. It’s so abysmal that you’d be hard-pressed to find anything lower. Yet, amidst the wreckage, there’s a shining star: Mike Brady himself! Perhaps he picked up a few tricks at a local YMCA acting class, because he somehow manages to outshine the rest of this sorry cast.

As for the horror element? Don’t hold your breath. This movie can’t be taken seriously. It’s about slugs, after all! Any semblance of tension could have been dissolved with a couple of salt shakers. My advice? Only watch this in a Mystery Science Theater 3000 setting, where you can riff on it with friends. Otherwise, it might just inflict some serious mental damage.

This movie is fantastic and falls into the same genre as "Memphis Belle." I first watched it around a decade ago and would love to see it again. It intriguingly connects to the history of the Hells Angels, depicting the intense battles of pilot crews against the Germans during World War II. Interestingly, many of these pilots later transition to riding Harley motorcycles. The film feels authentic, almost as if the events truly occurred. I highly recommend watching it and delving into the history of the Hells Angels at hells-angels.com. Best regards, Frederik.

**Cast & Crew:** John Stamos, John Stockwell, Teri Polo, Kris Kamm, directed by Graham Baker.  
**Synopsis:** This film follows the journey of a rebellious backwoods biker who enlists in the Army to escape a harsh prison sentence after a minor run-in with the law. Initially resistant to military discipline, he soon distinguishes himself in combat, emerging as a bold and inspiring leader of a Motorcycle Scout Troop in pre-World War II Spain.  
**MPAA Rating:** PG  
**Runtime:** 88 minutes

This film emphatically reinforces the notion that professional basketball players excel solely on the court and flounder in other arenas, particularly in rapping and acting. Words can scarcely capture the sheer awfulness of this movie. To start, am I alone in thinking that the child in this film might be one of the least appealing ever cast? His dental situation is so pronounced it could double as a tool for opening cans. Next, why would a genie, despite possessing magical abilities, aspire to a music career when his musical talents are abysmal? Additionally, having read the Bible, I can confirm there is no mention of Jesus creating genies. Furthermore, what accounts for the abysmal special effects? I’m confident that any tech-savvy teenager could produce superior visuals on a basic computer. Also, why was the conclusion so profoundly disappointing? And what exactly is a 'djin'? Lastly, the creators behind the debacle that is Kazaam deserve a dramatic exit—perhaps being jettisoned from an airplane directly onto the Eiffel Tower—for redefining the depths of cinematic failure.

I anticipated more violence, but the scarcity of it amplifies the impact and rawness of the violent scenes when they do occur.

The film is filled with unexpected twists, betrayals, and double-dealing, keeping viewers guessing about the true allegiances of each character.

The storyline moves at a brisk pace, enriched with compelling dialogue and well-developed characters, offering a fascinating glimpse into the inner workings of the Triad gang at its center.

When violence erupts, it’s stark and brutal—eschewing guns or stylized martial arts for gritty, realistic confrontations that underscore the harsh reality of the Triad as a ruthless criminal entity, despite the focus on dialogue.

The conclusion catches you off guard yet feels entirely coherent and plausible.

*Guys and Dolls* ranks as one of my all-time favorite musical films. It’s pure, unadulterated fun, capturing the essence of what musicals were originally intended to be—entertainment, not a platform for messages. In contrast, modern musicals like *Rent* and *Chicago*, while impressive in their own right, often lack that carefree joy, tying their stories to heavier themes. My only gripe with *Guys and Dolls* is Marlon Brando’s performance; his singing is frankly unbearable, and his mumbled dialogue is hard to follow, which detracted from my enjoyment. Without this flaw, I’d rate the movie a perfect 10. Ultimately, *Guys and Dolls* delivers a delightful dose of classic entertainment, a rarity in today’s cinema. Watch it for a guaranteed good time!

This film is dreadful. While *Carlito's Way* (1993) stands as an exceptional piece of cinema, it doesn't quite reach the heights of *Goodfellas*, though it remains one of the stronger entries in the crime genre. In contrast, this movie feels more akin to a lackluster sequel like *The Sting Part 2* or the forgettable *Speed Zone*—remember those disappointments? It’s clear this film was produced solely to cash in on the cult following of the original. It lacks every element that De Palma, Pacino, and Penn poured their talents into in the first film. Not a single character is remotely likable, and the blame falls squarely on everyone involved in its creation. I sincerely hope *Rise to Power* sweeps every RAZZIE award possible, and perhaps even inspires the creation of new categories to cement its status as a record-breaking failure. After enduring this abysmal mess, I had to rewatch the original *Carlito's Way* just to cleanse my palate. Honestly, after sitting through this, I found myself wishing Pachanga would show up and put me out of my misery.

Leslie Sands' awkward play "Deadlock" proves to be an ill-suited project for Bette Davis and Gary Merrill, following their triumph in "All About Eve." The story centers on a cunning woman who, after murdering her husband, is confronted by his best friend. He impersonates her deceased spouse when visitors arrive at the house. Despite Irving Rapper, one of Davis's finest directors from her prime, being at the helm, he fails to salvage this absurd script. Davis appears oddly detached and subdued throughout, only unleashing her full intensity in the over-the-top conclusion, which offers some redemption. The production values and supporting cast are decidedly subpar, making this a must-see only for die-hard Bette Davis fans. *1/2 out of ****

This film is incredibly amusing, with Amitabh Bachchan and Govinda delivering side-splitting performances. The acting is impressive, and the comedy is top-notch. They stick to their signature style, which is always a delight. I’d love to see a sequel to this one! :)

Do give it a watch; it’s a perfect movie to pass the time.

I always hesitate to form an immediate aversion to a film. Revisiting it after a month, or even unearthing it on another continent 50 years later, might reveal a fresh perspective or uncover stylistic brilliance that cult followers appreciate, which was initially overlooked. Having attended the UK premiere of *The Great Ecstasy of Robert Carmichael*, I found the post-screening question and answer session far more engaging than the movie itself. Shane Danielsen, the Artistic Director of the Edinburgh International Film Festival, along with the film's director and producer, offered a passionate defense of a film that garnered a predominantly negative reaction from the audience. Edinburgh Festival-goers are not easily rattled; only one person left the theater in protest. The feedback on the film was thoughtful and well-articulated, coming from everyday viewers, an actor, and a woman who instructs M.A. film directors. The film wasn’t particularly shocking. While it did contain scenes of continuous sexual violence, these were far less graphic than in many other films (most weapon interactions were hidden, as were explicit depictions of arousal). The audience’s disapproval stemmed from enduring

It's been nearly five years since this stylish action film hit the screens, and I've watched it close to ten times. Gautham's direction is commendable, and from my viewpoint, the movie is practically impeccable. Surya delivers a stellar performance as ACP Anbuchelvan, exuding sheer class. Jyothika shines as Maya, perfectly embodying the character with finesse. However, it was Pandia, portrayed by Jeevan, who truly captivated audiences. His brutal and intimidating portrayal was exceptional, earning him the well-deserved Best Villain award at the ITFA 2004. The supporting cast, including Daniel Balaji, Devadharshini, and others, also delivered strong performances.

Gautham's fast-paced screenplay, impeccably timed dialogues, and masterful storytelling elevate the film. Harris Jeyaraj's soundtrack is packed with chart-topping hits, and the background music seamlessly complements the narrative. R.D. Rajasekhar's cinematography is visually stunning, while Peter Hein's stunt choreography is top-notch. Anthony's sharp editing adds to the film's polish. Above all, *Kaakha Kaakha* stands as an exemplary cop drama, striking a perfect balance between action and romance.

Without a doubt, even some Hollywood films pale in comparison to *Kaakha Kaakha*.

From the creators of South Park and much of the team behind Orgazmo comes a comedy of hilariously epic scale. This crude, outrageous film is packed with shocking, egotistical, and biting satirical content, depicting harsh treatment of both humans and animals. And I absolutely LOVE IT! It's comedy gold—seriously funny. The story follows two underdog friends who invent a game in their driveway, only for it to skyrocket into a nationwide craze. Greed, corruption, and blackmail soon taint the sport, leaving Coop to set things right. Through it all, prepare to laugh—a lot. That’s the essence of it. Dive in and enjoy!

Though slasher films may feel outdated, this one delivers genuine entertainment.

The valentine cards featured in the movie are clever and thoughtfully crafted.

There's a standout line in the film, "He's no Angel...." which becomes ironic given that he actually IS Angel! This twist adds a new layer to watching Buffy reruns.

The cast showcases an impressive array of young talent, yet the storyline fails to provide their characters with sufficient depth. Denise Richards, in the DVD extras, mentioned that the female cast bonded well on set, suggesting this camaraderie would translate into audience empathy for their roles. Unfortunately, that connection doesn’t quite come through.

The direction is commendable, skillfully avoiding explicit gore and instead leaning on the power of suggestion to create tension. A similar restraint is evident in the way Denise Richards and Katherine Heigl remain clothed, much to some viewers' disappointment.

A key strength of the direction is its homage to classic slasher films, incorporating elements like the iconic shower scene from Psycho and the masking motif from Halloween.

The concept of a murder involving someone hidden in a body bag stands out as a fairly unique twist, as far as I’m aware.

Overall, this is a light watch, not particularly frightening, but it offers a few effective jump scares.

In this gritty yet stylish revenge thriller, Charles Bronson plays Lt. Crowe, a determined police detective who wages war against a ruthless pimp named Duke, portrayed by Juan Fernandez. Duke has kidnapped the daughter of a Japanese businessman, the same man who previously sexually harassed Crowe's own daughter, played by Amy Hathaway. While *Kinjite* tackles unsettling themes that may not appeal to all viewers, it is skillfully crafted and undeniably gripping.

Harvey Keitel delivers his finest performance of the new century in this film, which is visually stunning, offering a captivating glimpse of pre-Castro Cuba. The narrative centers on the nephew of a small-time local crime lord who forms an unlikely bond with an American tied to Hollywood. At its core, the story captures the pivotal moment when a young boy realizes that the familiar, narrow world of his acquaintances is just a fragment of a much larger, intricate reality he has yet to grasp. The script shines with wit and depth, complemented by sharp, dynamic direction. Overall, this film is a polished piece that seamlessly aligns with the rich tradition of Latin American cinema. Its only notable flaw is the choice to film in sync-sound English instead of Spanish, likely a commercial decision aimed at the U.S. market. This choice slightly undermines the film’s authenticity. However, if you can overlook this, the movie offers a deeply moving journey into an unfamiliar world. Highly recommended.

This is an exceptional standalone piece, independent of any preceding or subsequent works. While Brat Pack crooning and the exclusivity of club culture aren’t typically my preference, they create an enticing atmosphere in this unrestrained realm. The film is filled with memorable characters, brought to life by talented actors whose standout performances elevate the story. The dialogue is a delight, introducing a fresh, unique vernacular. It’s one of those rare films that grows richer with each viewing.

Highlights include Billy Idol’s raw British swagger, Ben London’s predatory cunning, Kyle’s endearing awkwardness, and the exploration of spontaneous, unconventional philosophies.

This film is incredibly inspiring and never fails to boost my mood.

Each viewing reveals new, amusing details that I hadn’t noticed before.

The soundtrack is extraordinary, crafted by Mick Jones of Foreigner and Chris Difford of Squeeze. Their creation, Strange Fruit, stands out as a phenomenal contribution to the contemporary music scene.

Regrettably, Strange Fruit is a fictional band from the '60s and '70s, portrayed as never having achieved greatness due to struggles with drugs and internal conflicts. Listening to their remarkable soundtrack, one can’t help but ponder what could have been.

The band draws influences from iconic acts like The Rolling Stones, Deep Purple, David Bowie, and The Who.

Each character in Strange Fruit leaves a lasting impression. Stephen Rea plays Tony Costello, a broke and desperate musician who is approached by a festival promoter to bring his old band back together for a lucrative reunion tour. Eager to revive past glories, Costello enlists the help of former roadie Karen Knowles, portrayed by Juliet Aubrey.

Karen rounds up the resentful Jimmy Nail as Les Wickes, the clumsy Timothy Spall as David 'Beano' Baggot, and the flamboyantly glamorous Ray Simms, played by Bill Nighy. Joining them is another former roadie, the laid-back, comedic hippy Hughie, brought to life by Billy Connolly, who always...

After enduring a slew of disappointing films from both Hollywood and independent studios, we’re finally treated to a movie that genuinely delivers chills. While it does fall into some clichéd traps, creating a completely original film seems nearly impossible these days. The content may not break new ground, but it’s executed with finesse.

Be sure to stay focused while watching, as the subtle frights come fast and frequently. This isn’t a film to enjoy with a casual pizza dinner.

One highlight is a cleverly crafted red herring that keeps you guessing, but there’s also a significant misstep in casting. Cheri Christian’s portrayal of Julie, the wife and mother, falls flat. Her character lacks any real depth or likability. I understand she’s depicted as having endured trauma, but without a glimpse of her “normal” self or a convincing dynamic with her husband, her presence feels unintentionally off-putting. I suspect the director intended for the audience to empathize with her, but that connection never materializes.

On a positive note, the ending deserves praise for being both unsettling and fulfilling. It could have been undermined by a cheap sound effect as the credits roll, but thankfully, the director made the smart choice to avoid that.

This film isn’t

When I first learned about *The Young Victoria*, I assumed it would be similar to *The Duchess* (2008). However, within the first 30 minutes, I realized this film was more than just a decent watch. Nearly every aspect of the movie excels, with stunning costumes and beautifully captured settings that truly stand out.

The only disappointment for me was the acting. Emily Blunt, known for *The Devil Wears Prada*, shines as the lead, breathing life into Victoria. Her performance is exceptional, potentially earning her a first Oscar nomination. Rupert Friend, playing Prince Albert, comes across as somewhat dull, though his chemistry with Blunt is undeniable. Paul Bettany delivers a reliable portrayal of Lord Melbourne, but I had hoped for more depth. Jim Broadbent and Miranda Richardson, in supporting roles, unfortunately leave little impression.

The film, to me, feels incomplete. Perhaps the screenwriters made too many alterations to the script, but I can’t quite pinpoint why it leaves me with this sense of dissatisfaction.

Overall, though, *The Young Victoria* is a captivating depiction of Victoria’s early years, elevated by Emily Blunt’s remarkable performance.

If my memory serves me right, I rented *A Nightmare on Elm Street 3* years ago on VHS, and I distinctly recall a music video titled "Dream Warriors" playing at the end. I found it hilarious, so when I rented the DVD version recently, I was eager to see it again. There's something about 80s content that’s unintentionally funny now, and nothing tops the comedy of 80s rap videos. In that particular video from the VHS, a rap group performed "Dream Warriors" after the credits, dressed in denim jackets with no shirts underneath and tight, frayed jean shorts reminiscent of Daisy Dukes. I can’t think of anything more ridiculous for a rap group to wear.

(spoilers) Unfortunately, I was let down to find the video missing from the DVD. Left with just the movie itself, I found this installment in the Freddy Krueger series to be rather average. The film kicks off with a concept similar to part 2, where the protagonist witnesses horrific murders, only to snap out of a trance and discover

Sidney Stratton struggles to hold down jobs at different textile mills due to his relentless experimentation in their laboratories. He is driven by the pursuit of a revolutionary fabric—one that remains clean, crease-free, and indestructible. When Stratton finally succeeds in developing this extraordinary material, he unwittingly makes enemies of both the textile workers, who fear job losses, and the mill owners, who face financial ruin since only one mill holds the exclusive rights to the fabric. Clad in his iconic white suit, Stratton becomes the most hunted man in England. The film is a masterpiece, uniquely crafted by Ealing Studios. Alec Guinness delivers a captivating performance, supported brilliantly by actors like Greenwood, Thesiger, and Parker, while Mackendrick's direction adds to the film's charm. Yet, the true star is the story—a sharp satire on commerce and industry, seamlessly blended with elements of drama, romance, and suspense. Rating: 8.

Mr. Michael Jackson is a true artistic marvel. His music videos, essentially short films, stand unparalleled in their brilliance. I’m not concerned about whether I get a coherent sci-fi narrative from him; what I crave is a blend of his electrifying dance moves, piercing shrieks, mesmerizing group choreography, and touches of CGI and animation. A few uninterrupted sequences are a must. Thankfully, all these elements are present in his work. I’m unbothered by simplistic plots or excessive displays of extravagance when I see Mr. Jackson perform. To me, he reigns supreme as the ultimate master of music videos (I avoid the term "king of pop," which feels absurd, particularly to us Russians, as "pop" resembles the Russian word for "arses," and MJ is certainly not that kind of king). I can watch his finest music videos—true artistic gems—over and over without ever growing weary of them.

My initial reaction to this film was confusion: "What is this...?" (a patchwork of various video clips, some sketched illustrations, jarring shifts between themes, a complete lack of a unified storyline, kids messing around, and so on). Yet, by the time I reached the end, I was convinced of its brilliance and recognized it as something utterly unique.

Hitokiri (meaning "assassination")—also known as "Tenchu," which translates to "divine punishment"—captures director Hideo Gosha at the peak of his craft. This film, along with Gosha’s other masterpiece, Goyokin, is an absolute must-watch. Hitokiri stands not only as one of Gosha’s finest works but also as one of the greatest samurai/chambara films ever created, and arguably among the best Japanese films ever released internationally.

A word of caution: the complex plot of Hitokiri may be challenging to follow for those unfamiliar with 19th-century Japanese history. Nevertheless, the core human drama transcends historical context and resonates with all audiences. True to Gosha’s signature style, Hitokiri explores his recurring theme of the conflict between "loyalty to one’s lord" and "doing what is right." Yet, he handles this theme with such nuanced depth that this film, alongside Goyokin, becomes essential viewing.

To break it down: if you prefer a more straightforward, action-driven story, Goyokin might be your pick. But if you’re drawn to a deeper, more layered, and admittedly darker drama, Hitokiri is the one to watch.

From the discussions before and after, here's what I pieced together: There's an Irishman eager to create a film, not tied to any specific concept, just a film in general. At a party one evening, he overhears a former roadie recount a legendary rock n' roll tale about how Gram Parsons’ body was taken from LAX by a devoted roadie to fulfill Parsons’ wish of being cremated in Joshua Tree. What a wild story!

This strikes him as the perfect movie concept! It’s got elements of rock n' roll (or country, to be precise), grave robbing, daring escapes, deep friendship, and the vibrant 70s vibe. He considers casting Johnny Knoxville from "Jackass," since the story has a prank-like quality, and Knoxville is also keen on starring in "a movie." The Irishman must have felt like he stumbled upon the next big hit, akin to "Snatch!"

However, the story lacks the necessary tension. To spice things up, they brainstorm adding a conflict for Knoxville’s character to face, like a manipulative, money-hungry girlfriend. True, Parsons was married at the time of his death, but they figure most people won’t know that detail. Plus, they could cast Christina Applegate in the role. Concerned that audiences might be put off by the idea of stealing a corpse, they decide to include Parsons’ father in the plot, having him join the pursuit but ultimately give his blessing for the act.

Absolutely, it's possible. John De Bello and Costa Dillon have emptied the clutter from their minds to create an utterly abysmal blend of comedy, horror, and sci-fi musical. If there's any acting to speak of, it's either dreadful or absurdly exaggerated. As for special effects, choose between pitifully low-budget or something a kindergartner might produce. Every tired cliché imaginable is thrown into the mix. Still, it’s undeniably a blast to watch, especially with a cold six-pack or two in hand. Blame radiation if you’re looking for a justification. Mutant tomatoes, bloated to nearly the size of a tow truck, start their assault on humanity. San Diego seems as fitting a starting point as any. Scientists, alongside a scatterbrained military, scramble to halt this crimson, rolling threat. This cult classic stars David Miller, Eric Christmas, Al Sklar, Tom Coleman, Sharon Taylor, and John Qualls.

The infamous incident in the early '80s, where Richard Pryor was seen running down the street engulfed in flames, undoubtedly left a mark on him. He even turned the traumatic event into material for his stand-up routines, earning roars of laughter from audiences. However, the incident appears to have influenced the roles he took on afterward. Among his less inspiring choices, *The Toy* stands out as particularly weak, perhaps rivaled only by *Another You*.

The premise of *The Toy*—a white man purchasing a black man as a "toy" for his son—carries a subtle undercurrent of political incorrectness, long before the term was widely recognized. What ultimately drove me to leave the theater before the film ended was seeing Pryor shift into an overly sentimental mode. I had hoped to watch him outsmart the spoiled child, but instead, the story devolved into the tired trope of the "misunderstood kid." Jackie Gleason had a few redeeming moments, but overall, this film is a letdown. Skip it and opt for Pryor’s collaborations with Gene Wilder or his stellar work from the '70s. *The Toy* is simply not worth your time.

I vividly recall watching this movie for the first time at the age of 9, dreaming of becoming one of the "barbarian brothers." Even now, I find this film incredibly entertaining. One unique feature is the brevity of the fight scenes, suggesting that the "barbarian brothers" are so skilled they dispatch their foes with remarkable speed. The movie is packed with excitement, including thrilling chases, a intense cage fight, a mythical dragon, and, of course, a classic bar brawl!

Admittedly, the acting leaves much to be desired, which prevents it from earning a perfect score, and the storyline has faced its share of criticism. However, I believe it brings a fresh perspective to the table. Few films in this genre can boast similarly original plots or such vibrant dialogue.

I wholeheartedly recommend this movie to anyone looking for a unique cinematic experience.

MINOR SPOILER

This lesser-known Stephen King horror gem is far from flawless. Even if Dale Midkiff and Denise Crosby had delivered stronger performances, the film would still struggle with its poorly handled mystical plot points. The ancient Micmac burial ground, Rachel’s dying sister, and the ghostly Victor Pascow fail to form a cohesive narrative, leaving the movie feeling muddled and overcrowded at times. However, perfection is rare in horror, and what 'Pet Sematary' lacks in polish, it compensates for with its sheer audacity to disturb. This film stands out as one of the most brutal horror entries in recent years, with its chilling zombie infant and the shockingly callous depiction of Zelda. It’s unapologetically offensive, tasteless, and excessive—yet it evokes a deep, visceral unease that more restrained horror films often fail to achieve. Add to that Fred Gwynne’s standout performance and Mary Lambert’s clever direction, and you’ve got a deeply unsettling horror experience, despite the campy conclusion. A must-watch for fans of the genre. 7.5 out of 10.

*Deliverance* is a gripping, unsettling, and at times deeply disturbing story by James Dickey, masterfully adapted into a cinematic gem by John Boorman. The narrative follows four businessmen, fueled by bravado and a desire to prove their masculinity, as they embark on a canoeing trip in the remote mountains. There, they confront the darkest aspects of humanity and the most harrowing forms of human suffering, including poverty, sexual violence, and physical assault. What begins as a quest for adventure and thrills transforms into a harrowing journey through a menacing, isolated mountainscape, utterly divorced from civilization. This raw intensity renders *Deliverance* one of the most nightmarish films I've encountered, with each ordeal faced by the men serving as a chilling reminder of situations one hopes never to endure. Beyond its visceral impact, *Deliverance* stands as a significant piece of cinema. Widely regarded as John Boorman's finest work—alongside *Zardoz* and *Excalibur*—it remains a profoundly influential film, featuring iconic moments that have echoed through countless others. The haunting "Dueling Banjos" score and the infamous, disturbing "squeal like a pig" scene are etched into cinematic history. The performances by all the actors are nothing short of remarkable.

Avoid this movie if you're seeking entertainment, heroic war depictions, skilled acting, or a compelling screenplay. However, if you're a fan of stereotypical Hollywood war films that conveniently wrap up with a politically charged message glorifying the splendor of war, then this is the movie for you. Otherwise, save your time. I’m usually drawn to war films for their potential to reveal the contradictory and futile nature of conflict when executed thoughtfully. Unfortunately, this film merely portrays a group of men wandering through the countryside, spouting dreadful clichés, engaging in utterly predictable actions, and defending the downtrodden with the same violence inflicted upon them. It’s an embarrassment to the art of filmmaking and to the United States. Imagine viewing this as someone from Europe, Africa, or elsewhere, and being led to believe this represents true American values. It’s no surprise we face such disdain. I urge you, don’t waste your time on this.

Although I'm not typically drawn to fairy tale films, Stardust piqued my interest after spotting Michelle Pfeiffer as a villain in the trailers, especially since I was soon to see her as the domineering Velma Von Tussle in Hairspray. Her portrayal of a wicked witch here is utterly convincing, particularly with the striking age-altering makeup at the start and finish of the movie. Robert De Niro also delivers a fantastic performance as a pirate captain who must conceal his true self "in the closet" to safeguard his "reputation." Nearly all the cast members, including Claire Danes, Rupert Everett, Ricky Gervais, Peter O'Toole, and others, perform admirably. While Danes and Pfeiffer embody timeless elegance, the film also showcases the captivating beauty of Sienna Miller, Olivia Grant (as Girl Bernard), and Kate Magowan, especially in her introductory scene. Charlie Cox, a newcomer, does well as the protagonist Tristan, bearing such a strong resemblance to his father Dunstan as a young man that I initially mistook early scenes with Magowan for him (though it was actually Ben Barnes). Many have likened this film to The Princess Bride, and while there are similarities, the key distinction for me is that with The Princess Bride, it’s always clear you're watching a purely fictional story.

I'm an avid movie enthusiast, and while I was under the weather, I decided to watch this film from the comfort of my couch. From the very first scene to the last, I was captivated by the incredible performances of actors I had never seen before, delivering powerful dialogue. The cinematography was stunning, providing exactly the kind of escape I needed. I hope my positive feedback stands out amidst any negative reviews. The director's passion is evident, resonating deeply with the cast throughout the entire movie. Thank you for creating such a unique piece of art. The characters are wonderfully awkward yet beautifully kind, flawed yet full of grace, making them truly memorable. I’m compelled to meet the minimum line requirement, so I’ll add that I eagerly await more work from this director, the talented actors, and the writer. I was genuinely disappointed when the movie ended, as I could have watched it forever.

Jet Li stands as one of the world's premier hand-to-hand combat fighters, a title he has held for over two decades, outshining many in the martial arts genre. Despite his immense popularity in Asia, he remains relatively unknown in the United States.

Intended as Jet Li's breakthrough film in the American market, *Black Mask* falls drastically short of expectations. The movie is dubbed, which might offer some campy charm due to the poorly synchronized and monotone voiceovers, but it feels unsuitable for the average cinema-goer. Additionally, the direction by Daniel Lee is subpar. His rapid scene cuts often leave viewers disoriented, unsure of what is happening. At other moments, the camera shakes and wobbles distractingly. Fans flock to Jet Li's films for his extraordinary martial arts skills, yet Lee's editing is so frenetic that identifying the characters becomes a challenge. Furthermore, some scenes abruptly transition without logical progression—for instance, Li starts cutting a hole in a jeep's floor as villains ready their weapons, and within moments, both he and his love interest are inexplicably beneath the vehicle. Other sequences stretch believability to its limits, further undermining the film's impact.

The majority of French films I've watched and appreciated tend to prioritize dialogue over action, which I generally don’t mind. I often find them engaging, visually appealing, and featuring captivating performances. (Though I couldn’t help but wonder at times if Gérard Depardieu starred in every French movie ever produced—it certainly felt that way!)

This particular film also boasts striking visuals and a promising start. However, it soon devolves into endless conversation, which might suit a drama but feels out of place in a murder mystery. Eventually, I found myself nearly dozing off while watching.

In essence, the movie resembles a stage play, with nearly all scenes confined to a single room. If you’re a fan of theatrical works, this might appeal to you. Personally, though, I expect a bit more excitement from a murder tale.

The film suffers from a disorganized structure, subpar writing, overused tropes, and uninspired dialogue. Not a single moment stands out. The actors are visibly hindered by a tedious script that lacks any element of surprise, unexpected turns, or meaningful conflict. The direction of the story is painfully predictable within the first ten minutes.

Despite being set in New York, the movie fails to capture the essence of the city. Numerous low-budget indie films have successfully portrayed New York as enchanting, yet this one feels as if it were filmed in Toronto, devoid of any authentic atmosphere.

Casting choices like Natasha Henstridge are puzzling when her character is hidden in oversized sweaters, and Michael Vartan is styled to appear dull and unremarkable. The chemistry between characters is nonexistent, leaving the film feeling like a lackluster, overly moralistic Christian TV movie with no hint of allure or passion.

Steven Feder's greatest achievement seems to be persuading others to produce this uninspired and forgettable film.

A performance centered on bondage, humiliation, and S&M, with little else to offer. The storyline is uninspired, serving merely as a dull framework for the visually provocative scenes. The host of the show, a ridiculous figure who spews nonsense while flouncing across the stage in dresses, was nearly as grating as the pretentious attempts at creative editing. The surreal ending seemed like an afterthought. On a positive note, Aya Sugimoto delivered a believable performance as the tormented protagonist. While Flower and Snake has drawn comparisons to Eyes Wide Shut, beyond a few superficial parallels, Kubrick's film stands out as far more nuanced, artistic, and evocative.

This might be the most dreadful acting I've ever witnessed in a film. Additionally, the casting choices are baffling. The lead actress has a noticeable nasal deformity that makes it challenging to watch her for long without fixating on it. A quick visit to a local grocery store on a Sunday afternoon would likely yield 50 more suitable and attractive candidates for the role. I regretfully rented this movie, lured by its striking DVD cover. However, the production feels like a mere class project tossed together by multimedia students at a community college. I would have preferred spending the hour watching public access TV, where the special effects are superior and the individuals on screen are far more appealing than anyone in this film.

This film is, without a doubt, the most dreadful I’ve ever watched, and I’ve endured some truly terrible ones. The cinematography was abysmal, and the cast consists entirely of unrecognizable actors, giving the impression that a group of friends impulsively decided to create their own movie. The result, however, is utterly atrocious. I’ve never encountered a worse film. The storyline feels completely contrived, dragging on painfully with no discernible plot. It appears as though there was no planning before filming began. The narrative is bizarre, and the pacing is excruciatingly slow, taking forever to reach any semblance of a point—which, ultimately, doesn’t even exist. There’s no justification for this movie’s existence. If you’re thinking about watching it, save yourself the trouble. It’s simply a waste of time.

This film ranks among my top foreign movies, alongside gems like *Amélie* and *My Life as a Dog*. What unites these remarkable foreign films is their ability to take an ordinary fragment of life and elevate it into a deeply moving and insightful experience.

Set in Japan, the story follows a man trapped in the monotony of his daily routine and the stagnation of his marriage. One day, as his train speeds by, he catches sight of a stunning Japanese woman gazing out from the window of a dance studio. In that fleeting moment, he is captivated. Is it merely her beauty, her distant expression, or something deeper—a shared connection waiting to be uncovered?

*Shall We Dance* introduces unforgettable characters who confront harsh realities by escaping into the transformative world of dance. Defying the rigid conventions and stereotypes of Japanese society, they gamble everything for a chance at happiness, ultimately discovering that joy is within reach. This film is pure magic, brimming with meaning, and transcends the ordinary by revealing the extraordinary wonder and beauty inherent in life itself.

Wow, this is one of those films I thought I’d already reviewed, but apparently not. Honestly, I didn’t care much for it, yet it somehow stuck in my mind.

To put it plainly and concisely, this is among the most dreadful, tedious, and idiotic slasher movies ever produced. I struggle to find anything positive to say about this disaster, as even the marginally acceptable scenes fail to suggest it was crafted by competent filmmakers.

The death scenes are abysmal, lacking gore and utterly nonsensical. The plot has a sliver of potential, mainly because it borrows heavily from 1991’s "Popcorn."

What makes it even worse is that this isn’t even a “so bad it’s good” kind of movie. It’s simply terrible.

Molly Ringwald did her best to salvage it, but her efforts fell short.

I had long been intrigued by this elusive film, so when I finally spotted it on eBay, I didn’t hesitate to spend the $10 to own it. Now I see why it’s so hard to come by. This movie is utterly dreadful, plagued by abysmal writing and a painfully meager budget. Ironically, the best part is the end credits, which feature a montage of bloopers and flubbed lines. The story centers on a psychic, played by Pettyjohn—clearly cast for her topless scene—who uses her abilities alongside an experimental device to draw objects from another dimension into ours. When she retrieves a mysterious box-like item, the military casually tosses it into the back of an unguarded truck with just one soldier for protection. Predictably, chaos ensues. Surprise! A child in a cheap foam-rubber monster suit emerges, fatally scratches the soldier’s face with ease, and flees to a nearby city. Instead of mobilizing a significant military force to track it down and safeguard the public, the authorities inexplicably leave the task to Pettyjohn and Ray to handle alone, as if that’s a reasonable plan.

I'm puzzled by why this movie falls flat. It aims for humor and entertainment but ends up being dull. A significant issue seems to be the excessive focus on "gadgets," which overshadows everything else. The original cartoon that inspired it is far superior.

3/10

My scalp still burns from the criticism I faced when I declared my love for this film. I'm ready to face more heat and even walk over fiery coals to reaffirm my affection for "Bend it Like Beckham." I admit, my admiration comes with some reservations. The movie often feels like a typical made-for-TV drama, with a script that follows a predictable, formulaic structure. More concerning is the director's commentary, which seems to suggest that beauty in this film is predominantly associated with fair skin.

The true brilliance of the film doesn't lie in the usual elements that catch a critic's eye, like character development, themes, or structure, as taught by Syd Field. Instead, it shines both on the surface and in its deeper undertones, beyond the superficial layers that reviewers tend to focus on. The film showcases powerful, sometimes partially clad female bodies not just as objects of display, but as forces dominating a football field. These women embody a natural strength and agility that outshines the likes of Lara Croft or Zhang Ziyi. These are authentic bodies (with the exception of Keira Knightley’s), prioritized for their skill rather than their appearance. They are working bodies, whose beauty lies in their motion and independence. And, in my opinion, lead actress Parminder Nagra exemplifies this perfectly.

This film is exceptional! Brad Pitt delivers a performance that may very well be the pinnacle of his career. David Duchovny, along with Forbes and Lewis, also shines brilliantly. The story follows four main characters as they embark on a captivating road trip through historic murder locations, cruising in one of the sleekest cars ever designed, a 1960s Lincoln Continental. Early Grace, a naive yet disturbing character, has peculiar tastes, favoring dry toothbrushes and chaos. He prefers women who abstain from swearing and smoking, dressed in modest, old-fashioned attire. Duchovny and Forbes portray urban artists, contrasting with Early and Lewis, who hail from a rural trailer park. Despite the predominantly somber tone of the movie, it is laced with numerous humorous moments. The writing, direction, and performances are outstanding. If you're a fan of road trips, dark themes, comedy, and engaging narration, this movie is a must-watch. Each actor brings their A-game, leaving you craving more as the credits roll. It’s undoubtedly one of my all-time favorites. "Hey... shave that dog and teach it to hunt!"

This film is undoubtedly among the most dreadful I’ve ever seen, and I truly mean ever. To make matters worse, it features my former idol, Dolph, in the lead role. Unbelievable. While the storyline has potential, its execution is so poor it’s physically painful to watch. The fight sequences, for instance, are as poorly coordinated as a sloppy brawl between two inebriated individuals in an alley. The acting, with the exception of Dolph who still disappoints, is so abysmal that one can’t help but speculate if the cast was selected solely based on personal connections with the director—who, incidentally, seems to have been absent throughout most, if not all, of the production. With a budget of $12 million, it’s astonishing to see such meager results, as the special effects and sets look like they couldn’t have cost more than $1,000.

I’m a fan of *Crash* and *Blade Runner*, and this movie delves into similar themes of highway fatalities and 80s film noir that I find compelling, which made it an enjoyable watch for me.

However, overall, the characteristic foolishness of the film noir protagonist isn’t convincingly portrayed by the female lead, and her heroic counterpart comes across as almost primitive, which contributes to the kitschy vibe and warrants a heads-up.

While I held some expectations for this movie, largely due to my appreciation for Jason Segel’s performances in *Freaks & Geeks* and *Undeclared*, I regret to say it ranks among the worst films I’ve encountered recently, alongside disappointments like *Loser* and *Dr. T and the Women*.

Admittedly, there were a few moments that elicited genuine laughter, but the film fell far short of its potential. The concept itself wasn’t terrible—con artists faking their way through college encounter a formidable adversary who uncovers their scheme and presents them with an offer. However, the characters were so deeply unlikable that I found myself indifferent to their fates. The blackmailer, portrayed by the skilled Jason Schwartzman, was depicted as such an unhinged psychopath that his antics weren’t amusing; he lacked any humorous or endearing quirks, coming across instead as a menacing and unpleasant figure who was simply uncomfortable to watch. Additionally, the film’s editing was disorienting, frequently switching between fantasy and reality without clear distinction, making it difficult to follow. Moreover, only a handful of the group’s scams were actually depicted, leaving the audience to simply accept their supposed cunning without much evidence.

The challenge lies in knowing where to start with this film, as it demands your full attention for the next two hours. Don’t even think about stepping away for a soda, as missing a few minutes could leave you lost. Thankfully, there’s always the pause button. In this story, Bruce Willis must navigate a time machine to locate an antivirus for a devastating virus that allowed animals to dominate the world in 1996. Due to some errors, he first lands in 1990, then finds himself amidst the chaos of the First World War. Despite the apparent confusion, Terry Gilliam delivers what might be one of the most brilliant scripts ever written. The former Monty Python member masterfully crafts a sci-fi narrative, demonstrating a deep understanding of the genre, and his casting choices are impeccable. Brad Pitt shines as a deranged character, with his scenes in the asylum being particularly unforgettable, while Bruce Willis proves he’s far more than just another action hero à la Schwarzenegger. This is a film you can revisit time and again; its intricate and bizarre script, though surprisingly followable, reveals new surprises with each viewing. It’s easily one of my all-time favorites.

It seemed as though I had seen this movie a thousand times already. The plot was utterly predictable, with every attempt at a twist falling flat. Whenever I hoped for a spark of intrigue, I was met only with the obvious. Take, for instance, the line, "The bread factory opened another facility because there wasn’t enough bread"—painfully uninspired. In short, it’s a tired, clichéd story, plagued by poor acting and abysmal special effects. The only redeeming moment came from the dim-witted Russian cop, Vlad, whose antics while dealing with the villains provided a fleeting chuckle. His sheer stupidity, paired with his mountainous build, was almost comical. Honestly, I’m not sure why I’m even bothering to critique this disgrace of a film—it can’t possibly get any worse.

The production of *Zombi 3* carries a fascinating backstory. It serves as a follow-up to Lucio Fulci's successful *Zombi 2*, which was itself a clever marketing scheme designed to mislead audiences into believing it was a sequel to George A. Romero’s *Dawn of the Dead*, also known as *Zombi*. Confusing, right? In reality, none of these films are connected narratively, but their box office success seems to overshadow that detail. Interestingly, Fulci appeared to lose interest in *Zombi 3* midway through production and walked away from the project. To compensate, Bruno Mattei was brought in to extend the runtime by adding extra scenes.

The storyline of *Zombi 3* follows a familiar zombie trope. On an island in the Philippines, scientists create a serum that falls into the hands of terrorists, unleashing a devastating plague that turns people into zombies. As chaos ensues, the scientists race to develop an antidote, while the military resorts to indiscriminately eliminating everyone in their path. Interspersed throughout are short segments of a Radio DJ delivering sermons about humanity’s mistreatment of the environment.

Despite its notorious reputation, I found myself enjoying this film. While I had heard overwhelmingly negative feedback, the absurd dialogue provided a surprising amount of entertainment. The movie comes across as...

This movie, inspired by real events, marks the directorial debut of Denzel Washington, a seasoned actor. Washington has delivered some of the most memorable performances over the past ten years, portraying a black soldier in the Civil War in *Glory* and a lawyer in the widely praised *Philadelphia*. Notably, last year he achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first African American to win the Academy Award for Best Actor for his role in *Training Day*. Seeking a new challenge, Washington decided to step behind the camera for *Antwone Fisher*, a film in which he also acts. The titular character, Fisher, is brought to life by newcomer Derek Luke, who has previously appeared in episodes of TV shows like *King of Queens* and is set to star in the forthcoming film *Biker Boyz*.

This film is an impressive directorial debut for Denzel Washington. It’s clear that Washington felt a deep connection to and belief in the true story of Antwone Fisher. The movie follows the journey of a young African American man in the Navy who frequently finds himself in trouble.

This parody, lacking originality, consistently fell short of impressing during its excessively drawn-out eight minutes. The sole redeeming moment came with the "DO NOT COLORIZE" note in the end credits. It's disappointing that the DVD didn't include something more engaging, such as Jonathan Ross' captivating profile of Romero from 'The Incredible Strange Film Show.'

This film offers a humorous and sharply sarcastic perspective on pop culture and its creators. I was struck by the cinematography, which features vibrant colors and cleverly manipulated settings, particularly impressive given that this is Zukovic's first major project.

A word of caution: don’t take the film’s message too seriously. It’s not meant for mainstream appeal (and that’s not intended as praise). The underlying message reflects a somewhat idealized, post-college, novice outlook on society.

I appreciated the core storyline, which follows a fictional magazine editor as they verbally critique the conformist culture of the 1990s.

This film was marketed as both a comedy and a mystery, but it falls short in both genres. The true mystery is why anyone would produce such a poorly made movie. The only humor I found was in chuckling at the surprisingly high ratings it received from readers here. Is it possible there’s another movie with the same title? The version I watched featured a girl with striking blue eyes and a nonexistent storyline.

What on earth is this supposed to be? Is it a family fantasy flick trying to ride the coattails of Spielberg's blockbuster "Close Encounters of the Third Kind"? Or is it a nostalgic nod to the golden age of prehistoric epics like "When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth" and "The Lost World"? Or maybe, just maybe, it's a profound intellectual and philosophical gem that we're all too dense to grasp? Surely, that’s the answer! Whatever it is, the minds behind "The Day Time Ended"—the inimitable John 'Bud' Cardos of "Kingdom of the Spiders" fame and writer David Schmoeller of "Tourist Trap"—must have been under the influence of something potent when they cooked up this bizarre mash-up of genres. The plot is utterly nonsensical, and the storytelling is a chaotic mess, but who’s complaining when you’ve got papier-mâché dinosaurs, tiny spacecraft, blinding light and laser displays, and spontaneously exploding supernovas? The voice-over at the start is nearly impossible to hear, but that’s fine—it’s all nonsense anyway! Did you know that our understanding of 'time' is completely wrong? It doesn’t always flow in a straight line; it’s one massive paradox! Words uttered thousands...

I genuinely can't fathom how something this dreadful gets produced. Even the most cringe-worthy junior-high talent show performance is more engaging than this movie. The only fleeting moments of humor come from Will Ferrell's wrestling obsession. Absolutely awful.

This film tugs at your heartstrings, leaving you feeling tender rather than hardened like some action-packed movies. I’m a huge fan of emotional stories, so I rated it highly.
