The acting was impressive, and the emotions were deeply felt throughout. I appreciated that the violence was minimal, offering a refreshing change. I would have scored it a 9, but the salute at the end held me back. Overall, it’s a solid movie with exceptional performances by the cast.

This movie was utterly dreadful! I’m baffled as to how it even reached the production stage. I have no issues with the cast; the blame lies squarely with the writing team. They recycled the tired, clichéd storyline of dancing to escape poverty—here, rebranded as STEP. Yet, this version is devoid of any meaningful plot, or at least one that could hold anyone’s interest. The use of Canadian actors in what’s meant to be an American setting further flattens the film’s impact. On a brighter note, the direction was commendable, and the cinematography was fairly impressive. It’s evident that the production budget was substantial. My only plea is for this team to step away from writing and hire skilled screenwriters who can breathe life into the dialogue and story. Ultimately, *How She Move* is more like *How She Fails*.

'Bruce Almighty' is poised to dominate the Academy Awards, clinching an unprecedented 14 Oscars! It is predicted to eclipse 'Titanic' as the highest-grossing film in history! Jim Carrey's fame will soar to such heights that he might declare his candidacy for the 2004 presidential election. Such grand visions could only materialize if the film's creators, including Carrey, wielded divine powers. This concept forms the core of Carrey's latest comedy hit, 'Bruce Almighty.' In the film, Carrey portrays Bruce Nolan, a TV reporter fixated on becoming the lead anchor, blaming God entirely for his misfortunes. God, brilliantly portrayed by Morgan Freeman, endows Bruce with divine powers to test whether he can perform God's role any better. Predictably, Bruce gets carried away with his new abilities, using them for personal gain. Carrey returns to his signature comedic brilliance in 'Bruce Almighty.' Jennifer Aniston delivers a compelling performance as Bruce’s girlfriend, avoiding any pitfalls. However, my highest praise is reserved for Director Tom Shadyac for keeping the humor tasteful, especially with the uproariously funny dog bathroom scene, which stands out as a highlight.

Undoubtedly, this is the most amusing of the Curly Stooges shorts. I’ve watched it countless times, and it never fails to bring a smile to my face. The pantomime sequences are absolutely hysterical. It’s a quintessential display of "musical comedy" at its best. Even those who aren’t fans of the knuckleheads often recall this one with affection.

Following the murder of the mob boss in "Central City," Robert Armstrong, playing the role of "Doc" Rogers, steps in to maintain the criminal empire. To ensure the continuity of their illicit operations, he enlists the late mobster's timid son, Richard Cromwell, who portrays Edward "Baby Face" Morgan, to helm the family business. The unsuspecting Cromwell is brought to the city and positioned as the President of his father's "Acme Protection Agency," a deceptive cover for a gang of criminals. While Cromwell naively sells insurance policies, his so-called employees operate an extortion scheme. Complications arise when Cromwell falls for a charming client, Virginia Clark, played by Mary Carlisle. As their romance blooms, the pair find themselves entangled in dangerous territory. "Baby Face Morgan" captures Cromwell and Carlisle towards the twilight of their once-bright film careers in this brief, light-hearted, and unobtrusive crime drama.

**** Baby Face Morgan (1942) Arthur Dreifuss ~ Richard Cromwell, Mary Carlisle, Robert Armstrong

As an Elvis enthusiast, I’m baffled by how this project even came to fruition. It is, without a doubt, the worst Elvis-related movie I’ve ever seen—completely devoid of humor, absurdly silly, and riddled with inaccuracies about The King. Seriously, Elvis’ grave in a public park? A reference to "Suspicious Minds" in 1958? These are just a couple of the many glaring errors. While a few cast members make an effort—Mike Starr is amusing, especially as an impersonator, and Tom Hanks’ cameo is a nice surprise—the actor portraying young Elvis is utterly terrible. Ultimately, the film lacks any sense of entertainment, growing increasingly tedious with each passing minute. If you’re looking for a low-budget, wild, yet genuinely funny Elvis-related flick, I wholeheartedly suggest "Bubba Ho-Tep" over this disaster.

I'm not going to dive into a detailed critique of this film. I acknowledge the numerous glowing reviews that have come before mine, and since I generally admire Maria de Medeiros, I've hesitated to voice any negative opinions. Nearly a year has passed with this reluctance. Yet, every time I spot that DVD on my shelf, I feel an internal sigh. Let the chorus of praise drown out my reservations! However, a word of caution to fellow cinephiles—proceed with care.

To put it simply and softly, here’s my perspective:

The political upheaval and regime change that form the film's backdrop also colored a chapter of my own life, filtered through the newspapers I read daily at my local middle-European pub. Back then, I kept up with the news, but I never fully understood the chaos unfolding. The reports were often neutral or laced with a conservative bias that disapproved of any factions disrupting order or challenging the status quo. Those were turbulent times, with unrest sweeping through Paris, Berlin, Prague, and parts of the U.S.—events I could comprehend more clearly. But whether it was dictatorship or otherwise,

If you're not familiar with Jimmy Stewart, this movie is among his lesser-known works from the later part of his career. While it doesn't stand up to many of his classic films, it's not a bad watch and serves as a tolerable way to pass the time, though it offers little beyond that.

Kim Novak plays a witch living in New York City who, for reasons that remain unclear, decides to enchant Stewart’s character to fall in love with her. As the story unfolds, the initially aloof Novak finds herself genuinely falling for Stewart—a serious breach of the apparent witch code.

The film’s portrayal of witches is peculiar. They are neither malevolent, sacrificing infants, nor overwhelmingly powerful. Their magic seems trivial and often pointless, like Jack Lemmon’s character using his abilities to extinguish street lamps. Even stranger, these witches are depicted as bohemian types, frequenting trendy bars where patrons don berets and listen to subpar jazz. Given my opinion on jazz, being a witch in this cinematic universe must be quite underwhelming!

Nevertheless, the movie carries a romantic charm.

I purchased this DVD as a gift for my brother, a huge fan of Michelle Pfeiffer, and decided to watch it myself earlier this week.

The film is fairly engaging, featuring two entirely distinct narratives. The storyline involving Michelle Pfeiffer is undoubtedly the more captivating of the pair. She portrays an up-and-coming Hollywood actress who has experienced a series of brief, unsatisfying relationships. Her life intersects with Brian Kerwin, a typical married man with children, after she rear-ends his car. Though their initial encounter is marked by hostility, he offers to drive her home when she feels unable to continue driving. A romance blossoms between them, ultimately leading to tragedy when his wife discovers the affair. The ending caught me off guard, but the sluggish pacing and uninspired TV-style direction drain much of the drama from the story.

The second narrative centers on an aging studio executive, played by Darren McGavin. This segment boasts a stronger ensemble cast, including Kenneth McMillan, Lois Chiles, Steven Bauer, and Stella Stevens. Each character seeks something from the studio boss, but when he is forced to resign, they come to the sobering realization that their careers are now at a standstill.

Eddie Murphy's "Delirious" is unabashedly offensive, vulgar, coarse, and indecent. These words aptly capture the essence of this distasteful and lowbrow stand-up performance. Murphy prioritizes shock over genuine humor in an attempt to captivate his audience. While he elicits a few laughs here and there, he largely derails with excessive profanity and inappropriate sexual humor.

Skip it! Unless you’re a fan of Eddie’s explicit style, this isn’t worth your time. I doubt I’ll give "Eddie Murphy Raw" a chance. I far prefer seeing Eddie within the structure of a film script.

Saturday, January 17, 1998 - Video

I was incredibly excited to watch *Planet of the Apes*, but it turned out to be a massive letdown.

The film's settings and masks are impressive, and they stand out as the only redeeming qualities. Everything else, however, is incredibly frustrating. Mark Wahlberg doesn’t seem to act at all; he merely appears on screen, looking out of place and unconvincing. The rest of the cast also fails to deliver compelling performances.

The most disappointing aspect, by far, is the storyline. It’s utterly absurd! For instance, there’s a scene where the apes are lying unconscious on the ground, yet the humans inexplicably refrain from attacking. Instead, they wait for the apes to regain consciousness. This is just one of many nonsensical plot points, and listing them all would take far too long.

To begin, I must express my strong support for Fanpro creations. I view them as a valuable means to extend the life of a beloved series well beyond its cancellation. Notable examples like Star Trek Voyages and Star Wars Revelations demonstrate commendable attempts in this genre. Consequently, I tend to be more forgiving of flaws in Fanpro projects that I might otherwise criticize harshly.

Now, turning to ST: HF. Let's start with the positives. The enthusiasm displayed by the cast across various ships greatly enhances the show's believability, and it's clear they enjoy their roles. Additionally, the special effects are quite impressive for a homemade production, avoiding any cringe-worthy moments. The storytelling, while not groundbreaking, is reasonably solid with the inclusion of continuous story arcs.

However, the production is not without significant shortcomings.

Firstly, while it's understandable that they must borrow footage, set designs, music, and effects from Star Trek, I find it unnecessary that they also heavily borrow from nearly every other sci-fi musical score out there. Themes from films like Aliens to Starship Troopers are noticeably present throughout the soundtrack.

I recently watched the movie on television and thoroughly enjoyed it. I'm a fan of a good mystery, and this one kept me guessing until the very end. Sean Connery delivered an excellent performance. I would definitely recommend it to a friend.

Or paying attention to, for that matter. Even the soundtrack is tedious.

Honestly, this isn’t the worst gay film I’ve encountered (that title goes to Regarding Billy), but it’s scraping the very bottom of the barrel.

This movie drags on endlessly. It’s not just that the plot is uninspired—in the hands of a skilled writer, it might have had potential . . . it could certainly have been far more engaging. Every plot twist is painfully predictable, visible from miles away. The dialogue lacks depth, and the humor feels stale. To make matters worse, the film is riddled with one-dimensional, clichéd portrayals of gay characters.

Nothing in this film convinced me that the circumstances or the relationship between the two main characters could exist, let alone feel authentic. There’s no chemistry, no spark, and no clear reason why these two are supposed to be in love . . . we’re simply told they are. It’s baffling, especially since they share no common ground and lack sexual compatibility. They bond over a book? Really?

The acting isn’t entirely dreadful, but the pacing is agonizingly slow. It’s almost reminiscent of a Jarmusch film in its lethargy, but without any of Jarmusch’s artistry.

This series was my introduction to Deighton’s writing and the genre during my younger years, and I truly appreciate this adaptation of the story. However, I must respectfully disagree with the previous comment. Based on my past readings, it wasn’t Holm’s performance that caused Deighton to oppose the release of the series, but rather the severe alterations made to all three books during their transition to the screen. A clear example is the rewritten border crossing scene that marked the end of Samson’s field career. This scene doesn’t exist in the book, the character who perishes in the minefield is absent from the novels, and the crossing in *Sinker* occurs from East Germany to West Germany, not at the Polish frontier. This entire subplot is a fabrication. Likewise, the modifications in *Set* undermine the story’s integrity. On the other hand, I felt Holm’s portrayal of Samson’s disorientation during his wife’s defection was outstanding, and he convincingly depicted an aging field agent struggling to overcome class barriers. Samson bears the consequences of his father’s idealism while being profoundly shaped by its impact on his life. As Clevemore remarks, had Samson pursued an education, he might have...

I'm a devoted fan of Jean Harlow, captivated by her undeniable star quality. Although I don't consider her films or her acting particularly exceptional, she truly shone in comedic roles. Her performance in *The Girl from Missouri* is outstanding, especially in the comedic moments, though the film leans more toward a romantic narrative. Harlow is mesmerizing in this movie, outshining the rest of the cast, whose performances feel uninspired and forgettable. It always astonishes me to remember that her stunning beauty concealed the reality of her poor health. In this film, she looks absolutely radiant.

Ever been ensnared by a movie in the theater, pinned to the perfect seat—dead center, your personal sweet spot after swapping places thrice—only to find yourself, what seems like 13 hours later, still stuck, restless and irritated, wondering, "When in the world is this movie going to END?" (We’ve all been there—think of films like *A.I.* or *The Village*.)

Well, *Visitor Q* offers a bizarre twist on that sensation. For the first 30 minutes, I was left questioning when the film would actually begin! It feels endless! So overly "artistic" that it’s almost painful. This was my first encounter with a Takashi Miike film. I’ve heard he churns out movies by the dozen, and if they’re all as self-indulgent and pretentious as this, I doubt I’ll be watching another.

I’m not inherently opposed to pretentious cinema. David Lynch ranks among my top 10 directors, but *Visitor Q* is just low-grade, crude, and distasteful in its pretension.

If it wasn’t already clear—I absolutely despised it.

Certainly, this is a step up from my experience with *Death Tunnel*. The death scenes showed some creativity, and the gore was quite satisfactory. It felt like a blend of *Wrong Turn* and *The Hills Have Eyes*.

However, there are several issues:

1.) During the kitchen scene where the "kids" (are they in high school or college?) chat about horror films, Shae’s dialogue is nearly a verbatim rip-off from *Scream* (1996), especially the part about big-breasted girls and so on.

2.) Wasn’t Steve just a knockoff Randy from *Scream*?  
3.) Other than the October setting, what did this movie have to do with Samhain? It felt entirely irrelevant. I can’t help but laugh at horror flicks from the '80s that tie up plot holes by blaming druids or tossing in a pentagram.

4.) I was surprised they threw in a Sam Raimi reference!  
5.) What was the point of Gary and his sister being in the film? Their characters contributed nothing to the story. And how is Gary supposedly psychic but unable to foresee his own death?  
6.) During Gary’s death in the bathroom (by then, the kills were pure Troma-style over-the-top), how could anyone downstairs hear his screams?

To clarify, Goldie Hawn hails from Washington (Takoma Park, Maryland), but that's beside the point. This film echoes the classic *Mr. Smith Goes to Washington*, sharing a similar core idea with a few twists. I recorded this movie from cable years back, largely due to my admiration for Goldie Hawn. While the plot is engaging, the idea of a cocktail waitress landing a significant government role simply for saving a high-ranking official's life stretches believability. The movie evoked mixed emotions in me—amusement and frustration in equal measure. I couldn’t help but laugh at the absurdity of some of the predicaments she encountered. (POSSIBLE SPOILER AHEAD). On the other hand, I felt anger at the thought of our government manipulating an ordinary citizen in such a way. Her final speech, though, was truly moving. If only more people in reality possessed that kind of courage.

This movie took me back to the cheesy "erotic thrillers" I’d sneakily watch on Cinemax late at night as a 13-year-old. I’d call this one softer-core, though, as it lacks any simulated intimate scenes. Still, there’s plenty of nudity—a strip club kicks off the film, we get a glimpse of Kane Hodder’s rear (or perhaps a stunt double’s), an out-of-nowhere 10-minute lesbian dance sequence midway through, and a nude female werewolf sporting a costume that looks straight out of a low-budget Munsters episode. Young teenage boys might be thrilled.

Beyond that, the werewolf transformation scenes feature some of the worst CGI I’ve seen in ages. The visuals are on par with the grainy full-motion videos from the old Resident Evil games. The wolf design is so terrible it defies description, and despite the laughably cheap costume, it’s shown far too often.

As for the plot and acting, they’re utterly nonsensical. There’s a bizarre backstory involving werewolves and hybrid-werewolves—apparently, the Darkwolf falls into the latter category. From what I could gather, though, hybrids do the same old thing as regular werewolves: appear human, transform into a wolf, and kill people.

Unbelievable, just how terrible can a film be? This was downright awful, not because of the gore—which was mostly comical due to poor CGI—but because of the abysmal acting, lackluster atmosphere, and misguided direction.

The storyline was atrocious. The protagonist's character arc was an absolute farce. After merely a few nights of trailing Vinnie Jones, he becomes so 'haunted' that he breaks down in tears while taking pictures of his girlfriend. Really? Are all New York photographers portrayed as this immature, impressionable, and fragile? His character evolution lacked any rationale or purpose, and by the film's conclusion, you'll find yourself laughing hysterically at the utterly predictable and ludicrous twist in his journey.

The gore scenes were nothing more than a feeble, insecure attempt to ride the wave of trendy MTV-style violence—full of CGI blood but devoid of any genuine emotion. These moments were unintentionally hilarious and jarring due to their overt self-awareness, complete with gimmicky camera angles and unnecessary flair.

Ultimately, this movie squanders yet another promising concept. What could have built a compelling atmosphere—until the ridiculous monsters appear at the end—is sacrificed for ostentatious, self-indulgent directing that screams 'look at me.' This film wasn't crafted for an audience; it was clearly made for the ego of its creator.

Beneath the masterful direction, production, and acting, as well as the anticipated drama, the script delivers a profound message:

"Listening paves the path forward." To let your voice thrive, listen. To blend your voice with others in harmony, listen. To connect with your inner self, listen. To understand the needs of any situation or person, listen. It seems the scriptwriters are revealing a fundamental "secret of life." Listening fosters self-awareness, sharpens the other senses—particularly sight—and broadens one’s perspective. Even the soul can be uncovered through this act. The brilliance of the film *As It Is in Heaven* beautifully portrays the unfolding of life, capturing not just its joys and sorrows but also its ultimate hope. This is all encapsulated in the lead character’s initial guidance to the choir:

"Just listen, it leads all the way."

"The Return of Chandu" stands out, if one might call it that, for featuring Bela Lugosi in the rare role of a hero instead of his typical villainous characters. Surprisingly, he even wins the affections of the leading lady.

The plot centers on the sinister Black Magic Cult of Ubasti, which seeks to abduct Nadji, the last Egyptian princess, portrayed by the captivating Maria Alba. Their goal is to sacrifice her to resurrect their ancient leader, who bears a striking resemblance to Nadji. Lugosi, playing the mystical Chandu with supernatural abilities, endeavors to foil the cult's nefarious plans.

Director Ray Taylor manages as best he can with constrained resources and heavy reliance on stock footage. Viewers familiar with "King Kong" (1933) may notice the reuse of the iconic giant doors from that film in several sequences. The acting, unfortunately, is largely subpar. Lucien Prival, believed to be playing the high priest, employs an exaggerated, theatrical enunciation typical of early sound films. As for the rest of the cast, their performances are best left unmentioned.

It remains puzzling why Lugosi, still a marketable name at Universal during this period, chose to take on roles in low-budget independent films like this one. Perhaps it was a decision driven by factors beyond mere career strategy.

I'm still unsure if this film had any meaningful purpose.

Despite being marketed as 'rebellious' and 'controversial,' the materials Maddox hands out to the students are disappointingly tame. The students are oddly quick to embrace ambiguous anti-authority messages and barely legible scribbles on flyers. Rebel, indeed.

I guess expecting a teenage rebellion movie without the cliché of a school fire alarm being triggered was too much to hope for.

Supposedly, a 'massive brawl on the football fields' involves just two people.

The characters' personalities fluctuate inconsistently. For instance, a football jock who fought with Maddox—and even got a staple to the face—is inexplicably friendly and apologetic the following day.

The lack of a proper resolution to the story leaves me thinking this could have been condensed into a 30-minute after-school special, especially if they had trimmed down the overdone, glitchy soundtrack attempts.

Undoubtedly, *Private Lessons II* stands as the finest film I’ve ever encountered. Originally a Japanese production with a rather clumsy English translation, it remains an absolute delight to watch. While much of the storyline is perplexing, its charm is unaffected. It reigns as the ultimate comedy, unintentionally hilarious in its execution.

This cinematic rarity isn’t available on video, but I’ve managed to catch it during late-night screenings on premium cable channels. My personal recording has been replayed countless times as I eagerly share this hidden treasure with friends and family, one viewer at a time.

Joanna Pacula portrays the tutor and romantic interest to the protagonist, Ken, seemingly just collecting a paycheck for her role. Ken, brought to life by Goro Inagaki of the Japanese pop group SMAP, delivers a committed performance and sports impeccable hair throughout the film. Stacy Edwards, known from *In the Company of Men*, also appears, likely relieved to have secured other roles following this project.

Deciphering the plot requires at least three viewings. With each rewatch, new quirks emerge, such as the bizarre abundance of vases—numbering at least 50—in Ken’s home, or other peculiarities that add to the film’s eccentric allure.

I can only hope that the viewer who called 'Dream Machine' one of Corey Haim's best performances and among the "best movies of the century" was joking. If I missed the sarcasm, I truly hope that’s the case.

'The Dream Machine' kicks off a string of subpar escapades that would overshadow much of Corey Haim's later career, with the notable exception of 'Prayer of the Rollerboys,' which was unexpectedly solid. In this film, Haim portrays Bernie, a laid-back college kid who believes a flashy car is the key to winning over his dream girl. As luck would have it, a wealthy woman, seeking revenge on her unfaithful husband, impulsively decides to gift her loyal piano tuner—Bernie—with a sleek Porsche Turbo. Unbeknownst to her, and tragically for Bernie, the car holds a dark secret: her murdered husband’s body is stashed in the trunk. Remarkably, in this movie, corpses neither decompose nor emit any telltale odor, leaving Bernie completely clueless. Even as bizarre events unfold, the naive young man remains oblivious to the suspicious nature of his situation. Most notably, a menacing figure tails him, determined to retrieve the body without drawing attention.

This film is nothing more than a lackluster, low-budget action flop.

To be clear, I’ve never been a fan of westerns. Having never watched one in its entirety, I chose to view "My Darling Clementine" and commit to seeing it through, despite anticipating discomfort. Initially, it was as torturous as I had feared. The acting struck me as comical, the typical desert, horses, and cowboy backdrop felt monotonous, and the music, along with its timing, bordered on unbearable. Yet, after giving myself a mental push to persist, the experience became somewhat more tolerable after the first 20 minutes. By concentrating on the cinematography and John Ford’s ability to transform even the most mundane scenes (in my opinion) into visually striking moments, I found the film increasingly engaging.

In the end, I can’t claim to have enjoyed the movie. Still, it was crafted well enough for me to remain seated until the final scene, and that alone is noteworthy to me.

Check out Eva Longoria and Paul Rudd in a film where a deceased girlfriend haunts the new one. You might recognize Longoria as Gabrielle from *Desperate Housewives* and Rudd as the man behind "Sex Panther cologne" from *Anchorman*. If you're hoping for a Golden Globe contender, you might want to adjust your expectations. But if you're game to escape reality for 90 minutes and enjoy a good laugh, this is the movie for you. The characters are hilarious and have great chemistry. The standout pairing is Paul Rudd and Lake Bell—Rudd brings the same humor he showcased on *Friends*, while Bell is both comedic and captivating. I watched it with my wife, and we both had a great time.

Famous Studios was renowned for their signature tension-and-release approach in cartoons, where a semi-main character often finds themselves in grave danger, only to be saved by the hero at the very last moment. This specific Casper cartoon stands out in my memory as the only one where death plays a direct role. Yet, even with death’s presence, the story still concludes on a positive note.

A recurring theme in Famous Studios’ animations is the idea that "virtue always prevails." Whether it’s Popeye reaching his spinach just in time, Baby Huey outsmarting the fox, or Little Audrey learning her lesson, the moral compass consistently points to triumph. That said, some of their cartoons delve into remarkably dark and somber territory.

Credit must be given where it’s due. While I hold a deep appreciation for Looney Tunes and "Tom and Jerry," I believe Paramount, through Famous Studios, was producing unparalleled cartoon content during that era. Their use of vibrant color, fluid animation, exceptional music by the talented Winston Sharples, precise editing, and memorable voice acting set a high standard. They delivered consistency and represented the pinnacle of what the art of animation could achieve.

In the era of digital fabrication, no computer can replicate the essence of an actor or writer. Unfortunately, films centered on deep character development are increasingly scarce. Duvall and James Earl Jones deliver performances that meet the lofty expectations of their audience with unwavering fidelity. I can't help but wonder if this film was originally intended for television, given the intimate, close-up style of its storytelling. To merely call the performances outstanding would be an understatement. The only element preventing this film from achieving cinematic masterpiece status is the absence of a remarkable cinematographer, though stunning visuals are not the sole measure of greatness. It’s astonishing how talents like Jones and Duvall consistently deliver such exceptional work in an age where many actors are reduced to mere subjects for digital rendering.

This film is a captivating masterpiece, particularly for those who admire horses, WWII narratives, and the stark beauty of the Hungarian Plateau. It weaves a poignant tale of bravery, empathy, and unwavering loyalty that resonates across generations. The horsemanship displayed is breathtaking, and the central horse's training journey is equally impressive.

I plan to purchase this movie and revisit it often. It’s an excellent choice for family viewing, and I wholeheartedly recommend it as a perfect "Family Night" film. While there are moments of violence, they are contextualized within the brutal reality of Nazi-occupied Hungary. The portrayal of the native people is compelling, showcasing their resilience and defiance even when facing imminent death at the hands of a Nazi officer with a personal vendetta against Brady. This film is hauntingly beautiful and leaves a lasting impression.

The past often seems brighter, and this holds true for children's television as well. Fraggle Rock is a prime example of this nostalgia. Even as a fourteen-year-old at the time of writing this, I find myself enchanted by the allure of Fraggle Rock. For anyone unfamiliar with the show (pun intended!), Fraggle Rock centers on a group of whimsical, silly creatures known as Fraggles, who, quite literally, live inside a rock. However, they aren't the only inhabitants. The rock is also home to other species, such as the industrious Doozers and numerous animated plants. Beyond the rock, on one side, resides an inventor-scientist named Doc and his dog Sprocket, who eventually forms a friendship with Gobo Fraggle. On the opposite side lives a family of Gorgs, who consider themselves the rulers of the Universe. The core group of Fraggles—Gobo (the brave leader), Mokey (creative and serene), Wembley (hesitant and Gobo’s close companion), Boober (a gloomy yet skilled homemaker), and Red (energetic and passionate about sports and spunk)—find themselves in bizarre predicaments in each episode, all while singing and dancing their troubles away.

Fraggle Rock is undeniably a show for all ages. While the intricate storylines might be challenging for very young viewers to grasp, the lively songs and dances ensure enjoyment for everyone.

I'm truly puzzled by the harsh criticism this movie has received. Sure, it follows the classic boy-meets-girl storyline, but it's executed with such style and finesse that the time simply slips away. Henstridge, who seems to have hit the genetic jackpot, is as captivating and enchanting as ever—proof that the magic of cinema's golden era is still alive. Vartan, too, delivers a solid performance and keeps pace with her charm.

The chemistry between the lead actors is electric; the film truly shines whenever they're on screen together, which thankfully happens often. Their dynamic is so compelling that you can't help but root for them to end up together.

Don't pay attention to the naysayers—if you're feeling down, this movie is the perfect pick-me-up to lift your spirits. And if you're already in a good mood, prepare to be absolutely overjoyed.

(P.S. I'm a 33-year-old guy from the UK, a hopeless romantic still on the quest to find my own Princess.)

The seventeen-minute dance sequence in George Gershwin’s 1928 orchestral composition, "An American in Paris," is an undeniable masterpiece. Choreographed with meticulous precision and exceptional style by Gene Kelly, this vibrant fusion of color, music, and movement remains astonishingly captivating. The sequence is divided into segments inspired by iconic artists—Dufy for the opening at Place de la Concorde, Manet for the flower market, Utrillo for a Parisian street, Rousseau at the fair, Vincent Van Gogh for the breathtaking Place de l’Opéra scene, and Toulouse-Lautrec for the Moulin Rouge, where Kelly dons his iconic white bodysuit. While the preceding 97 minutes of the film fall short of this finale’s energy, the 1951 Oscar-winning musical still offers moments of charm worth experiencing.

Under the direction of Vincente Minnelli and with a screenplay by Alan Jay Lerner, the film presents a surprisingly refined, though somewhat lightweight, romantic narrative centered on Jerry Mulligan, a former G.I. who stays in Paris post-WWII to pursue a career as a painter. Gene Kelly’s portrayal of Jerry, marked by a bold demeanor and dynamic dance style, oscillates between endearing and exasperating, yet he manages to capture the audience’s attention.

Cat Soup is a brief yet sufficiently extended experience that takes viewers on a bizarre and unforgettable journey. While browsing the anime section of my On-demand list one day, I stumbled upon this title and decided to give it a chance. Throughout the entire viewing, I found myself utterly stunned, my jaw practically on the floor. My mind oscillated between a complete blank and fleeting urges to scream, "TURN IT OFF!!!" Yet, I persisted, and in hindsight, I'm grateful I did.

The animation is breathtaking—deeply artistic, peculiar, and shadowy. I was captivated by its visual brilliance, but what intrigued me just as much was the seemingly elusive narrative that accompanies it.

The story follows a young cat-boy on a quest to recover his sister’s soul. In the opening scenes, she lies ill in bed and is soon visited by a figure resembling a grim reaper. Her soul is torn in two; the cat-boy manages to reclaim one half, while the other remains lost.

The remainder of the film, admittedly, becomes a bit hazy for me. I believe they return to a world that might be gradually disintegrating. Could the absence of her complete soul be the cause? The rest of the movie unfolds with this lingering question, weaving a tapestry of mystery and surrealism.

This movie was absolutely terrible. I only watched it as a lark, but it’s not even the kind of bad that loops back around to being unintentionally entertaining. It felt like the filmmakers crafted this specifically to provoke my irritation—and they succeeded spectacularly. It’s as though they cherry-picked every aggravating element from the movie *Priest*, tossed in a cast of unappealing characters, stripped away anything remotely interesting, humorous, or even vaguely attractive or witty, and then topped it all off with a heap of stale, moldy cheese. That’s the essence of this film: pure, unadulterated cheese. There’s no audience this could possibly resonate with, and no conceivable universe where this story could plausibly unfold. Why couldn’t a movie like this focus on celebrating life and joy? Why did they take an already absurd concept and make it even more outlandish and unbearable? Why didn’t they at least attempt to create something passable, or even a decent B-movie? Thinking about it now, what on earth were they even aiming to achieve with this disaster? I went in expecting a cheesy, campy romance, but instead...

When I first watched this movie in the 1980s, I was in my mid-teens and hesitant to see it, feeling I had outgrown the "Sesame Street/Muppets" phase and considered myself too mature for it. I can’t quite recall whether I enjoyed it back then or not. However, during my college years, I gave the film another chance, and it not only captivated me but also earned a permanent spot in my personal list of Best Films Ever.

This movie is bursting with humor that far surpasses the typical expectations for a Muppets production. While the Muppets have always managed to entertain both children and adults with their dual-layered jokes, this film takes it to another level. For instance, Janice is unintentionally overheard saying, “I don’t take my clothes off for anyone, even if it IS artistic.” There’s also a father warning his son that if he’s in love with Kermit the Frog, he doesn’t want to know about it. Another hilarious moment occurs when Gonzo performs mouth-to-mouth resuscitation on a chicken and quips afterward, “I think we’re engaged now.” These scenes, along with countless others, had me laughing uncontrollably. Combined with sharp dialogue and clever New York/Broadway insider humor, the film delivers the signature Muppet charm in a uniquely brilliant way.

This film is a profound disappointment, lacking any genuine emotional depth in a single scene. The characters are flat, stereotypically crafted, and utterly predictable, while the narrative follows a clichéd Hollywood fantasy of wish fulfillment.

It’s heartbreaking to see William Holden in such a role at 55, portraying a character meant to be in his early 40s, yet appearing closer to his 60s. Meanwhile, 20-year-old Kay Lenz is written to be inexplicably drawn to him. Frankly, the stray dog they picked up on the roadside exudes more charm and vitality than their supposed romantic chemistry.

Holden’s character, curiously the same age as director Clint Eastwood at the time of filming, is surrounded by dated symbols of 1960s pre-hippie allure: the bachelor pad, the retro hi-fi system, and lunches at Yamashiro. Yet, the movie itself is painfully outdated, a jarring mess of older generations clinging to the hope that the free-spirited youth of Sunset Strip and Laurel Canyon would be captivated by them and their oversized cars.

Disappointing. Youth culture was never so desperate for validation. And it’s disheartening to think that Bill Holden, in a quest to reclaim his youth, accepted such a cringe-worthy role.

This expansive (4-hour) adaptation of Rider Haggard's tale introduces a new female character and a superfluous subplot involving Russian soldiers in pursuit of a mysterious "Stone of Power" hidden with King Solomon's treasure. The cinematography is stunning, capturing the vast, untamed landscapes of Africa with striking clarity, and the performances are equally impressive. Patrick Swayze delivers a compelling portrayal of Alan Quatermain, while Allison Doody shines as the captivating Elizabeth Maitland, who enlists Quatermain to save her father. Standout supporting roles include Sidede Onyulo as Umbopa, Gavin Hood as McNabb, and the unnamed leader of the Russian soldiers (not listed on IMDb), all of whom leave a lasting impression. Despite Hollywood's tendency to meddle with a solid narrative during adaptations, this version is engagingly crafted. My only gripe is its excessive length; otherwise, I found it quite enjoyable. 6/10.

With an IMDB rating of 8.1, I had high expectations for this film, but it fell short. The opening is charming and humorous, with a lively, impromptu vibe. However, before reaching the halfway mark, the pace slows considerably, and the plot turns painfully predictable. Initially, the office characters are captivating, but as the film progresses, they lose depth, morphing into mere stereotypes rather than relatable individuals. This narrative feels overly familiar, a story I've encountered countless times, just dressed up with minor variations. I might have tolerated yet another clichéd romance if the dialogue weren’t so uninspired.

Worse still, the characters’ motivations in *Dead Letter Office* are inconsistent and unconvincing, adding to the disappointment. I can only hope this film finds its way to the archives of forgotten cinema soon.

The film lingers in ambiguity for an excessively long duration, offering scant explanations as it unfolds. This results in numerous bizarre sequences that hint at deeper significance, yet the storytelling renders them merely strange and incomprehensible. It almost compels a second viewing, though I have no intention of subjecting myself to it again. Had I watched this in the evening instead of the morning, I’m certain I would have dozed off. To me, the movie felt like a lackluster imitation of "Blade Runner."

The film is riddled with unresolved questions and implausibilities, leaving behind a hollow and forgettable impact.

Moreover, the film’s peculiar visual style does little to salvage it. Blending half CGI with half live-action, it falls far short of the impressive, spectacular, and inventive execution seen in later films like "Sin City" and "300." The decision to create half of the characters digitally also feels unnecessary and peculiar, especially since the character animation lacks quality.

Among all the films I've watched, this one ranks near the very bottom, only spared from the absolute worst by movies like *Haunted Mansion* and *Nothing but Trouble*. The pacing feels rushed, the narrative is unstable, and the performances are subpar. Some of the blame must fall on the original author, as the book this film is based on is overly dense and lacks coherence. Oprah delivers a tolerable performance as Bigger's mother, though she falls far short of her true capabilities. Other well-known actors also appear to be at their lowest in this production. The storyline follows an African American man who takes a job as a chauffeur. While driving the family’s daughter to a communist gathering, he becomes involved in a series of events. One incident leads to another, and the girl ends up intoxicated. Though the family he works for harbors no racial prejudice, he believes otherwise. Upon returning home, he puts her to bed, but she starts making noise. The blind mother hears the commotion, prompting Bigger to try to quiet the girl, only to accidentally smother her. Fearing the consequences of killing a white girl, he makes the seemingly logical decision to dispose of her by shoving her into—

This movie was an absolute disaster. Watching it was a painful experience. Nearly every action lacked motivation within the story’s context, the acting was abysmal (with P. Diddy being the standout, which speaks volumes about the film’s quality), and the plot was entirely predictable. While there were some nods to *Carlito’s Way*, like the dream of escaping to the Caribbean, these connections felt weak and uninspired. I found the love interest to be completely miscast, though opinions on that might differ. Going into it, I had low expectations, and somehow, even those weren’t met. I feel for Jay Hernandez, who’s actually a solid actor (*Friday Night Lights*), but he’s fortunate in a way—hardly anyone will likely see this film. I tend to give movies a fair rating if they capture my interest even slightly, so I’ll reluctantly give this one two stars. Here’s hoping for better next time. And for the record, I did enjoy *Carlito’s Way*.

I’m a huge fan of Neil Young’s music, and combined with the enthusiastic acclaim the film received in various alt-indie media outlets, I rushed to catch the earliest screening of *Greendale* I could find. However, my anticipation quickly faded as the film’s sluggish plot and lackluster lyrical drive left most of the audience either dozing off or deeply underwhelmed.

According to Neil, the project began as a soundtrack, and the characters became so vivid that they decided to turn it into a film. Unfortunately, this approach doesn’t lend itself to strong storytelling. None of the characters undergo any meaningful development, and when “important” moments occur, they fail to resonate with the audience, largely because the film’s technical flaws become overwhelmingly distracting by then. The movie is entirely driven by song, with characters lip-syncing the lyrics as they’re performed. This technique feels novel for the first verse or two, but it quickly becomes irritating and repetitive. It doesn’t come across as authentic or intentionally artificial—it simply feels out of place and intrusive.

The acting is subpar, with characters stuck in a single emotional gear throughout. The lighting is often inadequate, further detracting from the experience. The only redeeming aspect I can mention is a handful of scenes styled as newscasts, though even this technique is so overused in modern cinema that it hardly stands out.

I believe the first episode of this inaugural series was a fantastic success. It was thoroughly entertaining, and the actors delivered outstanding performances. I find it unjust for anyone to criticize it as poor, especially since it captured the essence of the era perfectly for its purpose. It frustrates me when people complain about historical inaccuracies; this is a Saturday night entertainment program, not a dry history documentary. The costumes and settings were spot-on for the tone of the show. What an incredible beginning! I’m eagerly anticipating what’s next. I’ve discussed it with many friends at school, and they’re all fans too. We agree it’s exceptional entertainment with compelling stories to match.

I rented this movie over the weekend, turned up the surround sound system, and was impressed by the incredible audio from the special effects. This film is an excellent choice for a rental; the special effects were intense enough to frighten my fiancée, though some appeared noticeably computer-generated. I didn’t catch it in theaters, but it’s the perfect pick for a spooky late-night stay-at-home movie. I highly recommend it!

This film is an exceptional cinematic experience. The performances by the entire cast are remarkable, with each actor embodying their character flawlessly. The storyline is captivating, revolving around Raj, who falls deeply in love with Priya. The couple ties the knot, and soon Priya is expecting a child. However, tragedy strikes, and they heartbreakingly lose the baby. In a twist of fate, Raj encounters Madhu, whom he persuades with a bribe to bear his child, despite not being married to her. The movie itself is outstanding, featuring brilliant dialogues and enchanting, melodic songs. The visual presentation is stunning, with vibrant picturizations, particularly the lively and colorful wedding song. Salman, Rani, and Preity deliver stellar performances, while the cinematography is breathtaking, capturing the beauty of Switzerland in a picturesque manner. The talented cast elevates the film, making it a delightful watch. It is undoubtedly worth the time and money. Rating: 8/10

Drawing from a real-life mining catastrophe, this early German sound film (complete with English subtitles) remains one of the most compelling docu-dramas in cinematic history. "Kameradschaft" features numerous non-professional actors and offers a haunting portrayal of the deep camaraderie among miners, transcending the French/German border divide. When a tragic accident strikes, it evokes the finest qualities in all involved, overriding any directives from above. A miner in distress is assured the support of his peers, even at the risk of immense personal sacrifice, including their own lives.

This movie evokes memories of the selfless bravery displayed by the NYFD in the wake of the 9/11 tragedy. Disregarding official protocols, these uniformed heroes were driven by a singular mission: to rescue lives and locate their fellow firefighters. Over 70 years after its release, "Kameradschaft" continues to convey a powerful and enduring message: a friend in need is truly a friend indeed.

I’ve watched this film multiple times at various short-film festivals, and each time it feels like I’m watching a movie trailer!

For a school project, the production and direction are impressive, but the story could use more depth to make it a truly captivating film. The character Tim Watcher, in particular, deserved a more detailed exploration. This is a recurring issue in some Portuguese short films—the scripts often remain too surface-level.

Nevertheless, I enjoyed the film...

Parabéns! (Congratulations!)

Many argue that Antz surpasses A Bug's Life, and while Antz is indeed a strong film, I found myself slightly more captivated by A Bug's Life. Apart from the Toy Story series, I can’t recall another Pixar animation that had me laughing so uncontrollably. The visuals are crisp, the storyline feels fresh without being didactic, and the voice acting truly elevates the film. Dave Foley brings a sincere charm to his role as a trouble-prone ant, while Kevin Spacey delivers a standout performance as the menacing Hopper. Haydn Panettiere also shines as Dot. The supporting cast, including Dennis Leary, David Hyde Pierce, and Madeline Kahn, is equally impressive, and the list of talent goes on. The script is exceptional—hilarious at times and occasionally poignant. While it may not carry the deeper social commentary of Antz, it offers pure, unadulterated entertainment. 9/10. Bethany Cox

Jason Lee's impressive physique makes a return! If that's your main interest, you've found what you're looking for. If not, you might want to skip this one.

As for the film itself, it’s riddled with clichés, featuring some poorly filmed but somewhat exotic fight sequences (incorporating Jeet Kune Do), along with subpar acting and cheap special effects. Jason Lee appears visibly uncomfortable throughout, and it’s easy to see why. This is far from a triumphant comeback.

The movie doesn’t even qualify as a decent B-movie. Yes, there’s a German-esque, bleached-blond villain reminiscent of a Rutger Hauer knockoff, but it lacks even the basics like a gratuitous sex scene or a single provocative shot. Nothing. Zilch. Even Starship Troopers 2 had the foresight to include the expected nude scenes (for more on that cinematic gem, stay tuned for our upcoming review of that awe-inspiring sequel...). I couldn’t shake the feeling that the writer was using this script to settle a personal score, so I’ll steer clear of discussing the “plot” or much else. I’ll just note that there are some subtle non-heterosexual undertones, and leave it at that.

On the plus side, at least there’s no Jean-Claude Van Damme in this one :)

Start by scribbling your script on a napkin. Why bother with anything more? We’re not aiming for a Hollywood blockbuster.

Next, cast amateur actors. Their inexperience will generate buzz at festivals. Why bother with seasoned professionals who’ve dedicated years to their craft? Then, bring on a cinematographer clueless about lighting. If the scenes are too polished, they won’t seem “authentic,” and festival judges might scoff. Who needs top-tier visuals anyway? Go a step further and hire a ten-year-old who’s never touched a camera to operate it. That raw, shaky footage will scream “amateur” in a way festival screeners will misinterpret as “realism.” Sure, it’ll drive away most viewers, but a handful of critics and pretentious audience members will hail it as “brilliant,” unable to fathom it’s just a mess.

Once that’s sorted, secure your spot at the Festival of Bad Movies, better known as Sundance.

What a tragic waste.

Michael Rooker is a competent actor, but he’s not suited for leading roles unless it’s in a low-budget film. His lack of charisma is evident, especially when compared to Ryo Ishibashi, who commands far greater screen presence. Unfortunately, Ishibashi isn’t the central figure, and the majority of the film focuses on the stoic Rooker.

Danielle Harris, known from Halloween 4 and 5, portrays Rooker’s daughter. She brings a charming and engaging energy to the role, though her character is written as somewhat dim-witted. One of her poor decisions tragically leads to the death of a key character. The film also features comedians Fred Willard, Bobcat Goldthwait, and Stephen Furst in unique roles, and their fates in the story are both surprising and memorable.

Vincent Schiavelli takes on the role of the Consigliere to the local Mafia Godfather, leaving viewers uncertain whether he’s playing it straight or for laughs. Tim Thomerson also appears, a familiar face in countless low-budget, direct-to-video action flicks and comedies. The presence of so many comedic actors contributes to the film’s tone, making it feel like a satire. Could this be a parody of a Yakuza movie? The ambiguity lingers.

I could hardly believe that this film would turn out to be a disappointment, yet I found myself let down. As a longtime enthusiast of Pekinpah's work, I stumbled upon this heavily discounted DVD and decided to take a chance on it. The opening credits, a signature element for Pekinpah fans, feature the striking inter-cutting of human and animal imagery. Here, they are accompanied by the non-diegetic sound of children playing in a schoolyard while a bomb is covertly planted—an excellent build-up of tension. Later, as the perpetrators, Caan and Duval, head to their next assignment, Duval shocks Caan with the revelation that his date from the previous night had an STD, a fact uncovered by rifling through her purse during Caan's intimate moment with her. The resulting laughter is brilliant and clearly serves as inspiration for a scene in Brian DePalma's *Dressed to Kill*, briefly at the expense of Angie Dickinson's character. However, the issue with *The Killer Elite* is that after those gripping opening credits, the film loses its momentum. Even *Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia*, with its superior production value, outshines it—a strong statement for those familiar with Pekinpah's catalog. I often use Pekinpah’s opening sequences as teaching material in lectures, but once the credits roll for *The Killer Elite*, I turn the film off.

Hello once more from the shadows. This film is often likened to "The Princess Bride," and while it doesn't quite reach the heights of that beloved classic, it stands as a highly entertaining and skillfully crafted piece in its own right. The plot feels somewhat peculiar, and the concept of the wall remains largely unexplained, yet the execution is solid, even generating significant tension at times.

Charlie Cox stars as Tristan, a young man who falls for the wrong woman, portrayed by Sienna Miller. In a bid to win her affection, he promises to retrieve a fallen star, who turns out to be the captivating Claire Danes. The outcome of their relationship is predictable, but the real suspense arises from the pursuit by a malevolent witch, played by Michelle Pfeiffer, and a prince, the son of King Peter O’Toole, both intent on seizing the ruby necklace worn by our celestial heroine. It’s a classic clash of good versus evil.

On their journey, they cross paths with an utterly bizarre pirate, unlike any seen even in the Caribbean. Robert DeNiro takes on the role of Captain Shakespeare, a character with a rough exterior but a surprisingly softer, more flamboyant side. Another memorable moment features the inimitable Ricky Gervais as a quick-witted trader, providing a few hearty chuckles along the way.

I had to sit through nearly the entire show dealing with teenage high school drama and family disputes, which I have little patience for. The worries of high school girls over their relationships are of no interest to me. Having already navigated my own personal hell with similar issues, I have no desire to watch fictional teens experience watered-down versions of the struggles I faced. My only reason for tuning in is the science fiction, and sadly, that element was barely present. Near the end, there were a few fleeting moments of sci-fi with the introduction of a proto-Cylon, which was promising but flawed. Its red eye-dot fixated on objects of interest, which contradicts the well-known Cylon trait of a constantly scanning eye that maps its surroundings. That red dot should never stop moving side to side.

I sincerely hope the writers correct this oversight before the second episode airs.

Disappointing. This is the result of a director showing up to work merely for a paycheck.

The intentions were commendable, with stunning locations and settings that promised a grand cinematic epic. However, the execution is abysmal. In certain scenes, you can catch background extras blatantly staring into the camera or watching the main actors, clearly clueless about their roles when "Action!" is called. The battle sequences are laughably poor, leaving you to question if these fighters are even trying. They might have caused more impact with a group hug. In slow-motion shots, individuals on the battlefield can be seen aimlessly walking or standing around, casually waving their arms.

Only the foreground action receives some focus, but to what end? The storyline is incoherent and fragmented, resembling a series of random events thrown together, often without even a semblance of chronological order. The dialogue is painfully simplistic, and the romantic subplot is more cringe-worthy and absurd than those found in low-budget Hong Kong action flicks.

Despite a hefty budget of 40 million dollars, which is evident in every frame, the outcome of this colossal endeavor, at best, is merely a polished, gleaming disc.

Around twenty minutes into the film, I found myself losing interest. The characters, quite frankly, lacked depth and failed to engage. While there were fleeting moments of entertainment, the pace would inevitably drag once more. Thankfully, my persistence paid off with a decent ending, though it wasn’t nearly compelling enough to redeem the preceding ninety minutes. Ultimately, I’d rate the movie as average, and given the impressive cast, I can’t help but view it as a letdown.

Panic In The Streets begins with a quintessential noir aesthetic, presenting a shadowy street scene that transitions with a camera tilt to a window, revealing a gritty card game in progress. This striking opening, paired with authentic location shots, foreshadows the intense atmosphere Orson Welles would later create in Touch Of Evil. One of the players dramatically flings open the window, a fitting gesture that not only introduces the unfolding drama but also symbolically unveils the dark underbelly of society to the audience.

Filmed in stark black and white, Panic In The Streets is elevated by a powerful ensemble cast and exceptional on-location filming in New Orleans. The settings—ranging from a somber mortuary to a bustling shipping office and the dilapidated interior of 'Frank's Place'—create a distinctive, often suffocating ambiance that could never be replicated on a studio set. These elements reflect the influence of Jules Dassin’s pioneering work in The Naked City from two years prior, which introduced a raw, documentary-like realism to the noir genre. Notably, Richard Widmark, who stars in this film, had previously collaborated with Dassin in the even more remarkable Night And The City, a testament to his versatility within the genre.

We purchased this movie as a prank for a friend, but it might have been the worst gag we’ve ever pulled. The film is nearly unwatchable, with abysmal acting throughout. It features possibly the worst child actor in history and a disappointing performance from Hasselhoff. The storyline is an absolute mess, and at times, we were so bored that we couldn’t even follow what was happening. It attempts to be gory in parts but ends up being simply ridiculous.

Absolutely awful.

Who would have guessed they could be this hilarious? Christopher Meloni and Janel Moloney, typically recognized for their remarkable performances in intense TV dramas like "Law & Order: SVU" and "The West Wing," shine together in a captivating romantic comedy that delivers plenty of laughter on the big screen.

The duo portrays the evolving relationship with remarkable finesse, making it impossible not to fall for Barry Singer (Meloni), even though he's a standup comedian with a harsh, misogynistic edge.

You'll find yourself cheering for Barry as he grapples with his insecurities about women and pursues Thea (Moloney) across the country, determined to win her over. Despite their stark differences, when Barry finally bares his soul, you'll be left questioning why Thea continues to push him away.

*The Souler Opposite* is a delightful film, boasting a stellar cast and a talented writer. It’s definitely worth a watch.

I’ve never watched any of the “Santa Slasher” films, such as *Silent Night, Deadly Night*, the original *Black Christmas*, or this particular one, *Christmas Evil*. I’m aware of their infamous reputation, often tied to groups like MADS (Mothers Against Deranged Santas). Curiosity led me to rent this movie after hearing it mentioned in a *Fat Guys At the Movies* segment.

Honestly, mothers should protest this film, but not because of the so-called “killer” Santa. The real issue is that this movie is simply terrible. It’s dull, drags on endlessly despite its short 92-minute runtime, and is, frankly, rubbish.

The story begins in 1947, when a young boy watches Santa come down the chimney, leave presents, enjoy some snacks, and magically float back up. The boy goes to bed but sneaks back to the living room, only to catch Mommy and Santa in a somewhat compromising moment. This event apparently scars him for life, though the scene is about as scandalous as the “Leg Lamp” moment in *A Christmas Story*. Disturbed by what he saw, he retreats to the attic and inexplicably cuts his own hand.

Fast forward to 1980, and this traumatized boy is now an adult working in a toy factory. We’re then taken through...

If you’re a fan of clichéd and formulaic rape-revenge thrillers, you’re in for a surprising delight. However, these types of films don’t resonate with me, and I struggled to find anything redeeming in this odd story. It feels like a relic from the 1980s, a time when such movies would have skipped theaters and gone straight to video. Gillian Anderson and Danny Dyer deliver passable performances despite a lackluster script and a dull premise. Yet, one has to wonder why Anderson, after her stellar portrayal of Lady Deadlock in last year’s BBC adaptation of Bleak House, would choose to be part of a project like this. The director’s influences reportedly stem from witnessing a near-rape and his background in documentaries, but even that doesn’t justify the absurd scene where rural dogs attack Dyer’s character—an moment so outlandish that I wasn’t the only one in the theater laughing. Equally baffling is the involvement of FilmFour and Verve Pictures, companies with a history of supporting excellent independent British cinema. Verve, for instance, distributed films like Bullet Boy, Code 46, and Red Road, making it hard to fathom why Straightheads is associated with their legacy.

That summer, I spent several days observing the filming of this movie, only to see that all that effort culminated in just two scenes in the final cut. The shooting took place at Sylvan Lake in the Black Hills, with commands like "Bring the wagon" and "Stop the wagon" echoing through the set. As a young person from Dakota, I eagerly awaited the movie's release and was not let down. The local buffalo herd was being thinned out during production, so the hunting scenes were disturbingly real. (Yes, Doris, animals were indeed harmed in the making of this film.) I couldn’t help but notice that the ending seemed to inspire Jack Nicholson’s performance in *The Shining*. This film is a remarkable Western with poignant social commentary from the 1950s. It deserves to stand alongside *High Noon* as a masterpiece of authentic Western drama or to be recognized as a powerful social statement, much like *Blackboard Jungle* or *Rebel Without a Cause* captured the spirit of 1950s youth.

This film can be described as a fair attempt, characteristic of a typical sixties movie, yet it falls short in delivering a sense of accomplishment. Maggie Smith delivers a credible performance, though it doesn't quite reach the heights of her potential. The rest of the cast, unfortunately, delivers subpar performances that detract from the overall experience. The film struggles to fulfill its intended genres, lacking both humor and drama, with only the romantic elements meeting a satisfactory standard. It fails to connect with its target audience, sending mixed and unclear messages. The plot and storyline are overly simplistic and poorly executed, leaving viewers puzzled about the film's quality and intended demographic. Despite these shortcomings, Maggie Smith's contribution stands out, and the storyline shows occasional flashes of promise.

4.

To begin, I acknowledge that I’m white, and I approach the sensitive topic of race with caution. That said, I’ve noticed a troubling double standard: hatred from white people toward black people is deemed unacceptable, yet hatred from black people toward white people seems to be excused, often with the justification that it’s somehow deserved. Where do I even begin? I wish I could find something positive to say about this film beyond its unintentional humor. Take, for instance, the absurd scene where Ice Cube and his friends take on a group of massive, intimidating, and ferocious-looking neo-Nazis—and somehow come out victorious, despite the neo-Nazis being twice their size. Then there’s the chase scene, which is unintentionally hilarious and utterly ridiculous.

This film fails to be a meaningful exploration of race, tolerance, or understanding. Instead, it’s a racist piece that reinforces tired stereotypes. The portrayal of the timid white character who, after being bullied by his black roommate, transforms into a skinhead is not just lazy—it’s downright terrible. I deeply regret watching this movie.

Save yourself the agony of enduring a poorly written, poorly acted, dull, and blatantly biased film. If you’re interested in a thoughtful take on race, rent *American History X* instead. That’s a real movie.

Allen ventures to the countryside, a place he loathes in reality, for a weekend getaway with his friends—archetypal successful, white, middle-class complainers often seen in his movies.

Typically, I find a spark of humor in Woody Allen's comedies, but this one is a complete misstep. Even his signature one-liners fail to land. The plot is virtually nonexistent, save for some contrived Shakespearean references, and Allen attempts to infuse the rural setting with a quasi-mystical vibe, which only renders the film more insipid and poorly conceived.

The movie fails on every front and is utterly tedious. The only redeeming aspects are the end credits rolling and the critical backlash that seems to have jolted Allen into recognizing that a haphazard script and casting friends do not automatically result in an engaging film.

Understanding the age of a film can help set expectations for certain outdated elements, potentially making the viewing experience more bearable. This was my mindset while watching *Revolt of the Zombies*. One should anticipate the heavy use of monotonous dialogue and exaggerated, outdated acting styles, as well as the rudimentary or even nonexistent special effects typical of that era. The film demands a significant stretch of the viewer's imagination—perhaps too much in this instance. The storyline itself is convoluted and hard to follow: during World War I, zombified Southeast Asian soldiers display remarkable prowess. Though doubts linger about the reasons behind this, there’s a pressing need to keep such a secret from falling into the wrong hands. Consequently, a team embarks on an archaeological expedition to uncover the truth. One member of the group discovers the secret to remote hypnosis and uses it for various ends, including temporarily eliminating a romantic rival for the woman he desires. In a gesture to prove his love, he relinquishes control over everyone—a grave mistake, as once freed from his influence, many of those formerly under his command seek to kill him to ensure he can never dominate them again. Even with adjusted expectations, the film falls below average. It is recommended only for the most dedicated enthusiasts of vintage cinema.

This film is intended to be a dark, suspenseful thriller centered on a man's search for a missing girl. Yet, just 30 minutes in, it veers into a comedic, absurd narrative filled with grating characters and disjointed scenes. It's impossible not to chuckle at absurd moments like Cage's unexpected Karate kick to a blonde girl or his bizarre "bear" punch to an elderly woman. From the outset, the dialogue, characters, and performances are subpar. I've always been a fan of Nicolas Cage, but his movie choices this year have been disappointing, with this one standing out as the absolute worst (so far).

I wouldn’t suggest this film to anyone seeking a gripping, intense thriller. If you’re curious about this story, opt for the original version instead. But if you do decide to watch this, be prepared to laugh at the dialogue and final scenes rather than take them seriously—it’s the only way to find any enjoyment in this movie.

Honestly, what was the thought process behind this? Over the years, the Columbo series has experimented with fresh ideas and occasionally strayed from its proven formula, but this film takes it to an extreme. It stands apart from other Columbo movies in a way that ultimately harms its quality.

The most striking departure from tradition is the absence of a murder, a cornerstone of the series. This film’s premise is entirely unique, placing Columbo in an unfamiliar setting and context. Additionally, the overall tone feels drastically different, adopting a more 'modern' approach that doesn't quite fit.

Director Alan J. Levi, who has helmed other Columbo films that adhered closely to the classic style, seems an unexpected choice for this project, given its radical shift in direction.

Even the character of Columbo feels altered, likely due to the unfamiliar circumstances he navigates while assisting his nephew after the mysterious disappearance of his bride post-wedding. The lack of the signature, lighthearted Columbo humor further detracts from the film's charm.

Richard Dix chose to retire, paving the way for Michael Duane to step into the role of Ted Nichols. Ted encounters a young French woman, Alice Dupres Barkley, portrayed by Lenore Aubert. After just two days of knowing each other, the impulsive couple decides to tie the knot with a Justice of the Peace. However, their plans are thwarted by a torrential downpour as they arrive at the Judge’s home, only to discover he’s away and won’t return until the following day. While they wait inside, an unseen figure tampering with their car’s engine by removing a crucial part hints at trouble ahead. This ominous act sets the stage for a series of mysterious events enveloping Alice Barkley, leaving poor Ted Nichols entangled in chaos before they can even exchange vows. It’s a compelling mystery, though I found myself missing Richard Dix. Enjoyable nonetheless.

When this film debuted in 1984, Prince was at the height of his popularity, making it a must-see for many. Essentially an elongated music video, the movie featured subpar acting—hardly surprising given it was the first big-screen venture for these musicians. Nevertheless, it remains highly enjoyable. Morris Day and Jerome Benton deliver timeless humor, particularly in their "The Password" skit, reminiscent of Abbott & Costello’s iconic "Who's on First?" baseball bit.

Appolina, known by a single name at the time, added a touch of allure with brief nudity and undeniable charm. Moreover, the film's soundtrack stands out as one of Prince's finest works. Though he later clashed with Warner Bros. and altered his name, during this era, Prince was undeniably at his peak.

While this movie may not be among the all-time classics, it offers plenty of entertainment value.

When I was nine, my parents brought me to see this film, and its impact has stayed with me ever since. I was utterly captivated by Elizabeth Taylor's beauty, unlike anything I had ever seen before. (She was just twenty-two during the filming of *Elephant Walk*.) As a child, my admiration was innocent, not romantic—I was simply mesmerized, unable to focus on anything else on the screen. I longed to sit at her feet, gazing up at her like a devoted puppy. Even now, as she approaches seventy-four and time has touched her, I still regard her as one of the most stunning and awe-inspiring women in history.

I’ve rewatched the movie multiple times over the years, and while it’s undeniably a melodramatic and sentimental story, it’s redeemed by several elements: Miss Taylor’s breathtaking presence, the gorgeous cinematography of the landscapes, a thrilling elephant stampede, and a poignant message about humanity’s hubris against nature.

Ultimately, spending a couple of hours with this film, whether on a movie channel or a rented video, remains a worthwhile experience.

In his first-ever film, the director delivers a series of gripping and spine-chilling moments. True to the finest traditions of horror, this movie keeps you on edge, with a constant knot in your stomach. The climax is exceptional, leaving a lasting impact. It's evident that the creators of *The Blair Witch Project* drew inspiration from this film's conclusion, which feels not like an end, but the ominous start of something darker. This is a remarkable movie, showcasing just a fragment of Japan's prowess in horror. With a perfect scare factor, it not only terrifies but also provokes deep thought, leaving you utterly unnerved.

"Rosenstraße" is a film centered on the courageous women of Nazi Germany, but it falls short due to its excessive length, lack of emotional impact, and occasional dullness. The movie is burdened by numerous clichés and subpar performances.

The narrative structure is poorly executed. Similar to James Cameron's *Titanic*, the story unfolds through the memories of an elderly woman reflecting on her past, providing a specific perspective. However, confusion arises when a second woman is introduced, also recounting events—not of her own life, but of others'. This approach feels like a fundamental flaw in storytelling. For instance, how could Riemann's character know intricate details about the little girl’s mother and her interrogation?

Additionally, the timeline of events is disorganized, with scenes presented out of order, leaving the audience unclear about when specific moments occur. Take the scene where Riemann proposes to Fabian—it’s unclear when this event takes place, and the setting misleadingly suggests the 1920s.

Riemann’s character, predictably, is a gifted pianist and, impressively, a Baroness. Her brother, returning from the Eastern Front, proudly displays his "Ritterkreuz" in several scenes, marking him as a decorated war hero.

Kimi wa Petto is an endearing tale of a girl who unexpectedly discovers a boy inside a box outside her apartment. Curious and concerned, she brings him inside to tend to his wounds. Before heading to work, she leaves a note instructing him to eat some food she prepared and then return to his own home. However, upon her return, she finds him still there. He expresses a desire to stay with her, suggesting a familial bond like that of a brother or cousin. In an attempt to discourage him, she jokingly proposes that he can only stay if he becomes her pet, with no rights and complete obedience to her commands—though not in any inappropriate sense. To her astonishment, he accepts the condition, and from that moment on, he is known as Momo, her pet.

This remake of the Zatoichi films mirrors the relationship between the "Star Trek" movies and their original series, but with a key difference: each of the original Zatoichi films outshines this glossy, modern reboot in entertainment value, intrigue, and craftsmanship, especially when depth is prioritized over polish. Without prior exposure to the originals, I might have found this visually appealing yet hollow; having seen them, I found its style mismatched and its substance lacking. The concept of resurrecting the iconic character in a grander, more polished format likely seemed promising, but it feels pointless beyond the pursuit of profit. The film merely puts on a spectacle, failing to evoke the essence of Ichi’s world and completely missing the mark on taking the character into new territory (compounded by the lead actor’s underwhelming performance). I had hoped for a story depicting Ichi in his later years, offering a graceful farewell and reflecting on his life’s journey; instead, this film recycles fragments of past movies, spiced up with gratuitous sex and over-the-top violence through special effects. It’s a far cry from the original experience.

The soundtrack of this 80s film is surprisingly underappreciated. I can picture John Travolta lending his voice to some of the tracks, though the movie itself epitomizes the quintessential 80s cheesiness. It’s evident that films centered on mechanical bulls, bartenders, and juvenile romances were all the rage back then. The highlight, undoubtedly, is Travolta’s comically bad Texas accent—quite a contrast to the authenticity of *Friday Night Lights*. For a deep dive into the decline of cinematic depth, I recommend starting with *Cocktail* and *Stir Crazy*. On a related note, *Made in America* starring Ted Danson and Whoopi Goldberg is a gloriously terrible film; I was amazed to discover I’d never seen it before. Another oddity in this genre is *Cadillac Man* featuring Robin Williams. It’s worth noting that huge stars like Tom Cruise, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, and John Travolta all took on prominent roles in these delightfully cheesy flicks.

This Chinese film evoked a profound sense of connection to a culture distant from my own. With an almost Buddhist perspective, it allows viewers to empathize with each character and find joy in the beauty of mundane, everyday tasks.

The performances are exceptional, with Xu Hzu embodying a complex blend of kindness and wisdom while also revealing vulnerability and pettiness. Er Min, the intellectually challenged brother, poignantly illustrates that wisdom and intelligence are not synonymous, demonstrating that profound insight can emerge from the most unexpected individuals in our world. This portrayal of China diverges from traditional Chinese realism, yet it brims with a unique humanity and authenticity.

I highly recommend watching it—you won’t be let down.

Although this film is far from impressive, I have some intriguing trivia to share about its production:

It was shot in 1976 at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, AZ, and also at Oak Creek Canyon near Sedona, AZ. Many of the extras featured in the movie were drama students from NAU at the time. As a freshman there that year, with a minor in theatre, I wasn’t part of the project for reasons I can’t quite recall. However, I knew several individuals who were involved, and I can share an unusual tidbit:

There’s a scene in the film where two main characters, during a hazing ritual, are shown running naked into the woods, filmed from behind. Interestingly, those aren’t the actual actors but two acquaintances of mine from the theatre department. I’ll keep the identity of these “stunt backsides” confidential for now, unless they choose to, shall we say, “uncover” themselves!

As a huge fan of Anthony Hopkins' acting, I was eager to see his skills as a writer and director. Unfortunately, I was deeply let down by this film. The narrative felt fragmented, and the cinematography was excessively dramatic, to the point where I was tempted to turn it off.
