While the actors delivered strong performances, their talents were sadly squandered. It's evident that not every actor excels in writing or directing, and Mr. Hopkins seems to be among them. In my 50 years of watching films, this stands out as the absolute worst. I urge Mr. Hopkins to focus on acting, where he shines brilliantly, and leave writing and directing to those with expertise in those fields. If it were possible to rate this movie below a one, I would do so without hesitation.

I believe Michael Ironside's acting career might be nearing its end if he's reduced to starring in such low-budget drivel. Surely, he has the talent to pursue more worthwhile projects instead of squandering his time on this nonsense.

This film had the potential to be much better with a proper budget, but its limitations are painfully evident throughout. There's a scene at an outpost that appears to be just outside a railway station, and I’d wager that’s exactly what it was.

One particular scene earned this movie a rating of 3 from me: the spacecraft landing and taking off over a lake, framed by lush forests. This moment was executed well, but the rest of the film is utterly forgettable.

Another scene, supposedly depicting a space outpost, looks suspiciously like an engineering plant—likely because it is—and fails to convince as the futuristic setting the characters claim it to be.

Overall, this movie is absurd, painfully underfunded, incoherent, and I can only hope Michael Ironside finds better roles in the future.

I watched this movie on cable last night, and it truly stands out as remarkable. What captivates me most is its subtle, understated tone paired with profound emotional depth. Henry Thomas, known for his childhood role in E.T., delivers a brilliantly reserved performance, embodying a man of few words with masterful precision. David Straithern shines as a captivatingly unhinged villain. Remarkably, for a Hollywood production, a baby plays a central role—not through contrived actions or dialogue, but simply by existing with a luminous presence. It’s striking to see how Thomas’ enigmatic connection with E.T. anchored that iconic film, while his tender bond with the baby forms the emotional heart of *A Good Baby*.

And then there’s the music—oh, what incredible music! Gillian Welch’s songs are enchanting, and the entire score, steeped in gorgeous hill country melodies, is a delight.

The film’s atmosphere is utterly captivating. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

This film appears to promote a pro-Muslim narrative.

Why do I say this? The protagonist has a Muslim father and a Christian mother, and spends the first 20 years of his life in a Christian village. By the film's conclusion, he appears to identify as Muslim, as suggested by his headwear, the retention of his amulet, and his overall attire. Additionally, he has a six-year-old child who wears similar headwear and is likely Muslim, despite the mother being Christian. It seems the main character has chosen to embrace Islam, and his child follows suit. Notably, none of the other prominent male characters, who are Christian, are shown to have children. Consequently, the film’s world appears to have a growing Muslim presence by the end.

Walt Disney, the iconic film producer, adapted three of the most beloved fairy tales into animated masterpieces that continue to be among the most cherished films of all time. His pioneering work began with the revolutionary "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs" in 1937, and concluded with the initially underappreciated "Sleeping Beauty" in 1959. Sandwiched between these was arguably his most fulfilling fairy tale adaptation, "Cinderella," released in 1950. Of the trio, "Cinderella" stays truest to its source material. However, unlike "Snow White," which became the quintessential version of the tale for many—whether for better or worse—"Cinderella" did not garner the same iconic status, despite its success. Although it revitalized Disney’s faltering finances much like "Snow White," it failed to secure the widespread recognition it undoubtedly merited. In this instance, Disney excelled by choosing not to alter the classic story, instead enriching and deepening its narrative for the cinematic experience. The outcome was nothing short of magical.

The film’s breathtaking animation, presented in delicate Technicolor, combined with impeccable voice casting, breathed vibrant life into the story—a brilliance that remains undimmed even today.

Television undeniably shapes societal trends, evident in the boom of cappuccino shops following the premiere of this superficial show. Moreover, it's unrealistic to think that real individuals, as attractive as these characters, face no personal struggles.

Furthermore, is it plausible that these characters can afford a luxurious Manhattan loft given their occupations? NBC seems to underestimate the audience's intelligence, even if it's just at a basic level. I know someone earning $100,000 annually as a web designer, yet they can only afford a small one-bedroom apartment in Manhattan for $2,200 a month.

I’d be eager to watch a series titled *Phriends*, featuring six unremarkable individuals stuck in dead-end jobs, residing in a rundown area plagued by constant sirens and weekly muggings, only for their landlord to raise the rent. That’s a show I’d tune into.

During the first 20 minutes or so (I watched it on a PS2, so I’m not exactly sure of the timing), *Alienator* introduces a captivating premise. I don’t recall ever seeing a slasher film where the villain is an alien from another world. But that intrigue quickly morphs into sheer astonishment when you discover the 'alien' is actually a massive bodybuilder woman clad in a steel bikini. Indeed, *Alienator* is utterly absurd.

That’s not to say I fault it for that. In the realm of schlock-horror, outright absurdity can often be a positive trait. Yet, the glaring foolishness of its concept is essentially the only thing *Alienator* has in its favor. It’s hilariously entertaining, but it’s also an absolute mess of epic proportions. The actors clumsily attempt gravitas with dismal results, potentially brilliant lines of cheesy dialogue are botched with alarming ineptitude, and the direction fails to deliver even a single memorable set-piece. By the end of the film, the original idea is buried under a mountain of complete nonsense that the creators heaped upon it.

On top of that, the 'Alien' merely vaporizes her victims, rather than...

I had anticipated a detailed historical account of the Apollo 11 mission, but instead, I received a collection of satisfactory interviews with Buzz Aldrin, Gene Kranz, and other key figures involved. Unfortunately, these were overshadowed by a melodramatic, disaster-obsessed voice-over that epitomized the most sensationalist tendencies of television production.

If the voice-over were removed and the program's narrative refocused to highlight the inspiring story of human perseverance and the triumph of achieving an extraordinary goal despite challenges, it could have been exceptional. As it stands, I feel that 45 minutes of my hour-long viewing experience were squandered. I wish I could reclaim that lost time.

I might be the only person in America who didn’t enjoy this film. It simply didn’t resonate with me—perhaps it’s just not my genre. I fail to understand the hype surrounding it; I found it only marginally entertaining, far from being hailed as a cinematic masterpiece.

The plot follows a man who rises from humble beginnings to become a drug lord. That’s a straightforward summary for an equally straightforward movie. Despite popular opinion, a storyline centered on mafias, drug trafficking, or criminal underworlds doesn’t guarantee greatness. Compelling storytelling is still essential, and that’s where I feel this film falls short.

I've watched numerous impressive Korean films, including thrillers and those with darker themes, but this one is simply terrible. The director appears to have a sadistic streak, managing to find a producer willing to back what can only be described as rubbish. The film offers no entertainment value whatsoever and fails to qualify as a thriller. It's astonishing that a movie like this was even made. While the acting is passable, the storyline and the lingering unpleasant feeling it evokes are dreadful.

I’m certain I won’t be watching any more films by this director. There’s a complete lack of filmmaking skill, and the supposed thrilling moments are a total letdown. The movie merely strings together poorly filmed scenes of a psychopath, wasting film with excessive blood and violence under the misguided belief that this creates suspense. This is an extremely disappointing film, and I strongly advise avoiding movies of this kind altogether.

Among the standout "Amitabh comeback" films, this one is a personal favorite. It captures the era when Govinda and David Dhawan were at their peak, delivering unparalleled chemistry. The songs are fantastic, embodying the quintessential "masti" vibe. This timeless entertainer is elevated by the versatile Anupam Kher's contribution. True to David Dhawan's signature style, the plot is packed with comical twists and turns. The well-timed cameo by Madhuri Dixit, now Mrs. Nene, adds to the chaos, making the climax an absolute laugh riot. Seeing Amitabh return with such vigor and wit after a long hiatus was a delight. While some might label it a stereotypical "Bollywood Masala" flick, I'd happily watch it anytime. For its unapologetic Bollywood essence, I rate it a solid 8 out of 10.

Good heavens! (And I say this as an atheist.) This so-called "movie" is utterly dreadful!

Much has already been covered by previous reviewers (those who gave this film a rating of 3 or lower), and I wholeheartedly concur with their assessments. I just want to highlight a few additional points:

Of the three men subjected to horrifying ordeals—consuming their own waste, being hacked by an axe, violated with a broomstick, and having their privates destroyed—the ex-boyfriend endures the most excruciating torment. He is forced to endure the girl's incessant, meaningless chatter at the kitchen table (as are we, though we at least have the reprieve of the mute button).

If the director had omitted the endless, pointless graveyard scenes and the bizarre inverted sequences, our misery could have ended after just 30 minutes.

The only redeeming aspect of this film, making it remotely tolerable, is a brief glimpse of Emily Haack's physique (worth one point, barely).

Skip it. Don’t buy it. Don’t waste your time or risk your mental well-being. My mind feels so scrambled after watching this that I’m compelled to immediately subject myself to (and perhaps suffer through) "Scrapbook" as a bizarre form of recovery.

As a devoted Trekker (or Trekkie, I’m not picky!), I endured all seven seasons of "Star Trek: Voyager," yearning for something better once it concluded, while mourning the loss of "Deep Space Nine" in 1999. My hopes were finally realized with "Enterprise." This show is incredible, offering a fresh outlook, strikingly unique characters, breathtaking visuals, and even a pop song for the opening credits—something that truly took me by surprise! I can’t find a single flaw. I’m ready to commit to 10 seasons of this gem. "Star Trek" has made a triumphant return, and "Voyager," you won’t be missed! Let’s keep on Trekkin’!

Rob Roy stands out as a cinematic gem, delivering an exceptional experience that is nearly flawless across every aspect. The film boasts remarkable performances from a stellar cast, a cleverly crafted and memorable script, stunning cinematography, and a captivating score by Carter Burwell. It is a rare treasure in the realm of cinema, leaving little room for criticism.

Comparisons to Braveheart, released in the same year, are inevitable. While Mel Gibson's Braveheart has its merits, it often feels overly deliberate and moralistic, lacking the replay value of Rob Roy. Braveheart strives to be a grand epic, but Rob Roy effortlessly draws viewers into its world with concise, gripping storytelling where every scene serves a purpose.

The film masterfully balances intense drama, thrilling action, and subtle humor. Its characters are richly developed, embodying the language and behaviors of their historical era with authenticity. Unlike many contemporary films, Rob Roy avoids reducing its characters to mere archetypes of virtue and vice.

For instance, while we root for the valiant Rob Roy to triumph, the film makes it clear that his challenges stem from complex circumstances, adding depth to his journey.

Numerous critiques in this discussion thread draw comparisons between this film and "The Mortal Storm" or "Casablanca." While individuals are free to make comparisons of their choice, the parallels between "The Mortal Storm" and "Watch on the Rhine" predominantly revolve around the plight of refugees endangered by the Nazi regime. On the other hand, the primary point of comparison with "Casablanca" centers on the perceived injustice by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 1943, when they awarded the Best Actor Oscar to Paul Lukas over Humphrey Bogart. This decision doesn't seem entirely unjustified to me. Lukas enjoyed a successful film career both in the U.S. and England—notably playing the antagonist in "The Lady Vanishes"—and his role in this film was arguably his finest. Meanwhile, Bogart delivered numerous exceptional performances beyond Rick Blaine. For instance, he was overlooked for his roles as Sam Spade in "The Maltese Falcon" and Roy Earle in "High Sierra" two years prior, both of which were outstanding. Moreover, he did not receive an Oscar for some of his most remarkable roles, including Fred C. Dobbs in "The Treasure of the Sierra Madre," the writer and murder suspect in "In a Lonely Place," and Captain Philip Francis Queeg in later works.

Certain aspects of this film undeniably feel outdated. For example, the crew is exclusively composed of white males. Additionally, much like many science fiction films before *Star Wars*, it often lingers too long in self-admiration.

Nevertheless, no other movie has so perfectly encapsulated the essence of Golden Age Science Fiction as this one. It even employs "electronic tonalities" for its musical score, enhancing the era's ambiance. Robbie the Robot embodies the quintessential Asimov robot, serving as a prototype for all subsequent robotic characters, from C3PO to Data.

The storyline draws directly from Shakespeare's *The Tempest*. Morbius mirrors Prospero, an exiled wizard whose secluded realm is disrupted by intruders. This film marked a significant milestone by presenting science fiction as a mature, adult genre, possibly for the first time.

Aldolpho (Steve Buscemi), an aspiring filmmaker, resides in a rundown New York City apartment, dependent on his mother to cover the rent. He is infatuated with his stunning neighbor, Angelica (Jennifer Beals), whose marital status remains unclear, yet he dreams of casting her in his film. When a mysterious man named Joe offers Al an unexpected financial boost for his project, it seems like a dream come true. However, the situation takes a dark turn when Joe involves Al in a scheme to steal a Porsche as part of the funding. Will Aldolpho manage to complete his film without losing his moral compass? And will Angelica agree to be his star? In this reviewer’s opinion, the movie falls flat. The script is dreadful, with a meandering, incoherent plot. Beals delivers her lines with an almost hostile edge, while Buscemi, though endearing, lacks depth. The film is riddled with objectionable content and unsavory characters. Additionally, the production quality is subpar, giving the movie a consistently cheap, second-rate appearance. Even if you have spare time, it’s wise to steer clear of this cinematic misstep.

I’m an avid movie enthusiast and usually commit to watching any film from start to finish to give it a fair shot. However, I’ve finally stumbled upon a movie I couldn’t bear to complete. The acting is painfully flat and emotionless, the CGI appears as though it was crafted by an amateur in a basement with basic tools, and the endless scenes of... just walking! This film drags on for a grueling THREE HOURS! I couldn’t even endure 15 minutes before resorting to fast-forwarding through the DVD. The alien encounters are frustratingly brief. Honestly, instead of calling this "War of the Worlds," it should be titled "War of the Endless Treks." And to think, this production cost 5 million dollars! Where did the budget go—perhaps the dramatic opening track?

On a brighter note, there’s one scene worth checking out: the initial alien attack on humans. It’s unintentionally comical—not due to the deaths, but because the skeletons continue to wriggle for a full 20 seconds after being reduced to bones.

So, as I was saying, if you’re a fan of dull, uninspired, and action-devoid films, this one’s a must-have for your DVD collection. But I didn’t pen this review for you; I wrote it for the

This film boasts a captivating story and stunning animation, clearly inspired by the works of Frazetta and Bakshi, which is undoubtedly a positive aspect. Fans of Conan the Barbarian or Dungeons and Dragons will likely find it appealing. The struggle between good and evil is distinctly portrayed, though the hero occasionally seems to adopt a neutral stance. In many fantasy films, Elves are often depicted with pale skin and blonde hair, while goblins and orcs are shown with darker complexions. However, those acquainted with the creations of Frazetta, Bakshi, or Tolkien understand that their works are free from racial bias. Fantasy enthusiasts are sure to appreciate this movie, though it is not suitable for younger viewers due to its violent content and suggestive themes. The casting is impressive, and both the cinematography and music are top-notch. I eagerly await its release on DVD and feel fortunate to own a well-preserved VHS copy.

ALMOST GOLDEN: THE JESSICA SAVITCH STORY

Aspect ratio: 1.33:1

Sound format: Stereo

This lackluster, soap-opera-style portrayal chronicles the ascent and decline of America's pioneering female TV news anchor. A sharper script, stronger direction, and a more compelling cast could have elevated this film, but the weak narrative hardly justifies the effort. A well-crafted documentary might have been a more fitting tribute to the subject. While the production values are typically polished in the standard TV movie mold, the result remains shallow and uninspired, offering little more engagement than outdated trivia.

The central crime narrative in *In Cold Blood* may appear somewhat subdued to those accustomed to the more sensational serial killer tales (like Gein, Bundy, or Dahmer) or the high-profile Hollywood cases (such as OJ or Manson). The basic details of the crime are straightforward and lack intricate twists: Perry Smith and Dick Hickock, portrayed by Robert Blake and Scott Wilson respectively, crossed paths by chance, plotted to steal from a safe in a Kansas farmhouse, and ended up murdering a family of four with a shotgun and dagger, only to escape with a mere 43 dollars. The resolution of the case offers little suspense; after a brief escape to Mexico, they returned to the US and were apprehended almost by fluke—a police officer pulled them over for driving a stolen car shortly after they assisted a boy and his grandfather collecting bottles for change. Their story concluded in 1965 with their execution by hanging.

However, the true strength of *In Cold Blood* lies in its storytelling approach, the quiet yet poignant moments, the compelling performances, and the masterful cinematic style brought to life by director Brooks and the exceptional, late cinematographer Conrad Hall.

This film narrates the poignant story of a deranged scientist who, following the tragic beheading of his fiancée, obsessively seeks out strippers in a desperate quest to find a compatible body for her severed head. Every character in this tale oozes a repugnance comparable to a snail's trail, with the main character being especially repugnant.

This film is a delightful treat for both hopeless romantics and avid sports enthusiasts.

Drew Barrymore delivers a stellar performance in this movie. As a longtime fan, it was refreshing to witness her reclaim her spotlight after a string of underwhelming projects. I was initially skeptical about Jimmy Fallon's casting, but he truly shines as Ben, the humorous, sports-obsessed charmer. The humor in this film is spot-on, with numerous scenes that had me laughing out loud.

Their first date takes a bumpy turn when Ben arrives at Lindsay’s apartment with flowers, only to find her sick from a meal she had earlier. Rather than walking away, he stays to look after her, helping her change into pajamas and even cleaning up the mess in her bathroom, later reassuring her with a lighthearted comment that she was 'very lady-like...no chunks.' Their relationship blossoms beautifully through the winter, but trouble brews with the onset of baseball season. Lindsay begins to see the extent of Ben’s obsession with the Red Sox and starts to understand why this seemingly perfect guy remains unattached. She tries to brush it off, seeing it as a silver lining given her own demanding work schedule, which allows her to focus on her career without guilt.

Robot Jox isn't hindered by a weak storyline or outdated effects, especially considering it was released in 1990. To put it in perspective, even RoboCop 2, from the same era, relied on stop-motion animation, a common technique throughout the 1980s. During that time, even the biggest blockbusters worked with the limited special effects technology available to them. It wasn’t until the groundbreaking release of Terminator 2: Judgment Day in 1991 that a significant leap in visual technology occurred, inspiring storyboard artists to push creative boundaries. Watching Robot Jox, however, will evoke nostalgic memories of Transformers, Gundam Wing, and even Power Rangers. The antagonist robot is genuinely intimidating, making you hesitant to confront it without a solid strategy. The film also delivers some standout moments, including the presence of a traitor or spy among the characters. Someone you believe is a loyal ally might turn out to be the last person you’d suspect, which is a deeply unsettling thought, don’t you think?

(Spoilers ahead?)

Although the historical accuracy of the film may be doubtful—especially in an era where the widely popular yet inaccurate *Lord of the Rings* has set a forgiving precedent for such liberties—I appreciated its artistic flair. While it doesn’t quite qualify as an art house piece, it occasionally delivers emotionally impactful moments.

I have two critiques: 1. The film feels too brief, and 2. The intermittent whispering voice remains an unexplained mystery.

Overall: 8/10

Quality: 10/10 | Entertainment: 7/10 | Replay Value: 5/10

Regardless of your familiarity with Ireland, "My Left Foot" is a film that demands admiration, particularly for Daniel Day-Lewis' extraordinary portrayal of Christy Brown, a man with cerebral palsy. Shunned by society for much of his life, Christy faces ridicule even when attempting to alert others to danger. Yet, amidst this isolation, he finds a beacon of hope in the control he possesses over his left foot. With it, he creates art and poetry, eventually gaining recognition.

The collaboration between Daniel Day-Lewis and director Jim Sheridan shines in this film, as it does in their later work, "In the Name of the Father," though "The Boxer" feels less essential. "My Left Foot" evokes a spectrum of emotions—sorrow, optimism, or something indefinable. Above all, Daniel Day-Lewis delivers a career-defining performance, making this film a masterpiece in every respect.

When the American writer Edgar Allan Poe travels to London, he encounters British journalist Alan Foster, who soon finds himself entangled in an unusual challenge. Skeptical of Poe's claim that his grim tales are rooted in real experiences, Foster agrees to a wager with Poe and his companion, Sir Thomas Blackwood, betting that he can endure a full night in Blackwood's eerie, haunted castle. Upon entering the desolate fortress, Foster realizes he is not alone; he is confronted by an array of striking women and men, along with a metaphysical doctor who reveals they are all doomed spirits, cursed to reenact the tragedies of their deaths on the anniversary of their passing. Watching this exquisite piece of classic horror for the first time, I was utterly captivated. The film struck me as both deeply unsettling and poignantly melancholic. Barbara Steele's beauty is captivating. The haunting musical score amplifies the terror twofold. The unexpected topless scene caught me off guard, adding to the shock. Synapse appears to have excelled in enhancing the visuals, as the film looks remarkably sharp for its era, presented in its Uncut International version.

After hearing positive feedback about this play, I decided to give it a chance when I found it on cable. However, I fail to understand how it "elevates" women or highlights their "struggles" through its central theme. If you're intrigued by narratives centered on women’s private matters and their impact on life, this might appeal to you. For me, though, it felt tedious and uninspiring. In fact, I found it somewhat derogatory.

I discussed it with a female friend who had also seen it, and she shared my negative opinion. So, it’s not simply a case of a man "not understanding" the content.

This film held great promise with my favorite actor starring in a historical drama set during the Independence War. It evoked memories of "Dances With Wolves" with its vast prairies, Native American elements, and military conflicts, as well as "Barry Lyndon" with its British ambiance and candlelit settings.

Regrettably, the script falls flat. The narrative lacks coherence, with abrupt jumps in time marked by captions like "5 months later" or "3 years later." The romance is utterly unconvincing, stretched to absurdity by the characters repeatedly crossing paths in a vast country like America. Worst of all, the ending completely derails the story—imagine a similar catastrophe in "Titanic."

Occasionally, a weak script can be salvaged by a talented director, but sadly, Hudson proves inadequate. Having previously faltered with "Greystoke," he repeats the same mistakes here: there’s no energy in the scenes, editing, or music. The film feels interminably long, tedious, and lifeless.

I had heard this movie marked a low point in Pacino’s career, and now I see why. Ultimately, this final film of 2006 mirrors my experience of the year itself: deeply disappointing.

I'm glad I didn't watch this movie during my pregnancy. I’m certain I would have been in tears or felt nauseous. The film was somewhat gruesome and deeply unsettling. Despite that, I found the baby oddly endearing in its own distorted way. As a mother, though, I couldn’t help but wince when Beth stabbed herself in the stomach and when Virginia terminated her pregnancy in the third trimester using rusty tools. Additionally, as an animal lover, I nearly broke down when the cat was brutally scratched to pieces. Yet, despite the baby’s eerie and sinister nature, I found myself hoping it would survive. And as bizarre as the movie was, I’m incredibly curious to watch the sequel.

Upon viewing the sets, staging, and editing, it's clear that this project suffered from a limited budget. Perhaps the presence of Bela Lugosi is intended to distract from such shortcomings. The story unfolds with young brides mysteriously dying at the altar immediately after their vows, only for their bodies to be snatched by the notorious horticulturist Dr. Lorenz (Lugosi) and his grotesque assistants. His aging wife (Elizabeth Russell) relies on injections of glandular fluids from these young virgins to maintain her eternal youth and beauty. A determined local cub reporter (Luana Walters) uncovers a chilling connection: each vanished bride adorned a rare orchid at her wedding, a flower Dr. Lorenz is uniquely expert in. As a classic horror movie storm gathers, a visit to the Lorenz estate turns eerie, heightened by the presence of a dwarf and a drooling hunchback. The cast also includes Angelo Rossitto, Tristram Coffin, Minerva Urecal, and Frank Moran.

I was eagerly anticipating this film due to its impressive cast, captivating location, and the remarkable direction of Michael Winterbottom. The storyline initially hinted at echoes of 'Don't Look Now,' with a family seeking solace in a new environment (once again, Italy) to ease the pain of their loss—or at least, that was my interpretation. As the film progressed, I found myself waiting for the narrative to develop and surprise me with an unexpected twist for this family in a foreign European setting. However, as time passed, I realized that nothing significant happens—absolutely nothing! There’s no depth to the characters; they come across as shallow and unengaging, preventing any emotional connection. The pacing of the movie builds an expectation of a dramatic shift, but it never materializes. The eldest daughter's interactions with local boys on Vespas seemed poised to steer the story in a fresh direction, yet it led nowhere. Similarly, the youngest daughter's visions of her deceased mother proved to be a meaningless and unresolved subplot. Even the father’s encounters with a woman who attempts to seduce him fail to add any meaningful dimension to the plot.

I attended a screening of this film at the Esquire Theatre in Cincinnati, OH, and now I’m utterly miserable.

Christopher Reeve would have been more convincing as a boxer than the lead in this movie.

As a cinematic experience, it was excruciating, but witnessing Bret Carr in person was the epitome of desperation.

The highlight of the film for me was a scene where BC gets hit in the face with what looked like a “C” battery. Though it’s unclear, the object appeared to come from a dildo, and the slow-motion effect made it oddly memorable.

“Shoot only the left side of my face… people become famous by demanding things!” Bret Carr declared. In a bizarre act of reverse psychology, B. Carr wandered the streets of Clifton in a chicken suit, publicly criticizing his own film. And honestly, he’s right to do so—this movie deserves the criticism.

My spirit felt raw and irritated after watching this.

Bret Carr lacks the charisma and intelligence to lead even a small following. That’s the impression left by the group of seemingly brainwashed, impressionable neo-yuppies who showed up to watch this Bret Carr creation.

Just reflecting on this film is an emotionally exhausting ordeal.

I'm not particularly a fan of Sylvester Stallone, and the only time I truly enjoyed his performance was in a minor, almost negligible role in the French film *Taxi 3*. Yet, I have to confess that this particular movie wasn’t as terrible as I had anticipated, despite my initial reservations.

In the story, Gabe, played by Stallone, is unable to save a friend's girlfriend, who tragically falls to her death from a 4,000-foot mountain peak. Devastated, he finds himself unable to continue his work as a mountain ranger. For nearly a year, he avoids the reserve entirely, but eventually, he returns. Shortly after his comeback, the rangers receive an urgent distress call from a group of hikers reportedly trapped in a snowstorm. However, the situation is not what it seems. The "hikers" are actually a band of robbers whose airplane crashed in the mountains after a failed heist involving stealing money-filled cases from a government plane in mid-air. With the cases scattered across the reserve, the robbers require the expertise of seasoned climbers to recover their loot...

Admittedly, this isn’t among the most intellectually stimulating films ever made, but it still manages to entertain.

I was required to watch this movie in school, and I found it dreadful. The film feels outdated, and the episodes are often confusing due to the blend of fact and fiction intended to heighten the story's appeal. Our teachers presented it as a special treat, but in reality, it was an excruciatingly dull experience. I've learned that most of the people featured in the film are not professional actors but perform their real-life roles, which frequently results in amateurish acting. Additionally, the storyline occasionally veers into the absurd and implausible. I was disappointed by the dialogue, wishing it carried more depth and significance. Although the movie aimed to be educational, humorous, suspenseful, and trendy, it ultimately came across as tedious, uninspired, far-fetched, and dated. I would advise against wasting time on this film, as you're unlikely to miss anything by skipping it.

If this series is intended as an upgrade from *Batman: The Animated Series*, I must say it falls short in a spectacularly disappointing way. The character designs are subpar, to put it mildly—Catwoman, for example, looks downright dreadful. What truly frustrates me, though, is how Batman is portrayed as a weakened figure, seemingly incapable of holding his own in a fight without the constant support of two, sometimes even three sidekicks. This is Batman we're talking about! I’m well-versed in the comics and understand that Nightwing, Batgirl, and Robin are meant to be his allies, but to have Batman openly admit he needs their help? It’s absurd. Can he not withstand a few blows? In *BTAS*, he could take on a dozen enemies single-handedly with ease. Is the implication that he’s past his prime? That’s just ridiculous.

Another issue I can’t overlook is the idea that Batman would permit a kid like Tim Drake to jump into combat so prematurely, without years of rigorous training. First, it’s utterly irresponsible—and irresponsibility is the last trait anyone would associate with Batman. Second, it deviates from the comics, assuming fidelity to the source material is a priority.

*Batman: The Animated Series* set an unparalleled standard with its groundbreaking animation, compelling narratives, and unforgettable characters. That show was, and remains, a true legend.

I sat through this movie from start to finish solely because I had made a promise to a friend. It doesn’t even possess the accidental charm that some terrible films offer. It might just be the most dreadful movie I’ve ever watched. I’m astonished that any distributor would agree to be associated with it.

While I gave this movie a dismal 2 for its utter lack of effort in crafting a decent horror film, it scored a perfect 10 on the unintentional comedy scale. I was utterly lost about the plot or the characters’ identities, but it didn’t matter—each scene was guaranteed to have me in tears of laughter. Dialogue is sparse, likely because filming began without a script. The absence of a coherent storyline adds to the film’s bizarre versatility; whether you watch it from start to finish or in reverse, you’ll be equally baffled and entertained. My favorite moment is the scene where inmates take turns running around outdoors, whacking each other with sticks, which the doctor hilariously labels as “treatment.” Pure brilliance!

In RKO's adaptation of Somerset Maugham's "Of Human Bondage," the characters are vividly portrayed, yet the film feels like a bare-bones rendition of the novel. Bette Davis delivers a career-defining performance as Mildred Rogers, dominating the screen and overshadowing much of the film's other elements. The story centers on Leslie Howard as Philip Carey, a man with aspirations of becoming a painter, only to be told he lacks artistic talent. As the narrative unfolds, Howard's character pivots to pursuing a career in medicine. His success in this field hints at misguided advice about his artistic potential; painting appeared to come more naturally to him. Additionally, the symbolism of his physical impairment, a "club foot," is highlighted and explored within the film.

Early in this adaptation, Howard's character becomes enamored with Davis' Mildred, a waitress. Davis' portrayal of Mildred is remarkable, reaching its peak in a powerful monologue where she venomously tells Howard that she had to "WIPE MY MOUTH!" after kissing him. While Howard also delivers a strong performance, the film falls short in explaining the depth of his enduring obsession and love for Mildred, rendering their acting efforts somewhat fruitless.

Nevertheless, the movie remains worth watching for the exceptional acting, bolstered by solid supporting performances. Bette Davis' iconic role as Mildred famously sparked a "write-in" campaign for recognition.

After watching apes for over an hour, I started feeling like one myself. I felt like a fool for spending money on this film. Please, keep your cash in your pocket and opt for a hilarious movie like Bridget Jones's Diary instead.

A captivating and fluid film, brimming with lyrical beauty, sweeps you along with a constant smile, even as it unveils truly startling events. One is left aghast at the treatment of the women, yet they ultimately emerge resilient, a testament to the remarkable execution of numerous scenes that could have easily faltered. This may well be Depardieu's finest role, undoubtedly his most authentic. Jeanne Moreau delivers a stellar performance in what must have been an immensely challenging part, tackling intense intimate scenes with men significantly younger than her. Miou-Miou shines with grace throughout, masterfully navigating her own complex sequences. At first, the film appears as a crude, misogynistic tirade or escapade, but as the narrative and characters develop, a far more compassionate and truthful image comes to light. Ultimately, this bold and unflinching film commands admiration.

*An Inconvenient Truth* is as overly simplistic and manipulative as the heavy-handed propaganda churned out by the most fervent and illogical Republicans. It wanders aimlessly along vague arguments before forcefully shoving a message down your throat: that humanity will perish in a few centuries—a fact already widely accepted. But frankly, why bother caring? Humans are inherently self-centered and destructive. I, for one, refuse to waste energy fretting over our inevitable extinction. Let’s just label it a "natural progression." Bring on the apocalypse. In the meantime, we’re stuck listening to the same shameless, biased politicians peddling yet another vision of a "new society." Don’t be deceived—control will still lie with the rich, the powerful, and the very fools who orchestrated these disasters. Nothing ever truly changes.

Al Gore, whose glaring hypocrisy permeates the film, is shown riding solo in a gas-guzzling vehicle and using a consumerist laptop. He resides on sprawling acres of land in a massive mansion, property historically exploited for destructive practices like cattle ranching, tobacco farming, and pig farming—contributing to methane emissions—and who knows what other damages. His wealth, built on exploitation and greed, undermines his message.

A dull, utterly predictable movie unfolding in a deeply unappealing location (lower Coachella Valley). The performances are as unpolished as any I've encountered. The script feels like a beginner's attempt from a Screenwriting 101 class. That said, it works remarkably well as a sleep aid.

I had high hopes for this indie film, but sadly, it fell short. The absence of a script, proudly announced in the opening titles, is painfully evident and ultimately undermines the movie. The storyline is a confusing jumble that’s not worth unraveling. I found myself disengaged within the first 10 minutes and struggled through the next 40, holding out for improvement, before finally skipping to the end—a decision that still felt like wasted effort. OZARK SAVAGE overreaches in its attempt to be clever, borrowing heavily from EVIL DEAD 2 and THE MATRIX for its strongest moments. Consequently, there’s little originality in OZARK SAVAGE, as much of it has been done elsewhere, and with greater success. This film would have been far more enjoyable as a concise 10-20 minute short; as a full-length feature, it feels overly drawn out and contrived. I recognize that short films don’t generate revenue, so I can understand the likely financial motivations behind extending it to over 75 minutes. Director Matt Steinauer displays significant potential, and I wish him the best in his future endeavors.

Revolver, neither the complete flop decried by UK critics nor the hidden gem its ardent supporters proclaim, represents at least a commendable effort by Guy Ritchie to infuse deeper meaning into his typical conman narratives. However, ambitious films that overreach often attract harsh criticism, particularly within the gangster/con-artist genre. With Luc Besson as producer, the film carries a distinct 'Cinema de look' vibe, set in a quasi-realistic fantasy realm blending American and British elements. It boasts stunning visuals, a few brilliantly crafted and edited action scenes, and exudes style, positioning it as enjoyable, if fleeting, entertainment. Yet, Ritchie’s aspirations extend beyond merely recycling his past works for profit; he has evidently invested considerable thought and research into broader existential themes. The film’s primary flaw, perhaps, lies in its attempt to incorporate too many disparate influences—Machiavelli, Godard, and the strategic intricacies of chess—along with an overload of motifs, techniques, and quotations scattered across the screen. "3lbs" appears to be a self-serving project for Stanley Tucci, allowing him to take on the roles of producer and a brooding, intense doctor. However, unlike the charismatic Dr. House, Tucci's character lacks any discernible personality. Additionally, in contrast to "Grey's Anatomy," the brain surgery cases in this series fail to captivate. Set in what is supposed to be a premier center for neurological conditions, the show surprisingly offers nothing engaging or thrilling. Even the minor conflict with a rival doctor falls flat, adding no depth to the narrative, and the inclusion of hallucinations feels equally uninspired. The pilot briefly explores the protagonist’s personal life as a father, but this subplot is dull and irrelevant.

Overall, "3lbs" is a disappointment. In a landscape saturated with medical dramas, this series fails to distinguish itself or offer anything noteworthy.

I stumbled upon the latter half of this film on cable late one night and was taken aback by its deeply somber tone. Even as one of the two victims reaches an extreme state of decay, the camera lingers unflinchingly. The prolonged scenes of his body being revealed and his emaciated, concentration-camp-like frame being sealed into a body bag are both poignant and profoundly saddening. I’d advise against watching this movie if you’re already feeling low. On the other hand, it’s probably not a good choice if you’re in high spirits either.

Avoid being swayed by the deceptive title "Werewolf Woman." European horror films often prioritize sex and nudity over genuine frights, but this movie takes it to an extreme. "Werewolf Woman" features a distasteful sex scene paired with the protagonist's descent into madness, resulting in the brutal murder of her partner. While this might be intriguing initially, enduring a hundred minutes of it grows tedious fast. Contrary to the title, she's not a werewolf but a schizophrenic woman whose ancestor was executed for supposed lycanthropy. The film struggles with its identity, shifting from a promising supernatural horror flashback in the opening ten minutes— which hinted at a potential cult classic— to a weak character study of the protagonist's repeated abuse and torment, and finally to a revenge narrative. By the end, the director claims this is inspired by a true story, which seems dubious at best.

On a positive note, there are a few redeeming qualities in the production. The titular character is visually striking, and there are some decent gore effects and nude scenes. However, these elements soon become repetitive. Additionally, the dubbed dialogue offers some unintentional humor with its campy delivery.

CITY HALL presents a mixed experience, blending snapshots of New York City's political scene with a moralistic narrative. Al Pacino plays a Dukakis-like political boss with presidential ambitions, delivering a performance that often feels somber or restrained. However, he truly excels in the moments where he dominates the screen with intense, dramatic flair. John Cusack, on the other hand, offers a subtle and impeccable portrayal, skillfully avoiding any exaggeration of a New Orleans accent or over-the-top emotion during the film's peak moments. Danny Aiello also impresses as a borough political leader, adding depth to the ensemble. On a side note, I’m a big fan of showtunes.

The primary issue with CITY HALL, despite its many strengths as a film, is its noticeable lack of drive. It often feels more like a documentary than a cinematic story. The action unfolds from a distant viewpoint, preventing the audience from fully engaging. Without this connection, viewers may grow indifferent to the characters and, ultimately, the storyline itself.

This sense of detachment can be alienating, turning what could have been a gripping and revealing conclusion into a lukewarm reaction of "Hmmm...uh...okay." As the saying goes, "You can't fight city hall," and this film seems to tread that line.

At the dawn of the 1980s, Warren Beatty both directed and starred in *Reds*, a sophisticated epic chronicling the birth of the Soviet Union through the perspective of the rebellious radical John Reed. The film was a thought-provoking masterpiece, blending entertainment with a powerful message, brought to life by a stellar ensemble cast. By the decade's close, Beatty pivoted to a starkly different project with *Dick Tracy*, a film that embraced pure, unadulterated fun. This vibrant spectacle featured some of Hollywood’s finest actors reveling in over-the-top performances, buried beneath layers of elaborate makeup.

The fact that Beatty could helm two such contrasting works—*Reds* and *Dick Tracy*—is a testament to his incredible versatility as a filmmaker and actor. In *Dick Tracy*, he skillfully brought the iconic cartoon characters of the original comic strip to the screen within a fresh, original storyline.

The plot centers on the city’s ruthless crime lord, Big Boy Caprice, who is determined to obliterate his rivals. The film kicks off with a brutal scene reminiscent of the Valentine’s Day Massacre, where Caprice eliminates Lips Manlis’s crew before disposing of Lips himself with a chilling “cement overcoat.” However, Caprice’s ruthless tactics soon draw the attention of the relentless detective, Dick Tracy.

Meanwhile,

This is the first segment of a brief animated clip that traces the origins of the Matrix, depicting the conflict between humans and machines that ultimately led to the Matrix's creation. The animation blends elements of Japanese anime with modern American animation styles, and its high quality reflects the talent of the exceptional directors involved in the project. It illustrates the early stages of AI development and humanity's exploitation of machines, culminating in the moment of their rebellion.

Setting aside any excuses about distributors, secondary directors, or script rewrites by unqualified individuals, let's evaluate this movie purely on its own merits.

This film is utterly terrible. It's a complete disaster. Instead of dissecting what might pass for a storyline, I'll focus on a few bewildering moments that left me utterly perplexed.

A small history class of just five students embarks on a field trip to an isolated part of Ireland, though it’s unclear whether they’re supposed to be Canadian or American. What is clear, however, is that the movie was shot in a Canadian forest, not Ireland. Among the group, one student is clueless about history and embodies the stereotypical "dumb jock" trope from classic 80s films, occasionally mimicking Randy from Scream. Another character could easily be mistaken for Chris Klein’s stunt double. He has a girlfriend whose fate—possibly death—remains ambiguous. Then there’s a brooding, detached character with no apparent reason for her attitude, and a blonde girl whose presence seems to be her only defining trait. Hooray for the blonde girl.

As for the depiction of Ireland, it’s reduced to a population of two—cousins, naturally. One of them, Gary, is obviously the same...

Unfamiliar with US television channels, I stumbled upon this program while browsing my in-laws' cable. Initially, I assumed it was a low-budget sci-fi flick, but after a few minutes, I began to suspect it might be a sharp satire of the extremes of Christian fundamentalism. Then it hit me—these folks are completely serious! I can’t recall the last time I encountered something so unintentionally comical. I hesitated to write a review, worried about offending religious viewers, but after seeing other critiques, I figured they could handle it. Here’s a tricky philosophical dilemma: how do you critique a genre of films without directly depicting the content you’re targeting? The solution seems to be crafting it so that only those who already disdain such films will get the joke. I imagine some liberals (yuck, say it with disdain!) might take issue with the filmmakers’ apparent disdain for audience members not captivated by the J**** C***** narrative, but I wasn’t bothered—it was just too amusing!

I found it quite engaging. The major plot twist didn't deliver the impact perhaps intended, feeling somewhat outdated, yet it still sparked my curiosity. It prompted deep reflection on a world devoid of plants and animals, enhancing my appreciation for our current environment. Charlton Heston delivers a strong performance, supported well by the rest of the cast, and the film's realism was unexpected and impressive. At times, it seemed to lack clear direction, and I wished for more background detail on the settings. Nonetheless, it remained a surprisingly thoughtful and well-crafted movie. My primary critique is that the ending left me wanting more; I was eager to see what would happen next.

7/10

I watched this movie just once, and that was more than enough. The film lacks a coherent plot, appearing to be little more than a relentless parade of psycho-sadistic violence with scarcely anything else to offer. I was drawn to it because it featured Zoe Trilling from the second "Night of the Demons," and I was curious to see her in a more conventional role. Regrettably, Tobe Hooper's script hardly gets started and leads nowhere, while Robert Englund overshadows everything, devouring both the scenery and any semblance of a storyline. Zoe, I can guess where you are now—distancing yourself from this movie!

This film ranks among the worst I’ve ever watched. Yet, it’s oddly captivating thanks to the little slave girl, Alice, and Jared Harris’s spot-on impersonation of Christopher Walken. Alice’s peculiar habits—smoking, drinking, and her eerie knack for appearing the moment her name is uttered—add a bizarre yet intriguing twist. Kudos to Jared for nailing the Christopher Walken mimicry, and to Walken himself for greenlighting this inclusion in the film.

This film is yet another deplorable offering akin to those often aired on Lifetime TV, which tend to depict the vile actions of a reprehensible woman in a sympathetic light. Similar to other objectionable movies like "The Burning Bed," "Enough," or "Monster," it focuses on a repugnant criminal and strives to convince the audience that she’s not entirely despicable. Spare us, please! I pose this challenge to the filmmakers: If LeTourneau were male and Vili a 12-year-old girl, would you have crafted a film that seeks to elicit sympathy and understanding for such a character? The answer is a resounding no.

Consider reversing the genders in this narrative, and the inherent bias becomes glaringly obvious, revealing why I and others deem this film utterly worthless. If the roles were reversed, there would be no effort to humanize the offender. Instead, we would likely witness a depiction of a monstrous man exploiting a vulnerable young girl, his predatory actions rightfully leading to incarceration, while his manipulated victim grapples with Stockholm Syndrome. The only reason LeTourneau escapes a similar portrayal in this movie is due to her gender.

Let’s be honest and call it what it is. LeTourneau

Despite our admiration for Al Pacino, watching him in this film was a disheartening experience. At what appears to be the tawdry conclusion of a once illustrious and principled career, Pacino delivers a performance marred by a disheveled appearance and a completely inauthentic, fluctuating southern accent that grates on the audience.

The narrative unravels erratically, burdened by numerous unresolved threads and implausibilities that baffle the mind before it disengages entirely.

Kim Basinger’s presence in the film is underwhelming, contributing little to the story. Her interactions with Pacino lack depth and fail to convey any genuine connection, leaving their supposed bond unconvincing and devoid of passion.

In contrast, Tea Leoni shines brilliantly, electrifying the screen with her presence. Her scenes with Pacino stand out as the most engaging moments of the film, though they fall short of redeeming Pacino’s overall disappointing portrayal.

Franco Rossi's 1985 six-hour Italian mini-series adaptation of *Quo Vadis* is a peculiar creation, meticulously crafting a believable ancient Roman setting with a straightforward, unembellished filming style (favoring close shots over expansive cityscapes). However, the drama is often subdued, overshadowed by frequent references to classical literature and history, causing the central narrative to fade into the background.

The series’ fragmented structure—particularly in the first episode, which relies heavily on voice-over letters—and its lack of narrative momentum make the full six-hour runtime both challenging and oddly unchallenging, frequently failing to engage the viewer. Yet, it possesses notable merits. Its strongest elements are the nuanced portrayal of Petronius, played by Frederic Forrest (whose dubbed voice mercifully enhances otherwise potentially flat dialogue), depicting a man so consumed by the cunning needed to navigate court intrigues that he has become emotionally numb. Equally compelling is Klaus Maria Brandauer's distinctive interpretation of Nero as an aspiring actor, obsessively calculating every gesture and word for the effect it will have on his 'audience.' Additionally, Max Von Sydow makes brief but impactful appearances across a few episodes, earning the series’ most powerful and heartfelt moment in a scene where he encounters a child.

This movie is truly incredible! It's important to recognize that Chinese folklore is both intricate and deeply philosophical, often weaving tales within tales. Even with my background in studying Chinese folklore from school, I found some elements challenging to fully grasp due to their complexity. My advice is to simply embrace what the movie offers. Dive into the experience, enjoy the journey, and celebrate the ride! Hooray!

I watched this film during a small screening hosted by my college's gaming club. We had been cautioned to expect a sort of "Reefer Madness" for the gaming world, and the movie did not disappoint in that regard.

Tom Hanks stars as Robbie, a young man returning to college after taking a semester off to "rest." As the story unfolds, we learn that Robbie had been deeply addicted to a role-playing game named "Mazes and Monsters." He becomes reintroduced to the game when a campus gaming group enlists him for a new campaign.

The film is unintentionally hilarious on numerous fronts. One particular scene shows the group "gaming by candlelight," which is the most fitting description I can muster. Although this was likely intended to appear somewhat "cultish," it’s far from accurate as any gamer would attest. Typical role-playing sessions occur in brightly lit spaces, often accompanied by snacks like Cheetos and soda.

While the acting doesn’t reach Oscar-worthy heights, it’s not painfully bad either. This role marks one of Tom Hanks’s early appearances, predating his work in "Bosom Buddies" and "Bachelor Party" by a couple of years. The supporting cast, though not particularly striking, delivers adequate performances.

I deeply apologize, but while I recognize that Fassbinder is often hailed as one of the most influential directors of post-war Germany, and many of his films are regarded as masterpieces, I find myself puzzled by the acclaim surrounding *Lili Marleen* when viewing it in 2004. The acting, particularly Hanna Schygulla’s constant, vacuous smiling, feels utterly unconvincing. The abrupt shifts between Nazi-era glamour and battlefield scenes come across as absurd, and the entire production appears rushed, as though it were slapped together in a mere two days in someone’s attic. Perhaps that rawness is what some interpret as "true art," but to me, it simply feels shoddy and inexpensive. When you place it alongside Visconti’s *La Caduta degli Dei*, I struggle to understand how anyone could still argue that *Lili Marleen* is a great film.

I’ve never read the book "A Wrinkle in Time," and to be completely honest, after watching the movie, I’m not sure I want to. I’ll start by admitting that I probably shouldn’t be reviewing this film. Next, I’ll point out that the TV movie adaptation is rather unremarkable. Why do I say that? Because I can’t even recall what happens in it. As I mentioned, it’s entirely forgettable. To be frank, no TV movie will ever surpass the brilliance of "Merlin."

How would I describe a TV movie? I’ve never written a review for one before, but I’ll note that they often feature recognizable faces. In the case of "A Wrinkle in Time," there’s just one notable star: Alfre Woodard (or Woodward, I’m not certain), the Oscar-winning actress.

The film is plagued by dated special effects, a barely engaging storyline, and scenes that leave you dumbfounded, muttering, “What on earth?” It’s an utterly disappointing movie that repeatedly elicits that same baffled reaction. What did I expect, though? It’s a TV movie, and they’re rarely of high quality. This one is no exception. "A Wrinkle in Time" feels like a complete waste of time—a massive drain on your patience. To cap it all off, you’ll likely forget it almost as soon as it ends. Well, perhaps not immediately, but close enough.

Contrary to the negative opinions of some reviewers, I believe this film is far from terrible and deserves a fairer assessment.

The performances are commendable, and the direction maintains a smooth and engaging flow. I appreciate the Tarantino-inspired technique of weaving interlocking stories, viewing it as an innovative approach for filmmakers to explore. It certainly adds a layer of intrigue to the movie. While the script could benefit from minor refinements, that is the only criticism I can muster. Nestor Cantillana delivers an impressive portrayal of Sylvio, and Antonella Rios captivates with her stunning presence, making the film worth watching for her performance alone.

I’d like to begin by expressing my admiration for Casey Affleck, an incredibly skilled actor whose work I deeply respect. I truly wish he were cast in more films that highlight his exceptional abilities. However, despite my appreciation for his talent, I must admit that *Soul Survivors* was an utterly disappointing film. 

The primary fault, in my opinion, lies with the weak script. Despite the presence of talented performers like Casey Affleck, Wes Bentley—who delivered a remarkable performance in *American Beauty*—Melissa Sagemiller, who did a decent job, and Eliza Dushku, a current Hollywood favorite, none of the actors seemed to connect with the material. It’s understandable, given the script’s shortcomings. Labeling this film as horror feels like a stretch; while it includes the expected twists and turns, they ultimately lead nowhere, creating only further confusion. The ending, in particular, felt deeply unsatisfying, as it failed to provide clarity or resolve any of the questions raised by the storyline.

I wish I could offer a positive review of this movie, but unfortunately, I can’t. Honestly, the only thing remotely frightening about *Soul Survivors* is

This film was rather harsh and intense. It was marred by significant implausibilities, a weak script, and poor performances, among other flaws.

The sole redeeming factor for watching this movie might be the occasional display of striking physical attributes.

I'm compelled to write this review because I was somehow misled into thinking Dark Remains was a noteworthy film. While it's not the worst movie I've encountered, it falls far short of being good.

The script is lackluster, the acting uninspired, and the direction feeble. Even without a budget for A-list stars, couldn't they have cast a more captivating lead actress? Watching a lackluster performer with a monotonous delivery throughout the film was tiresome. The plot felt clichéd and was poorly written. The special effects were sparse, and the repetitive "suspense" techniques used were unconvincing.

To give credit where it's due, Dark Remains isn't much worse than some episodes of Masters of Horror. However, it doesn't come close to the standard of quality cinema. I would only suggest Dark Remains to die-hard horror enthusiasts who are determined to watch every film in the genre, regardless of its quality. For everyone else, I advise investing your time in something more worthwhile—which shouldn't be difficult to find.

The Broadway success by John Van Druten is transformed into a cinematic gem, brimming with star power in this enchanting romantic fantasy. The story centers on a contemporary witch who captivates a prominent Manhattan publisher. While James Stewart is the headline star, Kim Novak truly enchants, emerging as one of the most captivating witches to ever grace the silver screen. However, the chemistry between the leads is a slight drawback; Stewart, with his silver hair, appears somewhat aged for the part. It's clear why he is smitten with Novak, but her attraction to him is less convincing, given their apparent mismatch in personality and perspective. (A delightful twist in the narrative presents witches and warlocks as Greenwich Village beatniks and bohemians.) Interestingly, the Stewart-Novak duo sparked far greater passion in "Vertigo," released in the same year, bolstered by a gripping suspense plot and Alfred Hitchcock's masterful direction.

The film's humor shines through its exceptional supporting cast, featuring a youthful Jack Lemmon as Novak’s warlock brother, Elsa Lanchester as their quirky aunt, and Ernie.

The year 1985 proved to be a remarkable one for cinema, potentially even exceptional. However, the fact that this particular film was overlooked for an award significantly reinforced the belief among fans that the Oscars are merely a decorative emblem for the elite within the industry.

Despite receiving 11 nominations, the film failed to secure a single win, reflecting the Academy's apparent disregard for one of its most talented directors. This director, snubbed by past biases, had to wait another eight years before the Academy finally recognized his genius, awarding him seven Oscars for *Schindler's List*—a film that, in my opinion, doesn't quite match the brilliance of this earlier work (and I say this as someone of half-Polish descent).

To be clear, *Schindler's List* is undeniably a masterpiece, and I’m not diminishing the merits of *Out of Africa*, which took home the top honors that year. Yet, in my view, it paled in comparison to this film—a profound tale of anguish and hope that moved me to tears, a rare occurrence for someone like me who seldom cries at movies.

Perhaps it was the extraordinary score or the breathtaking cinematography that left such an impact. More likely, though, it was the performances that truly elevated the film: Whoopi Goldberg, who demonstrated she was far more than a comedic talent; Danny Glover, an actor I hadn’t known prior to this; and, of course, Oprah Winfrey.

The rest, as they say, is history.

Having watched much of Ryuhei Kitamura's filmography, I've concluded that he possesses a real talent for action. His scenes are dynamic and rapid, frequently blending martial arts, gunplay, and samurai combat with camera work that skillfully captures the chaos unfolding on screen. In films like "Versus" and "Aragami," Kitamura showcased his creativity and proved his ability to deliver impressive results even on a tight budget. However, "Alive" stands as a stark contrast. To put it plainly, nothing happens in "Alive." The film, which runs over two hours, lacks action, character development, and a coherent plot.

Based on a comic by Tsutomu Takahashi, "Alive" explores the life of Tenshu Yashiro (portrayed by Hideo Sasaki), a death row inmate who miraculously survives his execution. Faced with a choice between a second execution attempt or participating in a bizarre series of experiments, he opts for the latter. Soon, he finds himself confined in a room with a rapist and, later, a girl infected with a peculiar parasite that trades its host's humanity for supernatural abilities.

Having heard countless praises for the 1990s Cracker series without ever watching an episode, I was thrilled to finally dive in. I had high hopes for the pairing of Jimmie McGovern and Robbie Coltrane, believing they were a guaranteed success. Unfortunately, I couldn’t have been more mistaken.

The heavy-handed polemics, reinforced by incessant and brutal flashbacks, were overwhelming. The production’s attempt at a cutting-edge aesthetic fell flat, with distracting visual effects and an almost juvenile font that grated on my nerves. Robbie Coltrane seemed to merely go through the motions during the two-hour runtime, delivering implausible and unexplained "insights," while the police were reduced to caricatures of incompetence. Consequently, the suspense failed to build, and the climactic scene just before the end (I’ll spare the details to avoid spoilers) was so absurdly poor that it ranks among the worst TV drama I’ve encountered in ages.

I have no desire to watch more of this, but I’m curious enough to explore the DVDs of the original 1990s series to see if they live up to their acclaimed reputation.

I'm from Sweden and recently watched this movie, and I found it to be decent. Despite the numerous negative reviews I've come across, it's important to consider that the audience for this two-part miniseries spans the globe, not just the USA. Additionally, many viewers may be unfamiliar with the original 1960s film or even the real-life events (murders) it depicts. Finding the original movie can be challenging, and even when it's available, some people are put off by black-and-white films. This newer version feels modern and vibrant with its color, and I believe it will resonate with its audience. Although it's 12 years old, this was my first time watching it. I'm eager to track down the original for comparison, but I haven't found it anywhere in Sweden. While the internet is an option, it’s not accessible to everyone worldwide. It's worth noting that this story is deeply rooted in American crime history, particularly significant in the USA during the 1950s and 60s, but it likely went largely unnoticed in other parts of the world.

I can somewhat see why certain individuals might emphasize this film's connection to the 1980s, but I wouldn’t claim it accurately portrays the lives of most people from that time, even in the most impoverished areas of Bradford. Rather, it exemplifies the heavy-handed agitprop nonsense that the Royal Court Theatre was producing back then. It’s full of self-righteous artistry aimed at tiny audiences, yet garners enough praise from influential circles to secure future projects for uninspired playwrights. The truth is, if you’re looking for a more authentic reflection of shared experiences, far more people would resonate with the heartfelt depiction of love and life in *Gregory's Girl*.

I’d be inclined to label this a 'kitchen sink' drama, but that would unfairly insult the plumbing trade. As for the quality of the script, this film is utterly drained of merit. For reasons I can’t fathom, it has gained a peculiar following among Guardian-reading cinephiles—perhaps they derive some thrill from vicariously “slumming it.” Take my advice and avoid this one. It’s a subpar film with a weak script that fancies itself profound.

I first encountered this video 15 years ago and was impressed by its quality then, an opinion I hold to this day. As a former English teacher at both high school and college levels, and an avid admirer of English Romantic poetry, I hold Coleridge in high esteem. Any element that could diminish the poem’s beauty or the narrative’s impact would not earn my approval. However, in this instance, every aspect effectively captivates the audience, particularly high school students. The visuals resonate with a generation raised on television, while Michael Redgrave’s narration lends an air of authenticity and gravitas. True, the project lacked a substantial budget; it is neither Star Wars nor does it feature CGI. Yet, the inclusion of Gustave Doré’s illustrations in the presentation is undeniable in its impact. The dismissive comment above, which in merely four lines labels the video as worthless, is both unjust and lacking in insight. My connection to the producer is not the motivation behind my words. Instead, I am championing a piece of artistry that I believe possesses merit on every level and is ideally crafted to introduce Coleridge’s poem to students.

What an incredible crime thriller! My wife and I caught this gem at the Toronto International Film Festival last week, and it stood out as the highlight of an already impressive lineup. It has quickly become my second favorite film of all time, right behind DR. STRANGELOVE. As we walked home, I was buzzing with emotion, eagerly discussing every detail with my wife.

I’ll keep the plot under wraps to preserve the thrill, as a movie of this quality is best experienced without prior knowledge. All I’ll say is that it follows two brothers, portrayed by Philip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke, as they plan a jewelry store heist in Westchester, New York. The narrative shifts across a roughly two-week span—before, during, and after the robbery—with one pivotal scene revisited multiple times. While this technique might typically break a film’s flow, it never falters here. Instead, the suspense, intensity, and stellar performances only intensify as the story unfolds. By the climax, I was gripping the edge of my seat, desperate to see how everything would resolve.

In 1999, I despised the debut episode of *Hippies* titled "Protesting Hippies" so intensely that I avoided the entire series afterward. Yet, when it aired on *The Paramount Comedy Channel*, I decided to watch it in its entirety and was pleasantly shocked to find it utterly hilarious. The lesson here? Never judge a comedy series by its first week!

Set in 1969, *Hippies* follows Simon Pegg as Ray Purbbs, the editor of an underground magazine called *Mouth*, reminiscent of *Oz*. Ray is surrounded by a quirky circle of friends: Jill, a fervent feminist; Alex, the easygoing type; and Hugo, a lovable dimwit. The show captures the boundless optimism of the youth during the late '60s, who believed they could transform the world through obscure magazines that hardly anyone read. Instead of mocking the hippies’ idealism, *Hippies* embraces it with warmth. Arthur Mathews’ witty scripts playfully satirize iconic elements of the era, from *Hair* and *Woodstock* to *The Graduate* and even the notorious *Oz* obscenity trial of the early '70s. The cast delivers stellar performances, with Julian Rhind-Tutt’s portrayal of Alex oddly reminding me of Richard O’Sullivan’s character from *Man About The House*. It’s unfortunate that a second series never materialized, perhaps due to initial skeptics like myself. If you overlooked *Hippies* the first time, it’s well worth a watch.

By the mid-1930s, Hollywood had begun to recover its stride following the challenging shift to talkies. While the technical hurdles of sound were swiftly overcome, it took more time to determine the visual style, narrative structure, and acting techniques best suited for talking pictures. *The Informer* stands out as a pivotal film in this era, demonstrating the profound impact of silent moments in storytelling and affirming the strength of visuals while still embracing the demands of sound and dialogue.

This isn’t to suggest that *The Informer* is merely a return to the heyday of silent cinema. Many silent films, after all, relied heavily on title cards and weren’t as visually driven as often remembered. What *The Informer* offers, however, is a bold confidence in stretching the spaces between spoken lines, prioritizing characters’ reactions over their words, and allowing scenes to linger purely for their atmospheric effect.

Director John Ford, despite his undeniable talent, seemed to invest effort in his projects based on his personal interest in the material. If he found a story trivial, his work could feel perfunctory. Fortunately, with *The Informer*, his passion for themes of community, honor, and the struggles of the working class shines through.

Is there an option to rate this film negatively? Unfortunately not. Allow me to express that this is arguably the worst movie I’ve ever attempted to endure. It was excruciating. The epitome of dullness. The storyline, if one can call it that, is buried under layers of obscurity. I rented this film with a friend, and after thirty minutes of holding onto hope for improvement, we resorted to skimming through parts in search of any redeeming moments. There were none. The premise—a guy getting abducted by two girls—might sound intriguing, but it’s utterly tedious in execution. Absolutely nothing of interest occurs. If you ever come across this film, do yourself a favor and watch "Plan Nine from Outer Space" instead.

"Bedknobs and Broomsticks" is an enchanting film that captivates the imagination of children with its charm and delight. This unforgettable movie follows the thrilling adventures of two adults and a pair of lively children. Though it might seem a bit dated at first, give it a chance—neither I nor my mother found anything to dislike. I was thoroughly captivated by both the storyline and the impressive animation, which are both remarkably well done.

This film is a wonderfully whimsical comedy that the entire family, including children, can enjoy together. Recommended for ages 7 and up, it offers a splendid mix of musical numbers and humor that will entertain everyone. The animation, with its smooth movements and appealing layouts, truly stands out and earns high praise. As an excellent family musical, "Bedknobs and Broomsticks" is a must-see. Don’t hesitate—head to your local video store and rent it today!

I viewed this movie at the 2006 Palm Springs International Film Festival, and it qualifies more as a movie than a film, having been produced by HBO for broadcast on their cable network later this year. The movie portrays Bettie Page as a fetish pinup specializing in bondage and discipline, as well as a B&D stag film actress with the potential to transition into mainstream acting. While Page was more multifaceted, the film briefly explores her other modeling endeavors but falls short of providing a comprehensive view of the 1950s pinup icon's career. Allegedly based on Richard Foster's book "The Real Bettie Page," the movie is filmed in black and white to evoke a sense of 1950s nostalgia. I own a copy of "Bettie Page: The Life of a Pinup Legend," which features numerous striking photographs documenting Page’s career. I must note that this movie, with Gretchen Mol portraying Page, meticulously recreates many of those iconic images. Mol, donning a black Bettie Page wig and brown contact lenses, embodies Page remarkably. She not only captures Page’s distinctive appearance but also mirrors her signature smile and mannerisms.

Three young girls, the last in line of the esteemed Gaylord family, one of America's most prestigious dynasties, lose their parents at a tender age. Just before departing for France to serve in World War I, their father entrusts the eldest, Fiona, with a firm directive to never sell their ancestral land. As the sisters reach adulthood, they find themselves forced to deplete much of their inheritance on legal fees to protect their estate. Due to specific ambiguities in their father's will, a man named Charles Barclay is poised to seize the Gaylord property, intending to develop it into a grand complex named Barclay Circle. Barclay's character draws inspiration from John D. Rockefeller, who famously acquired properties from wealthy New York families to construct Rockefeller Center.

The narrative of this film primarily explores the emotional and dramatic struggles of the three sisters. Fiona, portrayed with intensity by Barbara Stanwyck—though not among her finest performances—appears as a stern and controlling figure, harboring dark secrets from her past. Susanna, brought to life by Nancy Coleman, comes across as somewhat scatterbrained and is deeply infatuated with a contemporary artist named Gig Young. Coleman's portrayal captures...

This film might just be the most moving and inspiring I’ve ever watched. Though I’m not religious, there are moments when a masterpiece like this can evoke a near-spiritual reaction in me. It dawns on you that life truly holds profound meaning.

Initially, I was doubtful when I heard about this movie. The storyline seemed forced, and I worried it might be overly simplistic. However, as a fan of David Lynch, I decided to take a chance on it. Within about 30 minutes, I found myself completely engrossed. The film brimmed with such wisdom and compassion! Walking out of the theater, I felt as though I had gained a significant life lesson.

This isn’t a conventional David Lynch film, and it’s somewhat unexpected that he would create something like this after delving into the darker aspects of humanity for so long. Yet, it’s not entirely surprising that he can express deep emotions and insightful human truths, as I’ve seen him achieve this in his other works as well.

In this entertaining Bugs Bunny cartoon, the yet-to-be-named Marvin the Martian returns alongside his green canine companion, K-9. This time, Marvin's mission isn't to obliterate Earth but to land, abduct an Earth creature, and bring it back to Mars. Naturally, his target turns out to be Bugs Bunny. Initially, Bugs mistakes Marvin and K-9 for trick-or-treaters, but his confusion clears when Marvin uses a ray-gun to dramatically widen Bugs' rabbit hole. Bugs attempts several clever ploys to escape, including convincing Marvin that K-9 is plotting a mutiny. Despite his efforts, Bugs is eventually captured with the help of an Acme strait-jacket ejecting bazooka. Remarkably, this Acme gadget works flawlessly, leaving Bugs to rely on his cunning to manipulate K-9 into freeing him.
