Despite the deplorable condition of their home, their circumstances become more comprehensible when viewed through the lens of their mental health struggles. A commenter on a message board noted, "Little Edie has the coping skills of an eight-year-old," which brought to mind a poignant line from the 2009 dramatized film where Big Edie tells Little Edie, "If you're stuck, it's only with yourself!" These women possessed an abundance of gifts—beauty, talent, intelligence, and unwavering confidence in their beliefs and choices. Had Little Edie not been so self-critical after her initial setbacks, such as losing her hair, her job, and the love of her life, she might have succeeded. This self-criticism, I believe, is intertwined with her mental illness—a profound inability to recover from adversity and recognize that brighter days could be ahead. One can only wonder what might have been if she had resisted her mother’s desperate call, "Come home, Edie! Let me take care of you!"

Still, these women, though understandably insecure, shine with brilliance, evoke heartache, and remain endearing, even amidst the squalor of their home. Their extraordinary nature and the dynamic between them infuse their story with humor and depth.

Gédéon and Jules Naudet set out to create a documentary focusing on the lives of novice firefighters in New York City. Instead, they captured the only known video footage from inside the World Trade Center on September 11.

Previously having collaborated with James Hanlon's ladder company, Jules accompanied the captain to address a reported gas leak, while Gédéon remained at the firehouse to capture any potential developments. While out, Jules noticed an airplane flying unusually low over the city. He turned his camera skyward just moments before it struck Tower One.

Determined to document the unfolding tragedy, Jules requested permission from the captain to enter the Towers. Upon entering, he encountered a harrowing scene of two individuals engulfed in flames—a sight he chose not to record. He continued filming for several hours, capturing the raw responses of firefighters and others present at the scene.

The Naudet brothers were meticulous in ensuring their film did not focus excessively on graphic violence or gore. However, the authentic dialogue of the firefighters includes some rough language, and CBS demonstrated boldness in broadcasting it without censorship. To provide deeper insight, the Naudets combined their on-site footage with personal interviews, allowing the firefighters to share their thoughts and feelings about specific moments during the crisis.

Verhoeven's film was an absolute disaster. He is an appalling excuse for a director and ought to feel embarrassed by his work. By his own confession, he only read two chapters of the original book before losing interest and choosing to fabricate the entire story from nothing.

If Heinlein were alive to witness this travesty, he would have undoubtedly condemned it. The movie merely borrows the title, ridicules the political themes that form a significant part of the novel, and adds gratuitous content to keep the typical uninformed American viewer entertained.

While this anime adaptation isn’t flawless, it appears to stay largely true to the source material, from what I can discern.

This film is a compelling piece for its era, presenting a deep, expansive, and somewhat somber narrative that echoes John Ford's "The Searchers," though it lacks the same ferocity. The plot kicks off with momentum and maintains its pace, featuring numerous scenes with exceptional dialogue among Jeff Webster (played by Stewart), Ronda Castle, and Sheriff Gannon. It bears similarities to "Bend of the River" (1952), another collaboration between Mann and Stewart, yet it strikes a less sentimental and more captivating tone. However, there are minor drawbacks: the conclusion feels rushed and overly saccharine; Corrine Calvert, at 24, struggles to portray a naive French teenager convincingly; and the setting is the fantastical Mythic West, a realm where real-world laws and physics are irrelevant. These issues, though, are minor. James Stewart delivers a surprisingly strong performance as a brooding, detached man who believes he is solely self-interested, and the breathtaking mountain landscapes are unparalleled. Overall, this is an excellent Western costume drama.

If you ever hear the name "Joe Don Baker" whispered in warning, take heed...

*Final Justice* is a low-budget action flick centered on a sheriff from a small Texas town named Geronimo (mispronounced as Heronimo). He's a repulsive, abrasive, and crude figure relentlessly pursuing a criminal in Malta who murdered his partner back in Texas. The editing is so sloppy that his partner collapses twice in the same scene. Joe Don Baker, portraying Geronimo, lands in jail four or five times throughout the film, stalling the plot to a frustrating halt. Moreover, he guns down people with the reckless abandon of a Wild West outlaw, seemingly oblivious to the fact that he's in the 20th century. A female officer, reminiscent of Elaine from *Seinfeld*, is tasked with guiding him through Malta. She’s inexplicably the only one tolerant of this boorish redneck—perhaps she’s lost her mind!

The most captivating characters in this mess are the strippers at a local bar. Their dance sequences punctuate the film, and I found myself oddly drawn to these shady ladies. At the very least, they provided a welcome distraction from watching Geronimo bumble his way through every situation. The climax is both predictable and unsatisfying, leaving much to be desired.

It’s been ages since I last watched this comedy, and I’d forgotten just how absurdly bad it is. I’d rank it among the bottom two or three of Elvis Presley’s worst films without hesitation. Presley stars as Joe Whitecloud, a half-Native American bull rider who returns to his family’s rundown shack in Arizona, a place where his friends revel in endless late-night parties. His parents are portrayed by Burgess Meredith and Katy Jurado, with Thomas Gomez as his old Native American grandfather. Unfortunately, none of them bring anything noteworthy to the table, comedically or otherwise. The government has funded the family’s cattle operation, but they’re missing a crucial bull. Elvis performs a handful of utterly forgettable songs while being chased by a boy-obsessed girl and her firearm-wielding mother. The whole production feels like a haphazard mess, with the shabby setting almost reeking of manure, making it even harder to stomach. What baffles me, though, is that Elvis appears to be genuinely enjoying himself in the movie. It’s surprising, especially given how frustrated he became with being trapped in a string of subpar films.

Don't be misled by the presence of big names like Burt Reynolds, James Woods, and Anne Archer. Their roles are little more than cameo appearances, likely filmed in a day or less. Regardless of their reasons for joining this project, when you have talent like James Woods, you should utilize it effectively. The failure to do so is, in my opinion, a clear indication of poor direction. The storyline itself isn't terrible, and most of the cast delivers performances that are above average. However, Cuba Gooding Jr.'s acting is dreadful—so unconvincing that I nearly laughed during his dramatic moments, which is hardly a positive for a film intended to be serious. The action sequences are decent but miss the intensity needed to truly captivate. Once again, stronger direction could have made a difference. Additionally, the pacing feels off for a movie of this genre. It takes the protagonist nearly thirty minutes to get involved in the action, which is excessively slow for a 90-minute action thriller. The sole highlight is Angie Harmon, who puts in a valiant effort to carry the film. Unfortunately, the director fails to support her performance. Indeed, this movie had potential that was left unfulfilled.

When young Kevin inherits his late uncle's boat, he gathers five of his friends for a weekend getaway to Catalina Island. During the trip, they indulge in alcohol, engage in intimate encounters, and play games, sharing their deepest fears with one another. Tragedy strikes when Kevin drowns in the open sea, the boat's engine fails, and the group is subsequently tormented and killed by manifestations of their innermost fears.

Yesterday, I watched "Haunted Boat" on DVD with my wife, son, daughter, and three friends. Barely 30 minutes into the film, we abandoned it due to its disorganized and tedious nature, opting for a different movie instead. Curiosity led me to finish watching it later, though I soon regretted not simply going to bed. The film's muddled storyline is compounded by dreadful cinematography and camera work, featuring a cast that appears to be novice actors still honing their craft. Ultimately, this movie feels like a poorly executed student project from a film school. The screenplay is abysmal and overly pretentious, culminating in a ludicrous and utterly chaotic twist at the end.

Nikolai Gogol's tale "Viy" has been adapted into a new film and made available on home video in the US through Faith Films.

This adaptation significantly diverges from the original narrative, which centers on a priest tasked with guarding a witch's body, armed solely with his faith. Set in America but visibly shot in Russia—evident from the mismatched houses, clothing, and decor despite the presence of English signage—this film struggles to find its footing. The peculiar setting, which strives to depict rural America but falls short, contributes to its disjointed feel. Additionally, the film includes bizarre, deliberately ambiguous moments, such as the protagonist inexplicably transitioning from a reporter to a priest early in the story. Even the DVD's behind-the-scenes feature fails to clarify this choice. Another significant drawback is the abysmal dubbing; voices are either heard when characters’ lips are off-screen or, when visible, are glaringly out of sync with the lip movements. It remains unclear whether this poor quality is the fault of Faith Films or the producers, who, as suggested in the making-of segment, may have aimed to market the film to Western audiences.

Five Across the Eyes begins with five teenage girls driving home to meet their curfew. Along the way, they stop at a store, where they accidentally collide with another car. Choosing to flee the scene, they soon find themselves pursued and forced to stop by the driver of the damaged vehicle—a deranged woman wielding a shotgun. She terrorizes them, ordering them to strip and urinate on their clothes before inexplicably driving away. Traumatized, the girls believe their nightmare has ended, but the unhinged woman returns, seemingly determined to kill them as they struggle to navigate their way, lost and running out of gas.

Helmed by Greg Swinson and Ryan Theissen, with Swinson penning the script and Theissen handling cinematography and editing, Five Across the Eyes ranks as one of the most abysmal films I’ve ever encountered, if not the absolute worst. I genuinely struggle to recall a more dreadful movie. To be fair, I suspect many of the filmmaking choices were intentional, likely aimed at creating atmosphere and tension.

Initially, this documentary/fiction/cartoon appears both engaging and stimulating. However, anything that sparks thought invites closer examination. The truth is, this film blends metaphysics with speculation and unfounded assertions. The connection between science and spirituality that "What the Bleep..." tries to establish is not grounded in scientific evidence. For instance, the film references a Transcendental Meditation study suggesting that group meditation can lower crime rates in an area, specifically Washington D.C. In contrast, data shows the HRA (Homicides, Rapes, and Assaults) crime rate in 1993 was approximately 30% higher than the average from 1988 to 1992. There was no reduction in homicides during the study period. Moreover, every assertion linking metaphysics to science in the film has been thoroughly disproven.

Based on this, I believe the movie is either a misguided effort to sway viewers or simply a parody. Regardless, I recommend avoiding it to save your time.

If you're in search of a thought-provoking, lengthy film about science, consider watching Mindwalk (1990).

Although Louis B. Mayer reportedly showed little interest in signing the young Greta Garbo, her debut American film with MGM exudes stunning visual appeal. The production clearly benefited from exceptional talent, evident in the meticulous filming and masterful matte paintings. The movie possesses the refined elegance and artistry characteristic of the studio's finest works, retaining its breathtaking beauty even after 84 years.

As for Garbo, her appearance in this and other early American films differs noticeably. Though unmistakably herself, her makeup is subtler compared to the harsher style she would adopt just a year later. This softer look lends her a gentleness rarely seen in her later roles. Personally, I wish they had preserved this aesthetic, but given the iconic status she achieved with her signature style, who am I to question their choice?

The storyline centers on Garbo’s character and her family, who are unjustly evicted from their land by the landlord. Though the esteemed landlady, Doña Bernarda, cites the bank’s demand for payment as the reason, the true motive lies in her son’s infatuation with Garbo—a situation that prompts drastic measures.

Disturbing nightmares, unsettling premonitions, sacrilege, and forbidden desires pervade Paul Verhoeven's (debatably) finest work, a chilling portrait of a quintessential femme fatale who seduces her lovers only to destroy them. Brimming with bloodshed and sporadic violence, *The Fourth Man* is deeply unsettling. Men will instinctively recoil when Renee brandishes her scissors...

Soldier Blue is a film that aspires to be a deep and meaningful critique of human cruelty, the exploitation and violence inflicted by white settlers on indigenous populations, and a sharp, unflinching satire of the Vietnam War atrocities. Unfortunately, it falls far short of these lofty goals, resulting instead in a harmful, clichéd, poorly crafted, and deceitful piece of cinema.

As another critic aptly noted, the movie feels like a clumsy mash-up of two completely different stories. At its core, it’s a weak, trope-laden, and poorly performed "odd couple" romance—Strauss and Bergen gradually shedding their biases about each other’s ways of life and inevitably falling in love (how touching)—framed by two gruesome massacres that seem ripped straight from a Lucio Fulci horror film.

The film’s climax, drenched in gratuitous and voyeuristic gore, is utterly indefensible. It lingers on horrific close-ups of innocent Native American children being shot, slashed, dismembered, and impaled, while Native American women with exaggerated features are subjected to molestation, rape, and brutalization—all seemingly designed for shock value and ticket sales. There is no justification for such exploitative content, especially given its misguided purpose, and the execution of the massacre scene itself is appallingly poor.

This film ranks among the dullest and most poorly acted portrayals of Adolf Hitler's early years that I have ever seen. While Robert Carlyle is a talented actor, casting him as Hitler feels entirely misguided. Similarly, choosing Liev Schreiber to play Hitler’s close friend and aide, Haefengstal, likely provoked outrage from organizations like the Simon Wiesenthal Centre due to the inappropriate pairing of a Jewish actor with a Nazi sympathizer role. The casting decisions are simply disastrous. Far from being an engaging family film with a solid historical foundation, this movie epitomizes Hollywood's worst tendencies, exploiting a capable but underused supporting cast who appear to have faded from the acting scene over the last five years.

The exaggerated German accents (think "vee vill vin zis var") are an affront to Germans worldwide. My German mother was visibly angered by the inconsistent switching between American, English, and German accents within single sentences. Most of the supporting actors come across as lifeless as cardboard cutouts in a video store display. However, Jenna Malone’s portrayal of the tragic Geli Raubal stands out; she beautifully embodies the character’s innocence and turmoil.

This film might just claim the title of "The Worst Movie Ever." Without John Hurt's involvement, it could perhaps pass as a mediocre children's movie. The real tragedy, however, is that John Hurt, a titan of the screen, lowers his standards by participating in this disaster. I awarded it two points solely for Mr. Hurt’s presence, but I must deduct eight points for his failure to escape this project sooner. As for the rest of the cast, they are, quite frankly, dreadful. Janine Turner, despite her attractiveness, delivers a performance devoid of any skill. The lead actor is, to put it bluntly, abysmal. If you can avoid subjecting yourself to this cringe-worthy mess, I strongly advise you to do so. It’s so terrible, it’s almost painful to watch.

Over the years, I've watched numerous straight-to-video Steven Seagal films, and each one delivers a consistently low level of entertainment. While the action sequences provide some amusement, they’re often the only highlight. Seagal was at the peak of his career with films like *Under Siege*, *Under Siege 2*, and *Executive Decision*, at least in terms of action. However, in the last decade, his movies have failed to match the quality of his earlier work.

On a more positive note, this film does manage to use its runtime effectively at times, with decent action scenes and occasional bursts of wit. Just when the movie starts to feel tedious, a well-executed action sequence pulls it back from boredom. I genuinely think Seagal’s films would fare better if they featured recognizable supporting actors and actresses alongside him. A strong supporting cast is crucial, and their presence could potentially boost the popularity and reception of his recent projects.

I stumbled upon this documentary by accident on the UK channel More4, and I must admit it was incredibly engaging and thought-provoking. I’m eager to read the book that inspired it. The documentary explores Professor Jared Diamond’s theory on why some societies on Earth thrived while others struggled. His argument, which was new to me, centers on the crucial role of having the right crops and animals suitable for domestication—a perspective I found quite convincing. The documentary itself is visually impressive and well-narrated, avoiding the overuse of reenactments that often detract from modern documentaries. Diamond also strikes the right tone, avoiding the condescension that many intellectuals fall into when communicating complex ideas to a broader audience. While some label his theory as Marxist, I disagree and view it more as a socio-geological perspective. It was refreshing to encounter a theory on societal evolution that isn’t rooted in religion. I highly recommend watching it.

A few weeks back, the German channel "SAT1" hyped this film as the "TV-Event of the Year." Frankly, I’ve seen far better programming this year.

Initially, I wasn’t impressed by the movie, but the trailer quickly reminded me of two other disappointing films, *Titanic* and *Pearl Harbor*. The imagery was strikingly similar: the supposed "heroine" positioned centrally with her two love interests flanking her—sound familiar, *Pearl Harbor* fans? Honestly, the love story here feels like a watered-down version of *Pearl Harbor*’s already lackluster romance.

Despite my reservations, my curiosity about film patterns compelled me to watch this drivel. The story opens with a doctor abandoning his family to join a military campaign against Russia towards the end of the Third Reich, vowing to his wife that he’ll return. Flash forward to Spring 1948: Germany has been defeated, divided by the Allies and Russia, who are now locked in a battle for global dominance and ideological supremacy—capitalism versus communism. I’m sure you can predict where this is headed.

**Plot Summary**: A powerful crime lord is orchestrating a union of three rival mafias to fund the purchase of an island, intending to transform it into a hub for money laundering and other illicit activities. In a bid to disrupt this plan, the FBI targets one of the mafia heads for arrest. However, the operation goes awry, leading to a series of unexpected twists. The story evolves into yet another cliché "mismatched cop buddies" trope, featuring a determined female FBI agent paired with a rough-around-the-edges male ex-DEA operative.

**Review**: While the premise is far from original and borders on absurd, the movie's charm lies elsewhere. Its strength is in its humor—at least in the dubbed German version—which manages to entertain despite the weak narrative. The action sequences are also a highlight, particularly an unforgettable moment involving a shotgun and a rocket launcher. The primary focus, however, remains on the comedy, which strikes a balance between clever and absurd, delivering plenty of laugh-out-loud moments without veering into sophisticated satire or pure slapstick.

**Concerns**: On the downside, this film is blatantly unapologetic about political incorrectness. It prominently showcases legal drug abuse, portraying it as glamorous without any critique. This aspect was particularly troubling to me and, in my view, makes the movie inappropriate for younger audiences.

This film is among the numerous "Kung Fu" action movies produced in Asia during the late 1970s to early 1980s, characterized by low-budget sound effects, dubbed dialogue, and incredibly swift martial arts sequences. However, it stands out from typical films of its kind due to a solid storyline and abundant humor. The plot centers on dye factory workers who, after being ousted from their positions by oppressive Manchu thugs, enlist the help of a swindler, played by Gordon Liu, to intimidate their tormentors. His initial plan flops spectacularly, leading him to deceive his way into a Shaolin temple to genuinely master combat skills. Instead of training him directly in Kung Fu, the temple Master assigns him the grueling task of constructing scaffolding over the roofs of all 36 chambers. Unbeknownst to him, these mundane chores of stacking and securing bamboo poles are subtly honing his martial arts prowess, reminiscent of the training method in "The Karate Kid" where Mr. Miyagi imparts karate fundamentals to Daniel through ordinary household tasks like "wax on, wax off." The movie is infused with hilarious moments from start to finish, culminating in a flurry of action-packed scenes as Gordon Liu confronts his adversaries once more.

I genuinely believe this movie is fantastic, but like all films, it has its flaws. Some of you might not have seen Hilary Duff's *Raise Your Voice*, yet if you compare the two, you'll notice striking similarities. In *Brave New Girl*, Holly is desperate to gain admission to Haverty Conservatory, while in *Raise Your Voice*, Terri dreams of attending a conservatory in L.A. (though I can’t recall its specific name). Both characters are immersed in the world of music and face the challenge of performing at the end of the semester. It’s quite amusing how closely these two stories align. Personally, I prefer *Brave New Girl* over *Raise Your Voice*.

I recently rewatched *The Convent* for the second time, having enjoyed it on my first viewing. I thought it would be the perfect choice for a boozy Friday night—plenty of gore, a touch of style, and a sprinkle of humor. Unfortunately, I found myself unable to enjoy it as much this time around. It felt as though someone had tried to update cheesy cult classics like *Night of the Demons* for a contemporary audience, but in doing so, stripped away the elements that made the original engaging. For clarity, I’m not even a die-hard fan of *Night of the Demons*, though I did appreciate certain aspects of it. *The Convent* leans hard into the cheesiness but misses the charm. Apart from the main character (a likable performance by Joanna Canton), the goth girl, and a delightful cameo by Adrienne Barbeau, nearly every other character was painfully unlikable, embodying the worst stereotypes of idiotic, offensive jock culture. The film is further let down by a surprising lack of gratuitous nudity, which, combined with the dreadful dialogue, makes it tough to endure the characters and even harder to focus on the movie’s redeeming qualities. The evil nuns, however, stand out with their unique design and memorable presence.

"Transylvania 6-5000" is a minor yet sporadically amusing and endearing horror parody from the mid-1980s, featuring a recognizable cast and a script with several genuine laugh-out-loud moments. The story follows two bumbling journalists from a sensationalist tabloid who are reluctantly dispatched to Transylvania to investigate claims of the infamous scientist Frankenstein's return. The movie is sprinkled with delightful quirks and clever details, such as a miniature guillotine for slicing hard-boiled eggs and lab test tubes repurposed as cream and sugar holders at breakfast. However, the film falls short of its potential, dragged down by overly extended jokes and parody scenes that overstay their welcome. In comparison, the later Roger Corman production "Transylvania Twist," released four years after, offers sharper humor and comes more highly recommended. This film specifically spoofs the iconic Universal horror classics of the early 1930s, so familiarity with those movies is advised to fully appreciate the subtle gags and nods. Additionally, an inventive twist reveals that the Frankenstein character may only be acting the part of a deranged, villainous scientist.

I've always been a huge Batman enthusiast, captivated by the animated series and even Batman Beyond. I've occasionally delved into Batman comics as well. Naturally, I was thrilled to learn about this new series, but my excitement quickly turned to profound disappointment. This show is utterly lackluster and doesn't come close to the brilliance of the original series. It feels like an extended advertisement for toys, completely lacking in depth. Moreover, the treatment of the Joker—arguably the greatest Batman villain of all time—is baffling; they actually killed him off. I wish I could say his character design was the lowest point, but sadly, I can't find a single element of this series that feels creative or engaging. In summary (and trust me, I could elaborate further), do not waste your time or money on this show.

This adaptation of the notorious 1959 Kansas murders, drawn from Capote’s book, is captured in striking black and white by director Brooks and cinematographer Hall, lending it a documentary-like authenticity. Blake and Wilson deliver compelling portrayals of the killers, while Forsythe shines as the determined cop on their trail. The buildup to the murders, shot in the very house where the tragedy unfolded and accompanied by the eerie sound of whistling winds, is deeply unsettling and powerful. Brooks infuses the film with energy and employs creative scene transitions. The only drawback is its length; the conclusion feels protracted and somewhat moralistic.

This documentary, or rather mockumentary, perfectly illustrates the absurdity that can arise when people are overly passionate about certain topics. Frankly, I have a strong dislike for Cryptozoology; I view it as pseudoscience that undermines genuine scientific inquiry. On a positive note, the visual effects in this mockumentary were impressive, particularly the depiction of dragons. However, much of the information presented was completely fabricated, which is deeply disappointing, especially since it comes from supposed scientists. This is why I rate it a 1 out of 10 instead of a 0. A specific instance of misinformation is the concept of hydrogen production: While chemistry confirms that hydrogen can be produced in the stomach, it is implausible for it to occur in the quantities suggested. A credible explanation of what actually happens in a dragon’s stomach is necessary. Although hydrogen is present in many natural substances, the amount required to enable an animal of that size to fly is unattainable, and hydrogen cannot simply materialize from nowhere, rendering the idea impossible. Even more problematic is the notion of platinum involvement. This element is rarer than gold, and I struggle to comprehend how...

A touching movie featuring the exceptional talent of the late John Thaw, whose humble demeanor always shone through. Undoubtedly, he ranks among the top 10 actors of my generation in England.

He is best remembered for iconic roles such as Inspector Morse, Jack Regan in the popular 1970s TV series 'The Sweeney,' and as a barrister in 'Kavanagh QC.' This film is a must-watch for the whole family and a valuable addition to my DVD collection. The cinematography vividly recalls wartime Britain, resonating especially with those who experienced the evacuations from London during the German bombings. The dynamic between the two central characters, Tom and young William, is portrayed with remarkable authenticity and stays faithful to Michelle Magorian's book.

This movie was suggested as a solid action flick, but I wouldn't classify it as such. The plot felt overly complicated and difficult to track. Action sequences are sparse until the climax, and even then, the scenes are so dimly lit that it's challenging to discern what's going on. I had high hopes for a different experience, but unfortunately, this film didn't deliver.

If you have any interest in pirates, pirate films, the history of New Orleans or early 19th-century America, or Yul Brynner, I encourage you to watch this movie and form your own opinion. Ignore the underwhelming reviews from others. I found the film to be engaging, with solid acting (mostly), clever dialogue, and a captivating depiction of the charm and legendary allure of the privateer Jean Lafitte. While not every detail is historically precise—and I challenge you to find a historical film that is—I believe the movie accurately captures Lafitte’s significant role in New Orleans’ past and the complex, love-hate dynamic between the city’s “proper” residents and this beloved outlaw. Focus not on the film’s shortcomings, but on its strengths, particularly its portrayal of one of the most fascinating figures in New Orleans’ and American history.

Hey everyone, just check out the title! Hilarious, right? I recall watching this gem on a late-night Saturday Creature Features broadcast ages ago. It’s an absolute delight of a cheesy monster movie, complete with cringe-worthy acting and a pair of delightfully dim-witted hillbillies who elevate the kitsch to new heights. The two redneck boat rental characters truly steal the show! And you’ve got to see the boat scene with the English couple discussing the stars in broad daylight—pure comedy gold! It’s obvious the creators weren’t concerned with a coherent plot; they just rushed through production as quickly as they could. In short, if you’re a fan of 70s schlock, you’re in for a treat with this one.

I was initially hesitant about watching this documentary when it first aired on CBS. As someone who was in New York City on that fateful day, studying at Hunter College, I was reluctant to relive the devastation and horror. Yet, like many others, my curiosity drew me in. Watching the documentary brought tears to my eyes as all the memories flooded back; the intense images were simply staggering. I purchased the DVD on the first anniversary and have watched it several times since. The ability of these filmmakers to capture such footage is nothing short of remarkable. If you haven’t seen this documentary, I urge you to do so. While it is undeniably heartbreaking and will likely move you to tears, it stands as a powerful testament to one of the darkest moments in our nation's history.

Perhaps I'm overlooking something, as I've encountered more praise than criticism for *The Man Who Cheated Himself*, yet I remain unimpressed. I prefer my film noirs to exude a certain flair, with characters who embody the sharp wit, striking appearance, and commanding presence of Humphrey Bogart in *The Big Sleep* or Gene Tierney in *Laura*. Unfortunately, the characters in this film lack that distinctive charm or gravitas. Take Lee J. Cobb, for instance. His disheveled, just-rolled-out-of-bed demeanor is the antithesis of the polished, silver-tongued noir protagonist I expect. Similarly, Jane Wyatt as the femme fatale feels like a glaring miscast. She simply doesn't bring the necessary allure or menace to the part.

As for the storyline, it feels weary and uninspired, offering no fresh twists or originality to the genre. I could foresee the conclusion of *The Man Who Cheated Himself* within the first five minutes. And that climactic cat-and-mouse chase? Utterly lackluster. Stretching over ten to fifteen minutes of aimless action, it completely disrupts any momentum the film might have built.

Comedies are often dismissed as lacking substantial depth, but Arms and the Man by George Bernard Shaw challenges this misconception. The play masterfully blends comedic elements with profound philosophical insights, offering both an engaging storyline and meaningful commentary.

At its core, Arms and the Man functions as a distinctive and effective romantic comedy. The central character, Raina, is a young, dramatic, and somewhat shallow woman from a military family entrenched in conflict; both her fiancé and father serve as military officers. One night, she is startled by the unexpected appearance of an enemy soldier. Despite the risk, she saves him, fully aware that she must conceal this act from her family indefinitely. The soldier eventually departs, but returns after the war ends, compelling Raina and the other key characters to reassess their beliefs and connections.

What makes the play particularly compelling is Shaw’s ability to infuse deeper significance into a conventional comedic framework. Through his narrative, Shaw critiques social class structures, highlights the folly of war, and explores the essence of love. He achieves this with his characteristic Shavian humor while maintaining a gratifying plot. The richness of themes in the play is so abundant that much can be overlooked on a first encounter.

The opening scene is intended to depict the Legion's arrival in Paris on November 13, 1918. As the troops disembark from the train, they are dressed in the same uniforms worn by the French Army, including the Legion, at the outbreak of war in 1914. This glaring anachronism is a clear indicator that the war film you're about to watch is likely to be a flop. (By 1915, the French Army had recognized that fighting in red trousers and dark blue overcoats was impractical, transitioning Metropolitan troops to "horizon blue" and Colonial troops to khaki.) In contrast, the remake starring Claude Van Damme (spelling uncertain) managed to get the uniforms more or less accurate. It’s truly disappointing when directors overlook such details, especially when they invest significant effort into getting other aspects correct.

This mini-series proves to be more engaging than many others that boast larger budgets and loftier goals. On the entertainment scale, SOTD sits comfortably between "Kung-Fu" and "H R Pufnstuff." If it weren’t for its nearly 3-hour runtime, it would likely appeal greatly to children. The series is packed with adventure, action, and suspenseful "cliffhanger" moments, while keeping romance and other "yucky" elements to a minimum. Young viewers are often less bothered by obvious props like rubber swords, over-the-top acting, or repetitive scenes. (In fact, at least two sequences are repeated verbatim in the film, a nod to the old serials that used repetition to catch viewers up.) Additionally, kids tend to be more forgiving of Asian characters speaking American English and the casting of non-Asian actors in key roles.

Initially, I planned to rate this movie three stars, but I decided to award extra points to the director, producers, and cast for their dedication in seeing the project through. This film may not qualify as high art, but much like painting a house, it required significant time, effort, and commitment to complete.

Overall, it’s not something I’d readily recommend.

Georgia Rule ranks among the most disappointing films I’ve ever encountered, potentially even the worst. The entire movie exudes an unsettling, dreamlike quality that had me audibly exclaiming "what?" on multiple occasions—easily 7 to 10 times—during its arduous two-hour runtime.

The trailer markets it as a story centered on three generations of women, with Jane Fonda portraying the grandmother, Felicity Huffman as her daughter, and Lindsay Lohan as the defiant, overly sexualized, and underdressed granddaughter. This setup leads one to expect a predictable, breezy chick-flick focused on personal growth and familial bonding.

This couldn’t be further from the truth—a prime example of misleading advertising.

Featuring numerous distracting shots of animals performing "humorous" antics in the background of supposedly crucial scenes, a bizarre five-minute segment dedicated to an elderly woman visiting a doctor’s office for a weekly diaper change, and the shocking revelation that the film actually centers on Lindsay Lohan’s character experiencing sexual abuse by her stepfather, Georgia Rule carves out a unique and troubling niche in cinema. It becomes an unmoored, poorly acted, and inappropriate comedy that tackles deeply serious topics in the most uncomfortable, bizarre, and surreal manner. If Garry Marshall intended for this film to...

I’m always excited to discover films that explore underrepresented themes in global cinema. When I saw the trailer for "Water Lilies," I was eager to watch it, anticipating a fresh perspective: a candid depiction of teenage lesbian romance, akin to a female-led "Beautiful Thing."

The story centers on three 15-year-old French girls. Marie is slim, reserved, and has a tomboyish charm; Floriane is confident, athletic, and strikingly beautiful; and Anne is devoted, a bit overweight, and emotionally immature. The undercurrent of erotic tension between Marie and Floriane permeates the film, always present, whether subtly hidden or bubbling to the surface.

However, "Water Lilies" isn’t a tender exploration of emerging lesbian love between two teenagers. Instead, it delves into themes of sexual frustration, pain, boredom, and teens caught in conflicting desires. It also portrays, in at least two scenes, sex as a mechanical and joyless act. Moreover, the film reveals how screenwriters and directors can undermine their own work through excessive manipulation.

In the bonus features of the "Lord of the Flies" DVD, director Peter Brook remarks, "French cynicism begins with the awakening of sexuality," suggesting that the French view children as innocent angels, while seeing adolescents and beyond with a more jaded lens.

This film narrowly escapes the "video nasty" label, likely due to its release in 1994 when the controversy surrounding such content had waned in Britain. It largely recycles content from *The Boogeyman*, comprising about 75% of its material, and would likely have faced a ban for similar, albeit unclear, reasons as its predecessor.

Initially, I was puzzled, mistaking Annie (played by Kelly Galindo) for another character named Lacey. However, Annie is a distinct character haunted by psychic visions of a boogeyman akin to the one in the original movie. Fans will quickly recognize that they are not the same.

The plot thickens when Annie witnesses a murder in a bathroom through her visions, even discerning the location’s address. Accompanied by her psychiatrist and a parapsychology student—who looks like he stepped out of a cheesy romance novel or a butter ad—they investigate the house. Unsurprisingly, it’s the very same bathroom. Within 24 hours, a murder unfolds exactly as Annie had foreseen. Yet, the identity of the voluptuous victim and the motive behind her murder remain a mystery.

The narrative then pivots to a retelling of *The Boogeyman* storyline, interspersed with additional footage absent from the original. Notably, unlike the first film, the boogeyman is visibly depicted here. Unfortunately,

Regardless of opinions on Andy Milligan, if his real family bore even a slight resemblance to the dysfunctional clan in this movie, it's a wonder he didn't fare worse. Regrettably, the video version of this film includes explicit sex scenes inserted by the distributor to increase ticket sales. At various points, Milligan’s gritty cinematography and silent-era soundtrack are interrupted, replaced by attractive doubles for his less glamorous cast, engaging in intimate acts accompanied by trippy 60s guitar riffs. These additions are easy to skip if you're focused on Milligan’s original vision, though sadly, significant portions of the initial content were removed to accommodate these insertions. What’s left, though, remains captivating. I doubt I’ve encountered a more venomous maternal figure in any other film.

I have a strong dislike for most reality TV shows, and this one is even worse than the one featuring Paris Hilton. Yes, it’s his company, but how many seasons have we endured of “you’re fired” or “you’re hired”? After watching the show, I wouldn’t want to work for someone with such an inflated ego. Frankly, I find more entertainment in watching paint dry.

I’d be thrilled to see someone stand up and say, “Donald, I quit, and I’m taking some of your money to buy you a decent haircut.” Now, he’s even attempting to purchase fame through WWE wrestling. I hope he gets injured so I no longer have to see his pitiful face. It’s truly sad to crave fame so desperately, yet lack any real talent, and make a fool of yourself trying to buy it. If I could, I’d give this show a negative rating, but since I can’t, it gets a 1, which it doesn’t even deserve.

I believe this is a wonderful film, deeply rooted in Romanian culture through its scenery and atmosphere. It doesn't seem to aim for sensuality, though it emerges as a natural byproduct rather than a deliberate goal. The movie feels authentic and profoundly human, capturing my interest throughout. The actors, though not on the level of iconic stars like Sean Connery, deliver performances that never feel forced or subpar. They embody the essence of the film—ordinary people who can act convincingly. I feel the movie successfully achieves its purpose and evokes emotions, or perhaps rekindles them. I must admit, I might not be entirely objective. Above all, I truly enjoyed it, and that’s something I’m certain of.

Despite its English title, this film has scant connection to devils and focuses instead on a power-obsessed ruler in pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone and the ability to transform lead into gold, using virgin blood in the process. Jacinto Molina portrays Gilles de Lancre, a character who shows no remorse in ordering executions whenever he feels his authority is challenged or when he requires virgins for his sinister rituals. Driven by his lover and a hired alchemist, his actions stem more from greed and madness than any demonic influence, which is a bit disappointing. The movie does offer some engaging moments, such as jousting scenes and grown men clashing with large sticks, and it boasts a visually appealing style. However, beyond these elements, there’s little to praise. It lacks significant gore, offers no real frights, and, most surprisingly for a Molina/Naschy production, misses the mark on unintentional humor. As a result, it earns a rating of 4 out of 10.

I wasn't particularly eager to watch *The Flock*. Although Andrew Lau, co-director of the brilliant *Infernal Affairs* trilogy, was initially involved, he was removed from the project and replaced by Niels Mueller as an emergency director. I suspected that Lau had created a decent film, but it didn’t meet the studio’s expectations, leading to his dismissal and the hiring of a new director. Such changes often spell trouble (as seen with *The Invasion*), yet *The Flock* exceeded my modest expectations. While it’s not a remarkable film, it stands as an engaging and entertaining thriller. The character development is impressive, allowing me to connect deeply with the protagonists. Additionally, the dynamic between the two main characters feels authentic and believable, supported by solid performances from Richard Gere and Claire Danes. 

On the downside, one aspect that frustrated me—particularly at certain moments—was the overuse of editing gimmicks intended to inject the film with more "attitude" and style. These effects felt misplaced and arbitrary, detracting from the overall experience. Furthermore, I believe the film could have aimed higher in its ambitions. Despite these flaws, I would still recommend *The Flock* as a decent thriller. It’s far from unforgettable, but it offers a satisfying dose of entertainment.

While I wouldn't label Wargames: The Dead Code as the absolute worst film I've encountered—given it had a couple of passable moments—I can confidently state it's the most predictable movie I've ever watched. Every plot twist was telegraphed so far in advance that I anticipated each one at least ten minutes before it unfolded. The film lacked any trace of subtlety or cleverness, with no sign of intelligent craftsmanship behind the scenes. The purpose of every line, whether spoken or typed, was so blatantly obvious that immersing myself in the story became impossible.

I ended up laughing at the poorly conceived storyline and the clumsy efforts to win back the audience far more frequently than I found myself enjoying the film.

Unlike what some summaries suggest, the women in the film are not geisha but oiran, prostitutes residing beyond the renowned pleasure districts. Their lives and stories mirror those of many women from the Tokugawa era. While the narratives may not be profoundly revealing, their appeal stems from their ordinariness. The themes explored—love, friendship, and sacrifice—are relatable and timeless.

I was particularly impressed by the film's art direction and the performances. It felt as though I was peering into a distant time and place otherwise inaccessible to me. The actors, especially the four women portraying the central oiran characters, delivered captivating performances. I would recommend this movie to those curious about Japanese culture or to viewers who appreciate subtle, emotional storytelling. It excels in both aspects.

When it comes to horror films, I’m usually happy to overlook shaky production quality, disregard plot inconsistencies, and suspend disbelief for the sake of a thrilling scare. Unfortunately, this movie offers no such thrills. It doesn’t even have the charm of unintentional camp. The dialogue is dreadful, the acting is abysmal, and the direction is utterly incompetent. The kills are both predictable and clumsily executed, the soundtrack is grating, the cinematography is atrocious, and even the costumes are laughably bad. I genuinely pitied the actors, who clearly made an effort despite being burdened with awkward, forced dialogue and a glaring absence of guidance. It seems unlikely they had any rehearsal time either. Watching this film is an embarrassing and tedious ordeal, and enduring until the predictable “twist” ending demands extraordinary patience. Without a doubt, this is among the worst movies I’ve ever endured.

I rarely feel motivated to write reviews, but this film was so dreadful that I felt obligated to caution others. It’s an absolute waste of time. If you somehow decide to watch it, at least check out the “Making of” featurette. The writer/director appears to believe that casting the killer as a woman was a groundbreaking and audacious choice—an idea that’s far from novel. He and the cast spend their time...

Could anyone tell me the filming location of this movie? The aviation scene on the cliff is stunning and seems to be set in England. Yet, Ivy's apartment building resembles the Brill Building, complete with its intriguing elevators.

In the credits, Charles Mendl is noted as portraying "Sir Charles Gage." I might have missed him, but I don’t recall seeing him in the film. Could he have been the husband’s lawyer? I only remember that character being referenced in a phone call. Might he have appeared in the aviation or ballroom scene? Did anyone notice him?

Additionally, Herbert Marshall was 57 years old during the filming of this movie.

The highlight of An American in Paris is undoubtedly the extended ballet sequence at the film's conclusion, where Gene Kelly and Leslie Caron embody the essence of renowned painters. Having been introduced earlier as a street artist in Paris, Kelly's character finds a fitting culmination in this vibrant musical, brimming with energy, Gershwin melodies, and performances by talents like Georges Guetary and Oscar Levant. Kelly shines at his peak in this film, offering something distinct from Singin’ in the Rain. The combination of the entire movie with this stunning ballet sequence creates a remarkable impact, leaving audiences in awe. It’s no surprise that this scene capped off 'That’s Entertainment,' following a showcase of other iconic MGM musical moments.

"A Thief in the Night" is a film that largely went unnoticed by mainstream moviegoers, primarily due to its evident low budget and its focus on the Rapture of the true Christian church and the destiny of those left behind. Despite this, the story was compelling, captivating audiences and prompting them to reflect deeply on their personal relationship with Jesus Christ. It resonated with a wide audience, even depicting a pastor who preached the gospel yet lacked true belief, fully aware of the reasons for his exclusion from the Rapture. Both this film and its sequel, "Distant Thunder," are essential viewing. Even with the emergence of the newer, higher-budget "Left Behind" series, which explores the same narrative, the profound impact of "A Thief in the Night" remains undiminished. As a pioneer in this genre, it will forever hold a significant place in cinematic history.

In essence, this film is utterly without merit.

The concept of portraying the future through the lens of someone from the early 1900s is intriguing, but the absence of a gripping plot or engaging characters makes it impossible to immerse oneself in the narrative, rendering the concept ineffective.

It seems the entire movie was filmed using green screens, and we're expected to be dazzled by this. However, as someone familiar with graphics, the excessive softening used to mask the challenging issue of sharp edges in green screening is glaringly obvious. The colors are excessively muted, serving no purpose other than to diminish the visual appeal. Moreover, I fail to see why anything in this film would be considered innovative. On the contrary, the absurdly outdated graphics set a new low for poor quality—they don't even come close to the standards set by the decades-old Jurassic Park. The robot models are overly simplistic, dull, and completely uninspiring. Additionally, the strange, prehistoric-like creatures on the island remain entirely unexplained, adding to the confusion.

The storyline is atrociously bad, to the point of being almost unbelievable.

A 1957 J. Arthur Rank production featuring James Robertson Justice, Margaret Rutherford, and Wilfred Hyde White—surely, this promises to be a riotous comedy? Unfortunately, it falls flat. The entire film hinges on a single, repetitive joke: people's exaggerated reactions to a small alligator. The music, tossed in haphazardly, is both ill-fitting and utterly forgettable. Jeannie Carson brings energy to her dancing and handles the singing competently, but one can’t help wondering why she signed on for this project. Diana Dors also appears, her presence largely reduced to provocative shots meant to lure audiences through previews. Her acting isn’t terrible, but her role seems designed merely to draw leering gazes. Frankly, finding something to focus on besides groaning through this film is a challenge. Now available on VHS through eBay sellers, do yourself a favor and skip the purchase—it’s neither worth the cost nor the time. A comedy devoid of laughter, a musical lacking a single memorable song or dance.

I've always been captivated by Cream's music, despite their limited yet treasured collection of work. Even when their songs stretch to twenty minutes, as seen in tracks like "Spoonful" and "Toad" from *Wheels of Fire*, they still outshine more than half of today's rock bands. Their ability to connect on stage was showcased in one of the most eagerly awaited rock band reunions at the Royal Albert Hall last year. Though both the band and their fans have aged, the energy remains palpable, with superb arrangements of classic blues tunes alongside their original compositions. Performances of "White Room," "Badge," "Politician," "Spoonful," and "Sunshine of Your Love" are flawless, not missing a single beat. Clapton's solos exhibit a structure that sometimes eludes him when performing with his solo band. Ginger Baker's brilliance needs no elaboration. Jack Bruce's vocals remain robust, carrying a power that Clapton could never achieve alone. In short, if you missed last year’s shows, you missed some of the greatest performances you’ll wish you had witnessed.

"The Barbarians" might not be the greatest film any of us have ever watched, but honestly, it's hilarious! I can't even begin to explain how much I laughed the first time I saw it. The director clearly aimed to create a serious adventure movie, but it’s so terribly done that it becomes unintentionally comedic—one of the funniest movies I've ever seen. My advice? Watch it. And if you’ve already seen it, watch it again!

Before watching this miniseries, I was unfamiliar with *Jane Eyre*. Having explored numerous classics through books and adaptations, I often found them tedious, overly verbose, and overhyped, with plots that were only mildly engaging at best. However, this *Jane Eyre* miniseries shattered my preconceived notions.

Zelah Clarke delivers an exceptional performance as Jane Eyre. Her charming accent and the subtle yet resolute demeanor she brings to the role perfectly embody the young governess. Timothy Dalton is equally remarkable as Rochester, exuding a passion and intensity that convinces me he was destined to portray the enigmatic master of Thornfield Hall. After finishing the miniseries, I was so captivated that I couldn’t sleep that night. The storyline is both haunting and uplifting, the characters are portrayed with brilliance, and the narrative is extraordinary. Without a doubt, this is the finest adaptation of *Jane Eyre* ever filmed.

Later, when I read the novel, I was struck by how faithfully the miniseries adhered to Charlotte Brontë’s original work. *Jane Eyre* has since become my favorite book and film. If you’re seeking a transformative masterpiece, I highly recommend the 1983 BBC version of *Jane Eyre*.

This review focuses on the two-disc set accompanying the "Wonderland" DVD rental.

Included in the rental are "Wonderland" and a documentary about Johnny Wadd, both of which shatter the illusion propagated by "Boogie Nights." That film suggested that individuals in the adult film industry were more than just sleazy opportunists desperate for cash, portraying them as something other than contemptible, self-absorbed individuals. This revisionist take mirrors the way "Wiseguy" and its film adaptation "Goodfellas" dismantled the romanticized gangster mythos of "The Godfather" and similar narratives.

What struck me as particularly frustrating while watching these films—and likely will annoy others who enjoyed "Boogie Nights"—is the naivety of supposedly knowledgeable and worldly individuals. The character "Dirk Diggler" from "Boogie Nights" is clearly based on John Holmes, who, unlike his fictional counterpart, possessed no redeeming traits. Holmes was a criminal sociopath who exploited those around him, driven solely by self-indulgence, and was undeniably involved in the horrific Wonderland Avenue murders in Los Angeles in 1981. The film starkly reveals this harsh reality.

If this movie were produced in modern times, it’s easy to imagine Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant in the leading roles; in fact, it feels like a prime candidate for a future remake. While the film is enjoyable, it lacks any real substance. The casting of James Stewart is a near-fatal flaw, as he appears two decades too old for his character, resulting in a complete lack of chemistry with the stunning Kim Novak. The only standout performance comes from Ernie Kovacs, who brings a rare touch of wit to his minor role as an aspiring writer. (**1/2)

The documentary offers a fresh perspective on the theory of "Guns, Germs, and Steel." Through vivid depictions of various episodes, the series compellingly supports the theory while addressing and countering typical criticisms.

I was surprised to read user feedback claiming the series lacked novel insights, with some stating that the content mirrors what is taught in middle school. While this may be true, I found the innovative approach to familiar material and the surprising depth of analysis to be highly engaging, despite having learned these concepts years ago in middle school.

If you're curious about the reasons behind how things function, if you've ever disassembled a telephone to understand its mechanics, or visited a farm to observe its operations and see cows being milked, this series will captivate you. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Incredible! Stacy Peralta has delivered another masterpiece with a documentary on the evolution of big-wave surfing in America, rivaling the brilliance of Dogtown and Z-Boys. By weaving together exclusive archival footage and insightful interviews with surfing legends, the film immerses viewers in the bold, carefree world of the sport’s early trailblazers, whose unwavering passion laid the foundation for an industry that now impacts millions.

The heart of the film lies in getting acquainted with these iconic figures and their personal journeys, which infuse the documentary with a genuine warmth. Peralta’s admiration for these pioneers shines through as we listen to gripping tales, like Greg Noll stepping out from a crowd of mesmerized peers on the beach to tackle monstrous 50-foot waves off Hawaii’s North Shore single-handedly. Or Jeff Clark, who braved the treacherous Maverick break off northern California solo for 15 years before it was recognized as a premier surfing spot. Then there’s the almost mythical saga of Laird Hamilton, a modern-day surfing titan. Hearing Greg Noll speak of Hamilton with awe, calling him the greatest surfer of all time, sent shivers down my spine.

(On a side note, Noll, Clark, and others attended the Sundance screenings. Noll, with touching humility, called himself an old, past-his-prime surfer, visibly emotional during the event.)

The sole redeeming quality of "People I Know" is that it starkly highlights the kind of films Al Pacino should steer clear of. My initial disappointment stemmed from Pacino's attempt at a Georgia accent, which fluctuated between unconvincing and overly exaggerated. The dialogue and character interactions were abysmal, compounded by a flimsy plot. The supporting cast failed miserably to inject any intrigue into the film, and even an hour in, there was no hint of a coherent storyline. The narrative is dreadfully dull, and I found myself struggling to stay awake, resorting to physically jolting myself to maintain consciousness.

This film is almost guaranteed to leave you uninterested... steer clear at all costs.

This film is best avoided, as it seems destined for failure from the start. Ram Gopal Verma initially intended to remake the iconic Bollywood classic "Sholay," but after encountering issues with the original creators, he pushed forward with the project anyway. Unfortunately, it feels as though he stripped away all the essential elements that make a movie great—acting, script, songs, music, comedy, and action—and proceeded to shoot simply because the crew was already hired. What a waste of time and money. After delivering masterpieces like *Rangeela*, *Satya*, and *Company*, RGV pulls a disappointing move akin to Coppola’s missteps after *The Godfather*. What were you thinking, RGV?

As for the plot, though convoluted and difficult to follow, it mirrors the basic framework of *Sholay*. Ajay Devgn takes on the role of Heero (akin to Veeru from *Sholay*), while a newcomer, also named Ajay, plays a character reminiscent of Jai. The duo, portrayed as "bad yet amusing" friends, first assist a cop in apprehending a criminal. Later, a retired cop hires them as personal security to protect against a notorious villain, Bubban, played by Amitabh Bachchan. If you're unfamiliar with Bollywood tropes, rest assured—the good guys triumph in the end. There, I’ve just spared you three hours of your life!

Before World War II, American playwright Howard W. Campbell, Jr., portrayed with a weary staleness by Nick Nolte, enjoys a contented life in Germany alongside his actress wife, Helga Noth (Sheryl Lee). At the height of his personal fulfillment, Howard is recruited by an American agent (John Goodman) to serve as a spy for the Allies. Despite being fully aware of the perilous nature of the mission, he finds himself unable to resist the proposition. After the war ends and following the tragic loss of his wife, Campbell seeks refuge in the anonymity of a secluded existence in New York City, a choice that only deepens his psychological turmoil. The pivotal dilemma of both the film and Kurt Vonnegut's original novel remains: is Campbell a hero or a traitor? Director Keith Gordon and screenwriter Robert B. Weide provide hints but no definitive resolution, and it is this very uncertainty—this lack of closure—that sustains the captivating allure of "Mother Night." Initially, Nolte depicts Campbell as sharp and self-assured; by the film's conclusion, he appears either gripped by fear and doubt, or overwhelmed by fear yet utterly convinced of his impact—or debt—to humanity for his wartime actions.

In the 1970s, WPIX aired "The Adventures of Superman" on weekday afternoons for many years. Occasionally, they would interrupt the regular schedule of surrounding programs to broadcast "Superman and the Mole Men," a rare delight I eagerly anticipated. However, upon revisiting it recently, I was struck by its poor quality.

The film's flaws weren't rooted in the special effects, or the absence of them. Admittedly, George Reeves’ Superman outfit was far from impressive, with the foam padding meant to enhance his physique visibly protruding at the edges. The Mole Men’s costumes were even less convincing; the supposed furry texture was clearly substandard, with visible zippers, uneven sleeve hems, and poorly crafted, sagging fabric that wouldn’t deceive even a child. Yet, these were minor issues I could overlook.

The real problem lay in the forced plot contrivances. Repeatedly, Superman failed to take action to prevent the situation from worsening. When a lynch mob hunted for the creatures, instead of intervening to calm the frenzied group or searching for the beings himself, he idled, merely explaining the risks of the unfolding chaos to Lois.

A toxic chemical spill transforms ordinary people into flesh-craving zombies in this Andreas Schnaas film. The plot centers on two doctors struggling to endure the horrifying outbreak. As expected from a Schnaas production, the movie is riddled with subpar acting, laughably poor special effects, and an evidently nonexistent budget. The dubbing is absurdly bad, deserving of every bit of criticism it gets. Frankly, it's disheartening to even dedicate a single word to this disaster, let alone the required ten lines imposed by IMDb guidelines. My initial one-word review, "Crap," was deemed insufficient, forcing me to elaborate on the film's sheer awfulness. Honestly, it's a challenge to say more, but I believe I've met the line requirement now. In conclusion, this film is utterly terrible, and I strongly advise against wasting your time on it.

My Grade: F

This film is a reimagining of the 1978 Warren Beatty classic, "Heaven Can Wait," tailored to the sharp, stand-up comedy style of Chris Rock. The core story remains unchanged: Lance Barton (played by Rock) is prematurely pulled from life and strikes a bargain with Mr. King, God’s emissary, to return to Earth in a new body. Echoing Beatty’s plot, Barton selects the recently murdered Charles Wellington, a wealthy white man, driven by his attraction to Sontee Jenkins (Regina King), who coincidentally appears at Wellington’s home during the crime. However, this remake falters in its portrayal of Mrs. Wellington and her lover, whose roles are underwritten. The concept of transforming an elderly white millionaire into a Black stand-up comedian desperate to win Sontee’s heart feels forced and ineffective. Additionally, the visual gimmick of switching between Rock as Wellington and the ‘real’ white Wellington falls flat. While the original Beatty film wasn’t a flawless take on the afterlife concept, there was room for enhancement—sadly, "Down To Earth" misses the mark entirely.

I’m a huge fan of *Jane Eyre* and have watched numerous adaptations, each with its own merits and flaws. Unfortunately, this version ranks among the worst I’ve encountered. I felt no connection to Jane or Mr. Rochester. Charlotte Gainsbourg, portraying Jane, was somewhat bearable and certainly fit the plain appearance of the character, but her delivery lacked any trace of emotion. It was impossible to understand what Mr. Rochester could have seen in her.

Speaking of Mr. Rochester, William Hurt’s performance was even more devoid of feeling than Gainsbourg’s, if that’s even possible. How two such lifeless characters could fall in love remains a complete enigma, and it utterly failed to capture my interest. One can only wonder if the director, Zeffirelli, was disengaged during the making of this film.

In contrast, the Timothy Dalton version, though featuring an overly handsome Mr. Rochester, adheres much more closely to the novel. However, it’s Ciaran Hinds in the 1997 A&E adaptation who truly embodies the ideal Mr. Rochester, even if that version strays from the book in parts.

On a positive note, Geraldine Chaplin was impeccable in her role, a rare highlight in an otherwise disappointing adaptation.

This movie was a complete disaster. Despite the favorable rating on Rotten Tomatoes, don't let the positive reviews deceive you. It failed to be frightening, humorous, or even remotely clever. It couldn't even keep me engaged. I feel like I squandered two hours of my life on this utter debacle. The computer-generated monster was mildly intriguing at first, but after about 15 minutes, it lost all appeal. The dialogue was dreadful, possibly due to a poor translation. Another glaring flaw was the portrayal of the American characters—three of them were depicted as utterly devoid of depth, intelligence, or sound judgment. To meet the minimum line requirement, I'll add that the staff at the video store should have intervened when I picked up this title at the checkout counter.

After being impressed by Sandra Bullock's role in Miss Congeniality, I decided to watch Murder By Numbers. While Bullock excels in lighthearted, self-deprecating characters, her attempts at more dramatic roles (as seen in Hope Floats, Speed 2, and 28 Days) often fall short. In this film, her character is a confusing mix of all-knowing, bewildered, and sexually troubled, with a backstory that feels like unnecessary padding and fails to add depth to an already superficial role. The two teenage boys deliver passable performances, but their supposed forensic brilliance and taunting demeanor are undermined by glaring mistakes that practically shout their guilt. Chris Penn is underutilized as the painfully obvious suspect, and Ben Chaplin’s role as the obligatory partner and love interest feels equally wasted.

***Spoilers Ahead*** Beyond the lackluster acting, the film’s major shortcomings lie in a predictable, made-for-TV plot that never fully convinces you of the murder motives. As previously noted, the absurd errors—such as vomiting a rare food at the crime scene, an overly convenient framing of the school janitor, the boys openly associating in public, and a contrived love interest to stir conflict—shift the viewer’s experience from curiosity to disinterest and boredom.

The dreadful rendition of Jules Verne's timeless "Journey to the Center of the Earth" might elicit a comical noise—Verne himself turning over in his grave. This 80-minute travesty shares nothing with the original story beyond its title. The rest of this uninspired film is entirely new content, and frankly, not worth your time. The director has even admitted on IMDb.com that he only helmed eight minutes of the movie, with the studio clumsily attaching footage from Albert Pyun’s sequel to "Alien from L.A.," featuring Kathy Ireland. Apparently, due to budget constraints and international contract demands, the producers stitched Pyun’s work onto director Rusty Lemorande’s incomplete project. Do yourself a favor and steer clear of renting or purchasing this abysmal mess.

In stark contrast to Henry Levin’s 1959 period adaptation starring James Mason and Pat Boone, Lemorande’s version of "Journey to the Center of the Earth" is set in modern-day Hawaii. The story randomly unites two men, a British nanny, and a dog for what’s supposed to be the adventure of a lifetime.

I'm genuinely enjoying what I've watched of this cartoon so far. While the animation may not be top-notch, I honestly prefer this quicker, less expensive, cartoony style over the older style done in a similarly rushed and cheap manner. The older style only looked impressive with significant time and care invested in it, which was becoming increasingly rare. I find nothing wrong with the sharp, angular lines and simple black-dot eyes—in fact, I think they're quite charming. As a child, I never found Scooby-Doo's design especially cute, but my opinion might be changing now.

On another note, Shaggy has always been my favorite character, and surprisingly, I believe he holds the most potential for deeper development. Yes, the show strays from the classic "mystery-solving" theme, but that formula had grown stale anyway. Don't misunderstand me—I'm confident there are writers who could reinvigorate Mystery Inc.'s traditional adventures, which have felt lackluster recently. For now, though, this show offers a refreshing departure from the norm. Shaggy and Scooby are

I rarely feel compelled to write reviews, but this film was so unbearably awful that I can’t stay silent. The plot was painfully predictable, the acting was dreadful, and I found myself laughing during scenes meant to be suspenseful. It seemed the majority of the audience was equally unimpressed, chatting idly even during the film’s supposedly gripping climax. Molly Ringwald was the sole redeeming element in an otherwise agonizing production. As for the so-called “twist” at the end, it was anything but surprising. Some claim the movie wasn’t meant to be taken seriously, but I saw no sign of intentional irony or humor.

In short, *Cut* deserved to be left on the editing room floor. Save your time and money for something worthwhile.

I've been a longtime fan of the wonderful book 'Goodnight Mister Tom,' and it was only recently that I had the opportunity to watch its film adaptation. With numerous positive reviews circulating, my expectations were quite high. However, by the time the credits rolled, I was utterly disappointed.

This film falls far short of being a quality adaptation. 'Goodnight Mister Tom' misses the mark terribly, omitting nearly half of the book's content. Key characters and memorable scenes from the novel were conspicuously absent. The dialogue was sparse, the pacing felt hurried and overly rapid, but what disappointed me most was the lack of emotional connection and love depicted between William Beech and Tom—a central theme of the story. The casting choices were also underwhelming. I had hoped for a faithful and touching rendition, but the film strayed significantly from the source material. This adaptation is among the poorest I've encountered. It desperately needs a remake that is infinitely superior to this disappointing effort.

In recent years, chess-themed movies have been scarce, but this film transcends the genre. It’s not just about chess; it’s a profound narrative exploring the human desire for love and victory. John Turturro delivers a compelling performance as a man with psychological struggles, whose world revolves solely around the 64 squares and 32 pieces of a chessboard. For him, the game is his identity, his validation. Losing a match means losing the only thing that gives his life meaning, a sentiment Turturro portrays with heartbreaking beauty. Even the love of a woman cannot pull him from the depths of his tragic existence. This film prompts reflection on whether there are others like Luzon, consumed by an obsession with chess. Undoubtedly, such individuals exist. For chess enthusiasts, this movie is a must-see. It’s a thoughtfully crafted and skillfully executed piece of cinema that successfully fulfills its purpose. Regrettably, a sequel seems unlikely.

Like many other reviewers, this film has lingered in my thoughts for over three decades. I remember spending hours at the library, delving into every resource I could find about this story, and even reaching out to the PBS station for additional details. Despite my efforts, the only information I uncovered was that it originated from a newspaper article in the early 1900s.

Jumping ahead to 2002, after years of scouring eBay on a weekly basis, I finally stumbled upon a VHS copy of the movie. There was one other bidder, but I was resolute in securing it for myself. After winning, the other bidder contacted me, requesting a copy, which I gladly provided. Even with the VHS in my possession, my search continued until I discovered a website offering a DVD version of the film. You can find it here: http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html

Each person we encounter shapes our thoughts and subtly alters our behavior, leaving a lasting impression on us. "The Eighth Day" explores this concept (similar to "Rainmaker"). In the movie, Harry (Daniel Auteuil), a seasoned businessman skilled in sales psychology, crosses paths with Georges (Pascal Duquenne), a young man with Down's Syndrome who has run away. The compelling performances by both actors are the film's strongest asset. The opening sequence stands out, as Georges shares his unique perspective on the world's creation, while the final scene reveals what God crafted on the eighth day. Certain moments in the narrative are deeply frustrating for Harry, such as when the uninhibited Georges insists on buying expensive shoes despite lacking the funds—a scene that evokes both laughter and tears. A favorite moment is when a group of individuals with Down's Syndrome, on a trip to an art gallery, hijack a bus and invade the Paradis fun park. Among the many humorous mishaps, the standout is when Harry and Georges overtake a horse trailer on the highway, and Georges cheekily salutes the driver as they pass. Yet, the film also balances these lighthearted incidents with tender, heartfelt scenes.

I believe this production merits around 5 stars for its acting, though I recognize that my personal biases might influence this rating, making it more subjective than the objective assessment it deserves. However, I’m aware that such high ratings are often boosted by the fame of the actors involved, artificially inflating the perceived quality of the work.

That said, I take issue with productions like this. It feels like yet another attempt, similar to "Untraceable," to push a propagandistic narrative that justifies government overreach into personal rights. This is particularly striking given the current context, where ISP providers are attempting to "prioritize" or effectively censor information, while Americans and Canadians are actively resisting these measures. Unlike past efforts that vilified torrent file sharing to instill guilt about data transfers online, this production seems to aim at creating a sexually frustrated society. It appears that fear-mongering has become Hollywood’s standard, especially in thrillers—the most popular and influential genre of the past two decades. With such widespread viewership, these films are a powerful tool for shaping societal attitudes, often depicting extreme levels of violence to drive their message.

Clearly, those who rated this movie below a 5 aren't appreciative of sharp, playful humor. Keaton delivers a stellar performance here, as he does in much of his work. This isn’t an over-the-top, larger-than-life production; it’s pure camp and slapstick, brought to life by some of Hollywood’s finest and most adaptable talents. Piscopo also shines as the eager underdog with big ambitions.

If you’re looking for the most hilarious take on barely censored swearing ever captured on film, you can’t miss Dimitri’s unforgettable scene as Morone.

I rated it a 7.

I attended the Toronto Film Festival with high hopes for this movie, bolstered by its impressive cast and status as the festival's closing film. Surely, it had to be exceptional, I thought. Unfortunately, I was gravely mistaken.

Trouble loomed even before the screening began, as the director took the stage to reminisce about meeting a then-unknown Kevin Spacey while directing an episode of *Wiseguy*. Hearing that a *Wiseguy* director/writer was making his feature film debut didn’t inspire confidence. It seemed the only plausible explanation for Spacey—and the rest of the talented cast—agreeing to participate in this fiasco was that the director must possess some damning evidence, like photos of Spacey committing a heinous act.

This film is utterly dreadful! It’s a tired rehash of every hard-boiled cop cliché imaginable, offering nothing original. The acting is subpar, and the direction is even worse, reminiscent of a dated *Wiseguy* episode. It felt like the best-cast straight-to-video movie I’ve ever encountered.

A few particularly absurd moments in *Edison* stand out: Morgan Freeman inexplicably dancing around his apartment to rock and roll music for no apparent reason, and Justin Timberlake attempting to get “creative” in a scene that falls embarrassingly flat.

Apart from roughly 10 remarkable minutes featuring HB Warner on the heavenly train, the remaining 94 minutes of this film were utterly dreadful! The performances were abysmal, but the storyline was what truly horrified me. The acting was stiff and unnatural, even for the standards of early talkies, with the notable exceptions of Lee Tracy and HB Warner, both of whom are consistently impeccable. Rose Hobart delivered a completely lifeless and terrible performance as Julie, mirroring her equally dull portrayal in the otherwise commendable 1932 film *Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*.
