The rest of the cast was even more disastrous, their performances so poor that words fail to capture their ineptitude.

However, the story was an even greater offense than the acting. For reasons beyond comprehension, Julie is inexplicably devoted to Liliom, a despicable womanizer devoid of any redeeming traits. Despite marrying her, he refuses to provide for her, spending his days lounging in bed or associating with his shady, criminal friend (played by Lee Tracy). To make matters worse, he never utters a kind word to Julie and habitually subjects her to physical abuse. Astonishingly, Julie remains devoted to him, constantly rationalizing his behavior, which only seems to fuel his cruelty. Most disturbing of all is that the film presents this toxic narrative as...

To me, *A Matter of Life and Death* is nothing less than the greatest film ever created.

From start to finish, it radiates sophistication. It is intellectually engaging, deeply reflective, and serves as a poignant reflection of the post-war era and the dynamics between nations.

The cinematography is breathtaking, with the seamless blend of monochrome and Technicolor brilliantly highlighting the contrast between different realms. The characters and storyline are crafted with near perfection, and the meticulous attention to detail creates a wholly convincing fantasy.

No matter how often I revisit this film—and I have done so countless times—it never loses its emotional impact. It brings a smile to my face, draws laughter, provokes thought, and moves me to tears. Its relevance and allure remain as powerful today as they were in 1946.

If I could choose only one film to keep and rewatch, *A Matter of Life and Death* would undoubtedly be my pick.

This movie is visually stunning, crafted with a palette limited to just six or seven colors. When it debuted over 15 years ago, its unique color scheme left audiences in awe, setting it apart from anything previously captured on film. For me, these colors transform the film into a captivating spectacle. There are countless scenes so striking that I wish I could pause them, turn them into paintings, and study their artistic brilliance.

While the characters and storyline may not reach the same heights as the cinematography, they are delightfully exaggerated, particularly the villains. The renowned actors who portrayed characters like "Flatop," "Pruneface," "Lips," and "Mumbles" must have relished their time on set, embracing the over-the-top nature of their roles.

Warren Beatty and Glenne Headly deliver solid performances as Dick Tracy and his girlfriend Tess Trueheart, with Headly embodying the sweetness and gentleness her character’s name suggests. Charlie Korsmo also shines as the troubled young boy taken in by Dick and Tess. The vibrant ensemble of supporting characters is brought to life by talents like Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman, William Forsythe, Paul Sorvino, Mandy Patinkin, Madonna, and many other familiar names too numerous to mention.

Any potential intrigue in this content is quickly extinguished within the opening moments by a disclaimer stating that the events depicted are unknowable, merely the "whisper [rumor] most often told" about one of Hollywood's most notorious "mysteries."

So, there’s nothing fresh here (and E!'s "Mysteries & Scandals" offers a better grasp on this particular event, which isn’t saying much). What, then, do we receive?

We’re told that Hollywood is a den of vipers and debauchery—hardly a revelation. More compelling is the insight into what a fallen director might stoop to in order to reclaim influence in the entertainment industry or political sphere. It prompts speculation about whether Peter Bogdanovich is drawing from personal experience through these characters. Yet, the narrative is so cynical, distasteful, and convoluted that we’re left feeling complicit in watching nonsense masquerading as history.

The film’s tone carries an odd, frenetic energy that I found more annoying than entertaining. There’s no one to root for or connect with. And the brilliance of *Citizen Kane* overshadows the portrayal of the relationship between Davies and Hearst.

If you possess even a shred of empathy and care for others, this film becomes a challenging watch, particularly in its latter half.

In this portion, the narrative takes a dark turn as we witness a kind-hearted young boy being viciously attacked, followed by a mentally challenged man spiraling into distress after witnessing the cruelty inflicted on the child. The content is far from lighthearted.

Nevertheless, the movie is compelling, with strong performances throughout. Its story lingers long after the credits roll.

The character "Dominick," portrayed by Tom Hulce, is the mentally disabled man at the heart of the story. This role might be Hulce’s finest, showcasing his remarkable talent. He is cared for by a medical student named "Eugene," played by Ray Liotta, who rose to prominence the next year in "Field of Dreams" alongside Kevin Costner.

Dominick is a lovable garbage collector with a passion for "Hulk" comics and wrestling. He’s the kind of gentle, "slow" soul you can’t help but adore and hope will find happiness. When he loses control, it’s for deeply understandable reasons, and... well, I’ll leave the rest for you to discover. The film is worth your time, but brace yourself for an intense emotional journey that may leave you deeply moved.

This film stands apart from others, with the nearest comparison being a Woody Allen movie. However, while Woody Allen often explores the quirks of human nature, Bret Carr seems focused on unraveling the deep-seated insecurity that shapes our identity, for better or worse. In Lou’s story, this insecurity is the source of his stutter, linked to a specific childhood trauma unveiled through poignant flashbacks.

The world is filled with wonderfully neurotic individuals, and I believe each deserves a shot at redemption. Yet, the diversity of human character is what makes life so fascinating—perhaps we shouldn’t “fix” our neuroses any more than we should alter our physical features like noses or breasts.

Despite being an indie project made on a tight budget, this film boasts impressive production values and a remarkable scope. It feels like a unique, quirky treasure for the self-help audience. I’m eager to see what this filmmaker creates next and can envision a career trajectory similar to that of Woody Allen or Albert Brooks.

This film is undeniably among the finest I’ve ever watched. It’s an emotional journey, pulling me through laughter, tears, revulsion, joy, and love—all within just over two hours!

The cast delivers exceptional performances! I must highlight the lead actor, Michael Nyquist, whose work is truly outstanding. I’m also incredibly impressed by the actor portraying Tore, who brings such authenticity to the role of a mentally challenged young man. His performance evoked memories of Leonardo DiCaprio’s role in *What’s Eating Gilbert Grape*. And then there’s the breathtakingly beautiful “Gabriella’s Song,” which might just be the most exquisite piece of music I’ve ever heard.

I wholeheartedly urge everyone to watch and savor this masterpiece!

This specific Joe McDoakes short film clearly draws inspiration from the star-studded Warner Brothers production *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, a wartime morale-boosting extravaganza. In that film, Eddie Cantor portrayed both himself and an aspiring comedian struggling to break into Hollywood due to his striking similarity to Cantor.

In the McDoakes series, George O'Hanlon plays dual roles as himself and McDoakes, a man desperate for a shot at stardom. Similar to *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, several Warner Brothers contract players make brief appearances in this short, dropping by during their spare moments.

O'Hanlon’s character is dispatched by central casting for a minor, single-line part in a World War I movie, but it’s the lookalike McDoakes who receives the call. Overwhelmed by nerves for his big break, McDoakes obsesses over how to deliver his one line, even considering mimicking the style of a famous movie star to stand out.

After 86 frustrating takes, much to the annoyance of director Ralph Sanford and the tolerant Clyde Cook, who plays a British cockney soldier, they finally discover a fitting role for the hapless McDoakes in the film industry. This hilarious short, which earned an Oscar nomination, is well worth a watch.

This was an utterly deplorable waste of my time. The film lacks any semblance of a plot, and the acting is so abysmal that it could serve as a textbook example in acting schools of what to avoid at all costs. It’s nothing more than a shameless commercial knockoff of the earlier *Universal Soldier*, which itself barely rises above dreadful in terms of performance quality. It’s disappointing that VD feels the need to inflate his ego every few years, and even more disheartening that audiences are willing to spend their hard-earned money to endure this drivel. Such garbage tarnishes the reputation of martial arts films. In comparison, it almost makes the work of Segall, Norris, and Arnold seem like masterpieces.

Perhaps VD should follow Leslie Nielsen’s path and pivot to parodying his own genre. At least then, we could laugh alongside him rather than at his expense.

The direction of this comedy film is exceptional, with many scenes reminiscent of a comic book, featuring a darker visual style—though not in terms of story—than one might anticipate. While it may not claim the title of the funniest movie ever, especially for those who prefer crude, sexist humor found in films like Something About Mary or American Pie, it offers a different kind of comedy. The humor grows on you with each viewing, as certain jokes become more amusing over time. Fans of comic books or related movies such as Batman or X-Men are likely to appreciate the subtle, ongoing humor woven throughout. Even if you’re not a fan of the genre, you might enjoy the film’s playful, respectful mockery of it. For those who enjoyed the movie, the DVD includes some noteworthy bonus features. (8/10)

As a child, I found the weapon used by the murderer in the movie intriguing, though I admit my judgment was clouded by youth and naivety. Even back then, however, I could tell the movie’s plot was lackluster and tedious whenever the killer wasn’t wielding his glowing blade. What truly surprises me is the impressive cast involved in this film. I can’t help but wonder what script they read when they signed on, because the final product is undeniably dull and seems little more than a showcase for a lightsaber on a minimal scale. The storyline is often confusing, and the ending descends into complete chaos. The entire film revolves around aliens and that singular weapon. The narrative follows two children and a man who encounter extraterrestrials, then jumps forward in time to what appears to be a reunion of sorts. There are dead animals and other oddities to investigate, and for reasons unclear, the man acquires the alien weapon and embarks on a rather understated killing spree. Honestly, it’s hard not to question why this movie was even made.

Dolph Lundgren delivers a brooding and intense performance in this muddled mystery/thriller, which falls short of the intrigue promised by its cover. While Lundgren shines in his role, the plot is a chaotic jumble of overused B-movie tropes—think detectives, vengeance, moguls, prostitutes, and S&M—seemingly pieced together on the fly. The movie gains some traction in the latter half, but for a more satisfying Lundgren experience, opt for a rental of RED SCORPION instead.

The film was outstanding, though a few scenes with Esposito fell short. I loved how it reunited every detective from the series and tied up lingering plotlines that remained unresolved during the show’s run (thanks to NBC...). It was moving to witness Pembleton and Bayliss at their most vulnerable and authentic selves. Braugher and Secor delivered remarkable performances, though they’ll likely be overlooked as always. It was bittersweet to realize this marked the end of Homicide. Memories, recordings, and CourtTV reruns can’t replicate the thrill of tuning in every Friday. Nevertheless, the movie excelled in its purpose, offering a poignant portrayal of life after Al’s retirement and the deep, familial bond within the unit. I truly enjoyed it.

CREEP is a no-nonsense horror flick that unfolds in real time, focusing solely on the relentless attacks by a mutant in a deserted subway platform over the course of 85 minutes. It sticks to this premise without deviation. Director Christopher Smith stretches the tension as much as possible by crafting a believable cast of characters who have legitimate reasons to be in the locked subway. He also keeps the backstory of the titular Creep shrouded in ambiguity, with only subtle hints of illicit experiments from the 1960s underground, which adds a layer of intrigue that largely succeeds. Unfortunately, Smith pulls back from a potential twist ending involving more genetic monstrosities—despite earlier foreshadowing—missing a chance to embrace a classic horror trope. Yes, I admit, I was rooting for that predictable twist! Franka Potente, known from RUN LOLA RUN, delivers a strong performance as the frightened protagonist, while the supporting cast holds their own.

Unbelievable! Why would anyone bother creating a follow-up to a film that was already dreadful? While *Half Past Dead* was far from good, it at least had a clear sense of direction. *Half Past Dead 2*, on the other hand, seems utterly lost, lacking any purpose or identity. It merely occupies screen space for reasons that defy explanation. Here’s the gist of the plot: Twitch, portrayed by Kurupt of Tha Dogg Pound, is moved to a new prison where rumors circulate about a hidden stash of gold bricks. Chaos erupts when a riot breaks out among rival inmates, and one is shot by a man named Cortez, who then schemes to escape. During a conjugal visit, Twitch’s fiancée and Burke’s daughter, played by Bill Goldberg, are abducted by Cortez and held in an execution chamber. Burke, though hesitant, teams up with Twitch, and together they navigate conflicts with the absurdly foolish inmates while discovering that Cortez holds their loved ones hostage.

Opinion: This sequel is as pointless as *Universal Soldier: The Return*. The script is abysmal, the acting is atrocious, and the dialogue is laughably bad. Every character feels like a cartoonish stereotype. Yes, it’s a low-budget production, but that’s no justification for such a lackluster effort.

This film is incredibly strange, and I couldn’t quite grasp its purpose. It follows a group of North London delinquents who stumble upon a mute child in the woods, whom they believe to be some sort of prophet. This mysterious figure seems to influence each of them to alter their lives, often with catastrophic results. After roughly 90 minutes, the movie concluded, leaving me deeply unsatisfied and frustrated by its apparent lack of meaning. I felt no connection to any of the characters, as they were given no opportunity to become relatable or likable to the audience.

What was the intended message? Am I missing something obvious? The film felt excessively bizarre. What becomes of Runner? Why does Emilio shoot the child? That moment felt utterly illogical and pointless. Can anyone help me make sense of this confusing mess of a movie?

Where are the cannibals? Those drawn in by the title and the promise of encountering 'real cannibals' in this film will feel misled. Rather than delivering on that expectation, the movie introduces us to an eccentric man revisiting a village in Papua New Guinea, where he once had a romantic connection with a local decades ago. This man, Tobias Schneebaum, epitomizes New York Jewish identity, a detail woven into the documentary as he is often seen wearing his yarmulke.

In reality, there are no cannibals featured—just tales recounted by the villagers and Tobias himself. That said, the film isn't entirely disappointing. It captivates with its intriguing narrative and impressive cinematography. Schneebaum proves to be a compelling and likable figure, offering a window into a life starkly different from Western norms.

Unfortunately, it falls short of the expectations set by its cover and plot description.

Rating: 4 out of 10.

I’m generally not a fan of remakes, or as they’re now often called, “retellings,” but this movie genuinely irritated me. The original *Prom Night*, while not a cinematic gem in my opinion, at least understood its genre—horror. There are fundamental principles to crafting a horror film, and suspense is key to keeping viewers engaged. Unfortunately, this film failed spectacularly in that regard; it was anything but a gripping, edge-of-your-seat experience. The scares felt cheap and were painfully predictable. (Take, for instance, the overused trope of a cat leaping out of a closet, only to be followed by the supposedly “unexpected” appearance of the villain—a tired cliché this film couldn’t even execute properly.) If it couldn’t handle a basic scare like that, I had little hope for it to deliver on any other horror conventions.

Another essential element of horror is a relatable hero or heroine, yet this film lacked one entirely. The character I connected with most was the head detective. His composed yet pragmatic response to a killer’s escape was a refreshing touch—something more films of this genre desperately need. A dose of common sense in reacting to the unfolding chaos would go a long way. (If you’re fleeing from an axe-wielding maniac, for instance, you turn and—

Viggo Mortensen takes on the role of a new prisoner in a haunted penitentiary, where the warden, portrayed convincingly by Lane Smith, harbors a dark secret that may explain the brutal killings of guards and inmates by a supernatural force. Lincoln Kilpatrick plays a long-term inmate aware of the secret, living in constant fear for his life. Typically, prison films bring to mind action-packed features with stars like Stallone or Van Damme, or profound dramas like *Shawshank Redemption* or *The Green Mile*. A ghost story reminiscent of *Exorcist III* was unexpected, yet *Prison* delivers a chilling atmosphere and stands as the pinnacle of Renny Harlin’s directorial work. The film maintains a creepy tone and benefits from strong performances by a then-unknown cast. Lane Smith shines, portraying the warden not as the stereotypical embodiment of evil, but as a jittery, anxious figure, lending authenticity to a film that surpasses all expectations.

*** out of 4 - (Good)

What a delightful and unexpected surprise! This film embodies the essence of a true thriller. In a hurry, I dashed into the video store, picked up a movie without fully reading the description on the case, and simply crossed my fingers. To my amazement and joy, it exceeded all expectations. The actors delivered outstanding performances, bringing their characters to life with remarkable authenticity. The storyline was meticulously crafted, expertly written, and skillfully directed, captivating me from beginning to end without a dull moment.

I wholeheartedly recommend this film to thriller enthusiasts, particularly those who appreciate a well-paced narrative that holds your attention throughout. Without a doubt, it’s a perfect 10 out of 10 in my book.

As an avid horror movie enthusiast, I make it a point to catch all noteworthy releases in this genre, particularly those from my home country's cinema. However, I must admit that "Power of Fear" (known as "Vedma" in Russian) ranks among the weakest films I've seen. To begin with, it fails to evoke even a hint of fear, plodding along at a painfully slow and predictable pace that leaves no room for genuine terror. Honestly, it falls short in every aspect: the plot is absurd (I’m puzzled why Russian producers and directors chose to morph a traditional Ukrainian witchcraft tale into a dull, laughable modern American thriller. I completely concur with the previous reviewer—it utterly lacks any thrill), and the acting is dreadful and overdone. All the performers, including well-known Russian actors Valeri Nikolayev and Yevgeniya Kryukova, come across as stiff as wooden puppets. It appears they made no effort to act, merely reciting their English lines with zero emotion. Lastly, I’m baffled by the decision to shoot this movie in English using Russian actors. In my opinion, this was a significant misstep.

Initially, this film showed promise, but it ultimately fell short of expectations. The director, while skilled with impressive camera work and artistic vision— traits often seen in Asian cinema—struggles to craft a compelling narrative. The storyline felt disjointed, veering off in multiple directions without ever settling on a clear, engaging, or coherent path. In essence, the movie failed to match the descriptions provided in the press releases. On a positive note, the acting was commendable. The cast delivered strong performances, with Jude Law shining as he consistently does. It’s unfortunate, however, that he opted for a project with such a feeble script.

What starts as a reasonably smart satire about a dubious security monitoring firm quickly devolves into a dull and utterly absurd murder mystery. Despite the valiant efforts of David Arquette and the exceptional Stanley Tucci to salvage this disaster, some flaws are simply beyond repair.

For example, why does Gale abruptly transform from a loving, maternal figure into a bitter, intoxicated harpy at Tommy's parents' home? Why would Heinrich, despite being a shady character, risk destroying the company he’s dedicated his life to by robbing and potentially killing his clients? How does Tommy, who appears rational, come to suspect Heinrich of murder based almost entirely on a dream, and even if that were plausible, why doesn’t he alert the authorities? And why does Gale fail to set the alarm upon returning home, especially after reprimanding Howie for leaving it off? Naturally, these inconsistencies are essential for the storyline—though calling it a plot feels overly generous—to progress. Such lapses might be overlooked if they contributed to even a hint of humor. Yet, from Howie’s account of a date rape to the coroner’s mistaken identification of Gale to the concluding moments, nothing manages to elicit a laugh.

Let me put it this way: I feel compelled to warn you with a "Spoiler Alert" before disclosing that the F-word is thrown around excessively in this film—practically every other line. I found the movie utterly unappealing, burdened by constant allusions to sexual deviance, infidelity, and deceit. The profanity was simply over the top. I'm rating this film a "3," with two of those points solely attributed to Mira Sorvino's captivating dance moves.

The previous reviewer was quite lenient. While I somewhat enjoyed the first film, I can’t say the same for this one. The opening is tolerable, but the quality declines rapidly. I simply can’t picture Jon Bon Jovi as a convincing “tough vampire hunter,” and the vampire princess lacks both allure and menace. Many scenes are illogical; for instance, any reasonable person, especially a seasoned hunter, would grow suspicious of a mysterious woman appearing out of nowhere to seduce them. Additionally, the unexplained connection between Una and Jovi is baffling. The movie fails to clarify anything, and while you might overlook this in an engaging story, entertainment is sadly lacking here. This is easily one of the worst vampire films I’ve ever watched.

The late Dudley Moore delivered the standout performance of his tragically brief career in the 1981 film ARTHUR, a wildly humorous yet poignant story that evokes warm smiles, hearty laughs, and even a tear or two when you're in the right frame of mind. Moore earned a Best Actor Oscar nomination for his portrayal of Arthur Bach, a boozy playboy who "races cars, plays tennis, fondles women, but takes weekends off and answers to no one but himself." Arthur stands to inherit a staggering 750 million dollars, provided he marries Susan Johnston (Jill Eikenberry), a haughty socialite and the pampered daughter of a covert gangster. Complications arise when Arthur crosses paths with Linda Morolla (Liza Minnelli), a waitress and aspiring actress from Queens who shoplifts neckties as birthday gifts for her father. Moore's electrifying presence makes this one of the most hilarious performances in the past half-century. The late Sir John Gielgud clinched a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his impeccable role as Hobson, Arthur’s sharp-witted butler and closest confidant, whose apparent contempt for Arthur’s antics masks deeper, fatherly affection. Additional comedic flair is provided by Barney Martin as Linda’s father, Stephen Elliott as Susan’s father, and Geraldine Fitzgerald as Arthur’s eccentric grandmother. The film was skillfully directed with

It's no secret that the sex comedy sub-genre is oversaturated. Mere over-the-top raunchiness no longer cuts it. Having been exposed to countless crude jokes and behaviors, I now require a sex comedy to offer additional redeeming qualities to capture my interest.

Approaching *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, I had a fair idea of what was in store, thanks to the trailers I'd seen, complete with lines like, "Is it true that if you don't use it, you lose it?" What caught me by surprise, however, was the film’s genuine heart and sincere efforts at character depth. Sure, it features the eccentric, over-the-top personalities reminiscent of Adam Sandler films, and the profanity is abundant enough to overwhelm even Noah’s Ark, but beneath it all lies a meaningful love story and, surprisingly, a positive message.

The protagonist, Andy, is someone I found myself relating to, perhaps uncomfortably so. From the opening scene, I noticed we share a passion for *Mystery Science Theater 3000*—evident from the poster on his wall. As the film progresses, we’re introduced to his impressive collection of collectibles. Andy’s also into video games and displays a solid grasp of various trivia.

This lamentable waste of film could only be improved by Count Floyd appearing every minute. Astonishingly, they managed to assemble Steve Railsback, Susan Anspach, John Vernon, and Joe Flaherty on set, yet failed to produce anything resembling a real movie by a wide margin—think five miles or about eight kilometers. This film is utterly abysmal. From the mindless start to the equally mindless finish, there isn’t a single original line, idea, scene, or effect. The enchanting Susan Anspach from *Five Easy Pieces*? Dull. Steve Railsback? Dull. John Vernon? Dull. The giant bug? Dull. If this is supposed to be a horror film, then the Buttercream Gang might as well be a hardcore crime doc.

Honestly, every terrible movie reveals the root of its awfulness. Often, it’s right there in the opening credits—“Written, Directed, and Produced by” a single person. Or, at the heart of the story, there’s an utterly talentless actor, making it obvious why this disaster was greenlit. In this case, the revelation comes at the very end of the credits, where the film thanks a dozen obscure branches of the Canadian Government for their support.

At this moment, I’m cleansing my palate by watching MST3K’s riff on *Beast of Yucca Flats*.

This film is a disaster in every aspect—badly thought out, poorly performed, and dreadfully scripted.

Jon Heder is insufferably irritating, trapped in the same tired Napoleon Dynamite shtick, coming across as self-absorbed and clueless.

Diane Keaton, once again, portrays the same overbearing, mannish mother figure, obsessively meddling in her children’s lives while simultaneously showing too little genuine concern (reminiscent of her role in *Because I Said So*).

Anna Faris, despite being generally likable, is reduced to playing a shallow, brainless character in this movie.

Jeff Daniels delivers a mediocre performance, failing to leave any lasting impression.

Do yourself a favor and avoid this film if you value your sanity.

"All the world’s a stage, and all the men and women merely players"—or so the saying goes. But who decided that theatre ends at the edge of the stage or the theatre’s exit? Why shouldn’t the audience be active participants in the theatrical journey, woven into the very fabric of the story?

This film was a bold experiment, declaring, "Hey! You are the story, and it demands more than just your gaze—it craves your engagement." At times, the story comes to you; at others, you must seek it out.

Sadly, few paid heed, but that doesn’t diminish the importance of the message.

I had high hopes for this movie, especially since it was produced by Yashraj Films.

Jimmy runs a call center and is approached one day by Pooja Singh to tutor her boss, Lakhan Singh, in English. As Jimmy and Pooja grow closer, they fall in love and plan to elope. However, Pooja reveals she is indebted to Lakhan Singh, also known as Bhaiyyaji, and cannot leave. Despite this, they decide to steal money from him, only for Jimmy to discover that Bhaiyyaji is a notorious Don. Meanwhile, Bhaiyyaji enlists Bachchan Pandey to hunt down the runaway couple.

Featuring Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor, and Akshaye Kumar, the film is helmed by debut director Viay Krishna Acharya and produced by Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.

"Tashan" ranks among the most disappointing films I’ve ever seen. While the visuals are impressive and Kareena Kapoor shines (especially with her widely discussed transformation), the storyline is incredibly weak and often incoherent, with scenes that fail to connect logically.

(No spoilers, just plot overview) I'm baffled by the intense dislike for this episode. If you're looking for a truly terrible Smallville episode, check out Subterranean—that one’s a complete mess. Tom Welling delivers a solid performance, which isn’t something I often note, and Michael Rosenbaum is, as usual, excellent. The alternate universe storyline feels unsettlingly believable. The Martian Manhunter, last seen in "Static," reappears to warn Clark that the doctor running the asylum where they’re confined is a phantom from the Phantom Zone. To return to his own reality, Clark must eliminate this threat. Overall, this is a strong episode with impressive acting and a well-maintained pace.

This film transcends the simple narrative of a middle-aged man finding joy in ballroom dancing, though it certainly captures that charm. It is a profound story of rediscovering a zest for life, overcoming the burdens of work and financial stress to reconnect with happiness. An added layer of intrigue comes from the film’s exploration of shifting cultural attitudes in modern Japan, touching on topics as diverse as ballroom dancing and physical intimacy. Expect moments that will have you laughing aloud, others that might inspire you to dance, and plenty that will simply warm your heart.

For those who assume Japanese cinema is uniformly dense and difficult to approach, this movie serves as an excellent gateway to the contemporary scene.

Surprisingly, at 12 minutes long, this 1912 film is considered a full-length feature for its time. Very few films exceeded this duration back then, but its length is not what makes this peculiar short stand out. What truly distinguishes it is the cast—almost entirely composed of bugs! This quaint domestic comedy could have easily mirrored the works of stars like Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, or Max Linder, but this Russian production opted for an unusual twist by featuring insects (or possibly detailed models resembling them). With Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy yet to rise to fame, and Linder presumably occupied, the choice of bugs as actors might have been a creative necessity! Through the use of stop-motion, these insect characters move, dance, and fight with astonishing realism—far surpassing the effects seen in King Kong, which came out 21 years later.

The story opens with Mr. Beetle sneaking away for a night of revelry at a risqué club, leaving his wife presumably waiting at home. Unbeknownst to him, a local film enthusiast captures his escapades on camera. Meanwhile, Mr. Beetle remains oblivious to the fact that Mrs. Beetle is also entangled in an affair with a free-spirited grasshopper.

I’m genuinely shocked by what is considered entertainment these days. Themes of death (and mocking it), violence, sexual innuendos, adults menacing children, vulgarity, underage drinking, drug theft, dysfunctional parenting, a nightmarish babysitter, offensive stereotypes targeting African Americans, law enforcement, and overweight individuals, as well as children sneaking out at night—hardly the makings of a children’s film! Add to that the dark, frightening elements like a deceased woman possessing a house, imprisoning her devoted husband for over two decades, and terrorizing an entire neighborhood—how charming for young viewers. PARENTS, is this truly the kind of content you want your children exposed to? Is this the life lesson you wish to impart?

This film is far too unsettling for young children, and I worry that today’s teens might already be grappling with some of these harsh realities—why force it upon them further? As for adults, don’t expect to be frightened or entertained; the movie feels dull, forced, and utterly predictable. The characters are equally disappointing—oblivious parents, incompetent police, irritating and dim-witted friends, and cruel, scheming individuals.

Melissa Joan Hart delivers a stellar performance! This series is absolutely fantastic and unrivaled, with the possible exception of her equally remarkable role in *Clarissa Explains It All*. It far surpasses *Buffy the Vampire Slayer* in every way. This show is truly exceptional!

I first watched this film long after the television series had aired, and at first, I wasn’t impressed. However, as time passed and my memories of the series faded, I gave it another chance and found it utterly hilarious. Adapted from Neil Simon’s stage play, the movie retains much of its theatrical roots without being overly expanded for the cinema, which I consider one of its greatest strengths. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon deliver stellar performances as Oscar and Felix, while the supporting cast shines, especially John Fielder as ‘Vinnie.’ Even now, certain scenes bring me to tears of laughter—like Felix interrupting Oscar during a ball game with a dinner demand, Oscar losing it and chasing Felix around the apartment, the ‘Pigeon Sisters’ crumbling under Felix’s tearful tales, and, of course, the iconic cafeteria scene (which Nora Ephron later echoed in ‘When Harry Met Sally’). The dialogue is razor-sharp, with lines like Oscar’s quip, “They could be vitamins! He could be the healthiest one in the room!” when they fear Felix has overdosed. Simply fantastic!

I’m utterly astonished by how many people are praising this film in comparison to the original. It’s compelled me to share my thoughts! This sequel is clearly a shameless attempt to profit from the first movie’s success. The dialogue is dreadful, lacking the authenticity and depth that made the original so captivating.

The plot is absurd, the depiction of the French police is downright comical, and the characterization of Doyle feels completely detached from how he was portrayed in the first film.

Seriously, how many drug lords personally show up at the docks to oversee a shipment? The way Doyle effortlessly tracks down his target is beyond ridiculous. It’s as if the entire French police force was just sipping coffee until Doyle, the American hero, arrives to show them how real police work is done. What a farce. Imagine trying to uncover the biggest criminals in a foreign city armed with nothing but a tourist map and some brochures. Utterly laughable.

This is a truly terrible sequel, and anyone who disagrees must be out of their mind.

Following World War I, a team from the Allied nations embarks on a mission to Cambodia to thwart Count Mazovia's sinister plan to assemble a zombie-like army of soldiers and workers. With the looming threat of another war spurred by Mazovia's schemes, the expedition braves the treacherous jungle to reach Angkor Wat, undeterred by the dangers ahead. Among them is Armand, whose personal motives clash with the group's objectives, as described on the DVD sleeve.

A heads-up: the zombie makeup team staged a rebellion before filming even began.

Additionally, "Revolt of the Zombies" bears little connection to its alleged predecessor, "White Zombie" (1932), which featured Bela Lugosi. If the zombies in that film failed to captivate you, this movie is unlikely to fare any better. Dean Jagger, appearing younger than usual, plays Armand Louque, a man consumed by an obsession with the blonde Claire Duval, portrayed by Dorothy Stone. While supporting actors Roy D'Arcy as the sinister Mazovia and Teru Shimada as the loyal Buna deliver solid performances, they lack sufficient material to elevate the film from its mediocrity.

** Revolt of the Zombies (1936) Victor Halperin ~ Dean Jagger, Dorothy Stone, Roy D'Arcy

While *The Fluffer* may contain authentic elements of the porn industry, this does not compensate for its evident shortcomings in direction and acting, coupled with a distinctly average script.

It remains a B-grade production from beginning to its overly prolonged end.

It would be disheartening to consider this film as a representative sample of contemporary gay cinema to the wider audience.

One can only hope that its exposure remains confined to the gay film festival circuit, eventually fading into obscurity on video.

*The Fluffer* is set to premiere at the Queer Film Weekend in Brisbane on April 10, 2002. Its reception there might heavily depend on the level of intoxication from the preceding cocktail party—viewers may well need the assistance of alcohol to endure it.

It seems as though Shonda Rhimes' talented team may have delegated the scripting of this show to a less inspired group, perhaps in a place like MediocreLand. "PP" feels reminiscent of the numerous uninspired David Kelly series—initially intriguing but quickly predictable within a single season, much like Picket Fences, Ally McBeal, and more recently, Boston Legal. The cases presented are so bizarre that they fail to elicit any real empathy or sorrow, which is the core of compelling medical dramas: scenarios that resonate with the fear of "This could happen to me." Additionally, they lack humor.

The cast performs admirably, yet the storylines are lifeless and beyond revival. As a therapist myself, I must point out that Amy Brennan portrays an astonishingly inept, unethical, and poorly trained therapist. The writing for her character clearly disregards fundamental ethical principles and the concepts of transference and counter-transference, perhaps missing the mark set by any reputable institution like Stanford. Someone ought to hand the writers a copy of the Code of Ethics, especially considering the episode involving the nose-bleeding wife and the therapist's questionable involvement. No real therapist would act in such a manner.

The trope of women pining for men who have moved on is utterly overdone; we've all moved past the "Sex and the City" era. Addison's youthful, aggressive pursuit of the man she desires feels equally cliché and tired.

Diane and I caught an incredible film today in Fremantle, and we both concluded that among pastiche films, it stood out as exceptional. What captivated us were the short, five to ten-minute segments that made up the movie, each woven around the central theme of love in its myriad expressions.

The film is set across different Parisian arrondissements, lending a unique atmosphere to each segment. Although I’ve visited Paris a few times, I couldn’t easily identify the specific locations. I imagine, however, that Europeans, and especially the French, would recognize these iconic city spots instantly. Regardless, the stellar production quality draws viewers so deeply into each story that the settings become secondary.

The pace of the film is brisk, with each new scene unfolding while you’re still processing the last. Unlike the often sensationalized Hollywood fare, the narratives here are understated, reflective, and tender, mirroring the gentle nuances of real life, unmarred by the overwhelming gloss of mainstream media.

Brian Yuzna is frequently criticized as a director for his over-the-top, gory films, yet the reality is that his work is far from terrible. While the sequels to Re-Animator don’t reach the heights of the original, they still hold their own as respectable entries in the horror sequel genre. Return of the Living Dead 3 stands out as the strongest in its series, and Society comes remarkably close to being a surrealist horror gem. Though this particular thriller falls short of masterpiece status, it effectively showcases Yuzna’s knack for horror, with a plot that remains consistently gripping and captivating. It’s surprising that a horror film centered on dentistry didn’t emerge until 1996, considering a visit to the dentist taps into a near-universal, primal fear—akin to fleeing a predator in today’s world. While dentistry doesn’t personally unnerve me, it seems I’m in the minority. The story revolves around Dr. Feinstone, a perfectionist dentist who seemingly has it all: a lovely home, a thriving career, and a stunning wife. But his idyllic life unravels when he uncovers his wife’s infidelity with the pool cleaner, setting off a chain of events that impacts not just his life, but also those around him.

I picked up this DVD on a whim, completely unaware of what it was about, as part of a winter challenge to watch a movie every night. After enduring a string of disappointing American action-adventure flicks like *Ballistic*, *Daredevil*, and *Cradle of Life*, *Zhu Warriors* felt like a breath of fresh air with its strikingly original approach to filmmaking. While the plot is utterly absurd, I was captivated by the film's genuine sincerity, warm-hearted tone, and complete absence of cynicism. Visually, it’s a feast for the eyes. Though the special effects may not match Hollywood’s technical precision, the creators prioritize color, composition, and movement over realism, resulting in countless breathtaking scenes. One unforgettable shot features two superhuman characters perched on jagged rock spires, framed against an enormous rising moon, with the three elements in perfect harmony. In another, a princess-warrior soars through the sky, trailing her glowing sword like a homing missile. The vibrant colors burst from frame to frame, used not to mimic reality but to convey raw emotion.

The characters, much like those in comic books, are straightforward and uncomplicated, lacking deep complexity on their own but tapping into archetypes that strike a profound chord. Physically, several of the actors are absolutely mesmerizing.

As I’ve worked my way through the AFI’s list of the top 100 comedies, I can confidently say that this film ranks among the very worst. It’s not just disappointing compared to the 90 movies from the list I’ve watched, but it stands out as one of the most unenjoyable films I’ve ever seen. While drunks can occasionally be humorous, Dudley’s performance falls flat. Liza nearly salvages the experience, but ultimately, it’s not enough. If you’re looking for a standout role from her, I’d suggest watching Arrested Development instead. Honestly, the idea of Dudley laughing and drinking being comedic is baffling. I’d strongly recommend almost any other film on the AFI’s top 100 comedies for a better laugh. For a truly amusing take on a “drunk,” check out The Thin Man. And if you’re after a funnier movie overall, any Marx Brothers film will have you in stitches—especially if you’re as tipsy as Arthur.

I recently watched this film at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), and I can confidently say that Hal Hartley fans will be thrilled! Even if you're unfamiliar with his body of work, it’s not a problem—this movie stands strong on its own merits. I was so captivated that I’m already planning to attend the second screening. It was absolutely incredible, and I can’t wait to experience it again soon!

The film is incredibly humorous, with sharp, intelligent dialogue that keeps you engaged. Parker Posey delivers a remarkable performance in the titular role of Fay Grim. This latest feature revisits the universe and characters first introduced in *Henry Fool* (2000). Visually, one of the most striking elements is the frequent use of canted (or Dutch) angles, a signature style often seen in Hartley’s earlier projects, including shorts from the *Possible Films: Short Works by Hal Hartley 1994-2004* collection and in *The Girl from Monday* (2005).

I found it particularly fitting to watch this film on September 11th. The backdrop of Fay Grim’s journey in this narrative reflects the transformed world post-September 11, 2001. Without revealing too much, I see this film and its story-world as boldly political and thought-provoking.

Many dismissed Vanilla Sky as just another of Tom Cruise’s eccentric films, akin to Magnolia or Eyes Wide Shut, but it stands distinctly on its own. While often labeled as weird, I disagree; it’s more accurately described as different and perplexing. Weirdness belongs to the realm of Stanley Kubrick or Pauly Shore. Difference is exemplified by The Truman Show, and confusion by The Matrix or The Game. Unlike Kubrick’s often ambiguous endings, Vanilla Sky delivers a clear resolution. Everything falls into place, perhaps not instantly or even today, but eventually, it clicks. The confusion in Vanilla Sky mirrors the turmoil of David Aames, portrayed by Tom Cruise. That’s the crux of the film, the source of the so-called "weirdness" that repelled critics. Had they truly paid attention, as suggested by the title of the original 1997 Spanish film, they might have appreciated its depth. Beyond this, the film is worth watching for its exceptional soundtrack alone. Cameron Crowe masterfully weaves music to craft the movie’s atmosphere—a vital element often missing in cinema. With tracks like The Beach Boys’ "Good Vibrations" underscoring the emotional and dramatic peak, Crowe strikes an unconventional yet perfectly fitting tone. Vanilla Sky is, undeniably, a remarkable film.

The Biker Movie genre arguably consists of some of the most dreadful films in cinematic history. This particular film is packed with relentless fighting, copious bloodshed, clashes between bikers and Native Americans, and a shanty town that is systematically destroyed, shack by shack. The performances are utterly abysmal. Whatever became of Robert Walker, Jr.? He once appeared in significant studio projects, only to vanish from the spotlight. This film is genuinely awful, yet if it's been a while since you've watched a Biker movie, it might be worth a view. By the end, you might feel a tad sleazy for having sat through it!

"The Thief of Bagdad" captivates with the sinister portrayal of the malevolent magician Jaffar, brought to life by Conrad Veidt. Through deceit and dark sorcery, Jaffar schemes to usurp the throne from the youthful King Ahmad and to claim a beautiful princess from her protective father.

Ultimately, like all tyrants in tales and folklore, Jaffar succumbs to the forces of love and the overlooked commoner, represented by the spirited little thief, played by Sabu.

The dichotomy of good versus evil, light versus darkness, is masterfully depicted both visually and narratively. The script weaves a poetic, elegant, and strikingly beautiful story. The magician and his minions, cloaked in costumes that mimic the ominous flapping of black bird wings, strike under the cover of night, sowing destruction and fear.

In contrast, the noble hero is adorned in pristine white turbans and robes, while his princess is arrayed in delicate shades of pink and pale blue.

The film sets a new standard for breathtaking scenes, surpassing its predecessors. Through pioneering use of color, it unveils a fantastical realm previously unimaginable.

Featuring a magical flying carpet and a majestic flying white horse, alongside a towering genie, masterfully portrayed by Rex Ingram, and malevolent wizards, the movie enchants with its wondrous elements.

When you begin exploring fascism, the first concept you encounter is ostracism. This so-called "philosophy" is a sham, relying on scapegoats to prop up its ideology. Ettore Scola's film, arguably his finest work, centers on these marginalized figures, the outcasts of the regime.

The historical backdrop of Hitler and Mussolini's alliance is barely touched upon in the film. We catch fleeting glimpses of military parades, decorative garlands, and distant voices. Our protagonists are excluded from this celebration of masculinity. "Genius is inherently masculine" is the motto Antonietta—played with unparalleled depth by Sophia Loren—has stitched onto her cushion. Her world is confined to her kitchen, her pride rooted in her children. At the film's outset, she is a victim of this hyper-masculine society, though she remains unaware of her oppression, believing she ought to be content. Gabriel, on the other hand, is politically conscious. He recognizes the malignant force corroding his nation. Yet, as a gay man, he is an outsider, on the brink of arrest.

Despite the divides between them, they discover their shared humanity and become intimate. This act is one of defiance, especially for Antonietta, whose moral code should prohibit such behavior. To become an adulteress in a society where politics and religion collude to suppress women marks the beginning of her political awakening.

As I settled in to watch the 14th season of *The Bachelor*, titled "On the Wings of Love," I anticipated an "intriguing" experience. My exposure to the show had been sporadic in the past; I’d catch an episode or two, then miss several others. While I often find *The Bachelor* captivating and engaging, I can’t help but question its substance and ethical undertones.

"On the Wings of Love" follows Jake, a 31-year-old commercial pilot from Dallas, Texas, on his quest for genuine love—or at least as genuine as a reality TV dating show spanning a single season can offer. Jake is introduced to 25 stunning women from across the nation. His initial interactions with them are largely surface-level; after all, how much can one truly learn about another person in just a handful of brief, five-minute chats? From the outset, Jake is candid with the audience about his intentions. He isn’t merely seeking romance or a fling—he’s in pursuit of a fiancé or wife. We can only presume he has conveyed this same clarity to the women competing for his affection.

Following his tribute to classic film noir with *Chinatown*, Roman Polanski revisited the themes that defined his most iconic works of the 1960s in this unsettling psychological horror. Much like *Repulsion* and *Rosemary's Baby*, this film explores the paranoia and claustrophobia inherent in apartment life.

Polanski excels at crafting confined, suffocating spaces, and this may well be his most oppressive and restrictive work. The focus on looming side walls and distant vanishing points is more pronounced than ever, and even in the few outdoor scenes, the sky remains elusive. Yet *The Tenant* is not merely limited by physical space; it is equally constricted by its relentless focus on the protagonist. Trelkovsky, portrayed by Polanski himself, appears in every scene and nearly every frame. When he is absent from the screen, the camera often adopts his perspective. And wherever he turns, he is confronted by his own reflection glaring back from a mirror.

Few films delve so deeply into the isolation and inner turmoil of a single character. While some psychological thrillers, such as *M* or *Peeping Tom*, guide us into empathizing with their subjects, this film stands apart in its intense exploration of solitude.

As a child, this film held a special place in my heart, and having performed in its stage adaptation multiple times, it remains my favorite musical. I doubt any future screen adaptation of Oliver Twist could surpass the brilliance of this version.

Oliver Reed's portrayal of Bill Sikes stands out as my all-time favorite villain. His performance terrified me when I first watched it at the age of six, and now, as an adult, I find myself empathizing deeply with Nancy, the barmaid and prostitute who plays a pivotal role in helping Oliver achieve the life he deserves.

Jack Wild's depiction of the Artful Dodger was exceptional, and I believe no one could eclipse his performance as the cunning street pickpocket and loyal friend to Fagin. The music in the film is outstanding, particularly Fagin's numbers. I'm also relieved that Bill Sikes wasn’t given a musical number, as it would have felt incongruous with his dark and menacing character.

Carol Reed handled Nancy’s tragic fate with finesse, maintaining the film’s G rating by subtly portraying her brutal treatment while still conveying the severity of Bill’s violence toward her.

This movie is truly remarkable.

This musical genre encapsulates a perfect blend of humor, talent, romance, and action, all seamlessly woven together.

Frank Sinatra delivers an exceptional performance, and no further praise is necessary. Marlon Brando, despite not being a singer, captivates audiences with his portrayal of Sky Masterson. His lack of singing ability ironically enhances his character's charm. While the female performances in the film are decent, the male actors undeniably dominate the spotlight.

This film stands as a timeless classic, resonating with viewers of all ages. Its universal appeal brings smiles and laughter to every audience.

Undoubtedly, this is a movie worth watching and savoring!

While I respect personal preferences and believe everyone is entitled to their own tastes, I must say this movie was utterly disappointing with no redeeming qualities. I’m not particularly fond of Ani DiFranco, yet I can acknowledge her talent as a guitarist and songwriter. However, I find nothing praiseworthy in this film. Some argue it realistically depicts the challenges high school students face, but I find the portrayal exaggerated and implausible. The movie seems to aim for a "Naked Gun"-style comedy, yet the timing is clumsy, with awkward pauses between lines as if waiting for nonexistent laughter. The screenplay feels chaotic, clumsily squeezing in numerous controversial topics without fully exploring any, particularly the disturbing storyline of a student impregnated by a teacher. I didn’t laugh once during the film; instead, I felt insulted by its feeble attempt at humor and satire, leaving me to do nothing but roll my eyes in frustration.

I watched this movie just once, roughly 25 years ago, and even now, I consistently tell others it might be the finest film I've ever experienced. With no spoken words, only internal monologue, I was utterly captivated, often holding my breath to avoid making the slightest noise. I strongly recommend this movie and wish it were available on DVD.

WINCHESTER 73 follows the relentless pursuit of a man (Jimmy Stewart) determined to reclaim his cherished possession, a Winchester repeating rifle. The weapon continually slips through various hands, with Stewart in unyielding pursuit. Directed by Anthony Mann, this 1950 black-and-white film leans more toward crime drama than classic western, with its cowboys often resembling contemporary gangsters rather than traditional frontiersmen. Shelley Winters portrays a morally ambiguous woman traveling to a ranch with a potential suitor (Charles Drake). Though she eventually develops feelings for Stewart, her journey involves being passed between men. Winters stands out as the most layered character in a movie populated by eccentric figures. Keep an eye out for a young Dan Duryea as a deranged killer and Tony Curtis in a brief role. Will Geer, unfortunately miscast, plays Wyatt Earp.

I'll keep this brief. I consider this film to be exceptional. While some reviewers have criticized it for poor writing, substandard cinematography, an awful soundtrack, and a lack of realism in depicting life, I disagree. Though it might not be entirely credible throughout, the movie delivers a powerful message of hope that others seem to have overlooked. It conveys the possibility that it's not too late to rescue individuals from the horrors that plague so many lives. Gang violence is a harsh reality, isn’t it? Is it acceptable? Absolutely not! This film presents a vital social message that cynics might scorn, but it deserves commendation rather than criticism. I’ve watched this movie at least eight times, each viewing as enjoyable as the last, and each time it leaves me with a sense that the world can still be improved and isn’t beyond redemption (at least not until 2008). I rate it 9 out of 10. In my opinion, it’s nearly flawless. JMV

Did the filmmakers even review this movie before its release? The script is disjointed, leaping from one scene to another with little explanation. The opening fails to establish whether it's a prequel or a continuation, beginning with Superman's early days on Earth before abruptly shifting to a timeline after the previous film—without any clear indication to the audience. The result is utterly bewildering. Superman himself is depicted as feeble and in desperate need of antidepressants, coming across as a potential home-wrecker, a creepy stalker, and a deeply depressed, confused figure. Such a character rarely makes for a compelling hero. The ending is downright absurd; seeing Superman in a hospital bed was so frustrating that I almost wished for his demise. I’m half-expecting a Saturday Night Live parody where Superman appears on a talk show like Maury Povich, only for Maury to dramatically announce, “The results are in—Superman, you ARE the father!” In short, the acting by this Superman and Kevin Spacey is passable, but the script is atrocious. Overall, the film is virtually unwatchable.

This film is delightfully eccentric, and I must admit, the acting matches that unique vibe.

It tells the story of a young man aspiring to become a renowned Las Vegas illusionist. The plot weaves together his pursuit of fame, the aspirations of those around him, and the gritty realities of show business. I found the movie enchanting, with a few moments of genuine magic that elevate the entire experience.

Alan Arkin shines as the magician who never made it, and his mentorship of Max creates a blend of humor and heartfelt connection.

It may not appeal to all tastes, but if you enjoy films about personal journeys, I believe this one will resonate with you.

I’m revising my earlier review, which was deemed too harsh and rejected. I’ll aim for a more balanced tone this time. Honestly, though, a Chuck Norris movie where he isn’t the central figure just doesn’t feel right. While there was a decent fight scene toward the end, the rest of the film fell flat. It makes me question whether Chuck, a true icon, is still at the top of his game. Has age slowed him down to the point where he’s producing subpar work, relying on his legendary status to pull him through? Chuck is undeniably a phenomenal martial artist, and as seen in *Walker, Texas Ranger*, he’s a capable actor. The challenge is blending both talents effectively in his films, and unfortunately, this movie misses the mark. As a longtime fan, I’m disappointed. Chuck, please stick to being the lead in your projects—this supporting role just doesn’t suit you. - Gary

This film is not pornography, nor was it intended to be, and unless my uncle somehow becomes the global president, it should never be labeled as such.

With that clarification out of the way, I wholeheartedly recommend this movie. Its themes remain highly relevant, it’s humorous, the performances are excellent, and it poses thought-provoking questions.

I’m puzzled by the harsh criticism this film has received, which is one reason I have no plans to visit the US. Lena stands as a true trailblazer of the modern riot-grrrl movement, embodying confusion, curiosity, and sharp wit. While she can be angry at times, isn’t that a trait we all share?

**Spoilers:**

I was deeply let down by *Love's Abiding Joy*. Having eagerly anticipated watching it for a long time, I finally got the opportunity when it re-aired on Hallmark Thursday night. While I adore the first three films in the "Love" series, this one fell far short of my expectations. The entire movie felt heavy with sadness, riddled with numerous errores, and suffered from subpar editing, with many scenes feeling out of place. Additionally, I found the timing of baby Kathy's death to be overly abrupt, and Clark's presence in the film seemed oddly misplaced. The performances lacked passion; it felt as though the actors were disengaged, showing little emotion. There was also a noticeable absence of connection between Missie and Willie.

In my opinion, the scriptwriters should have stayed truer to the source material. With each successive film, the adaptations seem to stray further from Janette Oke's original works. Notably, the movie omitted any mention of the mine, the two boys, or Clark's injury related to it. Furthermore, I felt that Missie and Willie's responses to Kathy's death were inadequately portrayed.

This movie is an absolute blast. It's the kind of film you can kick back and enjoy without overthinking, as the storyline takes increasingly wild and hilarious turns. Featuring a stellar cast of familiar, talented actors like Sally Field, Teri Hatcher (at the peak of her fame), Kevin Kline, Elisabeth Shue, and Robert Downey Jr., they all brilliantly portray soap opera stars and producers with over-the-top flair. If you've ever watched a soap opera and wondered, "How did they even dream up this absurd plot?", then this movie is tailor-made for you. I've watched it several times, and with each viewing, I find myself laughing more and appreciating the exceptional acting even deeper. Don't go in expecting an Oscar-worthy masterpiece; this is purely a lighthearted, entertaining flick, not a pretentious dive into the human psyche. Just settle in, unwind, and let the laughter roll.

The initial bursts of creativity had me enraptured by their originality—from the reimagined Archers’ logo to the opening disclaimer, and the sweeping camera movement across the universe. It’s remarkable to consider that *It’s a Wonderful Life* was released in the same year. This is no mere coincidence, as the 1940s were rife with films exploring the celestial and terrestrial; however, compared to Alfred Junge’s visionary work, the fluffy, saccharine angels and glowing nebulae of other films appear dated and unworthy of mention.

The film maintains its stunning visual impact throughout, continuously unveiling striking concepts. I’m generally not fond of blending color with black and white, as one often detracts from the other, resulting in an unappealing contrast. Yet, here it’s executed flawlessly. Powell transitions between color and monochrome, and vice versa, with such ease that it feels utterly seamless, merely a shift in artistic tone. Both the color cinematography and the black-and-white sequences are strong enough to stand independently.

As for the narrative, this could be Pressburger’s finest screenplay—or it would have been, had the ending unfolded with a more coherent resolution.

Apologies, everyone. I understand this is meant to be an "art" film, but frankly, it was so unbearable that they might as well have handed out guns at the screening for people to end their suffering rather than endure it. While the scene design and cinematography were impressive, the story itself was excruciating to sit through. The lack of a soundtrack felt harsh and unforgiving. The excessively long shots dragged on endlessly—how long can you watch two people just sitting and talking, especially when their dialogue is nothing but complaints? I struggled to make it through this film. The performances were strong, but there’s only so much dark, somber, uninspired content one can handle. The only highlight for me was Maureen Stapleton in her red dress during the dancing scene. Beyond that, this felt like a derivative knockoff of Bergman, and I’m not a fan of his work either. Honestly, I think anyone claiming to have enjoyed an hour and a half of this is simply not being truthful.

I have long admired Chavez's opposition to globalization, but it was only after watching the film at the Amsterdam International Documentary Film Festival that I truly understood the extent of his accomplishments. The documentary recounts a coup and conspiracy orchestrated by Venezuela's elite, oil corporations, and corrupt Western governments obsessed with oil, aiming to oust the democratically elected President Chavez and revert Venezuela to a ruthless dictatorship. This film is essential viewing for anyone who values freedom and justice, and it serves as a powerful lesson to the global community. I applaud the Venezuelan people for taking control of their destiny and protecting their nation from entities like Halliburton and the Bush administration.

If you're in search of an accurate biography of boxer James Corbett, this film might not be your best choice. Instead, it offers a 1940s Hollywood spin on his life, transforming it into a more captivating and entertaining tale than reality might provide. Thankfully, the stellar performances, especially by Errol Flynn, and a charming script make the film's exaggerations easy to overlook.

Errol Flynn portrays James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett, a boxer from the Gay Nineties who clinched the world boxing championship in 1892. The movie traces his journey from modest origins to the pinnacle of his career, culminating in a title bout against John L. Sullivan. While the film could have centered on the fights, most are depicted briefly, with the exception of the climactic championship match. The spotlight instead shines on Corbett's bold character and his romance with the character played by Alexis Smith. The narrative is enriched by a talented ensemble of supporting actors, including Alan Hale, a regular in Flynn's films, whose performances, combined with sharp writing, breathe life into the characters.

A standout feature of the film is the impressive display of athleticism.

"The Muppets Take Manhattan" stands apart from other Muppet films in several unique ways. Notably, it is the only Muppet movie not under Disney's ownership. Even as of 2008, the rights remain with 20th Century Fox (originally released under CBS Fox), despite Disney holding the rights to the Muppets themselves. Additionally, the film features a non-linear narrative with unexpected twists and turns in its storyline.

While it's challenging to surpass the charm of the 1979 classic "The Muppet Movie," particularly due to its more iconic soundtrack, "The Muppets Take Manhattan" excels in its depiction of surprisingly grounded scenarios. Unlike the first film, where the Muppets simply travel to Hollywood and effortlessly secure a "Rich & Famous" contract upon meeting an agent, this movie portrays a more realistic struggle. It shows the Muppets grappling with the harsh realities of achieving success in the entertainment industry, learning that it demands hard work and perseverance. This serves as a significant, often underappreciated message for viewers willing to look past the fantastical elements of the story.

Last November, I had the privilege of watching this film at the Reno Film Festival, and I must admit it was an absolute delight. Despite a few minor technical glitches, the experience was thoroughly enjoyable. I was particularly impressed by the sharp writing and stellar performances, with the lead actor delivering an especially captivating portrayal. The film brims with emotion and clever humor, which added to its charm.

After the screening, I had the opportunity to chat with some of the filmmakers, who came across as genuinely warm and approachable. Overall, the movie left me with a deeply positive impression, and I wholeheartedly recommend it. The storyline was both engaging and relatable; as a woman, I found myself connecting with the lead character’s struggles, having faced similar challenges myself. This personal resonance made his journey all the more poignant.

The film excels in creating characters that feel authentic and easy to empathize with. The supporting friends in the story are crafted with such realism that they reminded me of people I know. I couldn’t help but wish my own conversations with friends could carry the same effortless coolness as theirs. In short, the movie is incredibly captivating, and I truly hope to see more films of this caliber in the future.

For those curious about the Soviet perspective on modern Russian history, this epic film is a gem. The narrative begins at the dawn of the 20th century, captured in the faded sepia tones reminiscent of vintage photographs. As the timeline progresses to the mid-1900s, the visuals transition to stark black and white, eventually blossoming into vibrant color as the story nears the 1960s.

The plot centers on a young boy from a remote Siberian village, whose life is profoundly impacted by the arrival and subsequent arrest of an anarchist during the Tsarist regime. Following the revolution, he aligns himself with the Bolsheviks and introduces Soviet communism to his community. His son, born to a local beauty, later battles the Germans in World War II. Upon his return, the village witnesses the rise of the oil industry, accompanied by a portrayal of Soviet economic optimism.

Though lengthy and deliberate in pace, the film is meticulously crafted and coherent. It is structured to be viewed in three distinct segments.

This film might appeal to staunch adherents of organized Christian doctrine, but for those with an open perspective who value free will, logical reasoning, the division between Church and State, and quality Science Fiction, it is nothing short of a dreadful farce.

Several recognizable actors appear in this production, seemingly either desperate for employment or compelled to impose their personal convictions on those of us deemed unbelievers.

I found amusement in this movie akin to the kind I experienced watching "Reefer Madness." Just as that film used fear to educate about drugs, this one attempts to instill "Christian" values by menacing viewers with the specter of hell and suffering for otherwise decent individuals who reject their worldview.

It left me roaring with laughter, yet simultaneously alarmed by the realization of how many people genuinely advocate for a return to the outdated societal norms of the 19th century.

For those who haven’t stumbled upon this hidden treasure or perhaps haven’t even heard of it, here’s something special. In the 1980s, Dennis Quaid was a major star, but by the early 1990s, he seemed to vanish from Hollywood. He made a striking comeback in 1993 with three films, all of which, sadly, flopped at the box office. I personally enjoyed two of them, and I’d like to dive into one that stands out.

"Wilder Napalm" is a wild, offbeat movie centered on two brothers, Wallace (played by Quaid) and Wilder (Arliss Howard), who possess a rare ability: pyrokinetics, the power to start fires with their minds.

Wilder, haunted by a tragic accident from his youth, has sworn off using his powers for anything frivolous. During their childhood, he and Wallace accidentally caused an explosion in an abandoned house, unknowingly killing a man inside. Now, Wilder works as a firefighter and is married to the eccentric Vida (Debra Winger), who, ironically, is under house arrest for arson (you’ll need to watch the film to fully grasp the irony). He hasn’t spoken to Wallace in five years, ever since Wallace pulled a cruel prank by setting his hair on fire at his bachelor party.

Wallace, on the other hand, revels in his fiery abilities and isn’t shy about using them.

I don’t believe this movie warrants the harsh criticism it’s receiving from certain reviewers. Admittedly, it suffers from an unnecessarily extended duration, clumsy editing, and an excessive dependence on tacky special effects. Moreover, it lacks the vibrancy necessary for a comedy to keep the typical viewer engaged without them glancing at their watch.

However, the film also delivers some genuinely hilarious lines, features a dedicated and skilled cast, and embraces the timeless underdog narrative. Macy, Stiller, and Azaria shine as the central trio, while Garofalo and Studi excellently contribute tension and diversity to the group. I must note that Reubens and Mitchell didn’t bring much to the overall impact of the movie, though each had moments to stand out.

As mentioned earlier, the storyline follows the predictable “underdog-triumphs” formula, offering no real surprises since the outcome is expected. What elevates the film isn’t the bizarre, flamboyant heroes and villains, but rather the sharp dialogue and dynamic interactions among the characters. At its core, these characters are childlike in spirit, driven by a desire to do good. The most compelling scenes are those that lend the film its emotional depth.

The performances by Fishbourne, who brings an oddly humorous quality to his role, and the briefly featured Ed Harris are noteworthy, in stark contrast to Connery, who seems unable to grasp the essence of his character and resorts to the physicality of an 80-year-old. The screenplay itself is incoherent; it feels like a 60-minute story with a forced happy ending, tacked on with an abrupt twist that lacks any logical connection to the characters or plot. It resembles more of a mishap than a structured script, perhaps useful only as a case study in screenwriting classes. The more one reflects on the details, the more this chaotic impression solidifies. Capital punishment, though introduced as a theme from the start, ultimately dissipates without deeper exploration or commentary. Despite the potential in the subject matter and setting, the execution falls short.

Harman and Ising's 'Old Mill Pond' stands as a remarkable achievement in the realm of animation. The exceptional talent and craftsmanship of this duo are vividly showcased in this cartoon, making it a standout in their body of work. It is unfortunate that many interpret this piece as offensive, when it was always meant to be a playful and entertaining work, with no intention of disrespecting Black individuals. If anything, it serves as a celebration of the vibrant humor and musicality associated with Black culture. Regrettably, I have not had the chance to watch this delightful creation in years, as authorities in England have labeled it too controversial for viewing in today's diverse Britain. If anyone knows where I might find a copy, I would be thrilled to experience this gem once more. I believe those who search for hidden messages or malicious intent in these decades-old cartoons—now over sixty years old—might benefit from adopting a more relaxed perspective. The world has evolved significantly, but that should not justify erasing or censoring historical works of art.
