It's the third installment, and by now, you can guess it's not going to be good. The original "Maniac Cop" wasn’t strong enough to justify a sequel, let alone a third film, so expectations are already low. But just how bad does it get? It's dreadful, teetering on the edge of unwatchable.

In one scene, as Maniac Cop unleashes a murderous rampage, a reporter dramatically declares, "What happened here can ONLY be described as a black rainbow of death."

Let’s break this down: 1—Rainbows are never black, and they can’t be. 2—Rainbows are benign, incapable of causing harm or death. 3—A competent news reporter, especially one valued by their agency, would surely find a more fitting description for the aftermath of a killing spree. "A black rainbow of death" is far from the ONLY way to capture such a tragic event.

This is the kind of absurdity you’re in for.

Upon rewatching this film, I was struck by how faithfully it adheres to the novel, aside from omitting the section about Cary's [Leslie Howard] childhood. Given the constraints of the era, which limited what could be depicted on screen (though the novel itself isn’t overly explicit), the film remarkably captures the character’s obsession with Mildred [Bette Davis], effectively conveying this intense emotion to the audience. I highly recommend this movie to anyone who has experienced unrequited love or been exploited by someone they cared for. I learned that Maugham was once requested to record an audio version of the novel for commercial release, but he broke down in tears during the recording session, unable to progress beyond the initial lines, leading to the abandonment of the project. It’s evident that the novel was a deeply personal work for him, and the film serves as a commendable adaptation of at least a portion of this heartfelt story.

I’ve rated this movie 1 star, though if given the chance, I would have awarded it a zero. As I inserted the DVD into my TV and settled onto my couch, I braced myself for some of the most notorious filmmaking blunders. Having checked the movie’s rating on IMDb and discovering it was the lowest-rated film, I approached it with a critical eye, ready to spot every flaw. Yet, nothing could have prepared me for the utter garbage that erupted from my screen.

The packaging might deceive you into thinking this film is passable at best. Don’t be misled. This movie should be pulled from every shelf worldwide.

The best analogy I can draw is that this film resembles porn, but stripped of any sex scenes. The acting—if it can even be labeled as such—is abysmal, the plot is riddled with holes akin to Swiss cheese, and the special effects are downright atrocious.

I urge you not to make the same mistake I did by renting this film under the illusion that it might be amusingly bad.

Ultimately, I’m not claiming I could produce a better film, but

I incorporated this film into a religion class I was teaching. In the story, a golden fish swims contentedly in its bowl in an apartment on an upper floor. Meanwhile, a young boy and his mother are out of the house. The boy, entrusted with money to purchase milk, stops at a carnival on his way back to play a game. Beside him is a man dressed in a black suit, his appearance somewhat intimidating. The boy accidentally drops the milk bottle, and it shatters. The man in the black suit kindly offers him money to buy a replacement. This scene intercuts with events unfolding at home. A black cat ascends the fire escape and slips into the apartment. It notices the fish bowl and observes intently. The fish, full of vigor, leaps out of the bowl. At this point, my students—a group of teenagers—and I are captivated by the fish’s fate. The cat seizes the fish in its mouth, and we all watch, breathless. Then, the cat gently releases the fish back into the bowl. The dual narrative weaves together the mysterious man in black and the enigmatic black cat, both of whom initially provoke suspicion but ultimately prove to be harmless. This film sparked an excellent discussion in my class.

When a movie boasts no fewer than five distinct titles, it often signals multiple issues and typically indicates significant shortcomings. *Necromancy* is a prime example, plagued by serious flaws and simply being outright terrible. I watched the version titled *Rosemary's Disciples* on video, and while I'm certain it differs from other cuts, I doubt any additional minutes or alternate versions could salvage it. The core issue lies in the story itself: the film begins with Laurie waking up as her husband drives her to a mysterious town called Lillith, where he has landed a new job at a toy factory catering to occultists (yes, the absurdity starts this early!). Entry to Lillith is guarded by a man with a rifle at the bridge, ensuring only those chosen by the town’s “owner” can pass. It soon becomes clear that every resident of Lillith is a witch, all under the command of Mr. Cato, the leader of this communal coven, who is obsessed with resurrecting his deceased son (hence the title *Necromancy*). The townsfolk engage in typical witch-like activities—

Prix de Beauté was produced during the pivotal transition from silent films to sound, a shift that occurred slightly later in Europe compared to Hollywood. Initially envisioned as a silent film, it was released in France with a dubbed soundtrack, featuring a French actress voicing over Louise Brooks' lines, while in Italy and other European regions, it retained its silent format. I had the privilege of viewing the impeccable new restoration of an Italian silent print by Cineteca di Bologna at the Tribeca Film Festival. Although I have yet to see the sound version, I believe the silent rendition is likely more gratifying, as reports suggest the dubbing is subpar—Louise Brooks visibly speaks English, making lip synchronization impossible. Moreover, the film is crafted in a distinctly silent style, relying on minimal intertitles and scant need for spoken words. Prix de Beauté narrates its tale through striking visuals and innovative cinematography. The opening immediately captivates with its dynamic montage of bustling city scenes and swimmers at a public beach. The film consistently focuses on visual intricacies—clothing, machinery, decor, and evocative symbols like a caged bird or a pile of debris.

This film is profoundly disappointing, with only a handful of redeeming moments or qualities.

The story begins with a pregnant Linda Blair frantically running down a hallway, escaping from shadowy pursuers—possibly monsters or individuals wielding pitchforks, though it remains unclear. She leaps through a window, only to awaken, revealing her advanced pregnancy. Curiously, the extent of her pregnancy fluctuates dramatically throughout the film.

Accompanied by an insufferable and potentially intellectually challenged young boy—whom I initially mistook for her son—Linda Blair journeys to an abandoned hotel on a remote island. It seems Italian horror directors have a knack for casting the most grating child actors! Already on the island are David Hasselhoff and his German-speaking, seemingly innocent girlfriend (a nod to the stereotype of Germans adoring Hasselhoff). He’s busy snapping photographs, while she’s engrossed in translating an obscure German text about witches, or so it appears.

Also arriving on the island are an older couple who have recently purchased the property, along with a real estate agent and a woman I initially assumed was their daughter. It turns out she’s an architect, and Linda Blair and the boy are actually the older couple’s children. Though it’s implied they all traveled to the island together, the film’s presentation makes it feel as though Linda and the boy arrived separately.

I watched "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival, and even two days later, it lingered in my thoughts. The film follows a prodigal son (Scott Cohen) who returns to his family’s custom furniture business after serving time in prison. It delivers all the hallmarks of a compelling drama—unforgettable characters, incisive and insightful dialogue, and a filmmaker’s keen visual sensibility through thoughtful cinematography.

Beyond these strengths, the movie offers something increasingly scarce in mainstream cinema: the unfiltered perspective of a seasoned storyteller. Director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin displays a fully realized talent, yet there’s a feeling that he, much like his central character, has earned his stripes through hard experience. He understands the struggles of ordinary people in this world and captures our deep desire to witness—or at least vicariously feel—triumph. However, Yellin holds too much respect for his audience to offer superficial optimism. Ultimately, we realize that Jake’s victory isn’t measured by financial success or familial approval, but in “the work” he is irrevocably tied to.

This central idea feels vital in a world—and a film industry—often fixated on profit over substance.

What’s the deal with the actors in this terrible film? Michael Dorn should stick to Star Trek projects. As for John Diehl, does anyone recall his role in Miami Vice? I enjoyed him in that, at least. But honestly, what can you expect from a movie starring a former Baywatch lifeguard in the lead role? Absolutely nothing, and that’s exactly what we get. None of the characters are remotely likable, the special effects are laughable (though not in a good way), and the story is an abysmal mess. There’s no logic to anything that unfolds on screen. It feels like the filmmakers were aiming for something akin to "Attack of the Killer Tomatoes," especially in that absurd scene where key figures discuss national security in what looks like a closet.

If you stumble across this movie on TV, do yourself a favor and change the channel—your television will thank you.

How did this film even come to be? I’m a fan of sci-fi and Bigfoot-themed movies, but I still expect a certain level of quality in the writing, without the overwhelming cheesiness found here. The special effects were disappointing, and the dialogue was even worse. Steer clear of this one at all costs. I only rented it by mistake, as it was in the wrong case—I was actually looking for the Sasquatch movie starring Lance Henriksen, which I still haven’t watched. The concept of this film had real promise, and there was potential for a solid little movie. I just can’t fathom how it ended up in such a sorry state. Walk into any high school and talk to students interested in film, arts, or English, and you’ll likely find someone who could have written a better script.

I was utterly captivated by just how terrible this movie turned out to be. Was there a deeper message or reflection intended for the audience? What was the significance of the pumpkins? Were the motel scenes meant to be striking or noteworthy? Does the presence of garbage bags on a rooftop across from a hotel hold any relevance? Why does the narrator so blatantly and unsuccessfully attempt to ridicule the people he interviews, clearly editing out the more insightful portions of their responses to emphasize mockery? The highlight of the film, ironically, was the interview with a film professor who predicts the movie’s failure even before its completion.

I am genuinely astonished. It seems the creator is desperately striving to appear intellectual or to gain the approval of the intellectual elite.

This ghost story by Kiyoshi Kurosawa is quite unconventional, featuring at least one unexpected jump scare that managed to startle me. However, overall, the film falls flat with its absurd plot. It follows a detective on the trail of a suspected serial killer, only to discover he might be implicated in one of the crimes himself. He is then inexplicably haunted by a striking Asian female ghost, leaving both him and the audience puzzled about her presence. As more murders occur and the culprits are quickly identified, his confusion deepens, with the ghost’s persistent haunting remaining a mystery. The storyline is not only nonsensical, but the ghost herself borders on comical, particularly in a scene where she soars across the city akin to Wonder Woman. The conclusion is equally perplexing, rendering the entire film incoherent and impossible to recommend. If it weren’t for the film’s overly serious tone, one might mistake it for a dark comedy. Apart from "Bright Future," this ranks as the least impressive work by Kiyoshi Kurosawa that I’ve encountered.

The movie *Evil Breed: The Legend of Samhain* demonstrates minimal creativity or dedication. It is filled with rushed, "slasher"-style killings and grotesque, disturbing death scenes. The acting earns a D grade, as the performers display scant talent, and their absurdly foolish behavior in the film raises serious doubts. The depiction of how individuals of their age group behave feels wildly inaccurate. The inclusion of random pornographic elements adds little value, and any potentially redeeming moments are swiftly overshadowed by horrific, stomach-churning violence. A prime example is the gruesome scene where a character is disemboweled from the anus, dragging on for an agonizing five minutes. It’s painfully clear how little resistance the young characters offer. This film might appeal to those who enjoy watching horrific deaths and near-torture scenarios.

What a dreadful waste of time—terrible acting, a weak plot, and abysmal directing. This has to be the most tedious movie I’ve ever seen! Some bad movies can still be entertaining (like Freddy vs. Jason), but others are simply atrocious. Unfortunately, this falls into the latter category. In short, don’t bother watching it.

This is, without a doubt, the most dreadful film I have ever watched!

I can confidently state that I have never encountered a movie as abysmal as this one!

And I truly mean never!

As an avid enthusiast of "B" horror films, I’ve seen my fair share of the movie industry’s lowest offerings.

I was drawn to this film by its captivating title. Honestly, what genuine horror fan wouldn’t be curious about a movie called "Vampires vs. Zombies"? Visions of the undead clashing in epic battles filled my mind. I couldn’t help but think, “I’ve got to watch this!”

Regrettably, I now wish I had never laid eyes on it!

To say the title of this movie is deceptive would be an understatement. There were no vampires battling zombies. In fact, there isn’t even a discernible plot! If someone asked me to summarize the movie, I’d have to admit I have no clue what it’s about!

There’s no plot!

There’s no storyline!

This film is utterly nonsensical!

By the end of this fiasco, I couldn’t help but feel pity for the

I had come across numerous positive reviews and comments about *Weeds*, and I was eager to dive into another captivating cable series, akin to *Entourage*, *The Sopranos*, or *Mad Men*. However, my excitement dwindled with each episode I watched from Season One, to the point where I couldn’t even finish the first six episodes.

The writing struck me as uninspired and overly contrived, with the portrayal of Black characters feeling particularly cringe-worthy. The dialogue often seemed unnatural, as if the writers were straining to sound witty and trendy. Genuine laughter on my part was a rarity.

I found the characters shallow and unlikable, failing to evolve in a way that made me care about their journeys. I was especially put off by the addition of the brother-in-law, whose behavior seemed predatory enough to warrant an appearance on *To Catch a Predator*. Additionally, the decision to write out the Hodes’ daughter, Quinn, by sending her to a boarding school in Mexico felt like a tired, clichéd plot device, almost as if the writers were daring the audience to stop watching.

With each episode, my dislike for the characters grew, compounded by noticeable flaws in the storyline that I couldn’t overlook.

On top of that, I’ve heard that Season Two fails to improve, so I decided to abandon the series altogether.

A childless couple, portrayed by Brooke Adams and Jeff Hayenga, consults a doctor, played by James Karen, in their desperate attempt to have a child. Their efforts succeed, but Adams gradually realizes that something is disturbingly wrong with the baby.

The film starts with a promising concept that is ultimately undermined by a weak script. While the premise holds potential, the storyline becomes frustratingly predictable as it progresses, with every plot twist glaringly obvious. The direction lacks finesse, showing a fundamental inability to effectively frame even the simplest scenes. Production quality is, to put it kindly, subpar and appears quite cheap. Additionally, the gore is excessively disturbing—particularly a harrowing scene involving a pregnant woman harming herself—and is marred by poor special effects. The movie completely falls apart toward the conclusion, revealing a clear lack of vision on how to wrap up the narrative.

Despite these shortcomings, the performances by Adams, Hayenga, and Karen provide some redemption. Their competent acting keeps the film marginally watchable, but that's the extent of its merits. Released obscurely in 1991, the movie remains largely unnoticed, and it's not hard to understand why. I rate it a 4.

"Seven Pounds" delivers a captivating performance by Will Smith and a narrative that pulls at your emotions with the intensity of a rock guitarist in full swing. This film surpasses the director's earlier work with Smith, "The Pursuit of Happyness," which I also thoroughly enjoyed. Keep an eye on director Gabriele Muccino; his films might slip under the radar without a big-name star attached.

Unfortunately, I unraveled Will Smith’s character’s plan early in the film, piecing it together from the opening scene where he reports his own suicide and the introduction of Rosario Dawson’s character with a terminal heart condition.

Despite this early revelation, I believe the writer/director made a wise decision in framing the story with those pivotal first and last scenes. They create a compelling sense of urgency and suspense, slowly unveiling the motivations behind a man’s extreme sacrifice. Watching the tender, evolving relationship between Smith’s and Dawson’s characters was deeply moving, even with the tragic outcome looming in the background.

I watched this movie with a friend, and...

When will this pain end? I’m exhausted by yet another rendition of A Christmas Carol. Filmmakers relentlessly churn out the same tired narrative, desperately competing to outshine one another, yet they consistently fall short. The story itself is flawed—preachy, outdated, and steeped in naive, conservative optimism. It assumes people change, but the endless stream of adaptations only proves we haven’t learned a thing.

It's a bad sign when John Cassavetes, known for his intense performances, appears to be merely coasting through a film, and "The Incubus" represents a low point for this talented actor, seemingly just cashing a paycheck. Given the over-the-top script and John Hough's excessively ornate art direction, it's hard to fault Cassavetes for his lack of enthusiasm. The plot revolves around a string of rape-murders in a small town, infused with a heavy dose of supernatural nonsense. Unfortunately, the direction drains any semblance of suspense or engagement from each scene, and Cassavetes often looks visibly frustrated. While the Incubus itself is a well-crafted creature in its brief appearance at the film's end, it’s hardly worth the slog to get there.

1/10

Prior to viewing this film, I came across a review claiming it might be among the greatest movies ever made. What a laugh! Indeed, tension builds scene by scene... but it's largely due to the irritating characters. From a little girl spouting nonsense and attempting to drown a boy, to a killer roaming freely without drawing attention (and who was that man speaking to the boy at the beach?), events unfold without explanation or closure. As I watched, the film appeared to head in one direction, only to veer off unexpectedly into another, repeatedly losing its way.

The acting is commendable, yet the script is dreadful. In every scene, characters say or do things that defy belief and realism, while the responses from other cast members and extras feel oddly out of place. The film fails to resolve any of the issues it raises, leaving viewers puzzled and ultimately feeling that their time has been squandered.

What an incredible episode! Last week's incessant cameos by Mellisa, focusing on the friendship between Annie and Brandi, nearly made me sick. But that was just the beginning compared to Mellisa's explosive outburst after getting fired. Watching her stumble around in her cast, unleashing a stream of profanities while demanding someone grab her purse, was hands-down the funniest moment I've ever seen on reality TV. Her relentless yells off-set for someone to fetch "all" her clothes—as if anyone would dare touch her garish wardrobe—were just icing on the cake. Mellisa, at 40 years old, still throwing tantrums? Unbelievable. Then Joan jumps in, hurling every insult imaginable at Annie and Brandi before dramatically storming off and quitting the show! Both Rivers are nothing but spoiled brats, kept on this long purely for ratings. Mellisa’s refusal to do an exit interview, coupled with her tears, only confirms what America already suspected—she’s a petulant child. Boo-hoo, she didn’t get her way! I couldn’t help but admire Annie’s candid confession to the cameras about manipulating Mellisa—and then watching her pull it off flawlessly. Despite everything, Mellisa remains the sharpest contestant by far and absolutely deserves to take home the win.

This film was created by a group of white men who share a school background. There's nothing inherently wrong with that, but the movie undeniably reflects this homogeneity. About 90 percent of the cast consists of white men of similar ages, giving the impression of watching a group of friends filming themselves at a boys' camp. The film lacks a coherent plot, relying instead on repetitive, gruesome action sequences that devolve into one bloodbath after another. While there are occasional humorous scenes and comedic moments, they fail to salvage the overall dullness and monotony.

The graphic cartoons interspersed throughout seem like a budget-driven choice to depict scenes beyond the filmmakers' means or capabilities, and even these are poorly executed. Whenever the action can't be portrayed by white men running around on a beach drenched in blood, the film resorts to subpar animation.

I was drawn to this movie after watching the trailer, which hinted at a Tarantino-esque style. However, the trailer showcases the best moments, and the rest of the film merely recycles the same tired, nonsensical humor. While it occasionally lands a laugh, the repetitive nature quickly becomes tedious.

I felt compelled to watch this film due to its bizarre plot, and it certainly met my expectations. At times, it’s an unsettling experience. Unlike other works by Meyer, the sexual content is surprisingly restrained. However, certain violent scenes feel excessively graphic and distasteful. The storyline is a mess, and some of the acting and dialogue are simply atrocious.

The movie awkwardly blends sado-masochistic fantasy with a glimpse into the cruelty and depravity of slavery, ultimately failing on every level. It seems as though Meyer attempted to offset the exploitative elements of sex and race by injecting a loftier moral message. He’s aware that the early scene of Lady Susan, dressed provocatively and brandishing a whip, evokes a guilty thrill with its dominatrix imagery. In response, Meyer tries to pivot toward a noble narrative of good triumphing over evil. Yet, these conflicting tones neutralize each other, leaving the film devoid of impact.

Ironically, its myriad flaws make it a must-see for those who revel in the craft of a spectacularly bad movie.

In a bygone era, there lay an enchanting realm known as France, where the people dwelled in contentment. The women were approachable, and the men reveled in their cherished pursuit: warfare, the sole amusement of monarchs in which the common folk could partake. This particular conflict was the Seven Years' War, and as the battlefield became littered with more fallen soldiers than living ones, recruiters roamed the land to refill the depleted ranks.

Thus, Fanfan (Gerard Philipe), discovered in a compromising dalliance with a farmer’s daughter amid a haystack, evades the bonds of matrimony by joining the Aquitaine Regiment. His decision is spurred by a prophecy from a gypsy, promising him renown and riches in the King’s service, along with the hand of the King’s daughter in marriage. Unbeknownst to him, the so-called gypsy, Adeline (Gina Lollobrigida), is actually the daughter of the regiment’s recruiting sergeant.

When Fanfan, saber drawn, boldly breaks from the recruits to aid a besieged carriage, he discovers none other than the Marquise du Pompadour and the King’s daughter inside. This encounter solidifies his belief in a lofty union, undeterred by Adeline’s provocatively low-cut attire. Meanwhile, Adeline herself begins to uncover her burgeoning feelings for Fanfan.

New York, I Love You comprises eleven short films, each approximately 10 minutes in duration. While the segments aren't directly connected, they share a central theme: love. Each story explores the quest for love, whether it involves a couple or simply two strangers engaging in casual conversation. The movie features a remarkable ensemble cast, including Shia LaBeouf, Natalie Portman, Hayden Christensen, Orlando Bloom, Chris Cooper, Andy Garcia, Christina Ricci, Irrfan Khan, Robin Wright Penn, Julie Christie, Ethan Hawke, Bradley Cooper, Rachel Bilson, and Anton Yelchin. With such an impressive lineup and a captivating concept, I had high hopes for a remarkable film. Unfortunately, New York, I Love You fails to coalesce into a unified whole, remaining merely a collection of its individual parts. Certain segments stand out as humorous, creative, and engaging, while others, such as those featuring Orlando Bloom with Christina Ricci and Ethan Hawke with Maggie Q, are disappointingly lackluster. The film feels inconsistent and carries an experimental vibe. Narratively, it resembles a project that might be assembled by a group of film students. Despite these shortcomings, there are shining moments, with one of the highlights being the touching segment featuring an elderly couple portrayed by Eli Wallach and Cloris Leachman, strolling together.

...a derivative imitation of numerous superior movies, most notably Steve Martin’s "LA Story." That film, at least, had the decency to be clearly fictional, despite featuring Martin's real-life girlfriend portraying his on-screen partner.

Indeed, unsuspecting viewers, "20 Dates" is a mockumentary, though I’m not entirely convinced that was Myles Berkowitz’s original plan. It seems he began the project with some degree of seriousness, only to realize early on that it risked being pitiful and humorless unless he exaggerated the scenarios into absurdity. Consequently, the film carries an awkward, low-budget, and disingenuous vibe throughout.

As someone astutely noted, the movie depicts two of the "dates" filing lawsuits and obtaining restraining orders against Myles, yet they still appear in the film—an impossibility without signed consent forms. Additionally, it strikes me that most of the women portrayed as "dates" are likely professional actresses (though not well-known, with the exception of Tia Carrere). They come across as far too conventionally attractive, poised, slender, and at ease on camera to be ordinary people.

Mr. Berkowitz commits a fundamental mistake by exclusively casting women who fit this strikingly beautiful mold...

Likely spurred by fans of her far superior work "Orlando," Sally Potter has crafted a self-indulgent project that falls flat. Taking on multiple roles as writer, director, lead actress, and even co-composer of the soundtrack—which includes a sentimental love song—Potter overextends herself. The result feels like an amateurish student film, created by someone who believes their personal romantic dramas and intense emotions are universally captivating. Unfortunately, Potter's character lacks appeal, and the target of her affection is equally unlikable, turning the movie into a cringe-worthy display of self-absorption thinly veiled as a homage to tango. Had she not starred in the film herself, there might have been a chance for success. Her acting, whether portraying herself or a fictional role, simply doesn’t measure up. The film ultimately comes across as pretentious, overly ambitious, tedious, and absurd.

A distinctly French quality of this film lies in the deliberate pacing used to develop the two main characters, which may demand some patience from the audience, particularly as neither fits Hollywood's conventional standards of "attractiveness." However, once the "heist" begins, the story accelerates rapidly, occasionally almost too fast. It transforms into a thrilling rollercoaster, and as long as you don't scrutinize it too closely, it remains quite plausible. This is the type of movie you can imagine Hollywood mishandling.

Kate Beckinsale truly shines in this production—absolutely stellar! It's a shame that Knightly doesn't match the charm of Jeremy Northam in looks. Mark Strong delivers an outstanding performance, and Bernard Hepton is flawless as Emma's father. The final scene, though an addition to the original novel, is beautifully crafted, depicting the harvest celebration where Knightly dines alongside both his workers and high society peers. Emma's acceptance of this new dynamic showcases her transformation, which feels a bit abrupt but is convincing enough to embrace. Samantha Bond is delightful as Emma's former governess and confidante, perfectly embodying the character as I envisioned her. In my opinion, the UK excels at adapting Jane Austen, capturing the essence far better than American adaptations, which often prioritize profit over quality. This version is a must-see!

I'll concede that the casting in the movie feels incredibly peculiar, largely due to the storyline, though I struggled somewhat to accept Pierce Brosnan in the starring role (even though he delivered a commendable performance).

The film is inspired by the true story of an Englishman who, in the early 20th century, lived among Canadian Indigenous peoples, presenting himself as a person of mixed Indigenous heritage. Remarkably, he gained such respect and popularity that individuals traveled from far and wide to attend his talks and join his guided wilderness expeditions—despite the fact that he had no Indigenous ancestry and his expertise was entirely self-taught from books or fabricated. The narrative focuses on this deception and the aftermath of its revelation.

Both the acting and the scenic backdrops are impressive, and I found myself genuinely enjoying the film (once I managed to overlook Brosnan's unlikely casting). It likely didn’t achieve broad theatrical release due to its intellectual tone—far from a typical Bond thriller or romantic tale, it’s a distinctly unconventional story about an extraordinary individual.

Following the disaster of Highlander 2 (which I still refuse to acknowledge), I believed no sequel could be so terrible as to bring me to tears. I was mistaken. I adored the original Wargames, but this sequel is a travesty, riddled with inaccuracies in both computer technology and elements from the first film. The original at least featured plausible hacks, whereas the writer of this movie clearly had no understanding of computers beyond basic word processing. I question whether they even saw the original. The acting is equally unconvincing. Do yourself a favor and avoid this film at all costs. Even if your TV is stuck on the channel and you can’t turn it off, do not watch it. This movie is a life-ruining catastrophe.

This movie is utterly dreadful. The cast appears painfully aware of its abysmal quality. It begins poorly and deteriorates further by the conclusion, becoming genuinely awful. The acting is abysmal, and the script feels as though it was improvised on the spot. Despite being marketed as a horror film, it lacks any genuinely frightening moments. Utter rubbish—1 out of 10.

I've been hooked on *Diagnosis Murder* since catching it on BBC1 during weekday afternoons about a decade ago, often while home sick from school. I know I shouldn’t admit to loving it, just as I shouldn’t confess my obsession with *Murder, She Wrote*, but I’m completely addicted to both. I even own the DVD box sets—yes, I’m aware that’s a bit embarrassing!

Dick Van Dyke is the heart of the show, portraying Dr. Mark Sloan, a physician at Community General Hospital in Los Angeles who moonlights as a consultant for the L.A.P.D. His son, Steve, played by Barry Van Dyke (Dick’s real-life son), is a police officer who frequently relies on his father’s expertise to solve suspicious deaths.

Joining them is Dr. Amanda Bentley (Victoria Rowell), the hospital’s resident pathologist. In the early seasons, Scott Baio played Dr. Jack Stewart, but he left the series in 1995, presumably for bigger opportunities. Unfortunately, that didn’t pan out—his career highlights since then are scarce, with a notable low point being his role in *Baby Geniuses 2: Superbabies*. Ouch!

Dr. Jack Stewart was eventually replaced by the younger Dr. Jesse, bringing a fresh dynamic to the team.

If you're a fan of movies featuring school bullies, courageous kids, funny little ones, and the bizarre act of eating worms, then *How to Eat Fried Worms* is sure to capture your interest.

The story centers on Billy, a young boy who, on his first day at a new school, falls victim to a prank when his classmates sneak worms into his lunch. The resident bully, Joe, along with his group of friends, begins to taunt Billy, mocking him with the nickname "worm boy."

Determined not to be intimidated, Billy retorts that he eats worms regularly. Skeptical of his claim, Joe and his crew challenge him to prove it. Billy boldly wagers that he can consume ten worms in a single day, with the consequence of showing up to school with worms in his pants if he fails.

Accepting the challenge, Billy, despite his queasy stomach, embarks on a quest to earn his peers' respect by eating worms in various forms—cooked, fried, or even raw.

While the premise might seem distasteful, the movie carries deeper themes. It highlights the essence of genuine friendship and the importance of accepting others as they are. Additionally, it sheds light on the reasons behind some children's bullying behavior.

I believe I've covered most of what I wanted to express, but I feel compelled to justify my perspective. I've rarely encountered a production as unprofessional as this one, and I mean that in every possible way. The camera work, boom mic handling, and other technical elements of this film are utterly substandard, but sadly, these aren't the only shortcomings.

In contrast to some classic independent films that are redeemed by strong scripts, compelling characters, and engaging plots, this film suffers from a dreadful script, abysmal acting, and, most disappointingly, grating and unlikeable characters.

It's a travesty that for every independent film like *Haiku Tunnel* that secures distribution, there are countless others that fade into obscurity. I can't fathom what connections the Kornbluth brothers might have at Sony, as it's the only plausible reason I can think of for how such an amateurish family project managed to get distributed. I'm genuinely perplexed by the decision to support this film.

The only aspect of this movie that sparks any curiosity is its title. Yet, even that turns out to be a disappointment. I hope this review prevents others, who might be drawn in by the title, from wasting their time.

I believe many people were let down by this sci-fi movie. Firstly, it was helmed by Tim Burton. Secondly, it’s a remake of a film considered a classic. Personally, I found it dull, distasteful, and absurd. If you’ve watched it, you’ll likely understand my perspective. Nearly everyone on IMDb agrees it’s terrible, and they’re absolutely correct! If you haven’t seen it, steer clear. It’s a total bore. 1 out of 10.

Just Cause initially appears to be a decent film, leaving you puzzled about the harsh criticism it received upon release. It’s passable, bolstered by a standout supporting role from Ed Harris. However, the final third takes a sharp turn into absurdity, culminating in a ridiculous scene where a murderer, with a flashlight bizarrely attached to his forehead, menaces Sean Connery’s wife—played by Kate Capshaw in her usual affected and unpersuasive style—and child, portrayed by a young Scarlett Johansson, in an alligator skinner’s shack.

This is the type of movie best watched on a plane, and even then, just once.

"Dressed To Kill" stands as one of the greatest thrillers in cinematic history. Its exploration of sex and violence marks it distinctly as a film for mature audiences. Brian De Palma reaffirms his unparalleled mastery of camera work in storytelling, crafting numerous dialogue-free scenes that rely solely on striking visuals and Pino Donnagio's exceptional score to convey the narrative. Shot in Panavision, the movie demands to be viewed in widescreen to fully appreciate De Palma's use of the expansive frame. When cropped for video, "Dressed To Kill" loses much of its essence. With strong performances from the cast, outstanding direction, and arguably one of the best film scores ever composed, "Dressed To Kill" is an essential watch.

I want to express that this production is heavily biased and lacks the neutrality essential for credibility.  

There are no credits provided for the individuals interviewed, leaving viewers unable to assess their credibility or relevance.  

The narrative is presented from a single perspective, which is risky. Such an approach can perpetuate harmful ideas to future generations, contributing to ongoing conflicts. While this isn’t the sole cause of wars, it certainly doesn’t help.  

You can watch this documentary, but I strongly recommend doing extensive research online beforehand. The Balkans, like much of human history, are incredibly complex.

This film serves as a revelation for those captivated by the dazzling lives of celebrities, shedding light on the struggles of well-intentioned individuals who are unable to enact change. The bomb blast sequence is strikingly realistic.

What you've been taught or read about simply doesn't align with reality!!!

It might just spike your blood pressure by 10%.

The performances by all actors are exceptional.

Certain scenes could have been omitted to make the movie more suitable for a teenage audience.

The content of this film is decidedly mature.

It's not a movie to watch with family.

The casting is outstanding!!!

Steve McQueen undoubtedly boasts a devoted fanbase. His charisma, arguably unmatched on the silver screen, remains undeniable. However, even McQueen's charm cannot salvage this dismal film, which appears to have been shot using a rudimentary brownie camera on the real streets of St. Louis.

In the movie, McQueen plays a newcomer with a clean slate, recruited by a fellow gang member to join in plotting a bank robbery. There are strong suggestions of a homosexual relationship between McQueen's character and David Clarke. The other members of the heist crew distrust him, primarily due to his lack of a criminal background.

McQueen's character also has a girlfriend, Molly McCarthy, who grows suspicious of his activities, particularly when he begins associating with tough individuals like Crahan Denton, James Dukas, and Clarke. Such company would certainly raise anyone's doubts.

Directed by Charles Guggenheim and John Stix, *The Great St. Louis Bank Robbery* suffers from uneven direction. Guggenheim, known for his documentary work, and Stix, with a sparse resume, seem to falter in their guidance. One of them inexplicably encouraged McQueen to mimic Marlon Brando poorly, detracting from his performance.

A group of three treasure hunters scours the West Indies in pursuit of a concealed fortune, as detailed on the DVD sleeve synopsis. The promise of gold heightens the tension among the crew as they near the treasure’s hiding spot. These deep-sea divers are determined to uncover the riches, but soon discover that greed and animosity spiral into deadly consequences. Their boat, named "Manfish," is not a creature but their vessel. The skeletal figure that hands over half of the treasure map to the robust Captain John Bromfield, portraying Brannigan, is strikingly depicted. The seasoned Victor Jory, as the Professor, holds the other map fragment. Lon Chaney Jr., playing the seemingly naive first mate Swede, adds to the dynamic, while the alluring Tessa Prendergast, as Alita, fails to safeguard the rum. Regrettably, significant editing and continuity issues detract from the film, which had the potential to be noteworthy.

*** Manfish (2/56) W. Lee Wilder ~ John Bromfield, Victor Jory, Lon Chaney Jr.

This is, without a doubt, the most dreadful film I’ve ever paid to watch, and aside from "They Saved Hitler's Brain," it ranks as the absolute worst movie I’ve ever endured. When it was released, I was an avid follower of SNL and SCTV, eagerly expecting what I believed would be the most hilarious film possible, free from the constraints imposed on television improv shows.

Evidently, the writers assumed that by tossing in some crude content, fart jokes, and shallow sexual humor, they’d craft a daring, side-splitting comedy. However, the game show parodies are merely tacky, uninspired rip-offs of Let's Make a Deal, laced with repulsive elements. The sitcom spoof featuring a single woman and her boyfriend was nothing more than cringe-worthy, juvenile humor. The stun gun commercial felt like something out of Sesame Street in terms of its comedic level. The LA subway sketch offered dull humor propped up by distasteful gore. And the French chef, blindly wandering while repeatedly muttering "there is no difference" in a French accent, was, frankly, tedious.

The sole redeeming moment came from a skit with Chevy Chase, which was amusing for all of one minute. That’s right, just 60 seconds of entertainment.

I absolutely loved this movie. Tobey Maguire delivers an outstanding performance as Jake, solidifying his place as one of the most talented actors I've ever watched. I was pleasantly surprised by the abundance of funny moments scattered throughout the film. Maguire handled the comedic lines with finesse, despite my never having seen him in a humorous role before. The story draws you in, making you deeply invested in the characters and their fates. I wasn't sure what to expect from Jewel's acting, but she exceeded my expectations with a commendable performance. The film is packed with thrilling scenes and offers an exhilarating experience from start to finish. I am undeniably a huge fan of Maguire's work. If you haven't already, be sure to watch *Cider House Rules*—it's truly one of the greatest films of all time.

I’m genuinely amazed that this film even got produced. The director, writer, and actor must possess an extraordinary level of charm in real life. I can’t fathom any other reason this script would have been approved. Here’s something to think about: while watching, I couldn’t help but feel pity for the actors. It was reminiscent of being at a stand-up comedy show where the performer is bombing, and you’re just sitting there, not laughing, but feeling awful for them because they’re trying so hard. I’m curious about the budget; it must have been minimal, given the noticeably poor quality of the film. I’d like to say the humor didn’t resonate with me, but honestly, to find it funny, you’d probably have to be the person who wrote it—or completely out of touch. Now picture that as a script... and somehow, this guy got it approved. That’s impressive, isn’t it?

Truly a dreadful heap of nonsense!

This film is a predictable, sluggish, soul-crushing, and mind-numbing ordeal that makes the thought of slashing your wrists with a dull, rusty bread knife seem almost appealing.

The acting is exaggerated, ill-suited to the sparse dialogue, and every scene drags on at least twice as long as necessary. The tedious minutiae of one career crumbling while another ascends are unbearably dull and mundane. The music might be enjoyable in isolation, but enduring the film to hear it is hardly worth it; three decent songs cannot justify the torture of watching this movie.

While sitting through this, I found myself praying for narcolepsy or for someone to put me out of my misery.

Never, under any circumstances, will I subject myself to this again.

The U.S. State Department might prefer we avoid this film due to their tensions with the Iranian government. Yet, it offers a surprising glimpse into Iran's civility, despite its focus on the profound struggle of women for basic equality—specifically, the right to attend a soccer match at a stadium, a privilege reserved exclusively for men. The movie is riotously funny and serves as a testament to freedom of speech and expression within Iran. I found it thoroughly captivating. The story follows five young women as they attempt to breach the police barricades at the ticket gates for a pivotal Iran-Bahrain soccer match. The comedy that unfolds—from their bus journey to the stadium, through their encounters with law enforcement and eventual detention, to the film's conclusion—is indescribably amusing. This classic is an absolute must-see and ranks among the finest foreign films I’ve watched in recent years.

I must confess that watching an Antonioni film in one sitting has always been a challenge for me, and this particular one was no exception—I ended up viewing it in three separate segments across multiple occasions. Ultimately, I came to see this as a blessing in disguise, as it shifted my focus away from conventional plot expectations and allowed me to savor each scene individually.

The initial segment feels quite disjointed, which isn’t necessarily a flaw, though it demands greater effort to piece together. However, once the narrative reaches the desert sequences, the patience pays off abundantly. The breathtaking cinematography is just one element of its impact; what truly renders these moments indelible is how the landscape becomes a dominant, almost tangible force. Its silence and immensity, imbued with a poignant mix of melancholy and liberation, both merges with and contrasts against the two young protagonists. Though the desert is lifeless, it somehow feels more intimate and less foreign than the urban settings of the opening. The visual interplay between the airplane soaring overhead and the girl’s car below creates a sequence of striking, memorable images.
